A portrait, engraved after the only photograph Pearl Bryan ever had taken in her lifetime, faces the text.

Fort Thomas, Kentucky, beautifully located near the Ohio River on the highlands opposite Cincinnati, becomes the scene of a crime that shocked a civilized nation at the close of the nineteenth century. The book recalls deeds of horror with grim, factual detail. Readers of true crime history will find a sensational, contemporary record of a famous murder.
29891-the-rector:
Mrs. Oliphant wrote The Rector as part of her Chronicles of Carlingford, in a new edition from William Blackwood and Sons. The arrival of a new rector is a great event in Carlingford. The town is considerable, pretty, mild, and sheltered, not far from town, with no manufactures and not much trade. Its good society is respectable, retired, and exclusive, and it has already put five per cent upon the house rents.

There are no Dissenters in Carlingford above the rank of greengrocer or milkman, so church folk feel the rector's coming keenly. His good reputation was common knowledge, though its source was not, and nobody knew what his views were. Oliphant builds a whole social comedy from that gap. The novel is a quiet, sharp study of a town and its church.
29916-go-mez-arias-or-the-moors-of-the-a:
Don Telesforo de Trueba y Cosio wrote Gomez Arias, or The Moors of the Alpujarras, a Spanish historical romance in three volumes, printed in London in 1828. Each volume holds fourteen chapters, with a conclusion and notes in the third. Trueba dedicates the work to Lord Holland, as a Spaniard grateful for Holland's steady interest in the prosperity and literature of Spain.

The preface begs the reader not to fear the hackneyed word preface, which often augurs an egotistical and prosy author. Trueba vows to avoid that fault and to claim no literary mask. The transcriber kept the original spelling, archaic forms like shew, extacy, and stopt included. The romance itself follows the Moors of the Alpujarras in the age of old Spain.
29932-the-harbor:
Ernest Poole published The Harbor in New York in 1915, with Grosset and Dunlap, by arrangement with the Macmillan Company. It was set up in February 1915 and reprinted again and again through that year and into March 1916. Book one, chapter one, opens with a seven-year-old narrator in his mother's pew in an old Brooklyn church, nursing a contemptuous grudge against Henry Ward Beecher.

The boy is too small for the pew, which is far too wide for the bend at his knees, and his short, fat legs stick straight out before him. He may not move, he is most uncomfortable, and he blames the preacher for this Sabbath torture. His mother once told him he was brought to church so small so that, grown up, he could say he had heard the great man preach before he died.
30020-the-matsuyama-mirror:
Mrs. T. H. James told this Japanese fairy tale in English as number ten of the Japanese Fairy Tale Series, printed by T. Hasegawa in Tokyo. A long, long time ago, a young man and his wife lived in a quiet spot with one child, a little daughter they loved with all their hearts. Their names are long forgotten, but their place was Matsuyama, in the province of Echigo.

While the girl was still a baby, her father had to travel to the great city, the capital, on business too far for mother and baby to join. The mother had never been farther than the next village. She felt fear and pride together. Her husband was the first man in all that countryside to visit the big town of the king and his great lords.
30261-claire-the-blind-love-of-a-blind-h:
Leslie Burton Blades tells the blind love of a blind hero in Claire, serialized in All-Story Weekly in four installments from October 5 to October 26, 1918. An editorial announcement praises the story for subtle insight, compassionate understanding of human nature, and an honest assault on love and living, the eternal problem. Lawrence Gordon, the blind hero of a triangle tragedy, plays out its destined path at Philip Ortez's mountain cabin.

The announcement notes that the author, like Gordon, cannot see, and that his family worked the Colorado mines. At nine, a refused dare ended with a giant firecracker taking two of his fingers and his eyesight. He later studied at the Colorado State School for the Blind. The novel asks how love and living look when sight itself is gone.
30645-stories-of-boys-and-girls-who-love:
John Wesley extracts Stories of Boys and Girls Who Loved the Saviour, a token for children, published in New York by Carlton and Porter at the Sunday-School Union. Contents open with Little Sarah Howley, A Happy Boy, Happy Mary, Praying Charlie, and A Poor but Happy Boy.

Later stories add A Babe in Christ, The Minister's Daughter, Little Jacob's Faith, Jacob's Sister Susannah, and The Merchant's Son. Pious Little Peter and The Dutiful Daughter close the list. Little Sarah, aged eight or nine, hears a sermon on the easy yoke and light burden, weeps, and wakes to her soul's need. Wesley offers short, earnest lives for young readers.
30673-sound-of-terror:
Don Berry wrote this short science fiction tale about Johnny Youngbear, a man who wakes before dawn in a desert house and drives toward a launch site. His wife begs him to be careful, and he answers with a shrug, as if the day may not be his. At the site stand blockhouses, a runway, a still B-52, and above them a tall silver ship straining, in the tale's image, to be off and gone.

The story's pull comes from dread of the unknown, the fear named in its opening tagline. Berry sets a plain domestic scene against huge machines and a cold desert sky, then lets Johnny walk toward a test or flight whose risks stay just out of sight. It is a tense, short piece about courage, fate, and what a man feels when he must face a danger he cannot name.
30685-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Held here is one slice of volume eight of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. This slice runs in alphabetical order from Demijohn to Destructor, so it holds the short, signed entries that fell in that range. It is a reference work, meant to be dipped into, not read straight through.

Its entries give plain definitions and brief histories, with cross references to longer pieces elsewhere in the work. A demijohn, for example, is shown as a large round bottle in a wicker case, while demise is given as a legal term for transfer by lease. Readers who want the flavor of Edwardian knowledge, or a quick check on a word from that era, will find this slice a handy, if dated, source.
30794-the-princess-of-ponthieu-in-the-ne:
Translated from the French, this romance first reached American readers in eight weekly parts in the New-York Weekly Magazine, from July to September 1796. Its setting is France under Philip the First, where the Count de Ponthieu and the Count de St. Paul stand among the great families of the realm. Ponthieu, a widower, holds wide lands and keeps a court of great splendor.

At the heart of the tale stands his only daughter, praised for wit and beauty, whose presence draws the bravest cavaliers of the age to her father's court. The Count de St. Paul has no child of his own, and his heir is a nephew, son of his sister, whose fortune rests on that hope. The story follows courtship, honor, and rank in an old French world, retold for readers of the new American republic.
31196-time-and-tide-by-weare-and-tyne-tw:
John Ruskin's Time and Tide, signed with the pen names Weare and Tyne, gathers twenty-five letters to a working man of Sunderland on the laws of work. The letters move from co-operation and contentment through legislation, expenditure, entertainment, festivity, and the authority of the Bible. They go on to wheat-sifting, dictatorship, episcopacy and dukedom, and trade warrants against theft by false work.

Later letters take up unjust profits, public education without class distinction, humility, broken reeds, rose-gardens, and the master, closing with landmarks, the rod and honeycomb, and hyssop. Earnest, moral, and often severe, the book shows Ruskin applying his gospel of honest work to the whole ordering of society.
31324-the-angel-of-the-revolution-a-tale:
George Griffith's Angel of the Revolution, in its fifth edition from the Tower Publishing Company in London in 1894, with illustrations by Fred. T. Jane, is a tale of the coming terror by airship. Dedicated to Cyril Arthur Pearson, whose suggestion prompted the story, it opens at the eleventh hour, in a house on Clapham Common, among an inner circle and the daughter of Natas.

Later chapters bring the airship Ariel, a wooing in mid-air, Aeria Felix, a navy of the future, and a battle in the night. They go on to a skirmish in the clouds, an embassy from the sky, the battle of Dover, beleaguered London, and Armageddon itself. Sweeping and prophetic, the novel made Griffith a pioneer of the air-war romance.
31357-the-ultroom-error:
Jerry Sohl's story, printed in Space Science Fiction in May 1952, opens with a dry record. A slip in the Ultroom let a Kanad departure from 1609 finish, yet so close to the thousand-day limit that the infant Reginald Laughton turned up on day 378 of his life. On an ordinary lawn, Nancy Laughton knits booties for a bazaar while her baby gurgles in a playpen. Then her brother Joe from Kankakee walks up, takes the child, and is set upon by a snarling mongrel.

The magazine's headnote explains the joke at the story's heart. Smith admitted he had made an error involving a few murders and a few thousand years, yet kept a sense of humor even in the Ultroom. Wry and unsettling, the tale treats time transfer as a bureaucracy where a clerical slip spans millennia.
31393-the-camp-fire-girls-on-the-field-o:
Margaret Vandercook's The Camp Fire Girls on the Field of Honor, published by the John C. Winston Company with copyright in 1918, follows the Camp Fire Girls into wartime service. Vandercook, author of the Ranch Girls and Red Cross Girls series, opens in an old house in New York City facing Washington Square. There a young girl in a Camp Fire costume, marked with crossed logs and a flame, works alone in a dismantled drawing room on a snowy winter morning.

The field of honor in the title points to the girls' wartime work, and later chapters explain how they came to serve. Written for girls, the book blends home life with patriotic duty, showing young women finding useful work in a nation at war. It is a period piece of unusual warmth, where campfire ideals meet the demands of 1918.
31467-the-ruba-iya-t-of-a-bachelor:
Helen Rowland's The Rubáiyát of a Bachelor, with decorations by Harold Speakman, was published by the Dodge Publishing Company in 1915 and dedicated to her husband, William Hill-Brereton. Its verses follow the quatrain manner of Omar Khayyam's Rubáiyát. They take up the bachelor's life with wit: spring scatters the vows of Lent into flight, the roast replaces the fish, and woman's eyes are bright, as one opening verse has it.

Rowland, known for her sharp observations on men, women, and marriage, turns the Persian form to modern courtship. Each quatrain is a small joke or judgment, meant to be read aloud and laughed over. The book's charm lies in that blend: an old form, a new subject, and a voice that treats love as both a game and a serious business.
31471-the-girl-in-the-mirror:
Elizabeth Jordan's novel The Girl in the Mirror, published by the Century Company in October 1919 and illustrated by Paul Meylan, opens at Barbara's wedding in the little city of Devondale, Ohio. Elm Avenue, the town's leading residence street, blossoms for one night into a brilliant thoroughfare of light, color, and movement, as automobiles pour through the gates of its homes. The wedding sets the story in a world of respectable families, mill towns on either side, and watchful social custom.

Later chapters follow Laurie, who meets Miss Mayo, loses a battle, and solves a problem, alongside figures such as Mr. Herbert Ransome Shaw and Doris, who takes a journey. Jordan, author of May Iverson and Lovers' Knots, builds a novel of young women, courtship, and reputation. Its mirror title hints at the double life of appearance and truth.
31508-euthenics-the-science-of-controlla:
Ellen H. Richards's Euthenics, the science of controllable environment, appeared in a second edition from Whitcomb and Barrows of Boston in 1912, with copyright in 1910. It is a plea for better living conditions as a first step toward higher human efficiency. Richards argues that the surroundings people can control shape what they can do and become.

She opens with a stark figure from the Report on National Vitality, which puts the yearly needless loss of capitalized net earnings near a billion dollars. Her book treats housing, food, air, and daily routine as levers for public health, and it makes the home and the town instruments of improvement.
3157-the-path-of-empire-a-chronicle-of-t:
Carl Russell Fish traces America's rise to world power in this chronicle. The Monroe Doctrine opens the story, followed by controversies with Great Britain, Alaska and its problems, and Blaine and Pan-Americanism. The United States and the Pacific, Venezuela, and the outbreak of war with Spain carry the narrative toward 1898.

Dewey and Manila Bay, the blockade of Cuba, the preparation of the army, and the campaign of Santiago close the arc. Fish writes a clear, compact history for general readers, not a work of theory. It shows how a republic that began by warning Europe away ended the century fighting and holding ground far beyond its shores.
31581-the-scarlet-lake-mystery-a-rick-br:
John Blaine's The Scarlet Lake Mystery, a Rick Brant science-adventure story, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1958. Its contents run from Spindrift and an assignment to a rocket base, through Las Vegas, Nevada, and Scarlet Lake. They continue to Project Pegasus, the sign of the Earthman, Careless Mesa, Project Orion, a ghost town clue, and being stranded in Steamboat. An illustration shows grim-faced men running to help still a holocaust.

Rick Brant and his friends face rockets, desert, and mystery, with science as their tool and adventure as their reward. Blaine's series, popular with boys of the period, mixed real technology with fast plots. Readers will find a vivid, mid-century juvenile adventure, where a scarlet lake hides a secret worth chasing.
31598-the-egyptian-cat-mystery-a-rick-br:
John Blaine's The Egyptian Cat Mystery, a Rick Brant science-adventure story, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1961. Its contents run from the Winston plan and the Egyptian cat, through Cairo, El Mouski, and Sahara wells. They continue to the cat having kittens, the Egyptian Museum, a midnight call, an uninvited visitor, and the Great Pyramid. An illustration shows a room searched inch by inch, with the caption noting that someone wanted the cat.

Rick and his friends follow the cat from America to Egypt, where an ancient artifact draws thieves and mystery. Blaine keeps the science-adventure formula moving, with travel, deduction, and danger in each chapter. Readers of juvenile adventure will find an Egyptian mystery with a feline clue at its heart, and a pyramid for a finale.
31692-homo-inferior:
Mari Wolf's Homo Inferior, illustrated by Rudolph Palais, appeared in If Worlds of Science Fiction for November 1953. Its sidenote describes a new race whose world is peaceful, comfortable, lovely, and completely static, and says only Eric knows the haunting loneliness that carried the old race to the stars. Eric cannot speak that loneliness, even if he dared.

The story opens on a starship waiting under a transparent plastic dome, gleaming and uncorroded through seasons, years, and centuries, while few men ever come to look at it. Eric meets the other children when he is four years old. Wolf's tale sets a restless old hunger against a perfect, changeless world.
31956-garth-and-the-visitor:
L. J. Stecher's short story Garth and the Visitor was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1958. It follows Garth, a brash ace reporter for a high school weekly paper, who is scared all the same. His head crest lifts in spasms, and the webbing between his fingers, still rudimentary, twitches as he prepares to answer a dare.

The dare is a newspaper interview with the Visitor, who has sat for thousands of years in an egg-shaped palace on a mountaintop, answering questions but never giving interviews. Readers get a comic science-fiction story about taboos that, as its headnote says, very urgently want to be broken.
32012-a-narrative-of-the-shipwreck-capti:
Horace Holden wrote this Boston narrative, published in 1836, about the wreck of the Mentor, an American ship, near the Pelew Islands in 1832. Holden and Benjamin H. Nute were cast away there, and for two years afterwards they lived among the inhabitants of Lord North's Island. The title promises exactly what follows: shipwreck, captivity, and sufferings, told by a survivor rather than by a distant historian.

Holden's preface argues that authentic accounts of little-visited peoples should be preserved, even when they seem of lesser importance. Readers therefore get both a personal survival story and a record of island life as the two castaways saw it. The book's value lies in its first-hand detail, its plain reporting of hardship, and its place among early American accounts of the Pacific islands.
32134-the-dictator:
Milton Lesser's short story, printed in Imagination in January 1955, is set in a society that claims perfect democracy, where all men are equal. Its tagline adds the twist: some still craved extra personal attention, and received it. Ellaby, the hero, looks ordinary by design: five feet nine inches tall, a hundred and fifty pounds, an intelligence quotient of 98.57, less than four hundredths off the mode, with mousey hair worn slightly long for a man.

Born at High Falls, Ellaby is physically weaker than sixty percent of men but stronger than sixty percent of women. He has trained since turning twenty to kill the Dictator, and he is now thirty. Dorcas Sinclair meets him at the pneumo-station, too big and strapping for a woman, the story notes, but otherwise unremarkable. Readers get a dystopia of enforced sameness, with an assassin trained inside it.
32279-the-children-on-the-top-floor:
Nina Rhoades's The Children on the Top Floor, illustrated by Bertha G. Davidson, was published in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in August 1904, copyright 1904. Rhoades was the author of Only Dollie, The Little Girl Next Door, and Winifred's Neighbors, and her new book is listed at one dollar in cloth. Its sixteen chapters run from A Mishap and Its Consequences and Betty's Temptation through Winifred's Thank Offering, Gathering Clouds, and Winifred to the Rescue.

Friends in Need, A Chance for Jack, The Doctor's Verdict, Suspense, A Letter and a Surprise, and At Navesink follow, with Drifting, His Lordship, Jack's New Friend, Something Happens, and Uncle Jack. An illustration shows little Betty Randall staring down at the debris of her three cream cakes. Readers get a girls' story of Betty, Winifred, and Jack, mishaps, temptations, rescues, and surprises on the top floor.
32287-know-thy-neighbor:
Elisabeth R. Lewis's science-fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy in February 1953, follows Ellen, a young office worker in San Francisco. She rents a cheap flat in the Tenderloin district, near Market Street, and keeps to herself on streets crowded with bars, sailors, and gamblers at night. Inside the building she knows only two neighbours by sight: Mrs. Moffatt in flat 404 and a stocky young man in flat 410.

Small alarms build from there, starting with a dead cat on a fire escape and growing stranger as Ellen watches her neighbours more closely. What looks like an ordinary, respectable block turns out to hide something far less ordinary behind its quiet halls. The story uses Ellen's wariness to ask how well anyone can know the people living just across a hall.
32403-human-error:
Raymond F. Jones's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1956, opens three years into the life of the first Wheel. The space station was watched by more amateur astronomers than any other object in the sky. When disaster strikes, over three hundred reports come in, and two observers film the event through ten-inch mirrors.

One film fails, but the other records the ship Griseda's approach, a pilot's fumbling correction, and a final collision. Behind the accident lies a government campaign spending a billion dollars to persuade people that men should feel shame at being men, rather than flawless machines. Jones argues the opposite: a person without error is not improved, but deadened. The story pairs a sharp accident inquiry with a warning about trading human fallibility for machine perfection.
3249-the-major:
Ralph Connor names this novel for its hero, the Major, and opens on a coward. A fight for freedom, an escutcheon cleared, and salvage follow, with westward ho and Jane Brown. The girl of the wood lot, a voice in the wilderness, and the closing of a chapter mark the later course. The spirit of Canada and the shadow of war hang over all.

Men and a mine, a day in September, and an extraordinary nurse fill the middle passages. Hospitality without grudging and the tragedies of love test the hero's growth. Connor writes of a man remade by duty, from cowardice toward command. War sharpens rather than settles character here, and duty remakes a man the army first called a coward.
32587-the-ambassador:
Sam Merwin Jr. sends Zalen Lindsay, a man from Mars, to speak for his world before the United Worlds assembly on Lake Pontchartrain. Lindsay tells Earth plainly that Mars will no longer take its surplus goods. Nor will Mars mine metal for pay it deems worthless.

Earth, in this tale, leans on computers to rule, yet the machines keep erring because men feed them poor facts. Lindsay's blunt speech, and the tests that follow, pit plain sense and nerve against a planet that trusts its machines more than its own judgment.
32609-the-children-of-the-poor:
Jacob A. Riis's The Children of the Poor, copyrighted in 1892 and printed in New York in 1908, studies children in the city's slums. Chapters treat Italian slum children, the great East Side treadmill, little toilers, truants, and the forces that make boys bad, alongside the fresh air fund, kindergartens, industrial schools, and boys' clubs.

Riis also tells individual stories, from Tony and his tribe to Kid McDuff's girl and Little Mary Ellen's legacy. Illustrated throughout, the book shows how crowded streets, work, and neglect shape childhood, and how schools, clubs, and charities can offer a different path.
32670-the-time-mirror:
Clark South opens on the eve of a wedding, when Mark Carter questions a mirror sent by Elaine Duchard's former suitor, Adrian Vance. Elaine defends the gift as mere politeness, but Mark distrusts Vance, who had expected to marry her himself.

The mirror proves to be a trap, pulling Elaine out of her own time and into a past age of coaches, swords, and a baron's men. Vance admits his plot, and Mark must chase his bride through danger to bring her home, in a tale of jealousy, revenge, and rescue across time.
32699-the-makers-of-canada-index-and-dic:
Lawrence J. Burpee and Arthur G. Doughty edited this index and dictionary of Canadian history. It was published in Toronto by Morang and Company in 1912. The volume serves as companion to The Makers of Canada. It gathers names, places, and subjects from the whole series into one alphabetical reference.

Entries give short lives and careers, with coded references to the volume and page where each figure is treated. Later sections cover manuscript sources in the Dominion Archives. They also list scarce maps and plans relating to Canada. A long list of abbreviated source works, from Bibaud to Who's Who, lets readers trace every entry back to its authority.
32831-the-lost-door:
Dorothy Quick sends an American heir to a French château with a fatal condition, in a story from Weird Tales of October 1936. The narrator inherits Rougemont, near Vichy, provided he spends six months of each year there. His father, who refused to see him in life, left everything with that one injunction. He cables his acceptance and urges his school friend Wrexler to come.

At Rougemont the two men find the portrait of Helene, Mademoiselle d'Harcourt, whose family gave the château its new name, Red Mountain. Both men have already met her, in dreams and on the stairs. When Helene raises her lips to Wrexler's, mist swirls and a door swings shut. The narrator beats on it until de Lacy pulls him away: the door is gone, and the library wall is lined with books.
32876-castle-of-terror:
E. J. Liston strands a detective and his prisoner in a dimension out of time, in a story from Amazing Stories of November 1948. Hale Jenkins escorts bank robber Bud Griffin by giant airliner, needling him over a platina fox jacket. A bartender's suspicion, not the girl Myrtle, gave Griffin away: a man who drinks beer and leaves no tips should not own such a jacket.

Mid-flight, Griffin shoots Jenkins in the shoulder, and both men seem to freeze for an instant before the fight ends. They wake among giants, gangsters, dwarfs, and Rip Van Winkle, at the castle of Lucretia Borgia. Lucretia serves course after course while Jenkins' anger grows, until he announces he is going, with Griffin. Lucretia answers that her guests leave only at her bidding. The tale turns on whether detective and prisoner can escape a hostess who keeps all time at her table.
32899-the-cosmic-deflector:
Stanton A. Coblentz's story, from Amazing Stories in January 1943, begins with Dan Holcomb bursting into a laboratory in triumph, waving a letter at his fellow worker Lucile Travers. He believes he has found a way to force the Earth out of its orbit. The tale's teasing note warns that pushing a planet out is one thing and pushing it back quite another. That gap between a bold idea and its control drives the plot.

Coblentz keeps the science at pulp speed, letting enthusiasm, romance, and danger share the stage. Dan's boyish energy charms Lucile even as his scheme grows riskier, and the story asks what happens when human pride takes on forces far larger than any laboratory. It is a short, lively warning about invention without a way back.
32903-the-victor:
Bryce Walton's story, from IF Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1953, drops its hero into a fight that is meant to end in death, not mere defeat. Charles Marquis hangs five thousand feet above tiers and walkways, caught between security officers closing in from both ends of a walkway, and finds his own hands will no longer obey him. Some paralyzing force has seized him at the worst possible moment.

Under the rule of the Managerials, Walton's future turns combat into a public test of ingenuity, and Marquis must outthink a system built to break him. The story moves fast, from steel beams and power-hung buildings to the cold logic of a regime that stages killing as order. It is a tense pulp tale about a man who refuses to die on schedule.
33177-narrative-of-the-march-of-co-a-eng:
William P. Seville's narrative records the march of Company A, Engineers, from Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, to Fort Bridger, Utah, and back, between May 6 and October 3, 1858. Seville served as an artificer in the company, and his account follows the daily grind of the trail. Camps, river crossings, and picket duty fill its pages, along with the strain of moving men and gear across wide, dry country in a time of trouble with the Mormons.

Revised under army direction and printed by the Engineer School in 1912, the paper adds to the history of the United States Corps of Engineers. Its value lies in its plain, on-the-spot detail, from a soldier who was there rather than a later historian. For readers of western and military history, it is a compact, first-hand view of an army march in the late 1850s.
33428-stevensoniana-being-a-reprint-of-v:
Stevensoniana, copyrighted in 1900, reprints literary and pictorial miscellany associated with Robert Louis Stevenson, the man and his work. Its contents range from biographical notes on Scotland, London, the Riviera, the Golden Gate, and the South Seas to an apparition and Stevenson's first works. The Bankside Press volume gathers scattered pieces into one book for Stevenson's admirers.

The collection suits readers who love Stevenson and want the small, odd pieces that surround a great career. Its mix of prose and pictures gives a sense of the man in many places. For students of Stevenson, it is a useful, affectionate scrapbook, preserving fugitive writing that might otherwise have been lost.
33634-the-night-operator:
Frank L. Packard, author of The Wire Devils and the Jimmie Dale adventures, writes a railroad story in this 1919 novel. The night operator of the title is Toddles, whose real name is Christopher Hyslop Hoogan. The men of the Hill Division nicknamed him on his first run and never called him anything else. Toddles is not strictly on the company payroll, and everybody says he is a bad one, yet he gets a good deal of business in his own way.

Ten chapters follow Toddles through Owslet and the 1601, the apotheosis of Sammy Durgan, a wrecking boss, a man who squealed, an age limit, the devil and all his works. Packard mixes railroad detail with melodrama, and the book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century adventure on the rails.
33689-oscar-wilde-art-and-morality-a-def:
Stuart Mason edited this 1908 volume defending Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray, gathering reviews and eight letters by Wilde himself, printed with his literary executor's permission. The book opens with Wilde's paradox that what the public calls an unhealthy novel is always a beautiful and healthy work of art. It also recalls Walter Pater urging the young Wilde at Oxford to write prose, which is so much more difficult than poetry.

Mason reproduces contemporary criticism, including attacks that Wilde answered with wit, arguing that an artist in England gains by being attacked, since his individuality is intensified. The volume documents the moral panic around Dorian Gray and Wilde's aesthetic defense of art's independence from moral judgment. It remains essential reading for students of Wilde, censorship, and the art-for-art's-sake debate.
3401-the-elevator:
William Dean Howells sets this short farce in a smart hotel drawing room, where a dinner table gleams under low gaslight. Mr Roberts waits in evening dress, watch in hand, while his wife arranges her train on the carpet and worries that guests will arrive before the dinner is at its peak. The humor starts in that fuss over timing and appearance.

When visitors do arrive, polite talk covers awkward truths, and a small social machine runs on manners. Howells lets character show through dialogue alone, with no narrator to explain motives. The piece is brief, easy to stage in the mind, and a good sample of the light comedies Howells wrote about American city life.
34034-the-belove-d-traitor:
Frank L. Packard wrote this romance, published at Toronto in 1915 by the Copp, Clark Company. Book one is set at Bernay-sur-Mer, in a house on a bluff, among keepers of the light and a beacon, where strangers enter the gates and a daughter of France waits. A question hangs over the book: who is Jean Laparde?

Book two, two years later, brings duplicity, an accusation, a secret model, flight, and a reported death of Jean Laparde. Packard writes of love, honor, and betrayal with high feeling. The novel offers a dramatic tale of a man torn between country and heart.
34120-farthest-north-vol-ii-being-the-re:
Fridtjof Nansen wrote this second volume of Farthest North, published in New York and London in 1897 by Harper and Brothers. The book records the voyage of the ship Fram from 1893 to 1896 and a fifteen-month sledge journey by Nansen and Lieutenant Johansen. An appendix by Otto Sverdrup, captain of the Fram, reports its drifting from March 1895.

Chapters follow preparation for the sledge expedition, the new year of 1895, a start, goodbye to the Fram, a hard struggle, travel by sledge and kayak, and land at last. About 120 full-page pictures and sixteen colored plates from Nansen's sketches aid the text. The volume stands as a classic of polar exploration.
34304-the-complete-story-of-the-galvesto:
The Complete Story of the Galveston Horror, edited by John Coulter, formerly of the New York Herald, chronicles the hurricane and flood that struck Galveston on September 8, 1900. The volume, copyrighted in 1900 and dedicated to the dead of that date, is written by the survivors, whose experiences the preface says are reported in their own words. Photographs taken on the spot illustrate the account.

Chapters follow the storm from south of San Domingo to the Texas coast, then the looting of corpses, bodies towed to sea, and pestilence among the ruins. President McKinley ordered army rations, tents and United States troops to the stricken city.
34415-for-the-allinson-honor:
Harold Bindloss wrote For the Allinson Honor, copyrighted in 1913 and reprinted in 1914, with a frontispiece by Cyrus Cuneo. Bindloss also wrote Prescott of Saskatchewan and Winston of the Prairie. Contents open with the tenant at the Firs, family pride, and a council, then reach the Lake of Shadows.

Later chapters bring first suspicions, a dream mine, an amateur miner, and an island of pines. Treachery, a silver lode, a cache, and an empty flour bag follow, with the truth about Rain Bluff near the end. Readers get a Canadian adventure novel where a family name must be cleared in the mining north, among ice, claim jumpers, and bush rescues.
34495-rob-nixon-the-old-white-trader-a-t:
Rob Nixon, the old white trader, is a tale by Kingston of the Canadian north-west. The tale opens on a rolling prairie midway across North America. Tall grass bends to the breeze with gleams of light flashing over it. Earth and sky meet with no break but far trees by a river. Bones of a dead man lie scattered in that lone wilderness waste.

A rusted rifle, powder-flask, sheath-knife, and flint tell the hunter's end. Locusts have eaten all the softer gear of the lost man's kit. No sound breaks the awe of that silence on the wide plain. Snows, storms, and rains have swept over the bones for seasons past. Then dark specks rise from below the horizon line, moving slow. They grow into one dark line of beasts with huge shaggy heads. Buffalo come browsing on, clearing the herbage as they advance north.
34592-behind-the-green-door:
Mildred A Wirt wrote Behind the Green Door, a Penny Parker mystery. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York in 1940. Sixteen Penny Parker books line the front pages. Tale of the Witch Doll opens that line. The Vanishing Houseboat follows it in order. Twenty-two chapters carry this tale.

Trouble for Mr Parker heads chapter one. A Rival Reporter enters at chapter two. Traveling Companions and Pine Top Mountain follow. Over the Barbed Wire and Penny Trespasses come next. The Green Door itself stands at chapter seven. A Coded Message and A Call for Help follow. Locked in the Cabin raises the stakes at ten. Peter Jasko Serves Notice heads chapter nineteen. Old Peter's Disappearance comes at twenty-one. The Secret Stairs open the end in view. A girl reporter at a ski lodge mixes news work with a shut door's secret in Wirt's brisk line.
34763-the-cat-and-fiddle-book-eight-dram:
The Cat and Fiddle Book, published at London in 1922, turns eight nursery rhymes into small plays for children to act at home. Lady Bell wrote the first six, covering the Cat and the Fiddle, Lucy Locket, Polly Put the Kettle On, Goosey-Gander, Oranges and Lemons, and Ride-a-Cock-horse. Mrs Herbert Richmond supplied the last two, Little Miss Muffet and Humpty Dumpty, and the volume is dedicated to ten grandchildren.

A producer's note gives plain stage directions: the tune of each rhyme is played twice on the piano, the nursery audience sings along, and screens stand in for scenery. The rhymes are printed in full after each little play so the performers can learn them.
34954-systematic-status-of-the-colubrid-:
Systematic Status of the Colubrid Snake Leptodeira discolor, by William E Duellman, came out from the University of Kansas in July 1958. The paper runs nine pages, with four figures. It stands first in volume eleven of the museum series.

Duellman notes that in his 1958 study of the genus he had seen no specimen of this snake. Gunther first named the species in 1860, from two snakes held in London and gathered in Oaxaca, Mexico, by Auguste Salle. Later writers put it in three other genera in turn. A fresh specimen from Oaxaca showed a vertical pupil, a split anal plate, and twenty one scale rows. Snake scholars get a close sorting of one rare Mexican species and its right place.
35037-napoleon-s-young-neighbor:
Helen Leah Reed published her short history for young readers in Boston in 1907. Reed tells how news of Napoleon reached St. Helena after Waterloo and how the exiled emperor came to live first at the Briars and then at Longwood.

Early pages set out the island itself, a steep rock far out in the south Atlantic, with Jamestown in its narrow valley. The chapter list then follows daily life near Napoleon through the eyes of a young host family. Ball gowns, horse taming, strict rules from the governor, visits, and a sad parting give a close and plain view of his last home.
35091-the-invisible-censor:
The Invisible Censor is a book of essays by Francis Hackett of the New Republic, published in 1921. The pieces first appeared in the New Republic. Their subjects range from whisky and Billy Sunday to Fifth Avenue, Chicago, Henry Adams and Yeats.

The title essay begins with a quarrel over Strachey's Eminent Victorians, which a distinguished friend of Hackett's called cheap. Hackett argues the opposite: the book fits exquisitely and never strains, because Strachey perfectly understood the invisible censor, the inner decorum that falsifies by omission. What the friend called vulgarity was Strachey's refusal to let appearances stand in the way of facts. The essay sets the collection's standard for criticism: judge the evaluation of decorum, not its acceptance, in books and in life.
35256-your-negro-neighbor:
Benjamin Brawley wrote Your Negro Neighbor in 1918. The Macmillan Company issued it at New York. Brawley had written a short history of the American Negro. The Negro in Literature and Art bears his name. Nine chapters fill the book. Your Negro Neighbor heads the first.

A history review of the Negro in America follows. The Negro as an industrial factor takes chapter three. Lynching gets its own grim chapter at four. Aspects of Negro education fill the fifth. Joanna P Moore, a great missionary, stands at six. Some critics and their fallacies take the seventh. The Promise of the Negro closes the book. Moore's portrait fronts the text in her honor. A Black scholar speaks to white readers in reasoned tones, asking them to know the neighbor Jim Crow kept strange.
35996-the-dawn-patrol-and-other-poems-of:
Paul Bewsher, of the Royal Naval Air Service and holder of the Distinguished Service Cross, wrote The Dawn Patrol and Other Poems of an Aviator. Erskine Macdonald in London issued the book, first in November nineteen seventeen. Bewsher gave the book to his father, his best friend and best critic. Press praise heads the volume.

A new domain has been won for poetry by the war, that of the air, the Daily Graphic says. The Times praises Bewsher for never straining for effect, with keen sensibilities devoted to duty. The Dawn Patrol marks a departure in English literature, the Graphic holds, sought by collectors in after years. The fable of Pegasus has come true, it adds. Poems of dawn flights, sea patrols, and lost comrades fill the pages. Readers get the first air war sung by a flying man himself.
36016-the-prussian-terror:
Alexandre Dumas wrote a novel of France in the grip of Prussian war. Garnett made the first English form of the book. It came out in London in 1916. A cry at the front names the Prussian as the foe. Bismarck and the house of Hohenzollern stand near the start.

Berlin scenes lead to duels, a charge, and a king's own hand. Benedict Turpin and Helen bear the tale's heart. Frankfort, Langensalza, and Sadowa mark the war's road. A free meal, a hurt man, and a hangman add grim turns. Dumas mixes court plots with the crash of hosts. Past tale fans get his full, swift hand.
36045-the-law-and-the-poor:
Edward Abbott Parry, a judge, wrote The Law and the Poor, a book put out in London in 1914. Parry gave the book to the man in the street, in hope he would take up his task. A line from Goldsmith heads the work: laws grind the poor, while rich men rule the law. The judge writes from long years on the bench.

Chapters trace debt law from old times, and jail for debt in England. He then shows how the courts work for a poor man day to day. Pay for hurt work, debt failure, and split homes each get a part. Parts on the police court, rents, the ale house, and the work house close the survey. Last parts weigh cures for his day and for days to come.
36252-sounding-the-ocean-of-air-being-si:
Sounding the Ocean of Air holds six lectures by A Lawrence Rotch. He gave them at the Lowell Institute in Boston in December 1898. The book came out in London in 1900.

Rotch ran the Blue Hill weather observatory in Massachusetts. He also served on world groups for the study of clouds and flight. His theme is the sea of air above us and how men probe it. The lectures share what kites, balloons and keen watches had learned. They show a young science at work, keen to read the sky for storms and safe travel. The book came out under a church press that backed learning.
3640-literary-taste-how-to-form-it-with-:
Arnold Bennett writes a practical guide to forming literary taste, with detailed advice on what to read and how to read it. He begins by clearing away a misconception. Many people treat literary taste as an elegant accomplishment, like good manners at a high dinner or skill on horseback, by which they hope to complete themselves for correct society. Bennett argues instead that taste grows from honest, steady reading.

The book lists classics, explains how to approach poetry, drama, and novels, and urges readers to keep notes and reread. Bennett writes for busy adults who feel ashamed of gaps in their reading. The guide suits readers who want a friendly, Edwardian path into serious books, without snobbery or academic jargon.
36553-education-in-england-in-the-middle:
Parry, head of the Training College at Carmarthen, wrote a thesis on schooling in England in the middle ages. It won a London degree in science and was printed in London in 1920. Parry says he read all the proof he could find before he wrote. Much of the work was done while he served in the war from 1914 to 1919.

The book tells what provision was made for schooling from the coming of Christianity to the eve of the Reformation. Parry seeks the forces that drove growth in learning through those long years. He notes that Leach wrote on the same theme with a unlike aim and unlike results. Church, kings, towns, and grants all play a part.
36750-st-nicholas-v-13-no-9-july-1886-an:
St Nicholas, volume 13, number 9, is an illustrated magazine issue for July 1886. The Century Company holds the copyright. A plate of La Fayette and the British Ambassador fronts the number. A life of La Fayette by Eugenia Hodge leads the text.

One hundred and nine years ago, in February 1777, a young French guardsman ran away to sea, she starts. A most singular running away it was. He did not wish to be a sailor, yet he bought a ship to run away in, for he was very rich. At nineteen he held a commission as major general in the armies of a land three thousand miles away. He had never seen that land, and could not speak its tongue. At a dinner in Paris he owned his sympathy with a downtrodden people, and the tale runs on.
36823-marjorie-dean-high-school-junior:
Pauline Lester's Marjorie Dean, High School Junior came out from the Burt Company in New York in 1917. It follows her freshman and sophomore volumes in the same school series. A front picture shows Marjorie sinking down at her mother's feet, looking low in spirits.

Chapter one finds Marjorie on a porch swing with Mary Raymond, dreading a parting due in one week. Mary is bound for Colorado, and both girls recall their first split two years earlier. Readers of the earlier books learn how Marjorie left Franklin High School for Sanford. Friendship, loyalty, and school life in a new town carry the story forward.
3687-the-ruby-of-kishmoor:
Howard Pyle writes a pirate adventure for young readers about the ruby of Kishmoor, a jewel famous for its size and color. The Rajah of Kishmoor had bestowed the ruby on his queen, and at her capture it fell into a pirate's hands. A prologue introduces a very famous pirate of his day, and chapters follow Jonathan Rugg, a mysterious lady with a silver veil, and a one eyed little gentleman in black.

Later adventures bring a stranger with silver earrings and a sea captain with a broken nose, all chasing the great stone. Pyle writes with the gusto of a storyteller who loved ships, swords, and treasure. The book suits young readers who enjoy classic pirate tales with humor and high color.
36906-marjorie-dean-college-senior:
Marjorie Dean, College Senior, by Pauline Lester, was published in 1922. Burt issued the girls' story at New York. Four college volumes stand in the series. Freshman, Sophomore, and Junior years precede this one. A high school series stands behind them. The books address girls of twelve to eighteen. Chapter one is A Question for the Future. A farewell hop fills the opening scene. Hal Macy and his sister Jerry give it at Sanford. Five Lookouts return to Hamilton College the next day. Marjorie waltzes with Hal and teases him kindly. She will miss General and Captain most, she says.

Hal ranks himself next, and she grants the old guard their place. The waltz In Sunny Gardens ends too soon for her. Senior year, with its partings, begins under that music.
371-literary-blunders-a-chapter-in-the-h:
Henry Wheatley catalogs the slips, ghosts, and false tales of bookish life in this amusing study. He takes his title from a jest in The Caxtons, where a grand History of Human Error never got past its first sheets. Wheatley then sorts real blunders by kind, from bad quotes to fake authors and phantom words.

Chapters treat authors, translators, book lists, and errata sheets, with tales of learned men caught out by their own print. Ghost words coined by misreading get a full airing. The book delights readers who love books, and it warns how fast one error in print can live for years.
37176-marjorie-dean-college-junior:
Pauline Lester wrote a college tale for girls from twelve to eighteen, printed in New York in 1922. Marjorie Dean is in her junior year at Hamilton College. Lester wrote the full set, from freshman to senior year, plus a high school set before it. The tale opens with music, as friends plan a serenade.

Phyllis Moore leads seven singers in songs to welcome Marjorie and her four chums, the Lookouts, back to Hamilton. Elaine Hunter sits on a grassy mound under a tree in one early scene. Friendships, class loyalties, songs, and small plots fill the year. The book gives its readers a warm picture of college girl life as its day imagined it.
37240-the-new-york-weekly-magazine-or-mi:
New York Weekly Magazine was a miscellaneous repository issued in the seventeen nineties. It ran for a little more than two years, from summer seventeen ninety five. Bound volumes gathered its two complete years for readers of that day. This text holds one of those bound yearly volumes in full.

Weekly numbers of that age mixed tales, essays, verse, and news for readers. A repository of this kind aimed to store varied matter in one place. The magazine belongs to the first years of American periodical print. Readers today can sample what New York readers took in each week then. Its short life still left two full years of print behind it.
37263-coelebs-the-love-story-of-a-bachel:
F E Mills Young wrote Coelebs, the Love Story of a Bachelor, published by John Lane at London in this edition of 1917. John Musgrave stands before his dining-room fire with the Daily Telegraph in his hands. He is not reading it. He watches his new housemaid set down his breakfast on the snowy damask, with sniffs that proclaim a soul above such service. He approves of her, and for three good reasons.

He always engages his own servants, which is the first and all-sufficient reason. She is by no means young, which is the second. She is plain and respectable, which is the third. The narrator remarks that plain people are generally more respectable than handsome ones. Temptation assails the beautiful more often, and virtue untested earns no self-esteem.
37284-dickens-as-an-educator:
James Hughes, inspector of schools in Toronto, wrote this study of Dickens as a teacher, copyrighted in 1900. Appleton reissued it in New York and London in 1913. The editor's preface claims Dickens as an educational reformer, the greatest England has produced in that line.

No one else, the preface argues, did more to win kind treatment for young children. To rob a child of its childhood, in the principle quoted, is a crime against the child. Hughes reads Dickens's novels, with their schools, masters and beaten pupils, as a force that changed how England taught and treated its young.
37338-the-crime-doctor:
The Crime Doctor, by Ernest Hornung, was printed at Indianapolis in 1914, with pictures by Frederic Dorr Steele. Hornung was known for Raffles, the amateur cracksman, and this book of eight tales turns his gift for crime toward a doctor figure. The contents open with The Physician Who Healed Himself.

That first tale begins with Topham Vinson, Secretary of State for the Home Department, walking home from Westminster at midnight. A young man rushes up with the minister's own gold watch, taken back from the thief who stole it in North Audley Street. Other tales promise a life preserver, a golden key, a hopeless case, and a second murderer.
37563-a-man-of-honor:
George Eggleston's A Man of Honor was published in New York by the Orange Judd Company, entered for copyright in 1878, and illustrated by Woolf. Eggleston gives the book to Marion, his wife. His preface is a confession: he has long been curious to know whether or not he could write a pretty good story. With press copies going out to the critics, he is in a fair way to have that curiosity satisfied.

The contents promise a comedy of a stranger learning a country. Nearly every chapter is named for Mr Pagebrook: he gets up and calls an ancient lawgiver, is invited to breakfast, eats it, learns the customs of the country, and makes acquaintances. Then come Miss Sudie and her apt quotation, a character called Foggy, a dinner with his cousin Sarah Ann, rivulets of blue blood. At last come lessons in the law from Mr Sharp.
37566-natural-history-of-the-ornate-box-:
John Legler studies the ornate box turtle in a University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper published March 7, 1960, running over a hundred pages with sixteen plates. Legler's subject is Terrapene ornata ornata, and his contents map a full life history. Study areas and methods in Kansas anchor the field work.

Sections treat habitat and its limits, mating, nesting, eggs, and the growth of shell rings year by year. Temperature relations fill many pages, from basking to tolerance of heat and cold, before hibernation and diet. Populations, home range, homing, injuries, shell repair, parasites, predators, and defence follow. An opening systematic section notes the genus is a land adapted emyid, set apart by a hinged plastron and a down turned beak.
3808-robur-the-conqueror:
Jules Verne launches Robur the Conqueror with a duel that misses both men and a cow, then lifts the tale into the sky. The Weldon Institute of Philadelphia, devoted to balloons, faces a visitor who scorns gas bags and promises a heavier than air flying machine. Soon its president Uncle Prudent and secretary Phil Evans wake as prisoners aboard the Albatross, a great aeronef with a golden sun on its flag.

The voyage sweeps across prairies, the Pacific, the Himalayas, the Caspian, Dahomey, and the Atlantic, while the captives shout their names in vain to cheering crowds below. The balloon Go-Ahead rises to challenge Robur and collapses in the attempt. Readers who like Verne's inventor tales will find a swift tour of the world from above, with a villain who flies beyond all law.
38164-english-book-illustration-of-to-da:
English Book-Illustration of To-day gathers four essays with lists of books, first printed in the journal The Library. Sketchley surveys living English illustrators in four groups: the decorative, the open-air, the character, and the children's-book artists. Alfred Pollard supplies the introduction, and Kegan Paul issued the volume at London in 1903.

Sketchley thanks the British Museum staff and the artists who checked their own entries. Plates sample the field, from Walter Crane and Laurence Housman to Joseph Pennell and William Strang. An index of artists closes the book. The lists of books run on from page 121 to the index.
38186-the-sailor:
The Sailor is a tale by Snaith, out in nineteen sixteen with drawn plates. Snaith was known for a shelf of past tales. The book stands in parts, the first named for the birth of its lead. It opens at night in the slums of a mill town of the mid lands, in the cold month.

A large wife in a torn dress stands at the gate of a junk yard with a cart whip in hand. Past the wall crouches a boy of thirteen years, bare of foot, in rags, with his face lit by fear. His aunt has sworn to wait up for him and to make his short coin up to a full one with the whip. The boy finds a hole in the old wall and squeezes past it to flee. That start marks the hard road of the sailor to be.
38286-the-protector:
The Protector is a tale of the north woods by Harold Bindloss. It was put out at London in nineteen eighteen. His past tales are named on the title leaf. The front plate shows a man sunk to the waist in a stream. Two steps took him to that depth, says the plate word. He had hard work to find firm ground at the next.

The list of parts runs to one and thirty. A friend in need heads the tale. A gust of wind, a day on shore, and a change of scene come next. The old land, the heights, and a storm stay fill the first run. A maid of the tale is named at the eighth part. The hero, Vane, is named in part past part.
38308-natural-history-of-cottonmouth-moc:
Ray Burkett wrote this study of the cottonmouth moccasin snake for Kansas University. The museum series issued it on October 27, 1966, in Lawrence. Seven figures in the text back the long research report. Contents run from kinship and range to food habits in detail.

Parts treat color, scale counts, teeth, and the snakes home ground. Courtship, birth of young, and litter size get close study here. Growth, shedding, and ways of taking prey fill later sections. The work is a full field science account of a feared swamp snake. The study came from the University of Kansas museum series.
38325-the-happy-warrior:
The Happy Warrior is a novel by Hutchinson, copyrighted in December 1912 at Toronto. Its first edition was reprinted seven times within three months, the title page boasts. A front picture by a named artist faces the title. Verses from Wordsworth stand at the front and give the book its name and its theme.

Who is the happy warrior, the poem asks. He is the generous spirit whom neither shape of danger can dismay, nor thought of soft happiness betray. He plays the one game of life where what he most values has to be won. The novel's first book calls itself a nice, short book showing the elements of chance. Its first chapter is a page of the peerage, placing the hero among the great families of England.
38539-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
A slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Johann Gichtel to a glory heading in the G volume. Transcriber notes explain subscripts, superscripts, and side notes in the plain text. Corrections are listed for the author list and the article on Gilgit. That article describes basins holding a system of glaciers. The slice forms part of a dictionary of arts, sciences, and general information.

Alphabetical slices let Gutenberg volunteers transcribe the vast edition in parts. Entries here pass through biography, geography, and theology. The author list corrections show the edition's scholarly apparatus. Readers tracing the G entries meet mystics, Himalayan districts, and glories in one file.
38918-vignettes-of-manhattan-outlines-in:
Brander Matthews made a set of short New York pieces that Scribner reissued in 1921, with pictures by Smedley. The book is given to Theodore Roosevelt in a letter of May 1894. Matthews tells his friend that he does not hold him a typical New Yorker.

That man, Matthews says, is not proud of his chosen city. He does not thrill at its strong, rough profile across the river. A few, Roosevelt among them, love the town for what it is. The pieces are not stories, Matthews owns, but vignettes. There are a dozen, one for each month of the year, an urban calendar of times and seasons.
39005-the-american-gentleman-s-guide-to-:
Henry Lunettes's American Gentleman's Guide to Politeness and Fashion, cast as familiar letters to his nephews, was issued by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1864. A new edition, carefully revised by the author, is this text. Epigraphs from Tennyson and Victor Hugo front the letters. The dedication inscribes the unpretending volume to his young countrymen. Letter one takes up dress at length: conformity to fashion with regard for one's own looks.

The contents promise anecdotes of Doctor Johnson, Byron's absurd influence on dress, and Washington's example. Collars, sleeve buttons, signet rings, and the bad taste of flash stones all get their rulings. Simplicity in dress is named the mark of true refinement. Later letters, by the contents, cover the wider conduct of a gentleman: conversation, company, and manners. The golden mean in dress is the first letter's rule. The book is a mid-century American courtesy manual in letter form.
39054-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume thirty of the Philippine Islands series, covering the year 1640. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the fifty-five volume set. The Arthur H Clark Company published it at Cleveland in 1905. The series prints contemporary books and manuscripts in translation. Political, economic, commercial, and religious conditions all fall within its scope.

Two works fill this volume. Antonio Alvarez de Abreu writes on commerce between the Philippines and New Spain. His extract appeared at Madrid in 1736. Diego Aduarte's history of the Dominican province of the Holy Rosary follows. Aduarte printed his chronicle at Manila in 1640. Facsimile title pages and an old Mercator map illustrate the volume.
39215-the-new-rector:
Stanley Weyman wrote this novel, first printed in 1891. The first two chapter titles play on a royal cry: the king is dead, long live the king. Here the dead man is Williams, rector of the small Warwickshire town of Claversham for nearly forty years, and the question is who will take his place.

For some days the living sits in abeyance, in the gift of Lord Dynmore, whose own whereabouts no one can pin down. His London agents tell one caller he is in the Cordilleras, another the Andes, a third the far north. Dynmore's memory is famed as eccentric, so his choice may surprise all. Later chapters promise awkward meetings, letters in a cupboard, a bazaar, and a rector's decision. Weyman builds a village comedy of clergy, lawyers, and gentry around one vacant post.
39262-bert-wilson-wireless-operator:
J W Duffield wrote Bert Wilson, Wireless Operator, a sea tale for boys with a nineteen hundred thirteen copyright. Sully and Kleinteich held the rights, and a Racine press reprinted the book in nineteen hundred twenty four. Duffield wrote other Bert Wilson tales of sport and speed. Sixteen chapters carry Bert from port to pirate seas.

A cry of amuck tears through a sleepy port at the start. A small man with a crooked knife leaps on a steamer rail. Blood stains the blade as he hunts fresh prey. Three young athletes walk down the pier toward him. Later chapters promise a ship in flames and a typhoon. Sharks, lost folk, and a pirate raid wait past the storm.
39280-lest-we-forget-chicago-s-awful-the:
Survivors and rescuers tell of the Iroquois Theater fire in Chicago, in a memorial book printed in 1904. Bishop Fallows wrote the introduction. A photo shows the crowd in front of the theater at the time of the fire. The fire struck on December 30, 1903, at four in the afternoon, during a show.

First hand tales by people who were there give the horror its force. Heroic work by rescuers stands beside grim facts, such as a fire escape door that could not be opened where many died. Building experts report on who bore blame for the slaughter of women and children. Past great fires are recalled, and faith is tested by grief in page after page.
39490-a-lad-of-grit-a-story-of-adventure:
A Lad of Grit is a boys' adventure novel by Percy Westerman, published in 1909. Blackie issued it at London and Glasgow, with pictures by Edward Hodgson. Its subtitle promises adventure on land and sea in Restoration times. A long list of Westerman's sea stories fronts the book. Captain Fosdyke's Gold and The Submarine Hunters stand among dozens of titles. The contents open with news reaching the hero's home.

How the tidings of the Restoration came to Rake heads chapter one. The arrest and escape of Increase Joyce follow. A journey to Portsmouth and judgement on the Dorset smugglers come next. The hero's first ship is the Gannet, in chapter five. Pedro Alvarez is found, and tells a strange tale of treasure. Westerman mixes history, smuggling, and sea peril for schoolboy readers. Grit, his title says, is the lad's chief equipment.
39698-the-impostor:
Harold Bindloss wrote a prairie novel printed at London, Melbourne, and Toronto. Bindloss had written Hawtrey's Deputy, The Liberationist, A Sower of Wheat, and The Pioneer. Rancher Witham opens the contents, then Lance Courthorne, Trooper Shannon's quarrel, and In the Bluff. Miss Barrington comes home, and Witham's decision and his coming to Silverdale follow.

An armistice, Maud Barrington's promise, Speed the Plough, and mastery recognized fill the middle. The unexpected, facing the flame, and Maud Barrington merciless come before With the Stream, Under Test, and Courthorne blunders. The face at the window closes the list. There was no blink of starlight in the murky sky, the tale opens, and a stinging wind moaned about the frame houses beside the trail. Wheat, pride, and a double name drive the plot.
39896-the-girl-next-door:
Augusta Huiell Seaman wrote The Girl Next Door, a girls mystery printed at New York in 1917, illustrated by Relyea. Seaman also wrote The Sapphire Signet and The Boarded-Up House. A frontispiece shows Marcia staring out of the window at the house opposite her own. She gave the book to Margaret Fagg and to her father's memory.

Contents open with Marcia's secret, the face behind the shutter, the gate opens, and a backward glance. A handkerchief in the window, Cecily revealing herself, surprises all around, the filigree bracelet, the lifted veil, and via wireless follow. The writing on the bracelets, puzzling it out, one mystery explained, and Major Goodrich assisting close the tale. Girls got Seaman.
40109-taxidermy-and-zoological-collectin:
Taxidermy and Zoological Collecting, by William Hornaday, calls itself a complete handbook for the amateur taxidermist, collector, osteologist, museum-builder, sportsman, and traveller. Scribner published the fourth edition in New York in 1894, with twenty-four plates and eighty-five text pictures. Hornaday had been chief taxidermist of the National Museum for eight years, and a collector for Ward's establishment for seven.

Chapters on collecting and preserving insects, by Holland, chancellor of the Western University of Pennsylvania, extend the book. A plate shows the head of a royal Bengal tiger mounted by the author. The preface greets the heyday of popular zoology: eager young naturalists crowding forward, and fine new museums starting up on every hand. Hornaday writes a full bench and field manual, from skinning to mounting.
40126-the-cock-and-anchor:
Cock and Anchor is a novel of old Dublin by Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu. Downey of London issued this edition in the year 1895 here. Brinsley Le Fanu drew the illustrations for his father's early tale. A note by the son tells the book's publishing history in full. It first appeared in Dublin in three volumes in 1845.

No author's name stood on the title page of that first edition. Curry of Dublin, Longman of London, and Fraser shared that imprint. Le Fanu later altered the story and reissued it as Morley Court. That reissue ran in the Select Library of Fiction for cheap readers. The son now restores the proper title, Cock and Anchor, in print.
40721-dan-carter-and-the-cub-honor:
Dan Carter and the Cub Honor, by Mildred Wirt, is a Cub Scout novel. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York with rights in 1952. Dan Carter leads Den Two in basketball at a church gym basement. Brad Wilber, the den chief, runs practice for the five Cubs there.

Pat Oswald and his gang jeer through the window at fumbling Chips. Chapters promise a freezer quest, a tapping bell, and payment refused in turn. A threatening suit, Halloween pranks, and measles crowd the boys year in fun. Old Terry demand and a locked door build the mystery strand. Cub honor is tested and proved in the final chapters.
40883-katerfelto-a-story-of-exmoor:
G J Whyte-Melville wrote Katerfelto, a story of Exmoor and its wild horse lore. Chapman and Hall issued the book in London in eighteen hundred seventy five. Colonel H Hope Crealocke drew its plates of chase and camp. Deadman’s Alley, the first chapter, opens in London in seventeen hundred sixty three.

John Wilkes, sent to the Tower that April, fills the street talk. A drunk chair man sings a crude Wilkes song in Covent Garden. Gentlemen at supper rage at the noise from their high room. Threats of a jelly beating fail to stop the dogged singer. His King Nabuchodonosor song grinds on in a flat key. The tale then turns west to Exmoor’s moors and horse hunts. Gipsy brides, moonlight rides, and hard runs fill its plates. Whyte-Melville of Digby Grand fame keeps the pace fast and gay.
40896-elementary-color:
Milton Bradley wrote this manual on color for teachers, in its third edition from his Springfield company, copyrighted in 1895, with an introduction by a Williams College physics professor. Bradley also wrote Color in the Schoolroom and Color in the Kindergarten.

The contents move from the theory of color through definitions to practical experiments with the color wheel, the color top, and Maxwell disks. The Bradley system sets six spectrum standards. Later sections classify harmonies, review Chevreul's work, and treat contrast of every kind. A full chapter takes color teaching into the schoolroom, with paper tablets, charts of broken colors, and color blindness, then outlines a whole course of instruction. Art teachers get the kindergarten king's system complete.
40918-on-some-ancient-battle-fields-in-l:
Charles Hardwick wrote a study of old fight fields in Lancashire, printed in eighteen eighty-two. He had first read its core as four talks to a town club of letters. For the book he spread those talks wide and backed them with far more proof. He cites the work of past and fresh hands in the same field.

Hardwick holds that the big past man may pass a fight site by, but the home student may not. Each small fact, tale, and old belief is worth close search. He finds that such tales, read with care, oft chime with broad truths of the past. The book thus blends hard fact, tale lore, and the charm of place.
41145-an-account-of-the-death-of-philip-:
Francis Cunningham, rector of Pakefield, published 'An Account of the Death of Philip Jolin' with Hatchard and Son in 1830. Jolin was executed for the murder of his father in the island of Jersey on October 3, 1829. An advertisement states the difficulty of the case. To determine the real state of mind in a criminal who shows signs of repentance under sentence of death is a work of much difficulty.

Professions of religion, Cunningham warns, are far oftener the language of alarm than of conversion, and every minister conversant in such cases knows it. He quotes Newton's wish to know rather how the man lived than how he died. The tract records the events of the last eleven days in the life of the criminal. His crimes had been great, but hypocrisy was not among their number, and he had received no previous religious instruction.
412-john-jacob-astor:
Elbert Hubbard profiles John Jacob Astor in this Little Journeys sketch of great business men. Hubbard opens with Astor's plain habits: early rising, steady work, and a life ruled by routine rather than luck. Wealth, he argues, follows habit, service, and the will to give value in return.

The sketch traces Astor from a poor German youth to the fur trade and New York land, where patience built a fortune. Hubbard writes in brisk, moralizing prose, full of maxims on work and thrift. The piece serves as both life and lesson, in the self-help style that made Hubbard's series popular.
41297-local-color:
Irvin Cobb's story set 'Local Color' appeared in 1916, after parts ran in magazines in 1914 and 1915. The title tale begins with a puzzle: Felix Looms, a writer of crime tales, left New York four years ago and never came back. He told friends he felt run down, gave a lawyer power to act for him, and stored his goods.

Looms was short, dark and shy, a man few people truly knew, so his going left barely a ripple. The book holds nine more tales, with names such as 'Field of Honor,' 'The Smart Aleck,' 'The Great Auk' and 'Smooth Crossing,' in Cobb's plain comic voice.
41393-the-confessions-of-a-collector:
William Carew Hazlitt wrote The Confessions of a Collector, printed at London in 1897. The first chapter traces how a love of old and rare books grew in him from youth. He tells of his kin on both sides, an uncle with a true feel for old things, and books bought in secret under his father roof.

Chapter heads promise tales of stalls, finds, and low prices, plus a plan to write on Venice though he knew it little at first. Richard Heber fills much of the next chapter, praised for vast stores of books, notes writ in flyleaves, and free loans to friends. Readers meet the joys, hunts, and luck of book men in a age of great sales.
41732-scotch-wit-and-humor:
A joke book of Scotch wit and humor, classified under subject headings, published at Philadelphia in 1898 with a table of authors. The contents alone run for pages of titles, each a small promise.

A Badly Arranged Prayer, A Beadle Magnifying his Office, A Canny Witness, A Consoling If: the jokes sort Scotland by type: ministers, beadles, elders, Highlanders, misers, and law courts. There are definitions of baptism and of fou, lessons in manners, and a piper's opinion of a lord. The humor trades on canniness, caution with money, and dry church talk. Readers get the Victorian idea of Scottish character in its purest distilled form, anecdote by anecdote.
41964-mark-tidd-editor:
Clarence Budington Kelland sends his boy hero into journalism in Mark Tidd, Editor, copyrighted in 1917 by Harper and Brothers. Binney Jenks narrates, opening with Mark's verdict that the Wicksville Trumpet is busted, though Binney allows it made one good paper in twenty years of weekly issues. A frontispiece caption shows Plunk and Tallow looking dilapidated and frightened.

Mark, fat enough to need a turn-table and stuttering like a locomotive under load, wants his father's leave first. Mr Tidd, grown rich on a turbine-engine invention, still wears overalls, keeps his machine-shop in the barn and reads Gibbon between inventions.
41981-the-jewels-of-aptor:
The Jewels of Aptor, by Samuel Delany, was published in 1962. Ace Books issued the novel at New York that year. Verses from an epic of its own world head the book. The Galactica, by the one-armed poet Geo, is their source. Leptar and Aptor war in that poem, as in the tale. A prologue opens on a beach after the events. A girl sits on a rock where the sand is wet. She has been shown a film of a cruelty done to a boy. It happened years ago and far away, she is told. A tight beam spied it out; the screen kept its record. Why show it to her, she asks. To teach her, comes the answer.

She is not sixteen yet, and a quick student. Telepathy is the lesson named.
41995-the-scout-and-ranger-being-the-per:
The Scout and Ranger gives the personal adventures of Corporal Pike of the Fourth Ohio Cavalry, printed at Cincinnati and New York in 1865 with twenty-five full-page engravings. The title page sets out his double service. He was a Texan ranger in the Indian wars. Afterward he was a scout and spy in Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and the Carolinas. He served under Generals Mitchell, Rosecrans, Sheridan, Thomas, and Sherman, and the book illustrates the secret service.

Pike gives the book to his late comrades in arms. A preface holds that whatever illustrates the spirit of the late great struggle must interest the American reader. Readers will not rest content, it argues, with mere outlines or battle pieces. They will search out details and incidents. These may be learned as well from a private soldier's career as from a major general's, the preface holds.
42135-the-unwilling-professor:
Arthur Porges wrote The Unwilling Professor, a science fiction story printed in Dynamic Science Fiction in January 1954. The Professor of the title has braved great perils to reach Earth. He thinks he knows what he is up against, but he has not counted on Fatty Schultz and Irv Lece.

Fatty and Irv are students at Bateman College, and both are failing mathematics badly. Their whole fraternity shares the trouble, in a college whose courses run from aardvark breeding to beer brewing. Irv's teacher told him his only hope was to start arithmetic over and retire to a cave. Porges plays the meeting of a learned visitor and two hopeless students for comedy, in the brisk style of the pulp magazines.
42520-a-marriage-under-the-terror:
Patricia Wentworth wrote a novel dated 1910 that won first prize in the Melrose novel contest in England. Three judges each picked the tale on their own, from a large field of seasoned hands. The tale opens at noon in August 1792, as Laure de Montargis wakes late in a grand bed in Paris.

Chapter heads trace a stolen cipher, a forced entry, and a town shut by a prison wall. Blood in the streets, the fate of a king, and a vote that can not be undone raise the stakes. A trial and a wedding, a burned great house, and a flight end the roll of threats.
42584-extinct-monsters-a-popular-account:
Extinct Monsters, a popular account of the larger forms of ancient animal life, was written by the Reverend Hutchinson and issued at London in a fifth, cheaper edition in 1897. Its front plate shows Triceratops, a gigantic horned dinosaur some twenty five feet long. A preface by Doctor Henry Woodward of the Natural History Museum praises the drawings prepared for the book.

Woodward notes how tales of giants and dragons may have grown from finds of mammoth and rhinoceros bones in caves. The book surveys the great beasts of past ages for general readers. It treats the restorations of extinct animals, such as those set up at the Crystal Palace grounds. Hutchinson wrote several popular earth science books, and this one brought fossil giants to a wide public. Illustrations by Smit and others help readers picture creatures known only from their bones.
42619-buckskin-mose-or-life-from-the-lak:
Buckskin Mose wrote his own life, and Rosenberg edited it with illustrations for Hinton at New York in 1873. His life ran from the Lakes to the Pacific, as actor, circus-rider, detective, ranger, gold-digger, Indian scout, and guide. Mose admits in his preface that money is one reason for the book. He insists there is a stronger one.

He means to show that the government's way of protecting the settler is good neither for the settler nor for the Indian. At times it leaves the settler unprotected; then it represses the independence that self-protection breeds. With the Indian it has no settled policy: at one time it bribes, and at another it lashes them into subjection. The officers and agents sent out, he says, are in nine cases out of ten ignorant of the people and the country, and not always honest. The adventures carry the argument.
4266-a-woman-s-way-through-unknown-labra:
Mina Benson Hubbard wrote this book to complete her husband Leonidas Hubbard's unfinished work in Labrador. She wanted to correct misleading accounts of his expedition. She includes much of his diary exactly as he wrote it. She adds George Elson's account of their last days together and his later efforts. A map of the region is included.

Her own journey crossed country recognized by geographical authorities in America and Europe. It was the only surveyed route over that region. The narrative moves through rivers, lakes, and portages, with the daily labor of travel. It stands as a tribute to her husband and a record of a woman leading an expedition through unknown land.
42676-natural-history-of-the-racer-colub:
Henry Fitch of the University of Kansas wrote this natural history of the racer, Coluber constrictor, issued in 1963 in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History. The study fills pages 351 to 468 of its volume, with plates and twenty figures. Contents open with methods and materials. A full description follows, covering color pattern, bodily proportions, scalation, and teeth.

Chapters then treat the snake's relationships, range, and change from place to place, and its habitat and ties to heat and cold. Home range and movements come next, then food habits in detail: how prey is taken, what the food is made of, and the kinds of prey. Breeding, eggs, and hatching follow, then growth. Death factors and means of escape, numbers and makeup of populations, and a summary close the study.
42914-gladiator:
Gladiator is a novel by Philip Wylie. Its first chapter opens like a fable, in plain once upon a time words. Once upon a time in Colorado lived a man named Abednego Danner and his wife Matilda. Danner was a professor of biology in a small college, the tale goes on, in a town whose name is cut short at the head of this copy.

The biblical names of the parents hint at the book's matter: a child bred by science to be more than common men. Wylie's strong man, raised in secret and loosed on the world, became one of the famous thought tales of its century. Later supermen of the comic pages owe his hero a clear debt. The fable opening keeps its feet in a small college town while the idea grows to world size.
43135-the-riddle-of-the-purple-emperor:
Mary and Thomas Hanshew wrote The Riddle of the Purple Emperor, a detective tale in the Scotland Yard Mystery Library, held in 1918.
