Its sleuth is Hamilton Cleek, the man of forty faces, once known to the police as the Vanishing Cracksman. A cast list at the front names his chief, Superintendent Narkom, his driver Lennard, and his young helper Dollops.

Lady Margaret Cheyne, an orphan heiress, stands at the heart of the case. Twenty five parts move through a house of shadows, a cry in the night, a shot in the dark, and a house with shuttered windows. Twin scarves, a twisted clue, and a trap build the puzzle, till Cleek untwists the threads in the last parts.
4343-how-and-when-to-be-your-own-doctor:
Dr. Isabelle A. Moser, with Steve Solomon, wrote this guide to natural hygiene and self-care, published in 1997. Its chapters tell how Moser became a hygienist, explain the nature and cause of disease, and cover fasting, colon cleansing, diet and nutrition, vitamins, and the analysis of disease states.

The book argues that the body recovers when given rest, clean food, and freedom from excess, and it teaches readers to help that process. Solomon's foreword sets the tone with a Shaker hymn on the gift of simplicity. Readers should note that its advice is alternative health teaching, not a substitute for medical care.
43996-the-american-joe-miller-a-collecti:
Robert Kempt compiles The American Joe Miller, a collection of Yankee wit and humour, printed in London in 1865. Adams and Francis made the book, and it was entered at Stationers' Hall. Two motto lines praise a teeming wit and a laugh that wets the cloak.

His preface owns the gap he fills. No good collection of American wit stands on this side of the Atlantic, he says. Jest books hold a few of Brother Jonathan's good things amid the wit of John Bull and Paddy. Scotland has had its Ramsay, and England its Timbs and Lemon. Kempt claims the first full haul of Yankee witticisms for English readers. Joke fans get a fat, dated store of them.
44464-under-one-sceptre-or-mortimer-s-mi:
Under One Sceptre, or Mortimer's Mission, is a tale by Emily Sarah Holt. Holt had writ Mistress Margery and The White Rose of Langley before. Shaw of London brought this new edition out in the year 1899. The subtitle calls it the story of the Lord of the Marches. Lines from Elizabeth Barrett Browning head the title page of the work.

Her preface calls Don Quixote the saddest book ever written by one judge. Yet the world needs its Quixotes, secular and religious, she argues there. Her hero is a Don Quixote who lived five hundred years back. He tilted at windmills and tried to free the captive lions there. The windmills stood firm, and the lions turned and tore him apart. Such spent heroism seems wasted, yet now and then the castle falls. Ireland's freedom in Christ stands as the hope behind her tale.
44804-betty-lee-junior:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote this school tale for girls, and the World Syndicate printed it in 1931. Betty Lee, Junior follows Betty through her third year of high school. A pep assembly opens the book with a bang of horns.

Golden Betty, small flies in the ointment, and baskets and humble friends fill the early list. Lucia dresses a doll and shares her secrets. Doris needs a sister, and carols mark the winter. Giving up a pleasant honor tests Betty's pride. Could Betty be stubborn asks one late head, before a fateful birthday party. An unhappy interview, a happy discovery, and Betty seeing a friend surprised close her junior year.
44808-betty-lee-senior:
Betty Lee, Senior is a school story by Harriet Pyne Grove, published in 1931. The World Syndicate Publishing Company issued the book at Cleveland and New York. Contents list twenty chapters for Betty senior year in the tale. Vacation Days and A Goldfish in the Ocean open the book in order.

A Merry Whirl of Good Times, The Storm, and A Surprising Rescue follow in the contents. Vacation Last Fling and Seniors carry the girls back to school in the list. One of Those A D Parties, The Seniors Entertain, and The Coveted Honor fill the middle chapters. An Intimate View for Janet, Valentines, Hearts and Masks, and An Exchange of Hearts come after in order. Grove wrote a shelf of such senior year books, in which the last year of school is a small republic of games, honours, and first love.
44819-kathleen-s-diamonds-or-she-loved-a:
Kathleen's Diamonds, or She Loved a Handsome Actor, is a novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller. The hosted copy is from a series volume first copyrighted in eighteen ninety five. Cleveland and New York publishers handled its later issue. Its contents run chapter by chapter in a teasing style.

The heads sketch a tale of love and crime round a diamond necklace. A romantic girl meets an actor who once rescued her at Newport. Her guardian forbids the match, then goes missing in a mysterious way. Kathleen defies the ban and offers her diamond necklace for sale. Murder, a fatal telegram, and a vow of revenge follow in swift order. Later heads promise a disappearance, a startling discovery, and a storm.
45302-my-pretty-scrap-book-picture-pages:
Cupples wrote My Pretty Scrap-Book, or Picture Pages and Pleasant Stories for Little Readers, published in London in 1874. The book opens with a frame: it is Dick's birthday, and his mother has wisely bought him this very scrap-book. The narrator invites the child reader to stand by while she turns the leaves.

Each page pairs a picture with a short story. Funny Uncle Toby suffers tickling and pranks on his wig. Naughty Judy tries on her sleeping mistress's fine clothes and admires herself in a fan's mirror. A little gleaner works in the heat because her parents are poor, and children caught in the rain shelter under a funny umbrella. A ship picture from the Bay of Biscay hints at a wreck, with a mast and a hen-coop floating by. Readers get a Victorian picture book that talks to its reader like a kind aunt.
45539-the-compleat-bachelor:
The Compleat Bachelor is a comic novel by Oliver Onions. Harper held the copyright in 1900. Stokes published the New York edition. Onions dedicated the book to Frank Gelett Burgess. The contents list fifteen episodes with playful titles. They include Sugar and Lemon and A Corner in Treacle.

The narrator is Rollo, a contented bachelor. His sister Caroline opens the first episode. She offers to drop him at his club. He insists on joining her tea visit instead. He calls it his first duty as a brother. The scene plays out in a drawing room full of chatter. Carrie shows off her middle-aged brother with pride. The episodes follow his calm path through society.
45656-the-ancient-cities-of-the-new-worl:
The Ancient Cities of the New World is a travel and dig report by Désiré Charnay. Its full title adds travels in Mexico and Central America from 1857 to 1882. Gonino and Conant turned the French text into English for this copy. Chapman and Hall brought the book out in London in 1887. Many pictures fill its pages, and it is addressed to Peter Lorillard.

The French minister of public teaching sent Charnay to study old American cultures. Lorillard backed the work with funds in a generous spirit, Charnay writes. The report sets out the finds of his trips across those lands. Charnay holds that the old cultures sprang from one Toltec root. He calls them far more modern than most men of his day thought. Correct spellings of names rest on his own preface note, he adds.
45701-christianity-and-problems-of-to-da:
Christianity and Problems of To-Day is a volume of lectures by various authors, printed by Scribner at New York in 1922. The lectures were delivered before Lake Forest College in 1921 on the foundation of the late William Bross. The book stands as Volume Eleven of the Bross Library. Its shelf-mates show the series' range.

The library list includes Dods on the origin and nature of the Bible, Thomson's Bible of Nature, and Bliss on the religions of modern Syria and Palestine. Royce's Sources of Religious Insight and Figgis on Nietzsche and the Gospel stand in the row. Prize volumes treat the problem of the Old Testament and the mythical interpretation of the Gospels. One lecture here opens among the Hebrew legends of Enoch, son of Jared, on the dim edge of history. The volume brings college Christianity to the questions of its day.
45885-dartmoor:
Arthur Salmon described Dartmoor in a volume of the Beautiful England series, with pictures by Haslehurst. The frontispiece shows Lydford Gorge, and plates follow of Wistman's Wood, Two Bridges, and the clapper bridge at Postbridge. Salmon opens with the name itself, which he calls misleading.

The moor, he notes, is not the moor of the Dart alone, but the cradle-land of the Teign, the Tavy, and the Ockment too. Saxons likely first knew it from the fertile South Hams, looking across a waste that seemed a region of mystery. Brent Tor, Tavy Cleave, Widecombe, and Dartmeet are among the places pictured. Walkers and stay-at-home travellers were the series' readers.
45932-the-gasoline-motor:
Harold Whiting Slauson wrote a handbook on the gasoline motor, issued in New York in 1913. The Outing Publishing Company held the rights that year. Slauson had written The Motor Boat for the same handbook set. Nine chapters run from types of motors to two-cycle motors.

The first chapter sets out what must happen for a motor to run on its own. Charge must enter, be squeezed, be lit, and be cast out in turn. Four-stroke and two-stroke forms get plain, careful contrasts. Valves, bearings, sparking, fuel mix, oil, and cooling each get a full part for owners and boat men.
45959-open-that-door:
Open That Door, by Robert Sturgis Ingersoll, was published at Philadelphia and London in September 1916. Nine chapters of essays make up the book. The first two are called Walled In and An Open Door. Later pieces treat reading fiction, history and the vote, and poets and readers. A motto from Cervantes heads chapter one: the brave man carves out his fortune. Ingersoll admits an author must have some ego to print his name.

Most writers, he jokes, limit their crowd: fat books for the fat, cook books for cooks. He claims no such modesty. Everyone wants the best of life, he says, from railroad president to ditch digger. His theme is the handicaps all people share, and the doors books can open past them.
46098-in-the-name-of-liberty-a-story-of-:
In the Name of Liberty, subtitled A Story of the Terror, is a novel by Owen Johnson published in New York in 1905. The story opens in Paris in August 1792, in a poor lane of the Faubourg Saint Antoine. Its epigraph quotes Madame Roland on crimes done in the name of liberty.

Chapters move through the taking of the Tuileries, the prison killings, and, a year later, hunger, plots, and the fall of the Terror. Figures named in the contents include Nicole, Barabant, Dossonville, and Goursac. The book blends love, risk, and street politics, and shows how fast hope in a new order can turn to fear.
4624-off-hand-sketches-a-little-dashed-w:
T. S. Arthur published Off-Hand Sketches, a little dashed with humour, in 1851. He notes that readers will smile at some slices of life pictured here, yet no smile here is bought by slighting humanity, good feeling, or virtue. Most episodes are true stories given a light imaginative colouring, and each carries a lesson worth taking to heart.

Contents include the circuit-preacher, the protest, and retrenchment, or what a man saved by stopping his newspaper. They go on to hunting up a testimonial, trying to be a gentleman, taking a prescription, and the Yankee and the Dutchman. Later sketches cover a tipsy parson, much ado about Mrs. Todd and Mrs. Jones, almost a tragedy, a new way to collect an old debt, and a shocking bad memory. Readers get short, funny, moral American sketches.
46369-torrey-s-narrative-or-the-life-and:
William Torrey wrote his own tale of captivity in the South Seas, printed at Boston in 1848. He was held by the people of the Marquesas for twenty-five months, in 1835, 1836, and 1837. Cast from the wreck of the brig Doll, he and one mate alone lived to tell it.

Torrey drew the engravings from his own sketches. A verse heads his title: a tale of grief, of constant peril, and of scant relief. He had served for years on English and American merchant ships in all a seaman's posts. His preface owns his small schooling with frank pride. Few castaway tales come so straight from the man's own hand.
46904-the-vagrancy-problem-the-case-for-:
The Vagrancy Problem, by William Harbutt Dawson, argues the case for measures of restraint for tramps, loafers and unemployables. King and Son published it in London in 1910. Dawson, who wrote several books on Germany, adds a study of the continental detention colonies and labour houses as models for England.

The title page carries a stern text from Carlyle. For the idle man, Carlyle thunders, there is no place in this England of ours. He that will not work, and save according to his means, should let him go elsewhere. The law has made for him no soft provision, but a hard and stern one. Dawson's own opening is milder in tone: English opinion, he says, is not only moving but maturing on vagrancy and its rational treatment. Foreign critics, he notes, call the English slow to listen.
46969-the-geologic-setting-of-the-john-d:
Geological Survey staff wrote a guide to the John Day Country in Grant County, Oregon, a famed spot for outdoor trips. The land takes its name from John Day, a Virginian who joined the Astor trek west in 1810. Lost and robbed on the trail, Day left his name on a river where he met with grief.

Gold finds in 1862 on Canyon Creek drew the first real rush of settlers to the place. Dredges later dug the river flats, and wood and ranch work now lead the local trades. A photo from 1946 shows the town, the river vale, and the Strawberry Range in one wide view.
471-the-bride-of-lammermoor:
Walter Scott tells a tragic Scots romance of feuding houses in this novel. Edgar, Master of Ravenswood, loves Lucy Ashton, daughter of the man who seized his family's lands. Their secret betrothal defies kin, law, and a mother's cold scheming, and the tale moves toward a grim, fated end.

Scott frames the story as drawn from a real Dalrymple family tale, told to him by kin near the events. Moor, castle, and storm set the dark ground. The novel endures as Scott's starkest tragedy, where love, pride, and revenge pull young lives toward ruin.
47423-vine-and-olive-or-young-america-in:
William Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, made Vine and Olive, a story of travel and adventure in Spain and Portugal, copyrighted in 1876. The book is the fifth volume of the second Young America Abroad series. A front picture shows the Academy Squadron off Barcelona. Adams gives the book to Henry Ruggles, once United States consul at Barcelona, with whom he saw a bull-fight at Madrid.

The preface tells the history of the Academy Squadron on its cruise along the shores of Spain and Portugal. A professor of geography and history lectures the pupils as they travel, and the ship's surgeon serves as a walking store of travel facts. The party crosses from Barcelona to Lisbon by way of Madrid and Toledo. A second trip runs from Malaga through Granada, Cordova, and Seville to Cadiz.
47455-the-fiction-factory-being-the-expe:
John Milton Edwards wrote The Fiction Factory, the record of a man who kept a story mill grinding for twenty two years, issued in New Jersey in 1912. In 1893 Edwards quit his post as paymaster for a building firm and lived by his pen, or as he jokes, by his good friend the typewriter. Night and Sunday tales had grown to dwarf his pay.

Twenty six parts tell how he bent the twig, chose methods, and won a big house as a patron. Nickel thrills and dollar shockers, lean years with the wolf at the door, and slow growth fill the tale. Lists of patrons and profits for the whole run close the book. It is a rare plain look at hack writing as a trade.
47569-birds-and-nature-vol-11-no-3-march:
Birds and Nature, volume eleven, number three, is the March 1902 issue of a magazine illustrated by color photography. An Easter carol and a poem on spring open the number. The first bird article treats the winter wren, which breeds chiefly north of the United States. Voices in the garden and the Leconte's sparrow follow. An Easter lilies piece, the call of the killdee, and the northern phalarope carry the bird pages forward.

The hairy woodpecker, a varicolored frog, and the domestic sheep have their articles. A piece on opal and one on the crocus serve the mineral and flower sides. The round-lobed liverwort and the violet get their pages. The spring migration of the warblers opens a series. The English walnut and related trees close the practical side. Such magazines taught natural history at the parlor table.
47570-birds-and-nature-vol-11-no-4-april:
The April 1902 number of Birds and Nature, volume eleven, number four, is a spring issue of the magazine illustrated by colour photography. Poems open it: a sonnet asking what time of year it is, and a verse welcome to April.

Short pieces follow on the black-chinned hummingbird, the burrowing owl, the western pine squirrel, Audubon's warbler, the veerie, and the red-backed sandpiper. An antelope tells its own life story, and other articles treat animal emotions, domestic cattle, and spring migration in central Mississippi. Plant studies of the arrow head, black cohosh, and calamus round out the number. The issue mixes verse, bird lore, and plain natural history for home readers.
47769-saragossa-a-story-of-spanish-valor:
Saragossa: A Story of Spanish Valor, by Pérez Galdós, reached English readers in a translation by Minna Caroline Smith, printed at Boston in eighteen ninety-nine. Napier's words on the siege head the book, calling the city a pillar of past glory. The narrator reaches Saragossa at night by the Puerta de Sancho. The clock in the Torre Nueva strikes ten as the party enters.

Four men have escaped a rope line of captives and walked from Lerma over hills and rivers. Their shared wealth has shrunk to a few coins, spent on bread by the Orphanage. Don Roque has friends in the city, but the hour is too late to call. They rest by the leaning tower and wait for day, free but worn out.
47816-the-silversmith-s-handbook-contain:
The Silversmiths Handbook is a craft book by George Gee, a gold and silver smith by trade. This is its fifth form, out at London in nineteen twenty-one. Its themes are the mix and work of silver, with its melts, its joins, its sham mixes, and the means to bar waste and to mend and gloss the work. A kin book on gold work stands past it in the trade list.

The front note says the trade long felt the want of such a book of facts. Work men, boys at the bench, and makes who use the stuff may find in it aid for their day tasks. Gee was led to the work by long use in the art and by the chance to learn its needs at first hand. Rules, mixes, and notes fill the book.
47881-birds-and-nature-vol-12-no-1-june-:
Birds and Nature, volume 12, number 1, for June 1902, is an issue of a monthly serial illustrated by color photography, edited by William Kerr Higley and published by Mumford at Chicago. Its banner calls it a guide in the study of nature, with forty illustrations in natural colors.

The contents open with verse: a sonnet on June by Helen Hunt Jackson and a song, Way of June, of dark red roses and larks lost in light. Bird studies follow in prose: the swallow tailed kite, praised in quoted words of Coues for its grace, Alice's thrush, the Carolina chickadee, and the violet green swallow. Fiction and incident mix in, with Dick, the story of a dog, and a true incident of lady birds. Nature pieces round out the number: springs, geysers and artesian wells, starfishes, the fire weed, the sea pink, the water ousel, and tobacco.
47882-birds-and-nature-vol-12-no-2-july-:
Birds and Nature for September 1902 is the second number of the journal's twelfth volume. The journal bills itself as illustrated by color photography. Poems and short nature pieces fill its pages alongside the bird studies.

A sonnet called September, by Helen Hunt Jackson, opens the number with praise of the golden month. A poem by Celia Thaxter on seaside goldenrod follows on the same spread. The Palm Warbler gets the first bird article, then the Long-Billed Curlew and the Everglade Kite. The Grasshopper Sparrow and the damsel fly have their own short pieces. Other items treat feldspar, cowries and shell money, and the Wisconsin Dells. A prolific peach tree stump and a happy family show the journal's range of curiosities.
48179-a-manual-of-the-hand-lathe-compris:
Egbert Watson's Manual of the Hand Lathe came from Henry Carey Baird in Philadelphia in 1869. Sampson Low sold it in London. Watson had lately written for the Scientific American. Seventy-eight engravings illustrate the directions. The manual covers working metals of all kinds, ivory, bone, and precious woods. It adds dyeing, coloring, French polishing, and inlaying by veneers.

Watson dedicates the book to his son Egbert Perley Watson. He hopes the boy will become a good man and a good mechanic. The preface calls turning an elevating, artistic pastime and a wholesome relief from business. Chapters treat the foot lathe, tools, scrapers, and screw cutting. Chucking, metal spinning, ornamental cutting, and fancy turning follow. Ornamental woods close the survey, from snake wood and tulip wood to granadilla.
48370-a-sermon-preach-d-before-the-right:
Andrew Snape preached a sermon before the Lord Mayor, aldermen, and citizens of London at the Cathedral Church of Saint Paul on Monday, January thirtieth, seventeen oh nine ten. The day was the anniversary fast for the martyrdom of King Charles the First. Jonah Bowyer in London printed the sermon in seventeen ten. Snape was chaplain to the Duke of Somerset and rector of Saint Mary at Hill. The court asked Snape to print the sermon.

The text is First Kings, chapter twenty one, verses nine and ten, on Naboth. It bids men proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high, and set two sons of Belial to bear false witness that he blasphemed God and the king. Snape applies the shedding of innocent blood to the solemn day. Church and city readers get high church preaching on loyalty, guilt, and a martyred king.
48475-on-the-stage-and-off-the-brief-car:
On the Stage and Off, subtitled The Brief Career of a Would-Be Actor, by Jerome K Jerome, was published by Henry Holt and Company in New York in 1891. Jerome says in his preface that he tried to see his stage days exactly as they were, rough road as well as smiling landscape, though time now gilds them. He thinks of the stage as a lost friend and sends its people a hearty God Speed.

The first chapter recalls the fever that takes a young man of about nineteen, who sees Romeo and Juliet and decides acting means making love in tights at three hundred a week. Jerome writes his own brief, blighted turn at that calling with comic hindsight.
48505-david-blaize-and-the-blue-door:
E F Benson sends young David Blaize through a blue door into a world where nursery things live in a Hodder and Stoughton tale. H J Ford drew the plates, which list flame-cats, a game-cupboard that wakes, and a dance with a giraffe. Front pages list Benson's David books in a row.

David calls on Miss Muffet, flees her spider, and finds a Mint-man in a bank in the plate list. Uncle Popacatapetl must be saved from that Mint-man by a telegram, the captions add. David rides a cow porter, uses a telephone in its tail, and earns a flying certificate from the birds. Noah chases him, a brigadier-general needs rescue, and David ends as a field-marshal who reviews his guard of honour.
49103-the-first-printed-translations-int:
The First Printed Translations into English is a list book by William Harris. Harris kept the borough book house at Bromley in his day. A Routledge house of London and a Dutton house of New York share the print. Its full name calls it a mate to school books of English book lore. Names of great far books stand in strict A to Z rank in the list.

Each name bears years of birth and death with a kind tag in brief. Works and their English turns stand with dates and house names. Edmond About French tales head the shown first rank of names. An old Greek love tale of Achilles Tatius stands in that rank too. Saxon priest Aelfric church talks, turned by Thorpe, close the first page rank.
4945-jane-allen-junior:
Edith Bancroft's Jane Allen: Junior opens on a late September day at Wellington College, where summer waves goodbye with fitful sunshine through stately trees. Leaves tremble before autumn's brush, buds burst in heroic tribute, and breezes cheer the pageant of farewell.

Jane and her friend Norma Travers face a new school year, with classes, friendships, and the small dramas of college life ahead. Bancroft writes in the girls' school-story tradition, warm and detailed about campus routine. Readers get a gentle college novel about growing up among friends, told in the season's turning light.
49709-tales-from-a-famished-land-includi:
Tales from a Famished Land is a book of stories by Edward Eyre Hunt, published in New York in 1918. It includes The White Island, a story of the Dardanelles. Hunt also wrote War Bread. Parts of the book first appeared in Collier's, the Outlook, and the Atlantic Monthly during 1916 and 1917.

Hunt served with relief work in Belgium and France during the First World War. His tales tell of hunger, occupation, and the people caught between armies. The first story is Saint Dympna's Miracle, and others follow refugees and soldiers. The book is dedicated to the memory of a friend, marked only by initials. Its realism comes from the author's own relief service.
49809-junior:
Junior is a science fiction story by Robert Abernathy, taken from Galaxy magazine for January 1956, with art by Weiss. A blurb says all younger generations have been going to the dogs, but this one was genuinely sunk. The joke turns on the sea folk raising of a strayed child.

Pater bellows for Junior, and Mater squeaks the name as a quavering echo. Junior has strayed off again, and if he plays in the shallows with the tide going out, the sentence hangs black. Pater leans upslope, scanning the shoreward reaches where light filters down through the murky water. The sea surface glints like bits of broken mirror. Mater peers toward the reef cliff and the abyss, sobbing that a sea monster ate him. Space tale fans get a sly tale of sea parents.
49877-the-mentor-the-revolution-vol-1-nu:
The Mentor, number 43, treats the Revolution, dated December 8, 1913. Albert Bushnell Hart wrote the number. Hart was professor of government at Harvard University. The issue stands in the series The Story of America in Pictures. Portraits of George the Third and George Washington head the page. Six gravures are listed: Lexington, Bunker Hill, Washington crossing the Delaware, the signing of the Declaration, John Paul Jones in fight, and the birth of the flag. Hart opens with a warning about worn words. Liberty and Revolution, he says, are taken like chocolate creams, without thought of their contents.

No, he insists, the forefathers were not all wise patriots in powdered wigs. A section on the military revolution follows. His painting of Washington, sixteen feet from General Howe, mocks schoolbook history.
49983-the-boy-scouts-on-the-roll-of-hono:
The Boy Scouts on the Roll of Honor is a boys' novel by Scout Master Robert Shaler, printed at New York in 1916. Shaler wrote many books in the series, from Boy Scouts of the Signal Corps to Boy Scouts with the Red Cross. This volume opens with chapters on nut gatherers and a deserted logging camp.

The contents promise a storm, a helping hand, and the duty of a scout. One chapter treats the peril of falling timber, and another puts Gus in the lime-light. Thanksgiving in camp and Sam redeeming himself gloriously come later in the book. Ten of the Sterling Boy Scout Books were sold bound in cloth at the price of this one. The series taught scoutcraft through adventure tales set in camps and woods. Shaler's books were part of the great wave of scouting fiction that followed the founding of the Boy Scouts.
5003-the-rover-boys-in-new-york-or-savin:
Arthur M. Winfield's Rover Boys in New York opens with the brothers planning a sail in the Dartaway, teasing Dick about visiting Dora at Hope Seminary and Tom about his dread of another storm. Sam, Tom, and Dick Rover banter like brothers who have shared many scrapes before.

The New York trip soon turns serious, as the boys work to save their father's honor against charges that threaten the family name. Boating, city adventure, and school loyalty mix in the usual Rover fashion. Readers get a boys' series tale where fun comes first, but family duty gives the adventure its stakes.
50089-the-paper-cap-a-story-of-love-and-:
Amelia Barr, author of An Orkney Maid and Christine, wrote The Paper Cap as a story of love and labor, issued at New York by Appleton in 1918. Stockton Mulford made the frontispiece. A rhyme at the head holds that a king may wear a golden crown, but a paper cap is lighter and sits tighter when the crown tumbles. Barr gave the tale to Samuel Gompers, the worker's friend, as a story of labor's forty years' struggle for the right of suffrage.

Her opening chapter treats the headdress of nations and callings: priests, soldiers, sailors, and traders all bear a covering of the head. The paper cap, the sign of the working man, first shows, she finds, with the agitation around the Reform Bill. The tale that follows weds a love story to the rise of the labor cause.
5054-the-dream-doctor:
Arthur B. Reeve's Dream Doctor follows Professor Craig Kennedy through cases introduced by his friend Jameson, a Star reporter summoned by his managing editor. The editor, sorting letters on his desk, reads one from a Constant Reader asking whether Professor Kennedy is really all the stories claim, and sends Jameson to get the real story.

Cases follow on a coke fiend, a submarine mystery, a wireless detector, ghouls, X-ray movies, and a death house, ending on a final day. Reeve's scientific detective uses new technology as his magnifying glass. Readers get early forensic fiction, where dreams themselves become evidence and the laboratory solves the crime.
5065-civil-government-for-common-schools:
This manual of civil government for common schools argues that textbooks fail pupils by stopping with theory. Students learn the science of government and the guaranty of republican rule. They do not learn how government works in their own town. They do not learn what causes a justice of the peace can try, or how a school district actually works.

To fill that gap, the manual begins with the school district. It proceeds through town, county, and state practice. It joins theory to the art of government as practiced locally. The work is cataloged without an author. Teachers and students get a practical civics book, written to make government visible in the places where pupils actually live.
5073-the-war-terror:
Arthur B. Reeve's War Terror gathers Craig Kennedy cases for a nation at war. Chapters cover an electro-magnetic gun and a murder syndicate. An air pirate, an ultra-violet ray, a triple mirror, and wireless wiretappers follow. A houseboat mystery, a radio detective, a curio shop, and a pillar of death come next. Arrow poison, a radium robber, and a spinthariscope add to the set.

Later cases add an asphyxiating safe, a dead line, a paste replica, a burglar's microphone, a germ letter, and an artificial kidney. Reeve's scientific detective meets wartime invention at every turn. Readers get pulp science detection at its most inventive, where each new device becomes both weapon and clue.
50744-a-british-rifle-man-the-journals-a:
George Simmons, a major in the Rifle Brigade, left journals and letters from the Peninsular War and the Waterloo campaign. Verner, a late officer of the same brigade, edited the papers and wrote the opening. Black of London issued the book in 1899, with three maps.

Simmons wrote home to his parents from Hythe and Dover in May 1809, then from camp after camp in Portugal and Spain. Year by year the record runs through the fights of 1809 to 1814 and the last great fight. The book is given to the Duke of Connaught, chief of the brigade, once called the 95th Rifles.
50889-half-past-alligator:
Donald Colvin published his story Half Past Alligator in Galaxy Science Fiction in September 1953, with pictures by Barth. A headnote jokes that sportsmanship makes a ball team, while foul play gets a backward race civilized. Bill Bradley manages a baseball game on a new planet among the Quxas.

Flat, piebald Quxas surge over the first-base line and squat around the third baseman. A half-tamed thrag breaks loose and canters across the outfield on five legs. Ray Bush steals second unnoticed, and Gust Mustas makes a shoestring catch over a hole some Quxa dug. After fourteen months of exploring, Bill loves the game, until Candace Mathews walks among the pneuma-huts and gloom returns.
50969-big-ancestor:
Wallace wrote a space tale that ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1954, with pictures by Emsh. Man's family tree was awesome enough to give every galactic race an inferiority complex, but then he tried to climb it, the blurb warns. In repose, Taphetta the Ribboneer resembled a fancy giant bow on a package. His four flat legs looped out and in under his wide thin body.

Only his head had appreciable thickness, crowned with a dozen long ribbons. Yes, I've heard the legend, Taphetta rattles to Sam Halden, a biologist. It's more than a legend, Halden answers. At least a hundred kinds of humans, each raised in strict seclusion on scattered planets, can yet interbreed with a minimum of trouble. Emmer the Neanderthal type stands near the scale's beginning. Deep roots call the races home.
51028-the-protector:
Protector is a science fiction story by Betsy Curtis, from Galaxy Science Fiction of February 1951. Stone illustrated the tale for the magazine in that issue. A blurb at its head says there is a fortune in a boxer who feels no pain in the story. This one did not feel it, except in odd ways, the blurb adds.

How come I live here on Gorlin permanent, the narrator begins in his own voice. Nobody is real surprised, he says, when a scientist writes that the primitive tribes of Anestha are dying out. The Anesthon natives are freaks anyway in the common view of his world. If your body does not feel any pain at any time, he argues, you need a nursemaid around you. Curtis builds her story on that one gift and curse: the painless man, prize fighter and ward at once.
51086-raymond-or-life-and-death-with-exa:
Sir Oliver J. Lodge wrote a book about his son Raymond, who died in war. The book came out in New York in 1916. Its full title claims proof that love and memory live past death. Lodge was a noted man of science in Britain. He gave the book to Raymond's mother and kin, with thanks for use of home notes.

Part one holds a life sketch and letters from the front. Part two gives talks said to come from Raymond through a medium. Lodge prints talks with Mrs. Leonard and a group photo case. Readers can judge the claims from the notes he shows.
51121-spoken-for:
William Morrison wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy in July 1955, with drawings by Emsh. A headnote says he was lost, as anyone could see, but she had no idea how entirely lost he was, nor why. Half of Jupiter's great disk and most of the other moons were below the horizon when the man stepped out of the plane and changed Carol Marsh's life. He was ordinary enough in appearance, and she was not ordinarily drawn to ordinary men.

It took him almost a minute to get his bearings and see her at all, and the troubled look in his eyes she held against him. A man should be confident and self-assured, she held, as John Burr back on Earth had been. Startlingly, it was with this newcomer, whose appearance she had every reason to dislike, that she fell suddenly and completely in love.
51148-common-denominator:
John MacDonald wrote this space tale for Galaxy, where it ran in July 1951, with plates by Don Hunter. Its head note flips the usual tale: high races love to share their lore with raw ones, and here the raw ones are Earthmen.

Scout Group Forty flicks back across half the Galaxy with a full study. Their find is a Class Seven culture on three planets of Argus Ten, rare and full of risk. The Bureau of Stellar Defense clamps a tight quarantine on the crew for thirty days. Film spools by the thousand go under the lens. Word leaks out, and doom-criers fill the news screens of Sol's three home planets.
5118-the-american-senator:
Anthony Trollope's novel, first serialised in 1876 and published in book form in 1877, brings an American senator to the English village of Dillsborough. His blunt questions about English customs, law, and land stir up the local families, especially the Mortons and the Masters, and expose the habits of a small rural community.

Around the visitor's tour, Trollope weaves courtship, family pride, and a dispute over poaching and property. The book works as both a comedy of manners and a comparison of two nations, with the senator's outsider eye sharpening every clash between old English ways and new American plain speaking.
51445-sordman-the-protector:
Tom Purdom wrote Sordman the Protector, a science fiction story printed in Galaxy Magazine in August 1960. Sordman is one of only four truly developed psionic adepts in the world. With drugs and preparation he can command the whole range of psi powers; without them, he still reads the feelings of people near him.

The magazine's blurb calls him the most powerful man in the world, yet the slave of a mad criminal's mind. The story opens in a beer hall on the eighty-first floor of the Hotel Mark Twain, where fourteen men hold a girl prisoner. Sordman insists on going up alone. Lee Shawn, a lawyer and lobbyist who fights laws against Talent, warns that fear will get him killed. Purdom builds the tale on power that cannot free its owner.
51658-how-to-become-an-actor:
How to Become an Actor was written by a prominent stage manager and printed in New York in 1900. The title page promises complete instructions on the duties of the stage manager, prompter, scenic artist, and property man. It tells how to make out a scene plot and a property plot. It also tells how to make up for the various characters seen on the stage. The introduction says the author has tried to show the mystic art of stage performance as clearly as possible.

His aim, he writes, is to enable the greenest amateur to erect a stage in his own drawing-room. The one cry has been how to get up a home performance properly, and with as little expense as possible. The first section treats the stage and effects, down to a curtain rigged from a sheet and rings.
51687-the-spy-in-the-elevator:
The Spy in the Elevator, by Donald E. Westlake, is a science fiction story. It first ran in Galaxy Magazine in October 1961, the note says. A narrator endures a day of small disasters, from egg to zipper. The stuck elevator caps it all on the worst day of all.

He means to propose to Linda that day, and time presses hard. Linda works as an ore sled dispatcher, where craft run on the dot. Robots that miss their hour are presumed captured and blown up in space. Her fixation on punctual time shapes every date they have ever had. Five minutes late once cost him four days of silence from her.
51699-the-god-next-door:
The God Next Door is a science fiction story by Bill Doede, printed in Galaxy Magazine in August 1961. Its headnote introduces the sand-thing: powerful, lonely and strange. No doubt it was a god, the note adds, but who wasn't?

Stinson lies still in the sand where he fell, gloating over the success of his arrival. Behind his ear, under a pencil-line scar, a buried cylinder holds the power that flung him from Earth to this fourth planet of the Centaurian system. He can almost feel the warm Missouri air, though he is light years from Missouri. A funnel-shaped cloud of dust stands off to his left. It spins on its axis and whines like a high-speed motor, though little wind moves his hair. The valley floor stretches between two mountain ranges, and the cloud does not behave like weather.
51758-from-an-unseen-censor:
From an Unseen Censor, by Rosel George Brown, ran in Galaxy Magazine in September 1958. The tale is told by a man whose Uncle Isadore was quick in life and, he jokes, is still quick though dead. Isadore had dared him to beat him, and the narrator took the bet.

The search leads to a crashed ship on Alvarla, a dull world of rock, dust, and dun heather. The craft sits tilted in a hollow, its blast pits fused into the stone. Dust films the hull, and the port seam can scarce be seen. Rene, the guide, says the ship has not been opened for months or years. He is sure no man could live sealed inside without air and water.
51782-doctor:
Murray Leinster wrote Doctor, a tale first printed in Galaxy Magazine in February 1961, with pictures by Finlay. Leinster opens wide, with suns, planets, cities, and spaceports spread through the cosmos. People build ships, remake planets, and fear nothing in that vast scene. Then, on one small planet, a single molecule changes itself.

The new molecule can copy itself, and men name the virus chlorophage. Leinster calls it the most terrifying thing in the universe to mankind. The scene then shifts to the Star Queen, in orbit round the planet Altaira. Lift-ships bring up many women and children, red-eyed from crying. A modern liner on the Regulus-to-Cassim run thus meets a plague tale.
51898-beauchamp-or-the-error:
James wrote this novel, Beauchamp, or The Error, in the Tauchnitz edition printed at Leipzig in 1846. The volume is number 107 in the Collection of British Authors. A list of James's other tales stands at the front, among them Morley Ernstein, Forest Days, The False Heir, and Agincourt. Chapter One is called The Attack and the Rescue.

The narrator refuses to say in which King George's reign the tale sits. Kings, he muses, fight and covet, hope and fear, and pass away, leaving a stone and a few dry lines. History, to him, reads like the pages of a dream-book. He jokes that the curl of a wig or the fashion of a sleeve-button would trip him up with the antiquaries.
52097-andy-gordon-or-the-fortunes-of-a-y:
Alger wrote this boys' novel for Hurst and Company at New York, in his series sold at thirty-five cents a volume post-paid. The Hamilton Academy stands on an eminence in the town of Hamilton, under Doctor Euclid, strict in his requirements and slow to accept excuses. Herbert Ross comes up the hill swinging a cane, a schoolboy with a high opinion of himself, hoping to cram his Virgil before the doctor arrives.

In the schoolroom he meets a cloud of dust. The boy with the broom is Andrew Gordon, called Andy, the janitor and the hero of the book. Alger's machinery is all here: the poor boy working his way, the rich boy's conceit, the lesson prepared too late. Andy Gordon belongs to the shelf with Strive and Succeed and Do and Dare: the Alger gospel that industry and honesty are a boy's real fortune.
52395-journal-of-my-journey-over-the-mou:
George Washington kept the Journal of My Journey Over the Mountains while he surveyed for Lord Thomas Fairfax. The work dates to seventeen hundred forty seven and forty eight. J M Toner edited the text with notes for an Albany press in eighteen hundred ninety two. The copy claims word for word care from the source.

Young Washington crossed the Blue Ridge in Virginia’s Northern Neck. Fairfax, Baron of Cameron, held the vast tract in claim. Plans traced from the source show Mount Vernon farms and fields. One plan marks a survey plot nicknamed Hell Hole. River front views at Hunting Creek join the set. The day book gives a teen surveyor at work in wild land that would soon fill with farms.
52398-silver-queen-the-fabulous-story-of:
Caroline Bancroft wrote Silver Queen, the story of Baby Doe Tabor, first printed at Boulder in 1950. Bancroft was a third generation Coloradan who wrote history for the Denver Post. Her family had deep roots in Colorado mining and lore.

The book tells the famed tale of Baby Doe and the Tabor silver wealth of Colorado. Bancroft drew on long study of western history and on her thesis work on Central City. Portraits and press images support the text. Readers get a vivid life story set in the boom and fall of a mining age in the West.
52610-ward-hill-the-senior:
Everett Tomlinson wrote a school tale, with rights held from 1897 and this printing issued at Cleveland in 1928. Ward Hill and his friends live at the Weston school. Tomlinson calls a school a small world of its own, with trials and wins as real as those outside.

He says the boys are real boys and the facts took place much as he tells them. Wins should spur young readers on, and fails should warn them off bad paths. The preface, signed at Elizabeth in New Jersey, holds that youth is seed time. What a boy sows then, and how much, shapes the crop he reaps as a man.
52902-a-naval-expositor:
Thomas Riley Blanckley wrote A Naval Expositor, printed at London in seventeen fifty. The book explains the words and terms of art used in building and fitting a ship for sea. The Lords of the Admiralty backed the work, and Blanckley gave it to them.

Entries cover the parts of a ship, their traits, and their sizes. They also list all goods taken into the stores, and what each is used for. A second part names the lesser officers of a ship and sums up their duties. Paul Fourdrinier cut the plates. Sea officers and builders were the audience.
5317-through-the-magic-door:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Through the Magic Door invites readers to shut the door of their room, leave the cares of the outer world behind. Readers plunge into the company of the great dead. However humble the bookshelf, Doyle says, its noble, silent comrades wait in ranks. Choosing a man from their files carries the reader through a magic portal.

The book's twelve chapters are essays on books and authors, written by the creator of Sherlock Holmes as a lover of reading. Readers will find a warm, personal guide to literature, in which Doyle shares his enthusiasms. It argues that books offer a fair land where worry cannot follow.
53256-the-room-with-the-little-door: The Room with the Little Door opens with an illustration of a prison door with bars, drawn around the book's title. The transcriber's note explains that the small floral decoration in most page headers survives in the electronic editions. Everything visible here is the door itself: the frame, the bars, and the little opening of the name. The book behind it is a prison novel, and its frontispiece does the work of a first chapter.
5332-the-love-sonnets-of-a-car-conductor:
Wallace Irwin's Love Sonnets of a Car Conductor parodies the sonnet in streetcar slang. It carries a harmless and instructive introduction by the fictional Professor Wolfgang Copernicus Addleburger of the University of Monte Carlo. Irwin, author of The Love Sonnets of a Hoodlum, gives his conductor a muse and a route, and lets him sing of love in the language of the car.

The introduction, by a scientist who reaches the transcendental by winding paths, sets the joke in motion. Readers get a light, comic volume of dialect verse, in which high poetic form meets low city life, and both come out laughing.
5333-every-man-in-his-humor:
Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humor, in its Anglicized edition, is the comedy that first made Jonson's name. The introduction presents Jonson as the greatest English dramatist after Shakespeare, a commanding figure and poet laureate whose strong personality shaped the course of English letters.

Jonson, grandson of a man from Annandale by the Solway, sets his comedy in London, where each character is ruled by a humour, a ruling passion or folly. Readers will find a lively, satiric portrait of Elizabethan city life, with young gallants, merchants, and soldiers, all acting exactly in their humour.
53407-dave-porter-s-return-to-school-or-:
Dave Porter's Return to School, or Winning the Medal of Honor, is a boys' school story by Edward Stratemeyer. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston published it in March 1907. Charles Nuttall drew the illustrations. It belongs to the Dave Porter series, whose earlier volumes stand listed.

The contents bring Dave back to Oak Hall after adventures abroad. A mystery opens almost as soon as he reaches the dormitory. The rivals of Oak Hall and a great football game fill the middle chapters. A kite, a widow's house, and work done in the dark add incident. Dave is carried off by enemies before the tale turns toward its climax. A cavern in the woods and an ice-boat race crowd the closing stretch. Dave's heroism and a confession clear the way to the medal of the title.
53892-an-ideal-kitchen-miss-parloa-s-kit:
Maria Parloa wrote a kitchen companion for all who would be good housekeepers. Estes and Lauriat issued the twentieth form at Boston, with rights from 1887. Parloa founded the first cooking school in Boston and led one in New York. An Ideal Kitchen opens the work with a plea for thought.

Builders lavish care on halls and parlors yet slight the kitchen, she writes. A little extra thought, not just money, would fix most flaws. Her New Cook Book held 1,724 receipts and drew wide praise. Home keepers gain a full, practical guide from a pioneer teacher of cooking.
54045-the-economical-jewish-cook-a-moder:
May Henry and Edith B Cohen arranged The Economical Jewish Cook, a strict recipe book for tight purses. Wertheimer, Lea and Company issued this third edition in London in eighteen hundred ninety seven. Boards bound copies sold at one shilling and sixpence. Both women held state cookery school papers for their craft.

Rich Jewish cook books took costly goods for granted, they say. Young house keepers felt the want of a cheap strict guide. Three aims shape the book from its first page on. Dishes must fit the dietary laws of the faith in full. Dishes must suit new wives at their first home stove. Dishes must serve the cookery classes now spread in town. Old high class treats slip in past their own strict rule. Passover and sick room cookery earn their own kind parts.
54124-war-the-creator:
War the Creator is a war story by Gelett Burgess, first printed in Collier's weekly. Huebsch published it in book form in New York in nineteen sixteen. Its hero is Georges Cucurou, called Coco, a shoemaker's son of Toulouse. The narrator knew him just before the war and met him again wounded.

Two months in the furnace of the fighting turned the boy into a man. The tale covers only the first six weeks of the war in France. It follows the bitter retreat from Belgium and the rally on the Marne. Georges was wounded as the pursuit began and sent home to hospital. There the narrator rebuilt his story from talks, a notebook, and letters. War, once seen as mere waste, shows here as a maker of men.
54168-english-lands-letters-and-kings-vo:
English Lands, Letters and Kings is a survey of English life and letters by Donald G. Mitchell. Volume 1, From Celt to Tudor, is the first of four volumes. The rest run From Elizabeth to Anne, Queen Anne and the Georges, and The Later Georges to Victoria. Each volume sold at a dollar fifty in cloth with gilt top, as the front pages state.

A note states that Gutenberg holds the other three volumes of the work, with their ebook numbers. A kindred book, American Lands and Letters, runs from the Mayflower to Rip Van Winkle. The images of the first pages can be seen through the Internet Archive, the note adds. The volume at hand opens the long march of English lands and letters, from the first Celts to the Tudor age.
54304-urith-a-tale-of-dartmoor:
Baring-Gould's Urith: A Tale of Dartmoor was published by Methuen at London in 1891. Baring-Gould had written Mehalah and Arminell before it. The first chapter, Devil Tor, sets the scene in the heart of the moor. Near two thousand feet above the sea stands a rude granite monolith, fourteen feet high, without a trace of any tool. A bow-shot off rises the hump called Devil Tor, whose topmost slab the stone seems to have been.

Local belief made the stone the Devil himself, erect in his eyrie, with the tor as his throne. He sits there only on Midsummer Eve, when bale-fires flame on every hill in his honour. The peat around has grown undisturbed since hoar antiquity; no shepherd, fisherman, or turf-cutter reaches the place. The tale unfolds against this desolate interior.
54409-new-england-joke-lore-the-tonic-of:
Arthur Crandall gathered New England joke lore as the tonic of Yankee humor, printed in Philadelphia in 1922. Crandall had written Optimistic Medicine. He gives the book to stalwart sons of New England whose straight thinking, unruffled poise, and never failing humor let them lead in the development of the country, he says. A rocky spring in Yankee land fronts the book.

Chapter one shows general characteristics, with the schoolmaster and his snow grave, drifted roads and right of way, post holes in the ice, and the man who took comfort at funerals. Conjugal infelicities, a confiding husband, and Dave leaving home fill chapter two. Dry, shrewd tales of farmers, butchers, and philanthropists preserve a regional voice.
54631-100-desert-wildflowers-in-natural-:
100 Desert Wildflowers in Natural Color holds photos and text by Natt N Dodge, put out by the Southwestern Monuments Association with a copyright of 1963. The front pages teach the ground first: what a desert is, why and when it blooms, and how to name what you find. A short guide to flower photos starts the set. Then the hundred run in order, each with its plate in true hue. Longleaf ephedra and common reed lead off.

Yuccas crowd the front: soaptree, Joshua-tree, Torrey, and giant, with agaves and sotol near. Poppies, lupines, and mesquite trees fill the mid run. The cactus clan closes strong: night-blooming cereus, saguaro, organpipe, three kinds of cholla, and the barrel. Wild plant fans get a bright field key to the dry lands in bloom.
54987-seth-s-brother-s-wife-a-study-of-l:
Harold Frederic wrote Seth's Brother's Wife, a study of life in the Greater New York, issued in New York in 1887. The tale opens on Lemuel Fairchild's farm, late in May, with a death in the house. Hired girl Alvira kneads pie crust and warns of a flare-up soon. Hired man Milton Squires peels apples on the step and shrugs her off.

Frederic lingers on the mean barns, lean cows, black mire, and broken gate in the sunset light. Nothing in the view is fair, and Milton is the least fair part of it. That harsh farm scene sets the tone for a close study of kin, pride, and want. The book was one of Frederic's early works of plain rural life.
55049-the-poems-of-madison-cawein-volume:
Volume One of The Poems of Madison Cawein is subtitled Lyrics and Old World Idylls. It was printed at Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with an introduction by Edmund Gosse. Photogravures after paintings by Eric Pape illustrate the volume. Cawein inscribed it to William Dean Howells, who first recognized and encouraged his endeavors.

The first part, Blooms of the Berry, holds short nature lyrics: Hepaticas, In Middle Spring, The Wood God, Pan, The Dryad and A Spring Shower. The second part, In the Gardens of Falerina, turns to old world tales in verse. Its pieces include The Gardens of Falerina itself, Blodeuwedd, A Guinevere, The Alcalde's Daughter, and Amadis at Miraflores. Cawein of Louisville, Kentucky, was famed as a nature poet. This opening volume of his collected poems shows both sides of his gift: the Kentucky woods and the romance of old Europe.
55690-william-hamilton-gibson-artist-nat:
John Coleman Adams wrote a life of William Hamilton Gibson, artist, naturalist, and author, published in 1901 and fully illustrated. A frontispiece shows Gibson, and another picture shows him at age forty one. A note explains that Gibson always wrote his signature without lifting the pen. Adams had written Nature Studies in Berkshire.

Adams ranks Gibson with Thoreau and John Burroughs as men who taught their generation to love nature. Thoreau, he says, challenged that generation to come out of doors and live in a shanty. Gibson worked as both artist and writer of nature. The book traces his life and work for readers who knew his drawings and books.
55728-hellenism-in-asia-minor:
Karl Dieterich of the University of Leipzig surveys the Greek stamp on Asia Minor in a study turned into English by Carroll N Brown. Oxford University Press issued it at New York in 1918. The American-Hellenic Society sponsored the printing.

His first pages call Asia Minor the land of Hellenic civilization at its height. Its cut-up coast held a chaplet of Greek democracies. They pushed inland and set their stamp on Persia itself. They formed the first rampart of the civilized world against Persian power. Salamis and Plataea ended that long struggle. A second part sums up Hellenic Pontus by D H Oeconomides. The survey argues that Christianity first sprouted in this Greek soil. Chrysostom and Basil were born or taught there.
56444-the-status-of-the-jews-in-egypt-th:
Flinders Petrie delivered The Status of the Jews in Egypt before the Jewish Historical Society at University College on April 30, 1922. The address is the fifth Arthur Davis Memorial Lecture. Petrie was Edwards Professor of Egyptology at University College. Philip Sassoon wrote a foreword. A plate shows a fragment of an ancient Hebrew papyrus, called the oldest in the world, found by Petrie himself; its rendering stands in an appendix.

Pages at the front place the lecture in its line. The first Arthur Davis lecture, Chosen Peoples, was by Israel Zangwill, whose works are also listed there. Other lectures in the line treat what the world owes to the Pharisees, poetry and religion, and Spinoza and time. Their speakers include Herford, Israel Abrahams, and Alexander, with forewords by Monash, Quiller-Couch, and Haldane. The lecture treats the Jews of ancient Egypt.
57021-the-christiana-riot-and-the-treaso:
The Christiana Riot and the Treason Trials of 1851 is a historical sketch by Hensel. It was prepared for a commemoration of those events in September 1911. The New Era Printing Company of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, issued it that year. A frontispiece shows three of the accused men after the trials.

Hensel writes in his preface of a lifelong tie to the subject. He was born near the ground where the events of 1851 took place. For over fifty years he had lived among their associations and memories. Law and liberty met there in a conflict that seemed beyond settling. Only the Civil War, he says, settled that quarrel at last. He offers the sketch to the Lancaster County Historical Society. His aim is to write without favour to either side.
57362-captain-lucy-in-the-home-sector:
Aline Havard wrote this sequel for the Penn Publishing Company at Philadelphia in 1921, with illustrations by Coleman. Larry Eaton calls the occupation of Germany the Home Sector, a little irony beneath his cheerfulness, as the Stars and Stripes rise over headquarters at Coblenz. Lucy Gordon, whose father is stationed there, walks the banks of the Rhine with him in the pale December sunlight. She wanted to sail home when the armistice was signed.

Her brother Bob is scouting over the Bolshevik lines in the frozen north, and Larry envies him. The contents carry the young people from the Rhine to the Dwina, into Germany, and through the mystery of the forest. A letter to Franz and a flight across the Channel close the book. The Captain Lucy books followed an American girl through the war and its strange peace, when home was the one posting nobody could order.
57546-e-mile-zola-novelist-and-reformer-:
Emile Zola, Novelist and Reformer, by Ernest Alfred Vizetelly, was published in London and New York in 1904. Portraits, views, and facsimile letters fill the plates. Vizetelly dates his preface from Merton, Surrey, in March 1904. Contents run in fifteen chapters from Zola's birth to his death. Early chapters treat his family, his first years, and bohemian drudgery in Paris. The Rougon-Macquart novels get a long central run.

Naturalism's advance and its battles fill the middle chapters. The Dreyfus case takes a full chapter near the end. An appendix prints the records of Zola's birth and death. Notes on English versions of his novels are added. The book is both a life and a defence of a contested writer.
57813-how-to-master-the-spoken-word-desi:
Edwin Gordon Lawrence wrote a self instructor for mastering the spoken word, printed at Chicago in 1913. Lawrence had written The Power of Speech, Speech Making, and The Lawrence Reader and Speaker. The book is given to William Edwin Hall in thanks and love. Faith cometh by hearing, Paul says at the front, and Shakespeare warns to mend your speech a little lest it mar your fortunes.

The power of utterance should enter every plan of self culture, Channing adds. How did other men become public speakers, Lawrence asks, since a study of their means is the apt answer. Voice, breath, gesture, and nerve are trained by set lessons. Ambitious clerks, preachers, and salesmen of the age bought such guides to rise by the tongue.
57961-mexican-copper-tools-the-use-of-co:
Mexican Copper Tools, by Philipp Valentini, was translated from the German by Stephen Salisbury and printed at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1880. The papers come from the proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society, in April and October 1879. Two studies make up the volume.

The first treats the use of copper by the Mexicans before the conquest. Pictures show copper axes in the arms of Tepoztla and other places. The second study treats the katunes of Maya history, a chapter in the early history of Central America. It gives special reference to the Pio Perez manuscript. Contents include tables of the twenty days of the Maya month, the eighteen months of the Maya year, and a translation of the manuscript by Perez himself. Readers get early American archaeology on metal and calendar together.
58266-war-what-for:
War What For, by George Kirkpatrick, is an anti war book for working readers. Kirkpatrick issued it himself at West La Fayette, Ohio, in nineteen ten. Five editions ran within a year, to the thirtieth thousand by May nineteen eleven. Lines from Hugo, Shakespeare, and a proverb front the book as warnings.

Kirkpatrick gives the book to the victims of the civil war in industry. By that he means his brothers and sisters of the working class. They furnish the blood, tears, cripples, and corpses in all wars, he says. Yet they win nothing from the wars they are made to fight in. A front picture calls wage freedom industrial despotism in disguise.
58604-the-olivia-letters-being-some-hist:
Emily Edson Briggs, writing as the newspaper correspondent Olivia, gathered letters that tell the history of Washington City across forty years. The book came out in 1906. Briggs writes as an insider who watched presidents, senators, and society at close range over a long career.

The letters cover a soldier's burial, Lincoln's birthday, and Senate scenes during the impeachment trial of President Johnson. Others treat Grant at his inaugural, the home life of the Grant family, and levees at the White House. Suffrage gets strong attention, with pieces on Elizabeth Cady Stanton and gatherings of the cause. Readers get politics, gossip, and reform all mixed in one lively Washington record. The letters show how power and society worked in the capital after the Civil War.
58721-unwelcomed-visitor:
William Morrison's story, printed in Worlds of If in October 1954, turns first contact upside down. Xhanph, the fully accredited ambassador from Gfun, is Earth's first visitor from outer space. All the way over he has dreamed of the reception: crowds, cheers, and the great men of Earth crowding to touch tentacles with him. He lands his ship with care in the middle of a large square, climbs out, and finds that no one is paying any attention to him at all.

People go about their business as if he were not there. Even a small dog sniffs at him without interest and trots off to more important business. Morrison's joke is gentle and pointed: Earth people are funny people, and the ambassador's hurt dignity carries a satire on our manners.
58952-the-red-chancellor:
Sir William Magnay's The Red Chancellor was published by Ward, Lock of London, Melbourne, and Toronto. Magnay had written The Man of the Hour and Rogues in Arcady before it. The frontispiece shows a plea from chapter eighteen: you may be my friend in this place where I have no friends.

Chapter one seats the reader in Duke Johann's chapel, where three men weigh a dangerous game. Von Orsova, a handsome captain of cavalry and master of the horse, has coupled his name with a lady's, and to couple their names is high treason. Von Lindheim gives the warning with a shrug and a lowered voice. The contents run on through a capsized boat, a duel, a stone sarcophagus, and a midnight burial.
59067-dancing-without-an-instructor:
Professor Wilkinson wrote this guide to dancing without a teacher, sold postpaid for fifty cents. It stands in a line of plain, cheap books of useful lore. Mate volumes in the line treat dreams, manners, fortune telling, and the lover's path.

The line calls itself popular information at a popular price, bound alike in size, style, and cost. Card tricks, coin tricks, and the key to hypnotism share the shelf. A book on how to be beautiful and a guide to letter writing serve other needs. Wilkinson's own task is the ballroom: steps and figures set out plainly, so that a shy beginner could learn at home with no master.
59211-the-marriage-of-elinor:
Mrs Oliphant wrote this novel in two volumes, issued as number 95 of The English Library by Heinemann and Balestier of Leipzig in 1892. Oliphant had written Kirsteen, Within the Precincts, and At His Gates. John Tatham, a barrister, sits at breakfast one summer morning when a letter comes in a fine, pointed lady's hand.

The writer asks if he has heard from Elinor of her new prospects and intentions, and whether he knows anything of the man. Elinor is hard to convince against her will, and the writer owns her own want of the power to persuade. Those mild words, Tatham sees at once, carry facts more surely than a full statement. He pauses and lays the letter down with a start.
59408-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Ralph Connor, with tables of contents for each volume. Thirteen works are listed at the front. Corporal Cameron, A Tale of the Macleod Trail, leads the set. The Doctor, A Tale of the Rockies, and Glengarry Schooldays follow. Black Rock and The Sky Pilot sit in the middle.

Chapter lists for each book fill the index. Corporal Cameron splits into three books of chapters. Heads name The Quitter, The Glen of the Cup of Gold, and A Question of Honour early. The Stonies, Sergeant Crisp, and Nurse Haley mark the late books. To Him That Hath, The Man from Glengarry, and The Foreigner close the main list. Michael McGrath, Postmaster and Beyond the Marshes are short addenda. The index serves readers who move through Connor's western tales in digital form.
59426-young-sioux-warrior:
Francis Lynde Kroll wrote Young Sioux Warrior, held in 1952 by Lantern Press and issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Charles H Geer drew the pictures. Kroll gives the book to L L C for firm, kind guidance of a young warrior long ago. Eleven chapters carry the tale of Little Bear.

Little Bear sits at the back of the great wigwam in Chapter One. Warriors form a circle round the council fire before him. He longs to speak in the long debate but does not dare. Big Buffalo urges a return to the main Sioux camp. Pawnees have driven the buffalo from the hunting grounds, he warns. Next they will attack this small party, he says. Flying Arrow leaps up and roars to drive the Pawnees out. Prints show a falls, a shelter, and a fat cow picked for food.
59674-homes-of-the-london-poor:
Homes of the London Poor is a housing pamphlet by Octavia Hill, reprinted in New York in 1875. The State Charities Aid Association sold the reprint at twenty five cents a copy. Hill articles had run in the Fortnightly Review and in Macmillan Magazine in London. A preface warns her system may not fit America in all its details.

Conditions of poverty and municipal government differ widely between the countries, it says. But the broad truths of humanity are the same everywhere, the preface argues. Helping the poor toward self support is the principle under all her efforts. Housing reform history counts Hill lady rent collectors as a founding model.
59766-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Bayard Taylor gathers his books tables. David Widger compiled the index for readers of the digital set. Beauty and the Beast, The Story of Kennett, and Lands of the Saracen lead. His Faust translation in English verse stands among the works listed here.

Northern Travel, a History of Germany, and Travels in Arabia follow in order. Joseph and His Friend closes the main list of Taylor volumes shown. Full chapter lists for each book let readers find parts fast in need. Kennett chase and will chapters show the shape of that novel. Saracen chapters open with life in a Syrian quarantine station scene.
59929-the-youth-of-the-great-elector:
The Youth of the Great Elector retells the early life of Frederick William of Brandenburg for young readers. George Upton translated it from the German of Ferdinand Schmidt, and McClurg printed it at Chicago in 1909, in the series Life Stories for Young People, with three illustrations.

In his preface, Upton says the story runs from the prince's birth to his accession on his father's death. Its scenes lie in the Thirty Years' War, still raging when Frederick William became Elector. The cast is famous: Gustavus Adolphus, Wallenstein, Tilly, and the Swedish chancellor Oxenstjern. Chapters move from the Elector's castle to a stag hunt, the Restitutions Edict, Holland, and the prince's flight.
60342-old-buildings-of-new-york-with-som:
Old buildings of New York City, with notes on their origin and occupants, fills a volume printed at New York in 1907. Number Seven State Street opens the subjects, then Fraunces's Tavern and the sub treasury. The Bank of New York, Saint Paul's Chapel, and City Hall follow. The Astor Library, the Langdon House, and Saint Mark's Church come next.

The Rutherfurd House, the Keteltas House, and the homes of Eugene Delano, James Lenox, and Robert Minturn fill the roll. Grace Church, the Society Library, the Cruger House, Abingdon Square, and Gramercy Square lead on. The Players, former home of Edwin Booth, and the homes of Samuel Tilden, Stanford White, and Cyrus Field close it. A writer lately stated that no one was ever born in New York, the text notes with a smile. The old city stands house by house here.
60553-the-criticism-of-the-fourth-gospel:
William Sanday, an Oxford church scholar, gave eight talks on the study of the Fourth Gospel at a New York seminary in October and November 1904. Scribner printed the talks in 1905 in a set of seminary lectures. Sanday gives the book to his American friends, who had called him across the sea.

Talk one surveys fresh books on the gospel, with the state of views in November 1903 as its start. Sanday says views had then swung farther from truth than at any time he could recall. Later talks treat methods, the writers stance, the tale form, the teaching on the Logos, and the gospels early history.
60585-the-life-travels-and-literary-care:
Russell Conwell wrote this life, The Life, Travels, and Literary Career of Bayard Taylor, printed at Boston in 1879 and sold in many cities. Conwell also wrote lives of President Hayes and histories of great fires. A poem about crowning the poet heads the title page, and a dedication in verse, drawn from Taylor's own journal, follows.

The preface calls the work a solemn yet pleasant duty. Taylor's death was still fresh, Conwell says, and tears still flowed. Yet no textbook of morals or history teaches the young so well, he argues, as the record of a virtuous, industrious, heroic life. Fables and fiction have their power, but the direct appeal of a noble life closed with honour beats them both.
60719-the-lonely-warrior:
Claude Washburn's 1922 novel opens on November 5th, 1914, with Edward Carroll sitting in his midwestern office, staring at the calendar instead of doing business. Carroll is vice-president of a cement works, a bank director, and the power behind copper mines.

A young man named Stacey is shown in, twenty-six or seven, handsome and restless with happy eagerness. Carroll has sent for him first, ahead of waiting callers, and the two gaze at each other across the desk. Harcourt, Brace and Company held the copyright, and the Burt Company issued this edition at New York. Stacey carries himself with the ease of good breeding and good schooling.
60963-the-impersonator:
Robert Wicks wrote a tale for Worlds of If in November 1960 about a man who wakes knowing he is not one. He opens his eyes on a laboratory. Two men in white coats bend over the table where he lies, and test him like a machine.

Clench your fingers, says one; blink your eyes. The tall man asks his name. Something deep inside trips, and the answers come. He is Paul Chandler, a worker in the science of ice. The World Council has set him to head Project Ice Thaw, a plan of weather control against a coming ice age. If it fails, the word is catastrophe. The tall man asks what manner of creature he is. A man, he says at last, and knows it is a lie.
60979-reminiscences-of-a-stock-operator:
Reminiscences of a Stock Operator is a trade tale by Edwin Lefevre. A Doran house holds its first right claim of nineteen twenty three. Lefevre gives the book to Jesse Livermore, the great hand of that game. A new front word by Benton Davis stands in this late print form. The tale voice went to work straight from gram school in part one.

He took a post as quote board boy in a stock trade house then. Quick at sums, he did three years of school math in one year there. Prices were mere counts to him, not coin per share, in those days. Why they changed he did not know or care in that first stage. Their shifts were his whole theme five hours a day in that room.
6108-boy-scouts-in-a-submarine-or-search:
G. Harvey Ralphson sends the Boy Scouts into a submarine to search an ocean floor, opening in the handsome, noisy clubroom of the Black Bear Patrol in New York, ablaze with light. The Sea Lion proves equal to her task, and through the night a chase goes on.

Chapters promise a dandy submarine, a wolf on the trail, two wolves in a pen, night on an ocean floor, the secret of the hold, and guard duty under the sea. Jimmie goes hunting, Jack makes a discovery, and a desperate prisoner and a bluff that didn't work follow. Ralphson mixes scout pluck with undersea adventure.
61128-seven-day-terror:
Lafferty wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of If in March 1962. Nine-year-old Clarence Willoughby has built a disappearer. Cut both ends out of a beer can, fit two pieces of red cardboard with peepholes in the ends, look through, and blink, and whatever you look at disappears.

His mother Myra admires his foresight when he refuses to try it on a sink of dishes, since dishes cost money and he does not know if things come back. She sends him to try it on Blanche Manners' cat instead, and the cat vanishes from the sidewalk. At the Plugged Nickel bar, Nokomis suggests his own paunch, then the fire plug outside. Its disappearance floods the streets, children play in the water, and fire engines stand apparatus-deep while Officer Comstock counts seven possible explanations. Clarence and Nokomis agree to tell nobody.
61257-world-in-a-mirror:
World in a Mirror, a story by Albert Teichner, appeared in Worlds of If Science Fiction for September 1962. Its headnote warns of a backward world, backward in a special and deadly manner. The narrator is the science chronicler of an interstellar expedition, and he did not want Hacker in the delegation from the start.

Hacker, a smart alecky kid of fifty whose great great uncle is president of the World Council, had caused a disaster. On the planet Rayna he took a bulldozer beyond the craft Terra One and flattened a hilltop. It proved to be an incubation bed for Raynan fledglings, and the eggs and five adult females were killed. The expedition fled. Now, landing among the Newtaneans, Captain Weber insists Hacker come along as chauffeur. The narrator and Barnes, the chief medical officer, protest; Barnes calls the kid no good at all.
61601-account-of-the-terrific-and-fatal-:
The Account of the Terrific and Fatal Riot at the Astor Place Opera House is a contemporary pamphlet history. Ranney published it in New York in 1849. The riot happened on the night of May 10 that year. The title page promises full and authentic particulars. More than fifty citizens were killed or maimed.

The first chapter paints the scene that night. Thousands gathered round the opera house in an aristocratic quarter. Inside, the English actor Macready tried to play Macbeth. Hisses and cheers fought across the house. Outside, a mob stoned the barricaded windows. Police arrested rioters within and were pelted without. The quarrel of Forrest and Macready, the rival tragedians, had lit the fuse.
61696-martian-terror:
Ed Earl Repp wrote Martian Terror, billed as a novelet of revolution among the Venusians, printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1940. Lolan, a Martian sub-commander, has no choice, the blurb says: he sorrows for Princess Mora's beaten, starved subjects, but duty commands him to loose his force-bolts.

The story opens on Lolan alone at a desk on a hot Venusian night, his ornate uniform collar open, writing a letter that might bring demotion or court-martial. In it he tenders his resignation as sub-commander of the Martian Army of Occupation on Venus. Readers get pulp space opera where the occupier's conscience is the first casualty.
62163-david-morgan-the-welsh-jacobite-a-:
William Llewellin recovers a rebel in David Morgan, the Welsh Jacobite, printed at Tenby in 1862. Mason made the pamphlet, reprinted from the Cambrian Journal of 1861. The sub title calls it a contribution to the history of Jacobitism in Wales. A Jacobite ballad sings out front, of the last hoof and horn and hide given to bonnie Charlie.

One of the most romantic episodes in English history opens the study. The last effort of the partisans of the expelled House of Stuart is its ground. The Rebellion of 1745, Llewellin writes, gave rise to striking incidents and romantic adventures. The annals of history show no greater personal sacrifices, he holds, nor more exalted heroism and devotion, than that struggle called forth.
62353-an-essay-towards-regulating-the-tr:
A trade pamphlet by John Cary, printed at London in 1719. This second edition adds an essay on paying off the public debts. Cary dedicates the enlarged work to the House of Commons. The first edition had gone to the Prince of Wales. Cary hoped to give the heir an early liking for trade.

His argument starts with the balance of trade. A favourable balance brings bullion into the kingdom. Manufactures keep that balance sound. They set the people to work and let them maintain themselves. Cary urges that English goods be worn at home first. Imports should favour goods bought with English wares, not with bullion.
