The essay shaped debate on workhouses, trade, and the poor.
62880-the-glebe-1914-01-vol-1-no-4-love-:
The January 1914 number of The Glebe, volume one, number four, is given over entirely to Love of One's Neighbor. The play is by the Russian writer Leonid Andreyev, in an authorized translation by Thomas Seltzer. The Glebe, edited by Alfred Kreymborg, was published by Albert and Charles Boni in New York. Each issue went to a single author, under a stated policy of absolute freedom of expression, and the magazine sold by subscription at three dollars a year.

Andreyev's play opens on a wild place in the mountains. A despairing man stands stranded on a narrow ledge of rock, beyond reach from above or below. Ladders, ropes, and sticks show that rescue has been tried and has failed, and a crowd gathers to watch. The scene sets up Andreyev's bitter joke about how neighbors love a spectacle more than a rescue.
62930-dick-merriwell-s-backers-or-well-w:
Standish, author of the famous Merriwell stories, wrote this Dick Merriwell tale for Street and Smith, copyrighted in 1907. Dick is pitching for Yale against the Tufts freshmen, and the game has gone tiresomely one-sided. At the beginning of the sixth inning the score stands seven to one. Tufts professed a hilarious confidence in hitting Dick's shoots and benders, and the confidence has oozed away. At Dick's own suggestion, Sam Kates comes into the box for a try-out.

The contents promise the mixture as before. There is a blackmailer, hush money, and a captive abandoned; then silver bullets, a terrifying trio, and a ghostly face. A holdup and the routing of the ruffians follow. The odds against Yale and Manhattan in the lead bring the baseball back at the end. Dick's backers, the title says, are well worth fighting for, and the freshman pitcher is the weapon.
6313-masterpieces-of-american-wit-and-hu:
Thomas L. Masson edits this fourth volume of American wit and humor, with Mark Twain pictured at the front and a roster running from Agnes Repplier to Harriet Beecher Stowe. Repplier pleads for humor, Marietta Holley writes an unmarried female, and Fitzhugh Ludlow offers selections from a brace of boys. Robert Jones Burdette cures rheumatism by movement, Oliver Wendell Holmes gives an aphorism and a lecture, and Artemus Ward writes business letters.

James Russell Lowell, Louisa May Alcott on Washington street scenes, and Samuel Minturn Peck join William Cullen Bryant on the mosquito and Danforth Marble on the Hoosier and the salt pile. The 1903 collection mixes essays, sketches, and verse, light in touch and broad in range. It is a sampler of a nation's funny bone, from parlour satire to frontier tall talk.
63298-the-new-democracy-a-handbook-for-d:
Walter Vrooman's The New Democracy is a handbook for Democratic speakers and workers, copyrighted by the author at St Louis. Its preface is dated June 1, 1897, and it outlines the methods of the National Volunteers of Democracy and of the Volunteer Speakers Bureau.

After the 1896 campaign, Democratic leaders set up a bureau of speakers for the continuous preaching of Democratic principles by new and young men. Vrooman complains that earlier handbooks were stuffed with statistics and figures that burdened and confused their readers. His own aims at a bird's-eye view of the political situation, with the best methods of work and speech.
63477-image-of-splendor:
Image of Splendor, by Lu Kella, was printed from Planet Stories of the summer of 1955. A head note says the run from Venus to Earth was a hard world for men, and for one trainee most of all. Bells roar as a red light flashes on the meter bank.

Trainee Burnerman O'Rielly races to Burner Four in his safety helm. Its fusion controls sit two points low, a fault no drill book says can occur in flight. Chief Callahan grills him through the helm phone. If one jet runs low at blast down, the ship may slew and crash with all hands. No one has passed his watch room since Venus, and bells guard each door. Women run the ship, from the chief to Captain Millicent Hatwoody. Space fans get a tense tale of blame, pride, and a slipped dial.
63761-a-letter-to-the-viscount-palmersto:
Charles John Vaughan, head master of Harrow, wrote an open letter to Viscount Palmerston in 1854 on the monitorial system of Harrow School. It was first printed only for private circulation among those concerned. Vaughan thanks Palmerston for his letter, valued the more because Harrow was the place of Palmerston's own education.

The question, Vaughan says, is not the system itself, which gives recognized authority to the upper boys. It is one method of enforcing it that draws anxiety: the power of inflicting corporal punishment. He cites Dr Arnold's defence of his sixth form's right to the cane at Rugby. Vaughan sets out Harrow's principles for Palmerston to judge.
64298-the-wavy-tailed-warrior:
John Breck told a set of woodland tales for children in his Told at Twilight books, and Doubleday, Page published this fifth book in 1923. William Andrews drew the pictures. The hero with the wavy tail is Stripes the skunk. His friends are Nibble the rabbit, Tad Coon, and Doctor Muskrat of the pond.

The first chapter opens with a strange scratching in the woods that sends the friends into a fright. Chapters that follow bring a fishing trip with a boy named Tommy, a pact between fishermen, and a battle of the potato bugs. The birds join a war, and the field mice rise in protest. One chapter asks where Tad Coon has gone. The tales are gentle and funny, with real habits of wild things woven into the play of the plot.
64352-the-illustrated-horse-doctor:
Edward Mayhew wrote The Illustrated Horse Doctor, printed at Philadelphia in 1862. It gives an accurate, detailed account of horse diseases, with the latest treatment and all requisite prescriptions, in plain English. More than four hundred pictorial representations accompany the text for non-professional readers. Mayhew gave the book to Sir Benjamin Brodie, who had rescued him from impending death.

Publishers had long felt a new book on horse diseases in simple language was a public necessity, their advertisement says. Mayhew's skill with the pencil proved only secondary to his use of the pen, to their surprise and profit. The acute stage of megrims illustrates the front matter dramatically. Horse owners got a Victorian veterinary guide.
64430-josie-o-gorman-and-the-meddlesome-:
Edith Van Dyne wrote this girl detective tale, printed in Chicago in 1924. Josie O'Gorman has already had one book of her own. Mack drew the frontispiece, which shows a torn package on a heap of filmy lace. Eighteen chapters follow Josie at work.

Josie takes a job as a sales girl, then moves to a new home on Meadow Street. Her black book, the folk in apartment three, and a trail taken up by the major drive the plot. Too many detectives crowd in, and a trap is set late in the hunt. Leslie turns detective too, and the tale ends with a win for Josie.
64655-space-trap-at-banya-tor:
W J Matthews wrote Space Trap at Banya Tor, a tale first printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1948. Jeff Thorne, famed as the Derelict of Mars, is its hero. The blurb says shows on the air made space crime look like fun and games. Thorne means to stop the real thing.

The tale opens as the head of the Planet Patrol boards a ship in full pomp. Word comes that Senator Chanler is dead, to the shock of his staff. The World Council gives his seat to his daughter Iris, a famed beauty from Venus. She throws her whole heart into the post. Pirates, patrol men, and Thorne soon clash in a trap that tests whose side each man is on.
64711-the-warlock-of-sharrador:
Gardner F Fox wrote The Warlock of Sharrador. Planet Stories ran the tale in March 1953. A Thing had slept for unremembered eons, the blurb says. It quested through star worlds in its dreams. Mankind kept it as a faint race legend. Now men must recall its name, the blurb warns.

Noorlythin is that name, and it walks among men and robots. The McCanahan wakes at a Senn dawn in the tale. A Thorn blaster floats before his face. No hand holds the gun in the air. Its trigger creeps back on its own. He flings his bedclothes up as a shield. Silk and moonylon billow in a geyser there. Little People whispered in his dreams that night. Their warning of Flaith's loveliness saved him. Pulp sword-and-planet fare mixes starships with a risen god in Fox's fast, gaudy style.
6482-the-coverley-papers-from-the-specta:
O. M. Myers edits The Coverley Papers from the Spectator, gathering every number concerned with Sir Roger de Coverley or arising from the Spectator's visit to his country house. Sir Roger appears in some seventeen other papers, but there he gets only passing mention or speaks where the subject, not he, is the interest. The contents list Addison, Steele, and Budgell numbers across the Spectator's run, with appendices on coffee houses, the Spectator's acquaintance, and Sir Roger's death.

Myers's introduction urges studying Addison in close relation to his time, for he was a true child of his century, not so much in opposition to it. A mid passage contrasts neighbours Laertes and Irus, whose ways of living are an abomination to each other. Laertes charges his estate yearly with a child's birth rather than let a new man equal him. The papers are Augustan comedy, gentle and observant.
64842-the-psychological-regulator:
Arthur Cooke wrote The Psychological Regulator, a science fiction tale printed in Comet in March nineteen forty-one. The scene is the year twenty sixty-six, in a vast numbered city. Nurse Markett Travenor works on floor twenty-four, ward five.

By her file code, Markett is a numbered person in a great register. She was born in twenty forty-six, of parents paired by science for their traits. Doctor Ward Alfreed is late, and a patient is coming up with him. The patient's card lists fears of falling, floating, and slipping. Three tries at self-killing failed for lack of skill. A device called the Regulator is advised.
64965-world-without-glamor:
Milton Lesser wrote this tale of colonists on Talbor with no glamor. The story ran in Imagination magazine in October 1953. Colonists had little time but work, bad for morale, it opens. Earth sent a special ship with a unique cargo for them.

Marsden lathers his face at a basin as Marie enters the cabin. Two years of marriage hold a smouldering resentment now between them. Broiling sun work leaves them bone weary and stiff muscled nightly. Chickens on Talbor, three dozen light years from Earth, mark the distance. Feeding their chickens fell to Marie each day after the field work ended there.
65078-how-to-become-a-lightning-calculat:
How to Become a Lightning Calculator is a short guide to fast work with figures. It came out in Boston in February 1894 as number two of the Multum in Parvo Library, a monthly billed as the smallest magazine in the world. Single copies sold for five cents and a year for fifty cents. A. B. Courtney was the publisher, at an address on Tremont Street.

The teaching starts with instant addition. The first rule is that accuracy must come first, and speed after. Quick adders, the guide holds, are in fact the most exact. The pupil is told to write the numbers in straight up-and-down lines, with no ragged rows. The mind is to be kept on the results, not on the numbers as such, as the first page of drills sets out.
65231-house-operator:
Tenneshaw wrote House Operator, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in December 1957. Rafferty, a gambler of the old school, walks into the Ganymede Casino with all the money he has left. He trusts poker and scorns the fancy electronic and psionic games the casinos now push.

Rafferty owes a large sum to Lee Walsh, a big-time gambler, and it falls due the next day. He means to triple his roll at the tables or go under. Walsh has teased him for always playing poker and urged him to switch games. The story sets a stubborn card man against a casino full of rigged wonders. Readers get a tight tale of nerve, debt, and one last run at the tables.
65375-the-poems-of-richard-corbet-late-b:
The Poems of Richard Corbet, late bishop of Oxford and of Norwich, appear here in a fourth edition printed in London in 1807. Octavius Gilchrist edited the volume for Longman and his partners, adding biographical notes and a life of the author. An oration on the death of Prince Henry, from Ashmole's Museum, is also newly included.

Gilchrist's life says Corbet was born at Ewell in Surrey in 1582, the son of Vincent Corbet, a gardener of eminence celebrated by Ben Jonson. The boy inherited five hundred pounds in money, payable at twenty-five. He was educated at Westminster School, then at Broadgate Hall and Christ Church in Oxford, before rising through the Church to his two bishoprics.
65400-youth-vol-i-no-3-may-1902-an-illus:
Youth for May 1902 is the third number of an illustrated monthly journal for boys and girls, published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia. A single copy cost ten cents, and a year's subscription cost $1. The cover promises serial stories, pictures, magic, and puzzles.

The lead serial is With Washington at Valley Forge by W Bert Foster. Its hero, Hadley Morris, carries captured dispatches to General Washington in 1777. A Memorial Day story, The Dandy Fifth's Last Triumph, is by Laura Alton Payne. Wordsworth's poem To May is reprinted as a selection. Two more serials run: Little Polly Prentiss by Elizabeth Lincoln Gould and A Daughter of the Forest by Evelyn Raymond. Wood-Folk Talk treats the bobolink. Parlor magic by Ellis Stanyon and a puzzle page called The Old Trunk close the number.
65728-the-inquisitor:
Conway Kroll takes no joy in his work, or so he tells himself each dawn. Randall Garrett's tale, from the December 1956 Imagination, sets Kroll over three prisoners in a bare room. He calls it interrogation; the tall young man spits back the word torture.

Miss Horniman must go first to the Inquisitor, though Leslie begs to take her place. Kroll shrugs and keeps the set order, mild as milk. Garrett wrote wry, sharp science fiction, often with a sting in the tail. The horror here sits in the calm voice of the man who runs the machine. The chamber next door holds the tool of his trade.
65805-nick-carter-stories-no-131-march-1:
Nick Carter Stories number one hundred thirty one is a week dime sheet of March thirteenth, nineteen fifteen. A Street and Smith house of New York brought it out at five cents. A Fatal Message, or Nick Carter Slender Clew, heads its scheme in full. Nick sits in a Shelby House food booth and hears two men talk. Thin board walls let each word through to his booth seat at lunch.

Those men speak loud, as if their theme bore no grave weight at all. Part names run through a doubt wire, a seized note, and night work. Patsy makes good and Chick craft fill the case parts in rank. A dark stage piece and world news fill the back of the sheet. A call for a John Dalton with no town book name starts the case.
65858-spruce-tree-house-trail-guide-mesa:
Spruce Tree House Trail Guide, for Mesa Verde National Park in Colorado, was a loan booklet on the trail. A note asks visitors to leave the booklet in the box at the far end of the ruin, or drop ten cents in the coin box to keep it. Visitors are warned not to climb on the walls or crawl through the doorways.

Station one gives the measure of the place. Spruce Tree House is the third largest cliff dwelling in the park, built in a natural cave 216 feet long, 89 feet deep, and 60 feet high. The dwelling held about 114 rooms and eight ceremonial rooms, and perhaps 200 to 250 people lived there at one time. It was occupied from about the year 1200 to shortly before 1300. Courts and kivas fill the later stations.
65995-the-mine-with-the-iron-door:
Harold Bell Wright, author of The Shepherd of the Hills and The Winning of Barbara Worth, wrote this Arizona romance. Appleton copyrighted it in 1923, the Ryerson Press issued it at Toronto, and Wright dedicated it to his friends in the old pueblo of Tucson. A frontispiece shows a girl catching a man's arm: the sheriff is here.

Chapter one, The Canon of Gold, opens on the Santa Catalina mountains above Tucson. Their granite heights and soft colors of red, blue, and purple lure the eye from every street of the city. Men still find color, Wright writes, in the Canada del Oro, and romance lives on there behind the lost mine's iron door. Thirty-five chapters follow through the Oracle store, the pardners' girl, Saint Jimmy, a prospector's story, Marta's flight, the sheriff's visit, and the lost mine, to chapters named Gold, Morning, and Freedom.
66469-the-book-collector:
Charles Nodier wrote this essay on the love of old books, in a print made at Cambridge in 1951. A plate by Honoré Daumier of 1844 stands at its front. It shows a man by a book stall in a state of joy: he has bought, for a sum of coin, a Horace printed at Amsterdam in 1780. That print is prized past words, the plate jests, since each page is shot through with faults.

The essay opens with a word of warn from the author. It will be as dull, he jests, as a speech by an old school man, for God, kind, and the schools have shut his fancy in a close cell. At least the reader can lay the book down, which is more luck than the author has.
66661-the-truth-about-an-author:
Arnold Bennett wrote The Truth About an Author, in a new edition of 1911. Doran at New York put out this form, with a fresh preface. Bennett had written How to Live on 24 Hours a Day. Sixteen chapters, numbered only, make the body of the book. It opens with a long roll of what its author is and does.

He resides on the literary world, a curious fourth-dimensional planet, he says. He follows the parasitic trade of talking about what people have done. He is a sort of public weighing-machine for bookish wares, he adds. He habitually thinks in articles and exists by phrases, by his own account. In passion he perceives chiefly a theme, and in tragedy a situation. Victimized by a literary temperament, he glories in his victimhood. Bennett traces that temperament from its first stirrings to its prime.
66849-captain-bill-mcdonald-texas-ranger:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this life of Captain Bill McDonald of the Texas Rangers, subtitled a story of frontier reform. A subscription edition was made at New York in 1909, with an introductory letter by Theodore Roosevelt. McDonald's creed heads the book: no man in the wrong can stand up against a fellow that is in the right and keeps on coming.

The contents follow McDonald from an old-time Mississippi childhood through emigration and adventure to the making of a Texan. He subdues bad men as a deputy, reforms Quanah, and gets even with the Brooken gang, whose outlaw drew one hundred and twenty-seven years of sentences. In No-Man's Land he holds up a bad gang single-handed and redeems the Strip. A chapter explains the Ranger service from the Fort Parker massacre onward, and Governor Jim Hogg appoints his old friend captain of Company B.
66886-from-immigrant-to-inventor:
Michael Pupin wrote From Immigrant to Inventor, his life story, with rights pages dated nineteen twenty-two and nineteen twenty-three. Pupin taught electro-mechanics at Columbia University in New York. He gave the book to the memory of his mother.

Pupin landed at Castle Garden, he says, with five cents in his pocket, forty-eight years before. Five hundred dollars, he argues, would not have changed his first path. Chapters tell the hardships of a greenhorn and the end of that apprenticeship. Study at Cambridge and Berlin follows, then a career at Columbia. Pictures show his birthplace at Idvor and his mother Olympiada. The rise of idealism in American science closes the tale.
67527-the-foot-prints-of-the-creator:
The Foot-Prints of the Creator is a work of geology by Hugh Miller. This American edition follows the third London edition of the book. Gould and Lincoln published it in Boston in 1868. A memoir of the author, by Louis Agassiz, accompanies the text.

Its subtitle names a fossil fish, the Asterolepis of Stromness. Miller had made his name with The Old Red Sandstone before it. He dedicates the volume to Sir Philip Egerton, a high authority on fossil fishes. In it he traces the history of creation through one division of life. The fish kind is at once the most ancient of backboned animals, he notes. It is also the most extensively preserved in the rocks of the earth. Against the popular author of a rival theory of creation, Miller argues his case.
67551-with-grenfell-on-the-labrador:
Fullerton Waldo wrote a book on a trip with Doctor Grenfell in Labrador. The book came out in New York in 1920. Grenfell wrote the front words for Waldo's tale. A plate shows Grenfell on a climb with three rope rungs broke. Waldo gave the book to Doris Kenyon in fond terms.

Saint Anthony, the mission's core town, takes an early part. All in the day's work shows the cure man's vast round. Grenfell stands as chief of trade, sport man, and man of God. Dogs and deer as work mates get a part of their own. A wide parish of coast folk closes the tale's scope. North fans get a warm tale of grit.
67576-thistledown-a-book-of-scotch-humou:
Robert Ford gathered this book of Scotch humour, character, folk-lore, story, and anecdote, in a new and enlarged edition printed at Paisley in 1913. John Duncan drew the pictures. Ford had edited ballad books before this one. The front picture quotes his claim that Scotch humour slips out most where it is least expected, on hillsides and at cottage fires.

Chapters take up the Scottish tongue, the humour of old divines, and the pulpit and the pew. Beadles, precentors, poets, and lawyers each get a chapter of jokes. Highland humour, rural life, and superstition fill the middle of the book. Jamie Fleeman, a famous fool, and Hawkie, a Glasgow street figure, close the set of characters.
67589-a-message-from-our-sponsor:
A Message from Our Sponsor is a science fiction story by Henry Slesar, taken from Infinity Science Fiction of October 1956. Lee illustrated it. The headnote gives the joke its edge: the foot in the door technique would work perfectly for any salesman, if he had an invisible foot. The story opens inside a radio broadcast beamed at Mars.

The announcer plays records for Martian fans and reads the sponsor's message with a straight face. Then the scene cuts to an office on Earth. The boss slams a file drawer in disgust. Before his desk stands a Martian salesman, shuffling his feet and rotating his cap with his third hand. He has come to straighten the whole thing out. Slesar built a career on such twists, and this tale sells its satire of advertising in advertising's own voice.
67615-nick-carter-stories-no-148-july-10:
Nick Carter Stories number 148, for July 10, 1915, holds the tale The Mark of Cain, or Nick Carter Air Line Case. Street and Smith put the weekly out in New York for five cents a copy. Chickering Carter shaped the text for print.

The tale opens in a phone exchange, where Helen Bailey works at a switchboard full of holes and plugs. Nick Carter waits in the business office and marks her held breath at once. Half a score of girls work the boards near her, too busy to note each other. Carter reads the small sign and moves fast, as he must in these tales. Readers of dime detective weeklies get pace, clues, and a hero who sees what others miss.
67618-nick-carter-stories-no-146-june-26:
Nick Carter Stories, number 146, is the weekly issue of 26 June 1915. Street and Smith issued it at New York for five cents a copy. Paying the Price, or Nick Carter Perilous Venture, is its lead tale. Mail terms for the weekly fill the front page of the number.

Single copies or back numbers cost five cents each in that price list. Three months came at sixty five cents and a year at two dollars fifty. Money was to come by money order, registered letter, or bank draft, the terms state. Nick Carter, the famed dime novel detective, faces peril in the headline story. Weekly story papers like this one fed millions of readers in 1915.
67790-the-mirror-of-the-graces-containin:
A lady of distinction wrote this guide to dress and manners, printed at Boston in 1831 from the London edition. Her motto holds that beauty, woman's weapon, must be feathered by the Graces, pointed by discretion, and shot by the hand of virtue. Chapters treat the female form and beauty at length, then dress and personal decoration in general.

Dress by station and dress in detail follow, with deportment, carriage, and dancing. An appendix takes up corsets, the ladies' passion for levelling all ranks of dress, and recipes. The preface argues that the body speaks our opinions, hopes, and fears to others before words can. The book joins elegance, simplicity, and economy, as its title promises, for young women of its day.
67858-aristotle-s-works-containing-the-m:
Aristotle's Works is a popular medical manual sold under the name of the famous philosopher. London booksellers published the combined volume. It joins three parts in one binding. The parts are the Master-Piece, directions for midwives, and counsel for child-bearing women. Useful remedies fill out the volume.

An opening notice praises the guide. Many women, it says, depend wholly on the skill of the midwife. The first part treats marriage and the womb. Its chapters cover false conceptions and untimely births. They give rules for each month of pregnancy. The midwife section then handles labour itself. It tells what to do in cases of extremity.
67968-how-to-use-and-enjoy-your-new-frig:
How to Use and Enjoy Your New Frigidaire Refrigerator is the owner's booklet for the 1947 Frigidaire line. The Frigidaire Division of General Motors copyrighted it at Dayton, Ohio, in 1947. Frigidaire and General Motors, the booklet boasts, stand behind the machine. More than nine million refrigerating units had already been built. The note on the cover lists the contents.

Instructions cover use and care, moving house, and the Frigidaire 5-Year Protection Plan. Recipes for salads and desserts add temptation. The index maps the parts by page. The Cold-Control sits on page 4, defrosting on page 5. The Super-Freezer, Meat-Tender, Cold Storage Tray, and Hydrator share page 7 and 8. Ice trays take page 9, and the Meter-Miser page 10. Cleaning, moving, and placement advice cluster at page 10. Frozen salads begin the recipes at page 12, desserts at page 14. The protection plan closes the booklet at page 23.
6802-white-slaves-or-the-oppression-of-t:
Louis Albert Banks, dedicating his book to parents who taught him love of liberty and hatred of oppression, writes on white slaves, the oppression of the worthy poor. He opens with Edison's note that ninety percent of coal's energy is lost in turning it to force, and asks if nearly as much spiritual power is wasted in average church life. Fervor in meetings, he notes, yields meagre results.

Banks, a Methodist preacher, urges churches to aid the poor in deed, not just in devotion. His tone is earnest, reforming, and plain. White Slaves is a passionate, period plea for social justice from a pulpit voice.
68106-nick-carter-stories-no-152-august-:
Nick Carter Stories number 152, dated August 7, 1915, carries the tale The Forced Crime, or Nick Carter's Brazen Clew. Street and Smith issued the weekly in New York at five cents. The story is edited by Chickering Carter, as the series' house name ran. Its first chapter is called A Tale of Burglars.

It opens with a victim telling Carter that a burglar has entered his bedroom three times. The detective takes up the strange case of a crime someone was forced to commit. Nick Carter weeklies were the backbone of American dime-novel reading for decades. They delivered a complete detective tale every week to newsstand buyers.
68116-nick-carter-stories-no-150-july-24:
Nick Carter Stories number 150, dated July 24, 1915, is a weekly dime novel. Street and Smith sold it at New York for five cents a copy. The House of Fear, or Nick Carter Counterstroke, fills this number in full. Chickering Carter edited the tale of the famous detective at work here.

Chapter one, The Dead Alive, opens at two in the morning on Fifth Avenue. Carter, disguised with grease paint, has hunted a crook all night in vain. A tipsy society man stops him to beg a match for his cigar. Carter reads the stranger dress, beard, and unsteady walk at a glance. Weekly terms, five cents single or two dollars fifty a year, front the issue.
68180-the-book-of-the-ancient-greeks-an-:
Dorothy Mills, who taught history at the Brearley School in New York, wrote this first book on the Greeks for young students. Putnam printed it in August 1925, with sixteen plates and a map. The Hermes of Praxiteles fronts the book.

Her span runs from the coming of the Greeks to Rome's conquest of Corinth in 146 BC. Crete opens the tale: its tales, palaces, dress, faith, and a day in Crete. Six printings by 1931 prove the book's wide use in schools. Mills had written The Book of the Ancient World before this. Clear, warm teaching fills these pages, made to give a first true grasp of Greek life.
6837-the-little-warrior:
Wodehouse opens The Little Warrior with Freddie Rooke gazing coldly at breakfast, eye-glass gleaming, at a poached egg Parker has placed before him. What is this, Freddie asks in pain; poached egg, sir, Parker replies. It looks just like an old aunt of mine, Freddie says, and orders it removed, then stands by the fireplace in his dressing-gown, shoulders to the mantel.

From that comic breakfast grows a tale of love, golf, and a little warrior's battles in London and New York. Wodehouse keeps the farce light and the dialogue crisp. The Little Warrior is a gay, classic Wodehouse novel, full of silly young men and sensible girls.
68463-the-salton-sea-an-account-of-harri:
George Kennan tells how men fought the Colorado River to save a rich farm valley, in a book printed in New York in 1917. Photos and maps fill the book. Sixteen years before, the land had been the dry bed of an old sea. Sun beat on it with near desert heat, and rain came seldom.

Irrigation made an oasis in the Salton Sink, then the river broke loose and ran wild. The flood cut deep channels and wrecked farm land. Harriman and the railroad threw dams, levees, and rock at the gap. Kennan tells the fight step by step, then tells what the valley owed and gained when the river was curbed at last.
68704-a-true-interpretation-of-the-witch:
A True Interpretation of the Witch of Endor, by Lodowicke Muggleton, reached a second edition at London in 1724. Muggleton calls himself the last chosen witness in his title matter. The treatise takes up the tale of Saul and the witch in the First Book of Samuel. Chapter one opens at verse eleven of chapter twenty eight. Friends had asked him to set his spoken answers in print.

He argues that no spirit can be raised without its body. If the spirit walks, he says, the body must walk also. He explains familiar spirits, voices, and shapes as tricks that fool the ignorant. Other scriptures that seem to show spirits apart from bodies are read his way. The book is a bold piece of early English religious dispute.
68739-come-into-my-parlor:
Charles E Fritch tells a bar-room tale of a reporter and a drunk friend, printed in Science Fiction Adventures Magazine in February 1953. Orban drew the pictures.

Charlie Bennet finds Johnny in a near-empty bar. Johnny stares at nothing, glass in hand, yet seems sober. The headnote says he is seeing things, like spider webs in the night sky. Bennet's job is to keep facts and fancies apart. The note adds that he is good at that, too good. Johnny swears he knows things about this cock-eyed old world that Bennet never dreamed. He drains his glass and demands more. The tale hangs on that gap: a drunk who sees truly, and a sober man trained not to believe him.
68929-beautiful-but-poor: Julia Edwards wrote this tale, put out as the eighth book of the Eagle Library by Street and Smith. The tale's name tells its theme in three words: a maid fair of face but poor of purse. The line it stands in was a weekly line of tales, at a price of a coin and half a dime. The house boasts that its tales are held by right and can be had in no other shape. Mrs. Georgie Sheldon is named as the chief star of the line.
68970-passed-by-the-censor:
Wythe Williams, Paris correspondent of the New York Times, wrote this war book, published in 1916. He was accredited to the French armies, and the former ambassador Myron Herrick introduces it. Georges Clemenceau contributes an endorsement from his newspaper.

Clemenceau praises the crowded picture: in it, he says, we recognize our men as they are, and the army as invincible in power, intelligence, and humanity. A letter from Senator Lafayette Young urges Williams to write his own experiences. He has been in the war from the start, and studied the soldier in and out of the trench. The title promises what the censor allowed through. American readers of 1916 get France at war, reported from inside the lines.
69213-the-13th-juror:
The Thirteenth Juror, by Leslie Waltham, was produced from Startling Stories for Summer 1955. The story opens with an excerpt from a future history of trial procedure, covering the years 2175 to 2543. Its author is a professor writing long after.

Even then, he says, in the start of the twenty third century, crime itself had ceased to exist. Lower emotions had been bred out of the people. Envy, hate, and greed were almost unknown. Every citizen wore a crude type of feeling recorder, checked from time to time by the Eye. Any drift from the norm brought a call for questioning. In the absence of actual crime, an emotion that might lead to crime was itself unlawful. Men were tried for too much anger, or too little pity. A trial only asked whether provocation warranted the response. Readers get a cold future court tale.
6934-the-radio-amateur-s-hand-book-a-com:
This handbook teaches the amateur how to receive and send messages without wires, from first set to working station. Its author, A Frederick Collins, won a gold medal for his wireless telephone at the Alaska Yukon Pacific Exposition in 1909. The book covers both wireless telegraphy and telephony, with numbered figures that match the text figure for figure.

Readers learn the parts, the circuits, and the practice of tuning, calling, and answering across the air. The opening pages sketch how the art grew and where it is used in daily life, so a beginner grasps the why before the how. It is a hands on manual for the 1920s listener turned builder, plain in speech and rich in diagrams.
6935-the-radio-amateur-s-hand-book-a-com:
A Frederick Collins, inventor of the wireless telephone in 1899, wrote this handbook for radio amateurs in 1922. Dedicated to William Marconi, inventor of the wireless telegraph, it claims to be a complete, authentic, and informative work on wireless telegraphy and telephony. Collins had already written on wireless telegraphy in 1905 and served as historian of wireless from 1901 to 1910.

The introduction promises first a word on the history of the art and its present day uses, before turning to the mysteries of sending and receiving messages without wires. Illustrations are keyed to the text by number, so a reader can follow each set and circuit. The book speaks to the early amateur eager to build, listen, and talk across the air.
69360-the-steeple-jack-s-instructor:
Clarence James Murray wrote The Steeple-Jack's Instructor for the Lee Publishing Company at Chicago, copyrighted in 1921. The title page prices the book at $2.00 and promises modern methods in full. Contents start with how to become a steeple-jack, then climb the smokestack step by step. Rigging without a gimblet wire, changing riggings, and steel stacks follow in order.

Murray claims fourteen years in the trade behind his secrets of the craft. He says he made as high as $170 a day at his best. Tanks, towers, standpipes, church spires, flagstaffs, and pole tops each get working chapters. Knots close the course, from square knot to bowline and half hitches. A nerve trade sells its tricks in plain print.
69425-paradisi-in-sole-paradisus-terrest:
John Parkinson, an apothecary of London, wrote this great garden book, Paradisi in Sole Paradisus Terrestris, first printed in 1629 and faithfully reprinted at London in 1904. Parkinson's own title page states the whole design. It is a garden of all sorts of pleasant flowers that English air will let be nursed up.

A kitchen garden stands beside the flowers, of all manner of herbs, roots, and fruits for meat or sauce used with us. Then comes an orchard of all sorts of fruit-bearing trees and shrubs fit for our land. The right ordering, planting, and keeping of them all, and their uses and virtues, complete the promise. A dedication carries the book to the queen, whose delight in fair flowers, Parkinson writes, passed that of all others, as she herself passed them in eminence.
69538-riches-have-wings-or-a-tale-for-th:
Riches Have Wings, or a Tale for the Rich and Poor, is a moral tale by T Arthur. The author wrote a shelf of such tales for home shelves in his day. This copy is marked as the fifth thousand of the print run. The book came out in New York in the year eighteen forty nine.

Parts trace trust in wealth, wild bets on gain, and a dream land of gold. Love bent by pride and by coin earns two parts of sharp note. Loss, a great wreck of funds, and a mind laid low fill the fall. Light in dark days and faith tried and proved chart the slow mend. Plain faith and thrift form the creed of the famed home tale.
69594-san-salvador:
San Salvador, a novel by Mary Agnes Tincker, author of Two Coronets, was printed by Houghton and Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1892. A psalm line stands as its motto: unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. The prologue opens in Venice, at the Palazzo Loredan on the Grand Canal.

The family has finished its midday breakfast, and coffee is brought in. The Marchesa, a widow, sits with her widowed daughter, a little grandson and his tutor, and her second son Claudio, usually the life of the family and its harmonizing element. Today Claudio is silent and preoccupied, and two deep lines between his mother's black brows promise a storm. She orders a private talk carried down to the garden arbor, and he follows, carefully avoiding the glistening wake of her sweeping progress.
70041-the-small-bachelor:
The Small Bachelor is a comic novel by Pelham Grenville Wodehouse. Doran published it in New York. The copyrights date to 1926 and 1927. The story opens on a roof near Washington Square. The narrator surveys the ground before the action starts.

The Sheridan Apartment House stands in the artistic quarter. A brick thrown from its windows would brain some sculptor or poet. On the roof stands a small penthouse bungalow. George Finch, its owner, comes from East Gilead, Idaho. A legacy freed him from earning a living. He came to New York to paint. He is probably the worst artist who ever held a brush. His man Mullett sweeps the roof. A booklet author named Beamish enters the scene.
70244-deems-taylor:
John Tasker Howard wrote this short study of the composer Deems Taylor, published in New York by Fischer and Brother in 1927. It belongs to a series of studies of contemporary American composers, and it sold for 25 cents. Howard thanks his colleague Paul Kempf for help with the life facts, and a studio portrait of Taylor faces the text.

Howard opens with a large claim: no man in America had done more good for the composing craft than Deems Taylor. By his own success Taylor proved that a composer could win fame in the United States without cheap sensation, and could live in a practical way while writing music of high fancy. The study traces how he did it, as proof that the path stood open for others. Music readers get a 1927 view of an American composer at the height of his powers.
70349-when-the-squadron-dropped-anchor:
Thomson Burtis wrote this navy tale of a man cast off in disgrace. Burtis had earlier written The White Slacker and The Green Serpent God. His hero, Graydon, stands accused of base conduct and loses the sea life he loves.

The tale opens in the still port of San Juan de Gracias. A cruiser's whaleboat waits to land Graydon on the beach for good. He stands at the gangway in plain clothes and a panama hat, head bowed. No one answers his last salute as he faces the flag. The head note promises that Graydon will yet find a way to serve his land and clear his name.
71180-the-grisly-horror:
Robert Howard wrote a tale that ran in Weird Tales in February 1935. A gripping tale of a ghastly horror that stalked the swamps of the Mississippi, the blurb promises. A tale of glorious heroism and the hunger of a black god. The horror in the pines opens it. The silence of the pine woods lay like a brooding cloak about the soul of Bristol McGrath.

The black shadows seemed fixed, as fixed as the weight of superstition over this forgotten back country. Vague ancestral dreads stirred at the back of McGrath's mind, for he was born in the pine woods. Sixteen years of roaming the world had not erased their shadows. No one in the river village would drive him to the Ballville estate, the road choked with stumps. A frantic appeal for aid, signed by his worst enemy, had brought him.
71592-survival-factor:
Charles De Vet strands two men in deep space in Survival Factor, from the September 1957 issue of Infinity. Orban drew the plates. The head blurb calls their foe an electronic bloodhound, wild and hard to foretell, on a fierce and crude world.

Wallace and Saxton form a survey team seven parsecs past the Rim. Three years back, mankind met a rival race with the same fast drive. Both sides now guard the worlds that lie between them. The alien bloodhound has picked up the team's trail. Wallace counts their time and finds room for one dip through the spacebridge. They must find a world fast, or die.
7191-modern-broods-or-developments-unloo:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's 1900 novel takes its motto from Tennyson: youth and age are scholars yet but in the lower school. Its chapters move from tortoises and hares through the Goyle, a first Sunday, and cycles. Clipstone friends, frescoes of St Kenelm, sisters, and snobbishness trace how a younger brood grows in ways their elders did not foresee.

Yonge watches family life with a moral eye, letting small choices, church Sundays, and social slights reveal character. The title's unlooked-for developments give the book its mild comedy and its sting, as parents find their children turning out unlike their plans. The novel stays close to home, where its quiet drama feels most true.
72407-the-god-on-the-36th-floor:
Herbert Kastle wrote this story, first printed in Amazing Stories in December 1963. Derrence Cale is a fraud who has hidden for eight years among the nine thousand employees of the Chester Chemical Company, playing at work.

He comes early, opens the public relations offices, and plays floor manager, duties nobody gave him. One morning he hears a high-pitched voice on a phone down the corridor of the 36th floor. The man behind the desk is new: Edwin Tzadi, fat, solemn, and meek, on his first day. The headnote adds Mercy Adrians, nineteen and good to look at. Cale, it says, was a phoney, but at least he thought he was a man. Readers get office intrigue with a strange edge.
72420-beside-the-golden-door:
Henry Slesar's story Beside the Golden Door ran in Amazing Stories in February 1964, with pictures by Schelling. Earth is dead, the blurb says, but Liberty still holds her torch aloft in some form. Only Deez, an alien visitor in the tale's frame, can say if that torch means welcome or mockery.

Ky-Tann, a metals stress analyst at the Roa-Pitin Spaceworks, hears from his wife Devia that Deez has come home a hero. Deez found a once peopled world that has set the archaeology commission buzzing like children. In a hundred years of searching, ships from Illyri had found only slugs, lichen, and sea beasts without minds, plus one dead culture's tools and art.
72796-jack-heaton-wireless-operator:
Jack Heaton, Wireless Operator is a boys' adventure novel by Frederick Collins, published by Stokes in 1919 with eight illustrations. Collins had written Inventing for Boys and The Boys' Book of Submarines. Jack tells his own story in twelve chapters. He begins with how he learned wireless and his first job as an operator, then serves through the sinking of a ship, the Andalusian.

The adventures widen fast. Jack catches seals by wireless, works in the tropics, and serves with Marconi himself. He becomes a government operator at Arlington and serves aboard a warship at Vera Cruz. A submarine chaser and a submarine follow, then the field artillery in France, and at last he is mustered out.
72892-how-to-become-an-inventor:
Tousey put out a youth guide that claims to teach how to become an inventor. The book was filed for rights in New York in 1898. Its pages mix hands-on tests with tool craft. Boys learn to use a saw, a chisel, and a hammer with skill. The first page says such skill saves cash all year.

Tests deal with photos, water force, and electric arts. Magnetism, heat, and the microscope get their own parts. Tool use and glass tools for sight round out the book. Plain tales, like a dear saw job, make the point stick. Young hands get a cheap start in craft and science.
72914-the-man-on-the-meteor:
Ray Cummings wrote a long space tale first run in Science and Invention in nine parts in 1924, and reprinted in 1941. A head note draws its odd world. On a small rock in Saturn's path, rocks burn and the water can be breathed. A man named Nemo and a golden haired girl named Nona live there as plain folk.

The Marinoid people dwell deep in its waters. The teller knows not where he was born, nor on what world. His first clear thought finds him a young man in a rubber suit and clear helmet, bruised and gasping. He tears the helmet off and drinks the sweet air. His body proves light as down in the small world's weak pull.
73053-island-honor:
Murray Leinster wrote Island Honor, a sea tale of the China Sea first told for magazine readers. Sailors on the slow yacht Shikar coast past mangrove swamps for two dull days and find a river mouth that should not be there. They tack in, miss the bar, and spot a white man's house with a flag.

A man named Vetter rules there as political agent for Kuramonga and acts as lord of all he sees. An aged island ruler faces a dreadful choice under tropic stars, the headnote warns readers at the start. White visitors help him decide in American fashion, the headnote promises in its bold opening lines. Readers get a tense tale of honor, power, and pride on a remote island station in the East.
73096-william-jordan-junior:
Snaith wrote a novel published at London in 1907, after a publisher's list of new six-shilling novels. It opens on a day of rain in London, cold, monotonous, and heavy on the streets, gathering mystery from a November night. Odd shapes emerge from the lamplight haze: a wet policeman, a dog, a sullen cabman, a lame horse.

Above all is the sound of continual water falling upon the great roar of London. In one of the narrow lanes leading from the City toward the eastern wilderness, night has erased the actual like a wet cloth drawn across chalk writing. Snaith, who had written Broke of Covenden, sets his young Jordan in that drowned city.
73266-behind-the-bronze-door:
William Le Queux's mystery novel Behind the Bronze Door was published in New York by the Macaulay Company, with a copyright of 1923. Gage drew the frontispiece, which shows a frightened woman turning from a weird knocker in ghostly stillness. The first chapter is called The Epidemic of Mystery.

Mrs Hartsilver presses the evening paper on her husband: another society tragedy, a well-known baronet found shot in his bedroom. The chapter recalls Lord Hope-Cooper, who drowned himself in the lake at Cowrie Park for no known reason. Viscount Molesley, found shot beside burnt papers, and the sudden death of Vera Froissart follow in the list. The contents add a hidden scandal, a confession and hush money.
73354-a-world-to-die-for:
A World to Die For, a story by Sam Carson, ran in Fantastic Universe in July 1954. Titans respect men who create, the tale’s motto declares at its head. It adds to the betterment of others that a Titan must aim. Surely it is brave to be a Titan and muchly in love.

An editor’s note presents Carson as a new name for these pages. He was a veteran writer and a radio and television editor, it says. A former roving newspaperman, he kept up with a son in nuclear physics. When Carson sets foot on an alien planet, the editor promises wonders. Its hills, valleys, and people pulse with light and vitality there. The note swears his desk bound travel magic is a rare thing.
73428-the-sea-horror:
The Sea Horror is a science fiction story by Edmond Hamilton, printed in the magazine Weird Tales in 1929. The narrator begins in retrospect: only now, knowing all the story, can he see how narrow the escape was.

From the first sailing of the Clinton expedition to a last flaming hour of combat, he says, a dark horror rose to overwhelm an unsuspecting world. Doctor Herbert Clinton held the chair of marine zoology at the University of London. He was the foremost British expert on deep-sea life, famous for proving the link between absent ultra-violet rays and the phosphorescence of deep creatures. His work on the forms of deep-sea life made possible the new K-type submarines, built on a fresh pressure-resisting design. Hamilton, a pioneer of the space opera, here turns his scale of menace to the ocean depths.
73430-history-as-past-ethics-an-introduc:
History as Past Ethics, an introduction to the history of morals, was written by Philip Van Ness Myers. Myers had been professor of history and political economy at the University of Cincinnati. He also wrote standard histories of the ancient, medieval, and modern worlds. Ginn published this book in 1913.

Its mottoes frame the aim. Ethics gives history its goal, one says, and no real understanding of history is possible without ethics. Another holds that scientific ethics must trace today's morality from the earliest morality on record, through its stages of growth. Myers accordingly surveys how the moral ideas of peoples have changed across the ages. He treats history as the record of man's conscience at work. The book served college classes as a first map of moral history, from tribal custom to modern duty, by a teacher who believed the past should school the present.
73548-the-story-of-the-rhinegold-der-rin:
The Story of the Rhinegold, told for young people by Anna Alice Chapin, retells Wagner's Ring cycle in plain prose. The book was copyrighted in 1897 and issued in New York and London in 1900. Chapin dedicates it to Eva Wagner, the Master's daughter, with thanks for her kindness and support. German names are kept in simple English forms.

Four parts cover The Rhinegold, The Warrior Goddess, Siegfried, and The Dusk of the Gods. Chapters move from the Rhine maidens and the giants Fasolt and Fafner to Wotan, Brunnhilde, and Siegfried at the forge and the dragon's death. Full-page plates show key scenes. The retelling lets young readers follow a vast opera plot as a clear, linked tale.
73576-a-kiss-for-the-conqueror:
Clyde Mitchell wrote A Kiss for the Conqueror, a science fiction story printed in Fantastic in February 1957. A blurb promises that from the innermost planet to the farthest reaches of space, one man plus one woman equals a story. Bolgar, lean and hungry, studies his face in a scrap of mirror on a barrack wall.

Tonight is the night, Bolgar insists, while Sergeant Pulley sneers from his bunk. Combs are rare in this world, razors are rotten green, and the only working faucet runs copper before it runs clear. Pulley wears a medal green with rust that he will not part with. An ion gun changes hands as a razor is borrowed. The scene is barracks poverty in a beaten future, with a date that plainly matters more than food. Mitchell builds his world from shortages.
73943-lancelot-biggs-master-navigator:
Nelson S Bond returns to his comic space freighter in Lancelot Biggs: Master Navigator, printed in Fantastic Adventures in May 1940. Sparks, the narrator, is taking firing orders at Sun City when Commander Allonby stares in disbelief. The Saturn should still be out among the planetoids on a transmutation experiment. Sparks realizes he is talking to Allonby as he was five months ago.

The cause is Biggs's new uranium audio plate, a time-speech-trap that catches voices from another time level. Retuning to the present gets the take-off order, but Biggs himself makes the lift. Captain Hanson comes to the bridge swearing, weakening in a promise not to commit mayhem on his first mate.
74108-how-little-bessie-kept-the-wolf-fr:
Mrs Coates wrote a penny tale for children in the Bouverie Series of popular stories. The tale stands as Number 11 in a long list of cheap tales for the young. Names in the set include Hesba Stretton, Amy Le Feuvre, and Mrs O F Walton. Each tale sold for a penny to wide young readers.

Little Bessie stands at the heart of the tale, as its title declares. Keeping the wolf from the door means holding hunger and want off a poor home. Work, faith, and a child's grit form the core of such tales. Young readers of the time got a short, warm lesson in courage at home.
74137-the-closed-door:
John Fleming Wilson opened his sea tale The Closed Door with a talk between the narrator and Gorham, a survivor of the wreck of the Shearwater. Gorham left the wreck in the last boat on a dark, stormy morning off the California coast. A woman beside him clutched his arm with relentless strength.

She was Sheila, wife of Captain Harry Owen, a seaman of ability who had never glanced at another woman since his marriage, or so all thought. Gorham hints she had never suspected who the other woman was. That hidden fact, he says, explains why the Shearwater was, in a way, deliberately cast away. The underwriters never probed the affair. A confession at sea drives Wilson's tale.
74266-the-history-of-germain-street-bapt:
The History of Germain Street Baptist Church, Saint John, New Brunswick, marks the congregation's first one hundred years, 1810 to 1910. The Saint John Globe Publishing Company issued it in 1910, and a prefatory note is signed T D Denham that September. The narrative reaches back before the founding for the first stirrings.

Joseph Crandall's autobiography is quoted on the Rev Edward Manning's visits of 1800 or 1805, when there was no Baptist place of worship or Baptist family in the city. Manning preached in houses on Germain and Dock streets, and George Harding became the first person baptized by immersion there.
74708-german-wit-and-humor:
German Wit and Humor is an anthology drawn from famous sources and sorted under subject headings, published at Philadelphia in nineteen hundred three. A portrait of Goethe fronts the volume. Contents begin with humour of the sixteenth century and move to the seventeenth. Chapters for gunners, doctors, and lawyers follow by trade and taste.

Composers and music lovers, travellers, and cyclists each get a chapter of jokes. Authors, scientists, artists, and stage folk are grouped in another. The German soldier and crowned heads close the visible list. In English dress, the book sold German laughter to American readers who knew Germany mostly through music and beer.
74984-wild-life-under-the-equator:
Wild Life Under the Equator is an African travel book told for young people. Paul Du Chaillu wrote it for Harper of New York in eighteen sixty nine. Du Chaillu also wrote Discoveries in Equatorial Africa and Stories of the Gorilla Country. Many engravings picture the hunts, camps, and beasts of his journeys there.

Contents open on Parrot Island and how the parrots build their nests. A leopard among the chickens and a night watch for leopards follow next. Elephant and buffalo hunts, a snake charmer death, and an African court appear. Gorilla hunts fill sundry chapters, with charms made of a great ape brain. Hippopotamus hunting and an African funeral close the early voyage tales.
7529-the-reverberator:
Henry James's novella opens in a Paris hotel's little reading room, where an old man leads a visitor to his daughter. The room holds a window with much curtain and no light, a Figaro the visitor cannot read, and a New York Herald he has already read. The visitor is George Flack, an American journalist of characteristic directness, and the girl is Francina Dosson, traveling with her father.

Flack's trade is the story, and the novella's comedy and sting come from what happens when private talk reverberates into print. Paris society, American innocence, and the press collide, as a young woman's reputation travels faster than she can control it. The Reverberator is James on journalism and gossip, witty, sharp, and quietly sad.
75303-stentor:
Stentor, or The Press of To-Day and To-Morrow, by David Ockham, was copyright 1928 and published in New York. Two long quotations face the title page, and they state the book theme. The new spirit in the Press, one says, aims at making statesmen subservient to its power.

Newspaper owners insolent pretensions, the quote continues, would reduce Downing Street to an annexe of Fleet Street. Can public opinion be free, the second asks, when half the leading journals are one man voice? There is a danger to the freedom of the Press, Janion, and that danger is you. A motto calls the book the abstract and brief chronicle of the time. Readers get a 1928 warning against press barons, built as a drama of quotations.
75338-the-heiress-of-mcgregor:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote The Heiress of McGregor, a tale of faith for young readers issued in Philadelphia in 1875 by the American Sunday School Union. Its second title, Living for Self, names the flaw the heroine must beat. Marion McGregor walks home from school to a plain brick farm house her kin have leased for years on a great Scots lord's tract.

Twenty two parts follow Marion through long talks with Aunt Christian, a mission meeting, and a clear call to new work. She moves to Hemlock Valley and labors at a hard place called Rock Bottom, through winter cold and doubt. Thanksgiving and home scenes soften the close of the tale.
75548-a-time-of-terror:
A Time of Terror tells of a great revenge set in London of 1910. Greening and Company issued the second form in London in 1906. Rights were taken in December 1905 across Britain, Canada, and America. The book is given to fellow citizens of this great Babylon, London.

A cast list names Marcus White, Sir John Westwood, and Detective-Inspector Henshaw. Chapters run from the Leaguers' first move to a great fire in Hyde Park. A murder, a shrine of luxury, and a mania gripping London crowd the plot. Readers gain a fevered tale of revolt and ruin in the near future.
76108-the-salem-horror:
Henry Kuttner's tale from Weird Tales for May 1937 brings the Salem witchcraft of three centuries past into a modern lodging. Carson rents the decrepit gabled house of Abigail Prinn in Derby Street, wanting quiet to finish a novel. The magazine's blurb warns that a horror out of the witchcraft days rears its form there again.

The house has a bad name: tenants keep leaving in haste, with vague tales about the rats. Legend calls Prinn a high priestess whose death in 1692 came mysteriously, near the time of the hangings on Gallows Hill. In the house waits the Witch Room, and a misshapen black rat that watches Carson with unsettling sense leads him toward it.
76137-through-trackless-labrador:
Through Trackless Labrador is a travel and hunting book by Hesketh Prichard, printed at London by William Heinemann in 1911. Prichard had already written Hunting Camps in Wood and Wilderness and Through the Heart of Patagonia. The book carries a foreword by Selous. It is illustrated with a frontispiece by Lady Helen Graham, a map of the route, and photographs. Prichard traveled in Labrador in 1910 with Gathorne-Hardy, who adds a chapter on fishing.

They then turn to the peoples and the game. There are chapters on the Eskimo, the winter masters of the Labrador, the settlers or liveyeres, and the Indians. A long chapter treats the caribou. The book closes by weighing Newfoundland and Labrador against Norway. It is a sportsman's survey of a country then almost unknown inland.
76142-children-of-the-moor:
Laura Fitinghoff wrote Children of the Moor, translated from the Swedish by Siri Andrews, with illustrations by Gustaf Tenggren. Houghton Mifflin Company in Boston and New York issued the book in nineteen twenty seven. A contents list shows over thirty six chapters. Chapter one is Seven Friendless Children. Wolves Tracks stands second. A Swedish famine tale is the heart of the book.

The Spectacle Man, A Bleak Morning, and All Hands on Deck follow. Separated and Where Is Martha Greta fill the early chapters. Two Little Maids, Earnings and the Money Question, and In the Place of the Dead follow. Per Erik and Anna Lisa, Ghosts on the Ice, and In a Den of Thieves deepen the peril. Flight, Fire, and In Their Own Green Cottage close the middle. Children get orphan courage in a hard northern winter.
76261-tales-of-terror:
Tales of Terror is a set of dark tales by Dick Donovan from 1899. Donovan was known for tales of the law and its hunt for crime. The front pages list his past books at their low trade prices. The tales here trade the beat for the chill of the grave.

A woman with strange eyes opens the set, with a tale that flows from hers. A light that burns on a corpse gives an other tale its name. A red bloom, a hoard of sea thieves, and a wolf spring fill the run. A white bird of ill luck and a fire tale come in the midst. The shade of a ruined church house waits near the end of the set. Each tale is short and aims at a cold turn of the spine.
76493-the-new-terror:
Gaston Leroux's New Terror was published by the Macaulay Company at New York in 1926. In England it appeared as The Burgled Heart. George Gage drew the frontispiece, showing Cordelia's form rising between two duelists. The narrator and Cordelia, first cousins, were betrothed by their parents from infancy. At twelve and eight they were already a charming couple to their families. He taught her to ride; she, bookish and gifted, drew and painted anything that caught her eye.

The contents move from betrothal and portrait through the wedding to an unexpected present. Doctor Thurel enters; the narrator discovers a change in Cordelia; a golden chamber and a thief follow. Anxiety about Cordelia's polygon revives, an appointment is kept, and a duel is fought. A terrible tale and the gold axe close the book's contents.
76875-monthly-supplement-of-the-penny-ma:
The hosted text is the monthly supplement of the Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number 16, for May 31 to June 30, 1832. The magazine brought cheap, useful reading to working people. Its pages mix news, history, and views of noted places.

The lead piece treats the Abbey of St Albans. In February a mass of the abbey wall fell through the roof into the aisle. The crash was likened to the loudest thunder. A repair bill of fifteen thousand pounds is named, and a public fund has been opened. The article then turns to the town's past. St Albans stood on the Roman city of Verulam. Great pieces of its wall of Roman tile still stand near the town.
77005-monthly-supplement-of-the-penny-ma:
The Monthly Supplement of the Penny Magazine, number 21, for June 30 to July 31, 1832, is one issue of the cheap journal of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. A plate shows the river front of Hungerford Market in London. The lead piece tells the market rebuilding.

An act of 1830 set up a company of owners for the re founding of Hungerford Market. The site of the old market was bought, with the houses round it. Many of those houses are pulled down. The architect of the new market is Mr C Fowler. The river front is done outside and forms a fine structure. The basement of the centre, next the river, holds the fish market. Wings are meant for taverns, joined by a colonnade with a terrace. Penny readers got town news cheap.
77025-the-house-with-the-silver-door:
The House with the Silver Door is a book for the young by Eva March Tappan. It came out in Boston and New York in 1913 from Houghton Mifflin Company, with pictures. A picture in the front matter shows the children who told the Moon Lady a tale. The book was made as an ebook in honor of the 25th year of Distributed Proofreaders.

The front pages list the other works of the author, all with pictures. Among them are When Knights Were Bold, Dixie Kitten, and An Old, Old Story-Book. The Chaucer Story Book, Letters from Colonial Children, and American Hero Stories stand in the list as well. The Story of the Roman People and The Story of the Greek People are named too. The volume at hand is a story book for children from a writer of tales and histories for the young.
77125-monthly-supplement-of-the-penny-ma:
The Monthly Supplement of the Penny Magazine covers the month from the end of July to the end of August 1832. The Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge issued the magazine at London. This number opens with a statue of James Watt, drawn from the work meant for Westminster Abbey.

The piece tells how three statues honoured the great improver of the steam engine. Chantrey, the sculptor, had modelled Watt from life before his death. A public meeting of 1824, chaired by the prime minister, began the subscription. A French guest marvelled that mere industry should win such thanks. The magazine carried cheap knowledge to working readers each week. Its supplements bound up longer essays like this one for keeping.
77142-monthly-supplement-of-the-penny-ma:
Monthly Supplement of the Penny Magazine, number thirty two, covers September 1 to September 29, 1832. The Penny Magazine was issued by the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. The lead article is the Thames Tunnel, with pictures of a transverse section and a drift way section.

As far back as 1802, the article says, a project was set on foot to open an archway under the Thames. It would run between Rotherhithe and Limehouse, not far from the line of the present tunnel. The engineer chosen was an experienced Cornish miner. He bored at the Horse Ferry and across the river, and reported firmly that the work would not cost as much as had been conceived. A subscription was raised, and a Thames Archway Company formed. Work began with a shaft eleven feet across, then ground troubles grew. Readers get cheap useful knowledge.
77270-monthly-supplement-of-the-penny-ma:
The Monthly Supplement of the Penny Magazine, from the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, devoted one whole number to a memoir of Sir Walter Scott. The number covers September 29 to October 31, 1832. The editors broke their usual plan for the occasion. A portrait from Chantrey's bust heads the sketch.

Scott had died that autumn, and his novels had made his name a household word. The writer knew Scott long and drew on private materials, though space cut the account short. Scott was born at Edinburgh on August 15, 1771, in a house at the head of the College Wynd. His father was a Writer to the Signet. The sketch traces the poet's rise for the magazine's working readers.
77729-the-kedge-anchor:
Kedge Anchor, or Young Sailors' Assistant, is a seamanship manual by William Brady, a sailing master in the United States Navy. The hosted text is the sixth edition, improved and enlarged, issued at New York in eighteen fifty two. Seventy engravings picture the gear and work it treats. Tables of rigging, spars, sails, and cables fill its later part.

Its title page lists its scope: rigging, knotting, splicing, blocks, purchases, and running rigging. The matter serves ships of war and other vessels alike. The book is dedicated to the navy and the merchant service. In his preface Brady owns he is better versed with the marlinespike than with the pen. He wrote the work in hours of rest from his duties, he says.
77765-monsieur-d-or:
John Louis Haney wrote a dramatic fantasy called Monsieur d'Or, printed at Philadelphia in 1910 in an edition limited to two hundred fifty copies. Haney had written a bibliography of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and a study of the name of William Shakespeare. Gold, gold, gold, gold, bright and yellow, hard and cold, chants a verse at the threshold.

Molten, graven, hammered, and rolled, heavy to get and light to hold, hoarded, bartered, bought, and sold, stolen and more, the verse runs on. A black laurel wreath round a flaming torch marks the title page. The play turns the love of gold into a figure, Monsieur d'Or himself, and lets fantasy judge the greed that rules men's lives. Haney gives the book to his parents.
78281-four-billion-dollar-door:
Four-Billion Dollar Door, a science fiction tale by Michael Shaara, tells of Sam Button, who gave his life to be the first man on the Moon. A blurb adds that, in one way, he was. The narrator warns that new history books his boy brings home are already rewriting the tale of Sam Button and the door, and hushing up the funniest part.

Sam was a long, lean man with blond hair that looked stuck on with glue. Townsfolk kidded him as Old Onward and Upward Button and joked that a flying saucer had scared his mother. Kidding never stopped him. He worked through school to a physics degree, then to guided missiles, so that when the chance came he would be readiest of all. Shaara mixes hero worship with dry humor.
78443-adventures-in-error:
Adventures in Error is a book of essays by Vilhjalmur Stefansson, printed at New York by Robert McBride in 1936, in a first edition. Stefansson was the Arctic explorer. His title names his subject: the errors that whole societies agree to believe. Eight essays make the book, from the standardization of error to the history of the bathtub in America.

The first essay states the case against standardized knowledge. Comte tried to coordinate the sciences a century ago, and many have tried since. Yet the accepted facts of a dozen years ago have become the error and folklore of today. You standardize knowledge, and while you are at the job the knowledge changes. Stefansson writes as an explorer who spent his career correcting the maps and the textbooks at once.
78526-incidents-on-a-journey-through-nub:
F Sidney Ensor wrote Incidents on a Journey in Nubia to Darfoor, a survey tale from Africa. W H Allen and Company issued the book in London in eighteen hundred eighty one. Ensor was a civil engineer on the work. A map shows his road from Old Dongola to El Fasher.

Egypt had seized Darfoor late in eighteen hundred seventy four. Ismael Pasha, the Khedive, then asked for a rail survey. Fertile tales from the land spurred the plan. Three old roads were too harsh or too long for rails. A fourth, the Wady Milkh, cut near straight from the Nile. Darfoor sultans had claimed that vale as theirs for two centuries. Ensor rode it with his crew and tells what befell them.
78539-helped-by-a-horse-doctor:
Helped by a Horse Doctor, by Tuttle, is a western tale told in dialect. Ike Harper, the narrator, walks in on a strange scene. His partner, Magpie Simpkins, stands in the cabin facing a fat stranger. The fat man makes signs with raised hands and crossed fingers. Ike takes the stranger for a hypnotist at work. With the Harpers, to think is to act: he bends his gun over the man's head.

Magpie answers by throwing the syrup pitcher, or so Ike guesses. Three shots through the closed door follow. Doc Milliken, the horse doctor, sews Ike's brow with a sack-needle and binding-twine. His verdict on the case is a dry joke: Ike was not hypnotized, he was assassinatized. Tuttle writes pulp west in a loose, comic voice.
78703-translator-s-error:
Translator's Error is a science fiction story by Charles Dye. Its premise hides in its first line: the mistake the men made was a perfectly natural one. The scene is Mars, where a project is at work to rehabilitate the dead planet. A great mural in a hall depicts scenes of the old Martian civilization.

Richard Potterboy, a beefy man with a big red face, runs the meeting with a politician's bluster. Beside him sits a little man with telescopic spectacles, Theodore McGinnis, the newly appointed historian of the Martian Rehabilitation Project. Philip Grisby arrives late and takes Potterboy's scolding in silence. The title warns the reader where the danger lies. Men are reading the records of a vanished race, and a translator's error in that reading may carry a cost none of them can see.
78911-survivor:
Irving E Cox Jr tells a tale of invasion in which gray men from an unknown place overrun the earth. The invaders kill without passion, much as men clear ants from a field they want to plant. Amid the ruin a father gives his small son a gun as the one legacy left to him.

The opening follows Vernon Randall Hume, a corporation lawyer of thirty-five, as he hides from a motor column in a swamp. Wounded, torn, and half mad with fear, he clings to his name and his old life like a charm. Only a day before, he had lunched at his club in a world now gone. Readers get a grim, close study of one man holding onto his mind while his world is wiped out.
78967-journal-of-a-tour-in-asia-minor:
William Martin Leake wrote a journal of a tour in Asia Minor, printed at London in 1824 with a map. His remarks compare the ancient and modern geography of that country. No country now affords so fertile a field of discovery as Asia Minor, the preface says. The traveller there traces vestiges of Grecian art amidst modern desolation.

Unfortunately, no province of the Ottoman empire is more difficult to explore in detail, he owns. The deserted state of the country often puts the common necessaries of travelling out of reach. In European Turkey the Turkish system is somewhat tempered by nearness to civilized Europe. Leake's marches fixed Greek sites for all later map makers.
79105-crowd-horror:
Crowd Horror is a boxing story by Robert Howard, from Argosy All Story Weekly of July 1929. Slade Costigan, a boxer with a slugger punch, stars as the hero of the tale. A deck line says he had everything, if he could fight off one great weakness. The narrator first speaks to him in his dressing room after a two round knockout.

Costigan had just flattened Battling Monaghan when the narrator hurried in to him. Six feet tall, broad shouldered, heavy armed, he shows the true fighting face. One eye is partly closed and his lips are bruised from the last round. Howard pulp energy drives this tale of the ring and its curse.
79386-the-death-s-head-meteor:
Death's Head Meteor is a story by Neil R Jones, from a magazine called Air Wonder Stories dated January nineteen thirty. An editor's note frames it as an aviation story of outer space. Weather changes were little understood not many years ago, the note says. Long range forecasting is only now becoming possible, it adds.

Space flyers will soon need to chart the spaces beyond Earth, the note argues. Meteors and great dust clouds drift between Earth and the sun. Such clouds cut off the sun's radiation and sway our weather, it says. Meteors may also hold strange and valuable elements worth seeking. The tale opens high in a hundred story building. A man sits at a desk before an array of dials. A glass bulb suddenly flares, and an electric spark cracks across a gap.
79533-neka-the-boy-conjuror:
A boys' adventure novel by Captain Ralph Bonehill. Street and Smith published it at New York and London in 1902. The subtitle calls it a mystery of the stage. Neka is a boy conjuror with a travelling circus. Thirty-seven chapters of incident crowd the contents. Storms, stage rows, fairs, and chases recur throughout.

The first chapter is a crash in the storm. Rain lashes a muddy road in near darkness. Bambo's International Circus wagons straggle along it in misery. A friend in need and a stage debut follow quickly. Chapter titles promise a king of fire and a race for money. A lawful guardian appears in the frontispiece caption. Bonehill wrote many such series books for boys.
79731-on-the-edge-of-a-moor:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote a tale of faith set on the edge of a moor. A fourth form came out in London with a church tract house. Le Feuvre wrote Probable Sons and The Carved Cupboard. A front plate shows a man who leaps out and grabs a bridle. A Bible line on bread cast on waters heads the tale.

Wild moor land sets the stage for the folk of the tale. Still land and grey skies open the book in calm words. Trials of heart and home test the faith of each soul. Le Feuvre writes for the young with a soft, firm hand. Her books sold at low cost in long lists of tales. Warm faith and moor air fill this one.
8106-captain-cook-s-journal-during-his-f:
Captain James Cook's journal of his first voyage round the world in HMS Bark Endeavour, 1768 to 1771, appears here in a literal transcription of the original manuscripts, edited by Captain W. J. L. Wharton, hydrographer of the Admiralty, and published in London in 1893. The volume includes maps, facsimiles, and a portrait with Cook's signature, and is dedicated to the Duke of Edinburgh for his interest in the British navy.

The journal records the voyage to Tahiti for the transit of Venus, the charting of New Zealand, and the east coast of Australia, day by day, in Cook's plain seaman's prose. It is the primary source for one of history's great voyages. For readers of exploration, it offers the Pacific as Cook himself saw it, without later romance.
840-lorna-doone-a-romance-of-exmoor:
R. D. Blackmore wrote this romance of Exmoor, where John Ridd, a sturdy Devon farmer, loves Lorna Doone, a maiden of the outlaw clan that haunts the moors. Blackmore calls it a romance, not a history, for its scenes, folk, and times are alike romantic. The tale moves from farm to moor, from love to feud and battle.

John's plain voice carries the story, with humour, dialect, and a love of the land. The Doones, fierce and proud, stand against law and neighbours, and Lorna's fate hangs on the feud. The novel has lasted as a classic English romance, beloved for its heroine, its villain clan, and its wild Exmoor setting.
8550-t-haviland-hicks-senior:
J. Raymond Elderdice wrote T. Haviland Hicks, Senior, for schoolboys, dedicating it to Master Lloyd Elderdice. Contents promise Hicks, wild west bad man, Leave It to Hicks, and Hicks's prodigious prodigy. A letter from Scoop Sawyer follows, with Hicks making a decision, making a speech, starting another mystery, Coach Corridan surprising the eleven, and Theophilus in further adventures.

Hicks, the senior boy, leads school stories in the classic pattern: sports, scrapes, and a wild west reputation tamed by school life. Readers of boys' fiction get a brisk, old-fashioned tale, where a school hero sorts out mysteries and teams alike. The book suits young readers and collectors of school stories.
8578-the-grand-inquisitor:
Feodor Dostoevsky's famous chapter, taken from The Brothers Karamazov, imagines Christ returning to Seville during the Inquisition and being arrested by the Grand Inquisitor. In H. P. Blavatsky's translation, the old churchman argues that people cannot bear freedom, and will trade it for bread, authority, and miracle. Christ answers with silence, and at the end kisses the Inquisitor on the lips.
