The passage stands alone as a fierce debate about faith, power, and human nature, which is why it is so often printed apart from the novel. Dostoevsky, then newly dead when this version appeared, uses the scene to press his deepest question: whether love can survive without force. Readers new to Russian fiction can start here and feel the novelist's full weight in a single short episode.
8729-the-dancing-mouse-a-study-in-animal:
Robert M. Yerkes, instructor in comparative psychology at Harvard, studies the dancing mouse in this first volume of the Animal Behavior Series. The book, dated 1907, grew from an essay that won the Cartwright Prize of the Columbia physicians and surgeons alumni in 1907, comprising its first twelve chapters. Yerkes dedicates it in love and gratitude to his mother, and opens with the mouse's characteristics, origin, and history, its markings and its method of keeping.

Dancing mice spin, circle, and sniff in patterns that made them favourites of fanciers and puzzles for psychologists. Yerkes tests their senses, learning, and behaviour with careful experiments, founding a field that would grow into modern animal psychology. The book remains a landmark of early behaviour study, readable for its clear methods and its affection for its small, whirling subjects, even where later science has moved beyond it.
8931-the-gem-collector:
P. G. Wodehouse published The Gem Collector in Ainslee's Magazine in December 1909. Later revised and republished in 1910 as The Intrusion of Jimmy, also known as A Gentleman of Leisure. A transcriber's note explains that the magazine version had two chapters headed chapter eighteen and ended with chapter nineteen, now relabelled nineteen and twenty. That one word in chapter six has been corrected from pubrescent to putrescent. The story opens in the Savoy Hotel supper room, all brightness and glitter and gaiety.

Sir James Willoughby Pitt, baronet, looks round through cigarette smoke and moodily judges the world flat, despite the geographers. From that bored aristocrat, Wodehouse builds a comedy of jewel theft, imposture, and romance in high society and country houses. Readers who know Wodehouse from Jeeves will recognize the early, breezier voice, and a hero who steals, charms, and reforms himself in the same breath.
9087-eleanor:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote this novel in 1900 and dedicated it to Italy, called here the instructress of the past and delight of the present. Its heroine, Eleanor, lives among English folk in Italy, where love, duty, and faith pull her in hard directions. A young visitor, Lucy Foster, and a priest, Father Benecke, shape the tale's turns.

Ward sets English reserve against Italian warmth, and lets her characters argue out questions of marriage, belief, and the claims of the heart. The prose is earnest and rich in place detail, from villas to loggias. Eleanor remains a good sample of the serious society novel at the turn of the century.
9097-robert-s-rules-of-order-pocket-manu:
Major Henry M. Robert, an officer in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, wrote this pocket manual in 1876 and printed it in Chicago. It sets out parliamentary law based on the rules and practice of Congress, but fitted to ordinary societies, conventions, and clubs. Part one gives rules of order; part two tells how to run a meeting.

For each motion Robert states its aim, its effect, and whether it can be changed or debated, in a set order any chair can follow. The book filled a real need, and it grew into the standard guide still used in meetings today. This first edition shows the system at its plain, practical start.
923-a-sketch-of-the-life-of-brig-gen-fra:
William Dobein James wrote this sketch of Brigadier General Francis Marion and a history of his brigade, from its rise in June 1780 until it disbanded in December 1782. The book adds descriptions of characters and scenes not before published, and an appendix with copies of letters from Marion's own hand.

James, who served with Marion's men, tells of swamp raids, skirmishes, and the hard life of partisans in South Carolina. His account is first-hand, plain, and full of local detail. The volume is a prime source for the Southern war, valued by historians for its eyewitness voice and its documentary appendix.
9457-travels-in-arabia-comprehending-an-:
John Lewis Burckhardt, who died before publication, wrote these travels in Arabia, issued in London in 1829 by the Association for Promoting the Discovery of Africa's Interior. The book covers the Hedjaz territories Muslims regard as sacred, with Mecca and Medina at its heart. An editor's preface links it to Burckhardt's Nubia and Syria volumes.

Those earlier travels won favor for merit and for their editor's fame as scholar and geographer. This volume, long delayed, proves no less worthy, the preface insists. It remains a classic of Arabian travel, careful, observant, and first-hand.
9588-my-summer-with-dr-singletary-part-2:
Part two of Whittier's Tales and Sketches holds My Summer with Dr. Singletary, a fragment of a tale. The piece opens on the doctor's death, then asks why this one man's life should claim our care. Singletary, an old man of odd ways, seldom left his home in later years. Yet death, Whittier writes, lifts the veil and shows the man as God's child, brother to us all.

The fragment meditates on joy and sorrow, pride and folly, and the sympathy owed to every life. Its tone is grave and tender, more essay than plot. A reader gets a short, thoughtful Whittier prose piece, and a glimpse of his Quaker faith in the worth of each soul.
9776-cicero-s-brutus-or-history-of-famou:
Cicero's Brutus, or History of Famous Orators, with his Orator, appears here in E. Jones's English translation, the first in the tongue. Jones notes that Cicero's fame needs no praise, and that the Brutus grew from his retirement during the civil war's African close. Cast as a dialogue, it sketches Greek and Roman speakers down to Cicero's own day. Lives and speeches blend into a hidden epitome of Roman history.

The Orator beside it defines the accomplished speaker, the ideal toward which the histories point. Jones writes for readers new to rhetoric. A reader gets Cicero's own school of eloquence, with lives of orators and a standard for great speech.
9811-the-adventures-of-hugh-trevor:
Thomas Holcroft's novel follows Hugh Trevor, a young man born into a family quarrel over rank and marriage. His rector grandfather disowns his mother for wedding a farmer's son, and Hugh grows up with little money and fewer prospects in late eighteenth-century England.

Told in Hugh's own voice, the story sends him through a string of jobs, patrons, and schemes as he tries to earn a living by his wits. Along the way Holcroft pokes fun at snobbery, the law, the stage, and politics. It is a lively, talkative picture of how a clever outsider climbed, stumbled, and kept going.
a-little-catechism-with-little-verses-an: John Mason gives a little catechism with little verses and little sayings for little children. The book teaches young learners in short lines suited to memory. Mason's other works on family catechizing and gospel doctrine stand behind the volume. The catechism serves parents, schoolmasters, and tutors of youth. Small children can learn the short lines by heart with ease.
a-sketch-of-the-life-of-brig-gen-francis:
William Dobein James, who served as one of Marion's militia, wrote this life of Brigadier General Francis Marion and the history of his brigade. The title page dates the work to April 1821 and covers the brigade from its rise in June 1780 to its end in December 1782. An appendix prints letters between leading men of the day, chiefly from General Greene to Marion.

Four chapters move from Marion's early life through the campaigns of 1780, 1781, and 1782 in South Carolina. James describes marches, ambushes, and the men who rode with the famous partisan leader. Because the author was there, his account stays close to the ground and to daily hardship.
a-woman-s-way-through-unknown-labrador:
Mina Hubbard's A Woman's Way Through Unknown Labrador tells how she finished the journey that killed her husband. Leonidas Hubbard starved in the Labrador interior in 1903, attempting the route from North-West River to Ungava Bay. In 1905 his widow set out to complete it. With George Elson, her husband's Cree guide, she traveled six hundred miles of unmapped river. The route ran up the Naskapi and down the George River to Ungava. Her party's race with the rival Dillon Wallace expedition gives the narrative its pulse.

Inside, the book is survey and elegy at once: maps corrected, rapids run, and a grief carried to where it happened. She was the first woman of European descent to cross Labrador's interior. Readers get a classic of women's exploration literature, written plainly by a widow who navigated by her husband's unfinished map and her own considerable nerve.
an-episode-under-the-terror:
Honoré de Balzac begins on the evening of January 22, 1793, the day after the execution of Louis XVI, as snow falls on a deserted Paris street. An old lady makes her way to a pastry shop in the Faubourg Saint Martin. She is a nun in hiding, and she comes for a box that is more than it seems. Clara Bell and others translated the tale.

A stranger follows her home through the snow, and fear gives way to a strange gratitude. The man, marked by the Terror's violence, seeks one small act of peace from the sisters. Balzac builds the short tale on dread, faith, and an uneasy mercy shown between enemies.
ashton-kirk-investigator:
John T. McIntyre's detective novel appeared at Philadelphia in 1910, with pictures by Ralph L. Boyer. Its hero, Ashton-Kirk, is a wealthy young investigator whom friends consult when a case baffles the police. Early chapters bring his companion Pendleton to his door, followed by Miss Edyth Vale, who lays a troubling matter before him and asks his help.

Clues gather around portraits of General Wayne, a Schwartz-Michael bayonet, and the confined violinist Antonio Spatola. Newspapers stir the case while Ashton-Kirk questions witnesses, inspects rooms, and tests Stillman's rival theory. Twenty-six chapters of interviews and deductions end with the investigator explaining why events fell as they did, in the formal manner of classic detective fiction.
bobby-of-the-labrador:
Dillon Wallace wrote Bobby of the Labrador, a boys' adventure novel from A C McClurg with pictures by Frank E Schoonover. Wallace knew the Labrador coast from his own trips, and the tale opens with a boat that comes down from the sea. A found child, Bobby, grows up with Skipper Ed.

Wolf packs, a foolhardy shot, and an iceberg that turns over test the boy. Bobby drifts on open sea, winters through famine, and is marooned in an Arctic blizzard. Jimmy's sacrifice and a lonely journey under drifting snow mark the late chapters. The mystery of Bobby's birth resolves at the close. Young readers get hard northern facts on ice, hunger, and dogs inside a fast tale of loyalty and grit.
boy-scouts-in-a-submarine-or-searching-a:
Boy Scouts in a Submarine, or Searching an Ocean Floor, by G Harvey Ralphson, sends its scout troop under the sea in the submarine Sea Lion. Ralphson, whose series also put the boys in an airship, in Mexico, and on motor cycles, opens lost on an ocean floor, with a conflict of authority aboard. The frontispiece shows the Sea Lion equal to a night long chase, which sets the book's pace at once.

Contents promise the dandy submarine, a wolf on the trail, two wolves in a pen, and a night on the ocean floor. Jimmie, the troop's irrepressible scout, goes hunting on the bottom. He demands a medal and proves foolish like a fox. Jack makes a discovery. The secret of the hold waits its turn. Ralphson's formula mixes naval technology, adult villains, and scout resourcefulness: boys on guard under the sea, solving with pluck what professionals cannot.
britannica-1911-abettor: Abettor is the headword of a short law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry traces the word to Old French abeter, to bait or urge dogs on, likely from a Scandinavian root meaning to cause to bite. In law an abettor urges, helps, or backs another in a crime. Presence at the act sets him apart from an accessory. Abettors count as principals and take the same punishment, unless statute says otherwise.
britannica-1911-adam-melchior:
Melchior Adam (died 1622) was a German divine and biographer. He was born at Grotkau in Silesia. The college of Brieg gave him his education. He became a Protestant during those years. In 1598 he went to Heidelberg. Various scholastic appointments occupied him there. His life's work was collective biography. He wrote lives of German scholars of the sixteenth century. Most of his subjects were theologians.

Five volumes appeared between 1615 and 1620. Heidelberg and Frankfort shared the publishing. Only twenty divines of other countries joined them. All his divines are Protestants, the entry notes. Bayle commended Adam's industry as a biographer. Bayle also acknowledged his own debts to Adam. The lives keep faults, yet remain useful. Scholars still consult them for that century.
britannica-1911-aicard-jean-francois-vic:
Aicard, Jean Francois Victor, a French poet and dramatist born in 1848, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Toulon on the fourth of February 1848, the son of Jean Aicard, a journalist of some distinction. The son began early, publishing Les Jeunes Croyances in 1867. A one-act play of his reached the Marseilles stage in 1870.

His poems include Poemes de Provence and La Chanson de l'enfant, both crowned by the Academy, plus a Provencal idyll, Miette et Nore. His most successful play was Le Pere Lebonnard, first produced at the Theatre Libre in 1890. Novels followed, among them Le Roi de Camargue and L'Ame d'un enfant. He also wrote La Venus de Milo, an account of the famous statue's discovery drawn from unpublished documents.
britannica-1911-aichinger-gregor:
Aichinger, Gregor, a German composer who lived from about 1565 to 1628, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry ranks him among the greatest German composers of the Golden Age. In 1584 he became organist to the Fugger family of Augsburg, the great banking house. He had taken holy orders before that appointment, though music, not church duty, drove his travels.

In 1599 Aichinger went to Rome for a two-year visit made for musical reasons. Proske, editing the great anthology Musica Divina, called him a priest of Regensburg. Proske was inclined to give him the palm, the highest praise, for the devout and unaffected mastery of his style. The entry agrees that impression holds up. The beautiful, somewhat quaint works of Aichinger printed in that anthology bear it out fully.
britannica-1911-angkor:
Forest north of Cambodia's Great Lake, Tonle-Sap, hides Angkor, the stone remains of the old Khmer civilisation. Two sites dominate: the walled town Angkor-Thom and the temple Angkor-Vat, both on the right bank of the Siem-Reap river. Lesser ruins dot the area, joined by an ancient stone bridge.

Building at Angkor-Thom ran from about 860 to toward 900. Its rectangle stretches nearly two miles each way inside walls twenty to thirty feet high, pierced by five grand gates. Within stand the royal palace grounds with the pyramid Phimeanakas, a terrace rich in relief carving, and the Bayon temple with its gallery colonnades. The account walks through each great structure, then credits the French and English travellers whose books brought the ruins to wide notice.
britannica-1911-ann-arbor:
Ann Arbor is a Michigan city. It is the county-seat of Washtenaw county. The Huron river flows through it. Detroit lies about thirty-eight miles east. Population grew fast in the late nineteenth century. It reached 14,509 in 1900. By 1910 it stood at 14,817. Foreign-born residents formed a notable share. Two railways and an electric line serve it.

The University of Michigan defines the city. That institution opened in 1837. Attractive residences fill many districts. The Huron valley offers picturesque views. Farms and orchards surround the town. The river supplies good water-power. Factories make agricultural implements and carriages. Furniture, pianos, organs, and pottery follow. Settlers founded Ann Arbor in 1824. Its name honours two founders' wives. Both women were named Ann.
britannica-1911-archchancellor:
Archchancellor means chief chancellor of an empire. The Holy Roman Empire used the title chiefly. It named the empire's highest dignitary. Medieval usage sometimes meant a chancellors' supervisor. Hincmar of Reims mentions a summus cancellarius. His work describes the Carolingian court order. A charter of Lothair I dates to 844. It names Agilmar of Vienne as archchancellor. Otto the Great's kingdom kept the office.

The office became attached to Mainz's archbishopric. Otto restored the empire in 962. A separate chancery organised Italian affairs then. Cologne's archbishop took Italy's archchancellorship early. Theory assigned German business to Mainz. Italian business fell to Cologne in theory. Practice often differed from that theory. The entry compares the office to Germany's modern chancellor. A Tübingen study of 1906 noted that resemblance.
britannica-1911-asor:
Asor is the topic of a brief article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is Hebrew for ten. It names a stringed tool of ten strings that the Bible names three times. Each time it stands next to the word nebel, a kind of harp.

The article weighs what the old Greek and Latin versions made of the word. It notes that no one is sure what the asor looked like. The best guess given is that it was a form of the nebel with ten strings in place of the usual twelve. Books on Bible music are listed for readers who want more.
britannica-1911-assessor:
Assessor comes from a Latin word for one who sits beside another. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it first to a trained lawyer in Rome. He sat by a governor or judge to guide him in the laws. That helper role still shaped uses of the word in later courts.

In Scotland town judges still use trained assessors for civil work. English high courts may call in assessors for any case by law. Sea cases often use Trinity House elders for their sea skill. In the United States the word names tax and rate valuers instead. In France and Germany it names junior judges on a court bench.
britannica-1911-averruncator:
Averruncator names a form of long shears used in tree work for pruning off high branches. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces the verb averruncate to Latin averruncare, to ward off or remove mischief.

From warding off harm, the word slid into senses like weeding ground and pruning vines. A guessed link to Latin ab, off, and eruncare, to weed out, even produced the spelling aberuncate. The New English Dictionary, the entry notes, regards that derivation as impossible, leaving the tool's name a small lesson in how word histories can mislead.
britannica-1911-bachelor:
Bachelor, in its widest sense a young man, comes through Old French from medieval Latin baccalarius, a word whose own root is still disputed. The entry traces it, probably, to the tenant of a baccalaria, a grazing farm, and notes one thread through all its later senses: subordination, a lower rank.

From that root the word spread to set classes of juniors. It named young monks and new canons in the church. It named knights bachelor, too poor or too young to fight under their own banner. From 13th-century Paris under Pope Gregory IX, it named holders of the first university degree. Those scholars were still classed as pupils on the road to master. Young man, farm tenant, junior knight, and first degree all hang on the one chain of meanings.
britannica-1911-baillie-robert-scottish-:
Baillie, Robert (d. 1684), called Baillie of Jerviswood, was a Scottish conspirator, son of George Baillie of St John's Kirk in Lanarkshire. Rescuing his brother-in-law, a Presbyterian minister illegally seized by an informer, in 1676 earned him a heavy fine and four months in prison.

Planning emigration to South Carolina in despair at his country, Baillie instead went to London and dealt with Monmouth's and Russell's party for redress. Arrested after the Rye House Plot surfaced, he honestly would not deny talk of a Scottish rising, though no proof tied him to the plot itself. Scotland fined him £6,000, held him close, then tried him for treason on 23 December 1684, found him guilty, and hanged him the same afternoon at Edinburgh's market cross. His treatment was long remembered as a Stuart crime.
britannica-1911-balaguer-victor:
Balaguer, Victor (1824-1901), was a Spanish politician and author. Barcelona was his birthplace and university. His precocity was truly remarkable. A first play reached Barcelona's stage at fourteen. A second play won him public crowning at nineteen.

From 1843 Balaguer led Barcelona's Liberals. He edited El Conseller as its proprietor. Catalan local patriotism grew under him. His first Catalan poem came in 1857. It addressed the Virgin of Montserrat. The troubadour of Montserrat became his pseudonym. He helped restore the Floral Games in 1859. Madrid politics then claimed him fully. In 1871 he became minister of colonies. Finance followed in 1872 for him. His history of Catalonia abounds in faults. It is inaccurate, partial, and unscientific. Attractive writing saved its influence nonetheless. Catalan pioneers keep his name alive.
britannica-1911-bar-harbor:
Bar Harbor is a well known summer resort in Hancock county, Maine, on the east side of Mount Desert Island. It sits on Frenchman's Bay in the township of Eden, some forty-five miles south-east of Bangor. The village had about 2,000 people in 1910, with far more in the summer season. Trains of the Maine Central line serve it. Ships also run to New York, Boston, and Portland.

The summer air is cool, often too cool for sea bathing, but the village has a large open-air salt water bath. Hills from 1,000 to 1,500 feet high ring the coast. The shore has deep inlets, bold cliffs, rocky isles, clear lakes, and wooded glens. Fine hotels and costly homes line the shore and the slopes behind it.
britannica-1911-bardoux-agenor:
Agénor Bardoux (1820–1897) was a French statesman, a native of Bourges who set up as an advocate at Clermont and openly declared his republican sympathies. He was elected deputy to the National Assembly in 1871 and re-elected in 1876 and 1877. In the chamber he led the left centre, standing firm for the republic but against anti-clericalism.

After the coup of 16 May, Bardoux ranked among the leaders of the famous 363 deputies. In December 1877 he became minister of public instruction and proposed republican laws, notably on compulsory primary schooling. He resigned in 1879 and lost his seat in 1881, but in December 1882 he was named senator for life. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his essays on the légistes and on Montlosier.
britannica-1911-barnum-phineas-taylor:
Phineas Taylor Barnum (1810–1891) was an American showman, born at Bethel, Connecticut, on 5 July 1810, son of an inn and store keeper. He began as a storekeeper himself and dabbled in the lottery mania of the day. In 1829 he started a weekly paper at Danbury, the Herald of Freedom. It brought him libel suits and a spell in prison.

New York in 1834 opened his real career. In 1835 he bought and exhibited Joyce Heth. She was said to have nursed George Washington and to be over 160 years old. She died in 1836, proved to be no more than seventy. In 1841 Barnum bought Scudder's American Museum and made it one of the most popular shows in the country. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his triumph with General Tom Thumb from 1842.
britannica-1911-baross-gabor:
Gabor Baross (1848–1892) was a Hungarian statesman, born at Trencsén on 6 July 1848 and educated at Esztergom, where he for a time taught. As chief notary of his county he built a local reputation, and in 1875 he entered parliament. He attached himself to Kálmán Tisza and stayed loyal even when the Bosnian occupation drove other supporters away.

His defence of the government then first showed his many-sided ability and genius for sustained hard work. Economics made his fame: secretary to the ministry of ways and communications in 1883, he mastered that hard department with great speed. On Kemény's retirement in 1886 he became minister himself. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his drive to remake Hungary's transport and trade systems.
britannica-1911-benfey-theodor:
Theodor Benfey (1809–1881) was a German philologist, son of a Jewish trader at Nörten near Göttingen, born in January 1809. Meant for medicine, he was turned to language study by his father’s careful teaching of Hebrew. Brilliant work at Göttingen and a year at Munich under Schelling and Thiersch set his course.

A wager pushed Benfey into Sanskrit: he learned enough in a few weeks to review a new book on it, a feat he later matched with Russian. His Lexicon of Greek Roots won the Volney prize, and from then Sanskrit led his work. He edited the Sāma-veda in 1848 and died at Göttingen in 1881, still preparing a grammar of Vedic Sanskrit.
britannica-1911-benton-harbor:
Benton Harbor is a city of Berrien county, Michigan, on the Saint Joseph river, a mile from Lake Michigan and joined to it by a ship canal. It lies near the state’s south-west corner, across from St Joseph. Its people numbered 3,692 in 1890 and 9,185 by 1910.

Three railways, electric lines and seasonal steamboats to Chicago and Milwaukee serve the city, and mineral springs draw visitors. The Israelite House of David, a religious community founded in 1903, sits near by. Fruit is the town’s great trade: peaches, grapes, pears, cherries and berries from the farms round it, plus baskets, cider and preserves made in the city. Known as Bronson Harbor until 1865, it became a city in 1891.
britannica-1911-bergk-theodor:
Theodor Bergk (1812–1881) was a German philologist born at Leipzig and taught there by G. Hermann. He lectured at the Halle orphan school from 1835, then held posts at Neustrelitz, Berlin and Cassel. In 1842 he succeeded K. F. Hermann as professor of classical literature at Marburg, moving later to Freiburg and back to Halle.

Bergk resigned his chair in 1868 and gave his last years to study at Bonn, dying at Ragatz in 1881. His fame rests on Greek literature, above all the Greek lyric poets. His Poetae Lyrici Graeci and his history of Greek literature are counted standard works, and his editions run from Anacreon and Aristophanes to Sophocles and a lyric anthology.
britannica-1911-berlioz-hector:
Hector Berlioz (1803–1869) was a French composer born at Côte-Saint-André, near Grenoble. His father was a physician who wanted him trained in medicine. The boy studied harmony in secret instead. In Paris he broke with medicine for good. He sang in a theatre chorus to live, then entered the Conservatoire. There he studied composition under Reicha and Lesueur.

The 1911 Britannica biography traces his self-education through Beethoven, Gluck, and Weber. It covers his mature works in turn. These include the Symphonie fantastique, the Requiem, and La Damnation de Faust. It also treats his treatise on instrumentation. Richard Strauss later revised that treatise. Early biographies that fixed his reputation close the entry.
britannica-1911-bijnor:
Bijnor, also spelled Bijnaur, is a town and district of British India in the United Provinces. The town stands about three miles from the left bank of the Ganges. Its 1901 population was 17,583, and it holds a large trade in sugar. American Methodists run a mission with aided schools there. An English high school for boys also serves the town. The district around it covers 1,791 square miles.

The district is mostly a level plain rising north toward the Himalayas. The Koh and Ramganga rivers cross it, and the Ganges bounds it west. Its 1901 population was 779,451, down two percent in the decade. Sugar is the great export, helped by small canals and hill streams. The 1911 Britannica entry closes with the district's Mutiny history. The nawab of Najibabad held Bijnor from June 1857 until British forces beat him at Nagina in April 1858.
britannica-1911-billroth-albert-christia:
Albert Christian Theodor Billroth (1829–1894) was a Viennese surgeon, born at Bergen on the island of Rügen. His family was of Swedish origin. He studied at Greifswald, Göttingen, and Berlin, taking his doctorate in 1852. A study tour took him to medical schools from Vienna to London. He assisted the surgeon Langenbeck at Berlin from 1853 to 1860. A surgery chair at Zürich followed, then Vienna in 1867.

At Vienna he spent the rest of his working life. The 1911 Britannica entry ranks him among the most distinguished surgeons of his day. His boldness as an operator matched his skill, and no emergency shook his coolness. In 1887 he gained a rare seat in the Austrian Herrnhaus. His surgical pathology textbook of 1863 ran through many editions and languages. He was also a fine pianist and a close friend of Brahms.
britannica-1911-butler-samuel-author:
Samuel Butler is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English author born in Nottinghamshire in eighteen thirty five. His grandfather is the bishop in the entry just before this one. He was schooled at Shrewsbury and at Cambridge and shone in classics.

The entry tells how doubt kept him from the church post his kin had planned. He sailed to New Zealand and ran sheep on high rough land there. In less than five years he came home with a small store of funds. That wild land gave him the scene for a famed mock tale of a lost land. A late sequel took the same hero back to that strange realm.
britannica-1911-canis-major:
Canis Major, the Great Dog, is an astronomy article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The grouping of stars sits south of the Zodiac, just below and behind the heels of Orion. A second, smaller dog grouping follows Orion as well. The Milky Way runs between the two.

Most of the entry centres on Sirius, the chief star of the Great Dog and the brightest star in the sky. The name is linked to Greek words for scorching, and one writer tied it to a word meaning the glittering one. Sirius and Procyon, the chief star of the Little Dog, were paired as two glitterers in old times. The article also weighs whether Sirius is the star meant by certain Hebrew words in the Old Testament.
britannica-1911-cawdor:
Cawdor is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a village and parish of Nairnshire, Scotland. The parish counted 925 people in 1901. The village stands five miles south south west of Nairn. Its castle is famed as the scene, by the tradition Shakespeare spread, of the murder of King Duncan by Macbeth, thane of Cawdor, in 1040. The entry dismisses the tale. The oldest part of the castle dates from 1454 and had no predecessor.

The castle stands on the rocky bank of Cawdor Burn. Its massive keep with small turrets is the oldest part. Buildings of the seventeenth century form two sides of a square. The entry also describes Kilravock Castle, a mile and a half west. The Roses have held it since 1293, father succeeding son without a break. Nearly every Rose bore the name Hugh. Queen Mary was received there in 1562. Prince Charles Edward stayed four days before Culloden.
britannica-1911-censor:
Censor is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Roman magistracy. The censors were two officials who ran the census. They registered each citizen to fix the duties he owed the community. The name comes from censere, to assess. Varro derived census from arbitrium, free discretion. That root idea of discretionary power never left the office. In time it attached itself more to morals than to burdens.

The entry treats the censorship as Rome's main tool for state control of conduct. Rome had sumptuary laws, but other magistrates enforced those. The censorship handled morals in a simple and complete way. It was said to begin in 443 B.C., to free the consuls from registration work. A law of 434 B.C. fixed the term at eighteen months. The office was at first patrician only. A plebeian censor appears in 351 B.C. From 131 B.C. both censors could be plebeian.
britannica-1911-chancellor:
Chancellor, a title borne by officers in most lands shaped by Roman rule, is traced in a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The duties bound to the title shift a great deal by time and place. Rank shifts just as much. The first chancellors were ushers in Roman courts of law.

Those ushers sat at the lattice screens that parted judge and counsel from the crowd. In the later eastern empire they rose to the work of notaries. Frankish kings took up the Roman model for their courts and coin. Under them the chancellors served a great officer who kept the seal. In time the chief chancellor became the kings head notary and seal keeper. Since learning then sat with the clergy, a cleric most often held the post. A bishop held it from the reign of Louis the Pious.
britannica-1911-charles-ii-roman-emperor:
Charles the Second, called the Bald, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was Roman emperor and king of the West Franks. He lived from 823 to 877. He was the son of the emperor Louis the Pious and his second wife, Judith.

His father tried to assign him a kingdom of his own. First came Alamannia in 829. Then came the land between the Meuse and the Pyrenees in 839. Both grants were at the cost of his half-brothers, Lothair and Louis. The two rose against the plan. When the emperor died in 840, war broke out among his sons. Charles joined with his brother Louis the German against Lothair. The allies beat him in the bloody victory of Fontenoy in June 841. The article opens the long tale of a realm split among heirs.
britannica-1911-charles-iii-roman-empero:
Charles the Third, called the Fat (832-888), was a Roman emperor and king of the West Franks, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells of his rise and his failings. He was the youngest of three sons of Louis the German. From his father he got the kingdom of Swabia. When his brothers Carloman and Louis died in turn, in 881 and 882, the whole of his father's lands came to him.

In 881 Pope John the Eighth crowned him emperor at Rome. Facing Norsemen camped in Friesland, he chose to pay them off rather than fight. In 884 the death of Carloman brought him the west Frankish realm as well, making his rule wide but weak. He blinded his rival Hugh of Alsace after taking him by treachery. For all his six trips into Italy, the entry says, he could not settle that land or free it from attack.
britannica-1911-charles-iv-roman-emperor:
Charles the Fourth, Roman emperor and king of Bohemia, was born at Prague on 14 May 1316 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of John of Luxemburg, king of Bohemia. At age seven he went to the French court of his uncle. There he took the name Charles, learned five tongues, and wed Blanche.

War in Italy with his father gave him early field craft in 1331. Back in Bohemia he ruled Moravia and fought for Tirol. In 1346 some princes chose him as German king against Louis the Fourth. He made wide pledges to Pope Clement the Sixth. That same year his father fell at the battle of Crecy, and Charles left the field wounded.
britannica-1911-charles-v-roman-emperor:
Charles the Fifth, emperor and king, opens a vast life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ghent in 1500, he was Philip of Burgundy's son. His mother Joanna was a child of Ferdinand and Isabella. Philip died in 1506 and left the boy his Netherlands lands. Margaret of Austria ruled those lands as his guard and guide.

Charles was declared of age in the Netherlands in 1515. Ferdinand's death in 1516 opened the Spanish crown to his house. In 1518 the cortes hailed him king with his mother at Castile. Maximilian's death then brought him the Habsburg lands in full. In 1519, against Francis of France, he won the imperial crown. Aix saw his crowning in October of the year 1520.
britannica-1911-charles-vi-roman-emperor:
Charles the Sixth is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Roman emperor born at Vienna in sixteen eighty five. He was the second son of an emperor by a third marriage. When the Spanish line of his house died out, he claimed its crown.

The entry tells how he was hailed as king in Vienna and sailed to Spain to fight for the throne. Most of his years there were spent in one loyal province. The entry finds him firm in will but weak as a war prince. He was too proud to take good advice and too soft with flatterers. His claim sparked a great war that is treated in its own entry.
britannica-1911-charles-vii-roman-empero:
Charles the Seventh, also called Charles Albert of Bavaria, gets a life story in the 1911 Britannica. Born in sixteen ninety seven, he was held at Vienna as a boy while Bavaria was held by foes. He fought the Turks at Belgrade and wed Maria Amelia of Austria. The match forced his house to back the claim of Maria Theresa to the Habsburg lands.

Once he ruled Bavaria from seventeen twenty six, high court costs drained his funds. He still chased the Austrian lands in secret with French help. Crowned emperor in seventeen forty two, he lost Bavaria to Austrian troops and ruled as a pawn of his allies.
britannica-1911-cherbuliez-charles-victo:
Cherbuliez, Charles Victor (1829–1899) was a French novelist and writer on many subjects, born at Geneva on 19 July 1829. His father André taught classics at the university there, and the family came from French Protestant refugees. Victor studied at Paris, Bonn and Berlin, taught at Geneva, and later took French nationality again. He joined the Academy in 1881 and died on 1 July 1899.

His first book appeared in 1860 and came out again in 1864 as Un Cheval de Phidias, a study of art in ancient Athens. Novels such as Le Comte Kostia, Miss Ravel and Samuel Brohl et Cie first ran in the Revue des deux mondes. For that journal he also wrote political pieces as G. Valbert. The entry praises his fresh, honest books, his wide knowledge and his clear, correct style.
britannica-1911-cleitor:
Cleitor was a town of old Greece in Arcadia, in the part that now maps to a district of the western Peloponnese. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it in a rich plain south of the highest peak of its range, near a stream of its own name. Close by stood a spring whose waters were said to kill a mans taste for wine.

The entry calls the town a place of weight in Arcadia, whose folk were famed for love of free rule. It spread its land over towns round it, fought in a great war of the age, and helped found a new joint city. As a league member it stood a siege, hosted league meets, and struck its own coin down to a late emperors reign. Its walled ruins still stand.
britannica-1911-cold-harbor:
Cold Harbor, a killing ground of the American Civil War, is set down in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Old and New Cold Harbor lie in Hanover county, Virginia. They stand ten miles north-east of Richmond, the South's capital. From late May to mid June of 1864 the armies clashed there. Grant led the Union force and Lee held a dug-in line.

The main Union attack fell on the third of June. Three corps charged and were stopped in eight minutes. An order to charge again was not obeyed at the front. The men there saw the strength of the line too well. As many as five thousand men fell in one hour. Grant lost fourteen thousand men across the whole fight.
britannica-1911-coleridge-samuel-taylor:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) was an English poet and philosopher, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens his life at his father’s vicarage. He was born on the twenty first of October 1772 at Ottery St Mary in Devonshire. His father, the Reverend John Coleridge, was a man of some mark. The father was known for great scholarship and simplicity of character.

John Coleridge ran the grammar school of the parish and served as its vicar. He held both posts from 1760 until his death in 1781. The poet was the youngest child of his father’s second wife. His mother, Anne Bowdon, had great good sense, the entry says. She was keenly ambitious for the success of her sons. On the death of his father, the boy gained a presentation to Christ’s Hospital school.
britannica-1911-coleridge-sir-john-taylo:
Sir John Taylor Coleridge, an English judge who lived from 1790 to 1876, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the nephew of the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Born at Tiverton in Devon, he had a brilliant career at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He was called to the bar in 1819.

Coleridge briefly edited the Quarterly Review in 1824, then gave the post to Lockhart. His fine edition of Blackstones Commentaries came out in 1825. He became a judge of the kings bench in 1835 and served for more than twenty years. He left the bench in 1858 and joined the privy council. In old age he wrote a warm memoir of his friend John Keble, which ran to three editions in a year. His eldest son became lord chief justice of England. His second son became a famed Jesuit writer.
britannica-1911-collector: Collector is a short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a class of officers, most of all in British India. There the word names the chief officer of a whole district of land. The post takes its name from the task of gathering the land tax. The same officer holds court powers and rules his district with a near free hand. In some provinces a deputy holds the same duties under a split title.
britannica-1911-condor:
The condor, Sarcorhamphus gryphus, is an American vulture and near the largest of living flying birds. Early writers gave it a size beyond the truth. It runs about four feet from beak tip to tail tip. Wing span runs about nine feet and, the entry holds, never past twelve feet. Head and neck bear no feathers at all.

The male wears a comb of bare skin on his flattened crown. Loose skin on his neck folds into a wattle. Adult dress is plain black, save for a white frill at the neck base. White patches mark some wing feathers as well. The middle toe is much drawn out, and the hind toe stays slight. Talons are straight and blunt, of little use for seizing prey. The female, against the rule among birds of prey, is smaller than the male. Carrion is the bird's chosen food.
britannica-1911-confessor:
Confessor is a word of the Christian church used in two senses. In the first sense it names a person whose holy life and death earn a set fame for sanctity. In the second sense it names a priest with power to hear confessions. The first sense came first in time. It was at times used loosely for all martyrs in the early church.

Strict use gave the name to a tighter class. It fit those who bore torment for the faith and then died in peace. When the age of torment passed, the sense grew wider still. Custom joined the name to holy men of the past at large. In time the Holy See kept the right to grant the title. King Edward of England is the famed case of a formal grant. The second sense links back to the entry on confession.
britannica-1911-cousin-victor:
Victor Cousin (1792–1867) was a French philosopher, son of a watchmaker, born in Paris on 28 November 1792. At ten he went to the Lycée Charlemagne in the Quartier Saint Antoine. He studied there until he was eighteen. The school crowned him in the old hall of the Sorbonne for a Latin oration. That prize came in a general contest of his school fellows.

Classical training at the lycée bent him toward literature. His Greek already stood out among his peers. He passed from the lycée to the Normal School of Paris. There Laromiguière lectured on philosophy at the time. Cousin later wrote that the day in 1811 when he first heard that teacher decided his whole life. Gratitude fills his account of that hour. The entry runs to near 49,000 bytes from there. It traces his school of thought and its wide sway in French teaching.
britannica-1911-crantor:
Crantor, a Greek thinker of the Old Academy, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was born most likely near the mid fourth century before Christ, at Soli in Cilicia. He studied at Athens with Polemo in the school of Xenocrates. He was the first man to write notes on Plato.

His famed work On Grief was a letter of comfort to a friend, Hippocles, on the death of his children. Parts of it live on in Plutarch and in Cicero, who praised it in the highest terms. Crantor gave most of his care to ethics, the study of how to live. He ranked goods as virtue first, then health, joy, and wealth.
britannica-1911-csiky-gregor:
Gregor Csiky (1842–1891) was a Hungarian dramatist born at Pankota in the county of Arad on 8 December 1842. He studied Catholic theology at Pest and Vienna and taught in the Priests' College at Temesvár from 1870 to 1878. In 1878 he left that church for the Evangelical Church and took up literature. Novels and church history came first and won some notice. Then he turned to the stage, where his success was instant.

Csiky's prize play, Az ellenállhatatlan, showed his marks of directness, freshness, and realistic vigour. A quick run of plays followed, among them Proletariate, Bubbles, Two Loves, and The Bashful. Each seized one feature or type of modern life and pressed it with unusual force. His diction stayed chaste and well balanced, a fruit, the entry suggests, of classical study. His translations of Sophocles and Plautus rank among the best Magyar versions of the classics. He died at Budapest on 19 November 1891.
britannica-1911-cultivator:
A cultivator, also called a scuffler, scarifier, or grubber, is a farm implement for breaking up land or stirring it after ploughing. The first all-iron model, Finlayson's grubber of about 1820, was a large harrow with curved teeth on wheels. It filled the gap between plough and harrow. The grubber stirred soil deeply without turning it over, and brought weeds unbroken to the surface. That double action set the pattern for all later forms.

The chief modern gain has been springy tines, made of spring steel or fitted with springs, which shake as they work. Rows of curved tines hang from a frame, raised or lowered by a lever. Two wheels stop the tines from digging too deep. Points or broad shares fit the stems, to stir soil or to lift weeds and clean the surface. Disk models use revolving disks, and steam power can drive the machine.
britannica-1911-curator:
Curator is a Latin word for one who takes care, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. In Roman law a curator guarded a spendthrift or a person of unsound mind. More often the word meant the man in charge of the estate of a youth past childhood but under age twenty five. Such youths were called minors in the legal sense.

While a tutor cared for the person of a child, the curator cared for the wealth. The term lives on in Scots law for the guard of a youth in the later stage of minority. Under the Roman empire the title was also borne by many state officers. Some ran the corn and oil supply of Rome, some kept order in its fourteen districts, and some had charge of the great water channels of the city.
britannica-1911-delisle-leopold-victor:
Léopold Victor Delisle, a French bibliophile and historian born in 1826, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Valognes, in Manche, in October 1826. At the École des Chartes his career was remarkably brilliant. His leaving thesis dealt with public revenues in Normandy in the twelfth century.

To the history of his native province he devoted his early works. One study covered the condition of the farming class in medieval Normandy. It condensed a huge mass of facts drawn from local archives. It was reprinted in 1905 without change, and remains authoritative. In November 1852 he entered the manuscript department of the national library. Of that library he became head in 1874. The article follows a scholar whose life was spent among old charters and records. His Normandy of the middle ages was rebuilt from its own papers.
britannica-1911-ecuador:
Ecuador, a republic of South America, is the subject of a long country article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Colombia bounds it on the north and north-east, and Peru on the south-east and south. The Pacific Ocean washes its western shore. The opening section deals wholly with its borders, which were still unsettled in 1909.

Large tracts were claimed by all three republics at once. A pact of 1894 named the Spanish sovereign to settle the disputes, but nothing came of it. In 1904 Colombia and Ecuador agreed to put their quarrel to the German emperor. The article warns that the maps of Ecuador are very faulty. They draw its lands reaching east to the frontier of Brazil. In fact Peru held much of that eastern ground, along the Napo river. What Ecuador truly held east of the Andes was a wedge between two rivers.
britannica-1911-equator:
Equator is the great circle round the earth set midway between the two poles. A 1911 Britannica entry gives the word roots and then sorts three kinds of equator. The name comes from a Latin verb meaning to make equal in measure. The land equator splits the globe into north and south halves of equal span.

Its plane stands square to the axis of the earth in the entry account. The sky equator is where that same plane cuts the dome of heaven. It stands midway between the sky poles just as on earth below. The magnetic equator is the line where the downward pull of earth magnetism fades to nil.
britannica-1911-euphranor: Euphranor of Corinth worked in the middle of the fourth century B.C., says a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the one Greek artist who shone as both sculptor and painter. Pliny lists his works. His paintings include a cavalry battle, Theseus, and the feigned madness of Odysseus. His statues include Paris, Leto with her children, and Philip and Alexander in chariots. The entry notes his care for proportion, his leaner body forms, his love of heroic themes, and his written treatise on proportions.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-i-emperor:
Ferdinand the First, Roman emperor, who lived from 1503 to 1564, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Alcalá de Henares in Spain. His father was Philip the Handsome, son of Maximilian, and his mother was Joanna, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile and Aragon.

Raised in Spain, Ferdinand was the pet of his grandfather, who hoped to build him a Spanish and Italian kingdom. That plan failed, as did a later bid to make him, not his elder brother Charles, the next emperor. Charles took the empire and all the family lands, and Ferdinand had to accept a lesser place. In 1521 Charles granted him the Austrian archduchies and duchies, with Tirol and the Habsburg lands in south west Germany soon added. He also wed Anna of Hungary at Linz that year.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-ii-emperor:
Ferdinand the Second, Roman emperor who lived from 1578 to 1637, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Charles, archduke of Styria, and Maria of Bavaria. Born at Gratz on 9 July 1578, he was trained by the Jesuits. He finished his schooling at the university of Ingolstadt.

That training made him the pattern prince of the counter reformation. In 1596 he took up the rule of Styria, Carinthia, and Carniola. After a visit to Italy he began a planned attack on Protestant faith in those lands. Turks raided his borders all the while, yet he pressed on with his design. Many Protestant subjects were forced to choose between exile and conversion. Worship of their kind was stamped out in full. Care for the wealth of his lands came second to that aim.
britannica-1911-fletcher-giles-author:
Giles Fletcher, an English writer who lived from about 1548 to 1611, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Eton and at Kings College, Cambridge, and became a fellow there. He took a law degree in 1581 and sat in parliament for Winchelsea. He was sent on state work to Scotland, Germany, and Holland.

In 1588 Fletcher was sent to Russia to seek a pact and better terms for English trade. He was lodged poorly in Moscow and treated with contempt. Still, he won sole rights for English traders on the Volga. On his return he wrote a full account of Russia in 1591. It covered the land, the state, law, war, the church, and daily life. Traders feared his frank words would harm their work.
britannica-1911-fliedner-theodor:
Theodor Fliedner, a German Protestant divine who lived from 1800 to 1864, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Epstein, near Wiesbaden, the son of the village pastor, he studied theology at Giessen, Göttingen, and Herborn. After a year of teaching and preaching, he took a call in 1821.

That call was to Kaiserswerth, a small town on the Rhine below Düsseldorf. To help his people and endow his church, Fliedner travelled in Germany, Holland, and England raising support. He met with much success. In England he observed what was being done for prison reform and met Elizabeth Fry. German prisons were then in a bad state, with prisoners crowded and idle. Fliedner took up the work almost alone. He was refused leave to be imprisoned himself to study prison life. He was allowed, though, to hold services in the Düsseldorf prison.
britannica-1911-floridor:
Floridor, the stage name of Josias de Soulas, a French actor who died about 1671, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born in Brie early in the seventeenth century. His father was a gentleman of German family who had moved to France and become a Catholic. The son entered the French army first. After promotion to ensign, he quit the army for the theatre.

Floridor's first Paris appearance came in 1640. Three years later he was called to the company at the Hôtel de Bourgogne. There he played all the leading parts in tragedy and comedy and became the head of his profession. He was a man of superb build, with a flexible, sonorous voice and rare elegance of manner. Louis the Fourteenth held him in particular esteem.
britannica-1911-francis-i-emperor:
Francis I (1708-1765), Roman emperor and grand duke of Tuscany, was the second son of Leopold Joseph, duke of Lorraine. His mother was Elizabeth Charlotte, daughter of Philip, duke of Orleans. He was born on 8 December 1708. Through his grandmother Eleanore, a daughter of the emperor Ferdinand III, he was kin to the Habsburgs. The emperor Charles VI favoured the family, who had served Austria with distinction, and he planned at first to marry his daughter Maria Theresa to Francis's elder brother Clement.

When Clement died, Charles took the younger brother as her husband instead. Francis was brought up at Vienna with Maria Theresa, on the understanding that they would marry, and real affection grew between them. At fifteen he was set up in the Silesian duchy of Teschen. The entry follows the Lorraine prince who became emperor as Maria Theresa's husband.
britannica-1911-francis-ii-emperor:
Francis II (1768-1835) was the last Holy Roman emperor, and, as Francis I, the first emperor of Austria. He was the son of Leopold II and of Maria Louisa, daughter of Charles III of Spain. He was born at Florence on 12 February 1768. In 1784 he was brought to Vienna to finish his education under the eye of his uncle, the childless emperor Joseph II. Joseph was repelled by his nephew's cold, retiring character and treated him, it is said, with impatient contempt, which confirmed the young man's natural timidity.

After Francis married Elizabeth of Wurttemberg in 1788, uncle and nephew got on better. At the close of Joseph's reign Francis saw service in the ill-run war with Turkey and kept a careful diary. His wife died in childbirth on 18 February 1790, two days before Joseph himself died.
britannica-1911-free-reed-vibrator:
Free reed vibrator is a thin metal tongue fixed at one end, swinging freely through a slot to make sound. It works in instruments such as the accordion, concertina, harmonium, and some organ reed stops. Driven by compressed air, the tongue checks and releases the stream in turn, breaking it into regular puffs of air. Those puffs, not the reed vibration itself, produce the tone.

Pitch depends on the length and thickness of the tongue: longer means slower swings and a lower note, thicker at the fixed end a higher one. Greater wind pressure swells the volume without changing pitch, a prized trait of the free reed. The entry sorts instruments by how the sound is reinforced. Some reeds sit in pipes, some work with air chambers as in the harmonium, and some have no resonator and sound rich in harmonics but harsh.
britannica-1911-galba-servius-sulpicius-:
Galba, Servius Sulpicius, was Roman emperor from June 68 to January 69, born near Terracina on the 24th of December 5 B.C. He came of a noble family unconnected with the six Caesars. Praetor in 20 and consul in 33, he won a name in Gaul, Germany, Africa and Spain for skill and strictness. On Caligula's death he refused his friends' invitation to bid for empire and served Claudius. In 61 Nero gave him Hispania Tarraconensis.

When Nero meant to kill him in 68, Galba rose, and after Nero's murder he took the title Caesar and marched on Rome. He never won the soldiers or the people: he refused the praetorians their reward and disgusted the mob by his meanness. Led by favourites, he adopted Piso as successor, a choice the praetorians read as fear. Otho, passed over, won them, and Galba, carried in a litter to meet the rebels, was butchered near the Lacus Curtius.
britannica-1911-ghor:
Ghor is a region article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ghor, or Ghur, was an ancient kingdom of Afghanistan. In the middle ages the name covered the highlands east of Herat. It reached eastward almost to the upper Helmand valley. Local use still kept the name in the article's day.

The entry fixes the region within the mountain country of western Afghanistan. Ghor forms the southern part of a great block of strong high ground. The northern part bore other names in medieval times, Gharjistan and Juzjana. The basin of the Herat River, and all land south of it, made up Ghor. Modern use narrows the name and leaves the Herat valley out. The article traces how the bounds of the name shifted across the centuries. Readers get a careful placing of a kingdom remembered in Persian and Afghan history.
britannica-1911-goldast-ab-haiminsfeld-m:
Melchior Goldast ab Haiminsfeld (1576-1635) was a Swiss writer, an industrious but uncritical collector of documents on medieval German history and constitution. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born on 6 January 1576 near Bischofszell, of poor Protestant parents. Poverty cut short his studies at Ingolstadt and Altdorf and dogged him all his life.

A rich patron at St Gall opened that convent's library of medieval documents to him, and his life's work began. Service followed under the duke of Bouillon, the baron von Hohensax, Saxe-Weimar and the count of Schaumburg, with war driving him to Bremen in 1624. His biographer lists 65 works by him, including collections of old German tales and of Swabian and Alamannic writers. He died at Giessen early in 1635. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; his entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-goldstucker-theodor:
Goldstucker, Theodor, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a German Sanskrit scholar. Born at Konigsberg on the 18th of January 1821 of Jewish parents, he read Sanskrit there. In 1838 he moved to Bonn, then went on to Paris. In 1842 he brought out a German version of an Indian play.

From 1847 to 1850 he lived at Berlin, where Humboldt praised his work. His bold views on state life made the rulers there distrust him. In 1850 he moved to London for a fresh start in life. Two years later he took the Sanskrit chair at University College. His chief work, on Panini and Sanskrit letters, came out in 1861. He helped found the Sanskrit Text Society in that time.
britannica-1911-governor:
Governor is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from a Latin verb meaning to steer a ship, then to direct or guide. In general it names one who governs or holds authority. In a narrower sense it names an official set to govern a district, a province, or a town.

The article fixes the word in two great uses. In British colonies and dependencies, the crown's own man on the spot bears the title. Such men are ranked as governors-general, governors, and lieutenant-governors, by the standing of the land they rule. Their powers shift with the post, but in all cases they stand for the authority of the crown. In the United States, the official at the head of every state government is likewise called a governor.
britannica-1911-gregory-the-illuminator:
Gregory the Illuminator is the reputed founder of the Armenian Church. The 1911 Britannica entry tells his legend as legend. His father Anak, head of the Parthian clan of Suren, was bribed by the Persian king to murder the Armenian king Chosroes. Anak was slain by his victim's soldiers, and the infant Gregory was rescued by his Christian nurse.

Raised a Christian at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory entered the service of Tiridates, the murdered king's son, to atone by fidelity for his father's treachery. At a feast of Anahite he refused pagan sacrifice, and his birth was revealed. Tiridates threw him into a deep pit at Artashat, where he languished fourteen years while persecution raged. The legend then turns to Rome, to the nun Ripsime fleeing Diocletian, and to her martyrdom in Armenia. Gregory's release and the king's conversion complete the founding story.
britannica-1911-herzl-theodor:
Theodor Herzl (1860–1904) founded modern political Zionism. Born in Budapest on the 2nd of May 1860, he died at Edlach on the 3rd of July 1904. Most of his career belonged to Vienna, where he won high repute as a literary journalist and dramatist. Yet his fame rests on one work: reviving Jewish hopes of a restored political life.

Herzl pitied Jews under persecution, but was moved still more by the blocks met under assimilation. In Europe Jews were refused social equality and fair entry to the army, universities and professions. In 1896 he published his pamphlet Der Judenstaat, urging national reunion over merging by intermarriage. He did not at first insist on Palestine, and his plan was secular, economic and political. His work gave fresh life to Jewish culture and to Hebrew as a living speech.
britannica-1911-hildebrandt-theodor:
Theodor Hildebrandt (1804–1874) was a German painter, born at Stettin, a pupil of Schadow. In 1828 he followed Schadow to Düsseldorf, where the new academy had called his master. He began with pictures from Goethe and Shakespeare: Faust and Mephistopheles (1824), Faust and Margaret (1825), Lear and Cordelia (1828).

His Robber (1829) and Captain and his Infant Son (1832) showed a kindly realism that won the public. The picture that made his fame is the Murder of the Children of King Edward (1836). After 1847 he gave himself to portrait work and built a large practice at Düsseldorf, where he died in 1874.
britannica-1911-hortensius-quintus-dicta: Quintus Hortensius was sole ruler of Rome in the year two eighty-six before Christ. When the folk, pressed by rich men they owed, withdrew to a hill, he was charged to end the strife. He passed a law that made the votes of the crowd bind on all, with no need for the high house to grant them. A twin law made fair days fit for law work. He is said to have died while still in that high post.
britannica-1911-hortensius-quintus-orato:
Quintus Hortensius, surnamed Hortalus, a Roman orator who lived from 114 to 50 before Christ, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At nineteen he made his first speech at the bar. Soon after, he defended Nicomedes of Bithynia, a client king who had lost his throne to his brother. From that time his standing as an advocate was secure.

Hortensius belonged to the aristocratic party, and under Sulla the courts were in senatorial hands. Cicero hints that he did not scruple to use that friendly bent of the courts. Many of his clients were governors accused of plundering their provinces. He served in the Social War, then rose through quaestor, aedile, and praetor to consul in 69 before Christ. The year before, he clashed with Cicero in the case of Verres. From then on, his supremacy at the bar was lost.
britannica-1911-john-i-roman-emperor:
John the First is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an East Roman emperor from 925 to 976. His surname was Tzimisces in the old tongue. He was born of a famed family of Cappadocia. He helped his uncle win the throne of the empire. That uncle then stripped him of his command by a plot. John struck back by a plot to kill his uncle.

The wife of his uncle joined him in that plot. Picked as ruler in his stead, John had to prove his claim. He drove new Russian foes out of Thrace in war. Hard fights broke their strength on the Danube. He moved groups he doubted to guard his north edge. In 974 he turned south against the Abbasid realm. He won back inland Syria and the Euphrates reach. He died on his return from a second such drive.
britannica-1911-john-ii-roman-emperor: John II Comnenus (1088-1143), called John the Good, was an East Roman emperor. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives him as eldest son of Emperor Alexius, whom he followed in 1118. His mild and just rule earned him praise as a Byzantine Marcus Aurelius. Pure conduct lifted the tone of his court, the entry says. Wars against Hungarians, Serbs, and Seljuk Turks brought wins but little lasting strength. He died after a wound on a boar hunt in April 1143.
britannica-1911-john-iii-roman-emperor:
John the Third, called Vatatzes, ruled the East Roman realm from 1222 and died in 1254. The 1911 Britannica entry praises his skill as a soldier and as a ruler. He followed his father in law Theodore Lascaris on the throne. By good rule he made a small remnant state the strongest and richest power in the Levant.

He first secured his east border by a pact with the Turks. Then his fleet pressed the Latins in the Aegean and his army won in the open field. A joint siege of Constantinople in 1235 failed, yet he gained sway over Thessalonica and Epirus. The entry credits him with laying the ground for the later recovery of the great city.
britannica-1911-john-iv-roman-emperor: John IV Lascaris (about 1250 to about 1300) was an East Roman emperor as a child. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives him as son of Theodore II, who died in 1258. Michael Palaeologus made himself regent soon after that death. In 1261 he deposed and blinded the boy ruler. John was then held in a far castle, where he died long afterward. The entry closes with pointers to Gibbon and to a Greek history of Nicaea.
britannica-1911-keim-karl-theodor:
Karl Theodor Keim (1825–1878) was a German Protestant theologian, born at Stuttgart on the 17th of December 1825. His father was headmaster of a gymnasium, and Karl had his early schooling there before going to the Stuttgart Obergymnasium. In 1843 he went to the university of Tübingen, where he studied philosophy under Reiff, a follower of Hegel, and eastern tongues under Ewald and Meier.

F. C. Baur, leader of the new Tübingen school, was then lecturing, and Keim was deeply marked by him. His first published work, on the reformation of the city of Ulm, came in 1851. In 1850 he visited Bonn and heard Bleek and Rothe among others.
britannica-1911-kjerulf-theodor:
Kjerulf, Theodor, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Norwegian geologist. Born at Christiania on the 30th of March 1825, he read at its university. He went on to study at Heidelberg in Bunsen's lab rooms. In 1858 he took the geology chair at his home university.

He was later put in charge of the state survey of Norway's rocks. That survey was set up in large part through his own push. His works on the rocks of Norway were many and of weight. They dealt most with the south of the land and its old rock lines. Ice age marks in the rocks also drew his close study. His main results came out in a book of 1879. He also wrote works of verse in his life.
britannica-1911-koko-nor:
Koko-Nor, also written Kuku-Nor, is a lake of Central Asia in the extreme north-east of Tibet. The Chinese call it Tsing-hai, and the Tanguts call it Tso-ngombo. It stands 9975 feet above the sea, 30 miles from the west frontier of the Chinese province of Kan-suh. It lies among the eastern ranges of the Kuen-lun, with the Nan-shan mountains to the north. The lake measures 66 miles by 40 miles.

Half a dozen islands rise in it. On one stands a Buddhist monastery to which pilgrims travel. The water is salt, yet fish live in it in plenty. The lake often stays frozen for three months together in winter. Its level rises and falls a good deal at times. The river Buhain-gol flows into it from the west. The nomads who camp round its shores are Tanguts.
britannica-1911-labrador:
Labrador is a peninsula of British North America, bounded by the Atlantic, Hudson Strait, Hudson and James Bays, and the Gulf of St Lawrence. It runs from 50° to 63° N. and covers about 511,000 sq. m. Recent surveys show much of it is well-wooded country, not a land of awful desolation, with resources in forests, fisheries and minerals.

The interior is mostly a plateau rising toward the south and east, with lowland fringes on some coasts. The only mountains run along the Atlantic coast from the Strait of Belle Isle to Cape Chidley; in the south they rarely pass 1500 ft., but in the north they reach a general level above 2000 ft., with sharp peaks between 3000 and 5000 ft. Forest covers the south up to 53° N., built of nine tree species — white birch, poplar, cedar, spruces, balsam fir and larch — and the river valleys hold valuable timber.
britannica-1911-laird-macgregor:
Macgregor Laird (1808–1861), Scottish merchant and pioneer of British trade on the Niger, was born at Greenock, the younger son of William Laird, founder of the Birkenhead shipbuilding firm. In 1831 he and some Liverpool merchants formed a company to develop trade in the Niger regions. In 1832 the company sent two small ships to the Niger. One, the "Alburkah," a paddle steamer of 55 tons designed by Laird, was the first iron vessel to make an ocean voyage.

Laird went with the expedition, led by Richard Lander, whose forty-eight Europeans nearly all died of fever or wounds. Laird ascended the Benue from its confluence with the Niger, the first white man to do so, and formed an accurate idea of its course. The party returned to Liverpool in 1834, and Laird and Oldfield published their Narrative of the expedition in 1837. The venture failed commercially, but the experience shaped his later Niger work.
britannica-1911-lechler-gotthard-victor:
Gotthard Victor Lechler, a German Lutheran divine who lived from 1811 to 1888, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Württemberg and studied at Tübingen under Baur. In 1858 he took three posts at Leipzig at once. He was pastor of Saint Thomas, teacher of church history, and head of the Lutheran church there.

Though Baur taught him, Lechler did not join the Tübingen school. He held that Paul and the first apostles show both range and accord, not a sharp split. His first great book dealt with the age of the apostles and the age just after. The work he prized most told of John Wiclif and the road to the Reformation. It reached English readers in a translated form. His book on English deism is still valued.
britannica-1911-leopold-i-emperor:
Leopold I (1640-1705), Roman emperor, was the second son of Ferdinand III. Church life was planned for him at first. His elder brother died in July 1654 and changed that path. Crowns of Hungary in 1655 and Bohemia in 1656 followed. Election as emperor came at Frankfort in July 1658.

His reign ran forty-seven years. For most of it he faced Louis XIV of France. Leopold never led troops in person. War still filled his rule. A Swedish war closed at Oliva in 1660. Turkish war then broke out in 1663. Victory at St Gotthard came in August 1664. A twenty-year truce at Vasvar followed. Later notes mark his zeal, his Jesuit links, and his love of music and the hunt.
britannica-1911-leopold-ii-emperor:
Leopold II (1747-1792), Roman emperor and grand duke of Tuscany, was born in Vienna on 5 May 1747. He was a third son of Maria Theresa and Francis I. Priesthood was his first planned path. His brother Charles died in 1761. Tuscany then fell to Leopold as his share. Marriage to Maria Louisa of Spain came in 1764.

His father died in 1765 and left him the grand duchy. Five years passed under guides set by his mother. A Vienna trip in 1770 won him a free hand. Twenty years of reform in Tuscany followed. He cut old curbs on trade and on the person. Tax rules grew more sound. Works like the draining of the Val di Chiana paid their way. No army drained his funds, so the state rose in wealth.
britannica-1911-llantwit-major:
Llantwit Major is a small market town in Glamorganshire, South Wales, a mile from the Bristol Channel. It has a station on the Barry railway, five miles south of Cowbridge. Its people numbered 1,113 in 1901. A mile north-west of the town, diggers found the remains of a large Roman villa in 1888. The villa stood in a square yard of about eight acres. The site may be part of a Roman town named in Welsh tales as Caer Wrgan.

The villa seems to have been the scene of a massacre, perhaps by Irish pirates in the 5th century. Some forty-three human bones and the remains of three horses were found in the yard. Some scholars place the Roman station of Bovium at Boverton, a mile east of the town. Others place it at Ewenny or at Cowbridge. On the coast stand two camps, one called Castle Ditches.
britannica-1911-lop-nor:
Lop-nor is a lake of Central Asia in the Gobi Desert, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies between two ranges of hills, one to the south and one to the north. Old maps drawn from Chinese accounts placed it in one spot. In 1876 the Russian traveller Przhevalsky found two basins a full degree of latitude to the south.

He took those basins for the old Lop-nor, but found their water fresh. Baron von Richthofen held that the true Salt Lake of the Chinese could not be fresh. A lake with no outflow, fed by a desert stream, must turn salt, he argued. Sven Hedin then found a string of lakes at the old mapped place. He held that the two groups trade water, and that the north lakes creep west under wind and sand.
britannica-1911-louis-i-emperor:
Louis the First, called the Pious, was a Roman emperor of the early middle ages, third son of Charlemagne. Born in France, he was crowned king of Aquitaine as a small child. The 1911 Britannica entry says he was well schooled, but his tastes ran to the church more than to war, so aides ran much of his realm.

The entry still credits him with real war craft in the guard of his lands. He fought Saxons and Avars and led a host into Italy. On the deaths of both elder brothers, his father had him crown himself as joint emperor, and he soon ruled alone. His byname came from his zeal to clean the court, reform friars, and give with a free hand to the church.
britannica-1911-louis-ii-emperor:
Louis the Second (825-875), a Roman emperor, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of the emperor Lothair the First. He was named king of Italy in 839 and took up his home in that country. A pope crowned him king at Rome in June 844. He at once claimed the rights of an emperor in the city, and the claim was flatly refused.

The article follows his long rule in Italy. In 850 another pope crowned him joint emperor at Rome. He then wed his cousin and took the rule of Italy into his own hands. He took the field against the Saracens and held a diet at Pavia. On his father's death in 855 he became sole emperor. The split of his father's lands left him nothing outside Italy, which stung him into leagues against his own kin.
britannica-1911-louis-iii-emperor:
Louis the Third, called the Blind, was a Roman emperor who lived from about 880 to 928. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica makes him a son of Boso, king of Provence. His mother was a daughter of the emperor Louis the Second. Charles the Fat took the boy under his care in 887. Provence lay in wild disorder at the time. Only in 890 was Louis owned as king there.

In 900 he went to Italy to seek the crown of empire. He was chosen king of the Lombards at Pavia. The pope crowned him emperor at Rome in February 901. His hold on north Italy soon slipped. His rival Berengar drove him out, and he swore to stay away. He broke that oath and came back in 904. Berengar caught him at Verona in 905, put out his eyes, and sent him home to Provence.
britannica-1911-lucilius-junior:
Lucilius Junior was a Roman writer and a friend of the younger Seneca. The 1911 Britannica article deals with one main question about him. He may have written Aetna, a Latin poem on why volcanoes erupt. The poem has also been linked to Virgil and to other Roman poets, so its author is not sure.

The article weighs clues of date and place to test the claim. Lucilius knew the work of Seneca, and he held a post in Sicily, where Mount Etna stands. He also wrote verse on Sicilian themes. Against this, a letter of Seneca seems to ask for Etna as a side theme, not a whole poem. The text lists the old sources and modern editions used in the debate.
britannica-1911-lycurgus-orator:
Lycurgus, who lived from about 396 to 325 BC, was one of the ten famed orators of Athens. The 1911 Britannica article says he came of an old priestly house, the Eteobutadae. He is said to have learned from Plato and Isocrates. When the threat from Philip of Macedon grew plain, he stood with Demosthenes as a chief of the national party. He left foreign affairs to his partners. His own field was the order and the funds of the city.

For twelve years, from 338 to 326 BC, Lycurgus ran the funds of Athens. Law barred him from the post in name for part of that span, so he worked through his son and a tame stand-in. He raised the yearly income of the state from 600 to 1,200 talents. He grew the fleet, fixed the dockyards, and built an arsenal. He rebuilt the theatre and the stadium too.
britannica-1911-magee-william-connor:
William Connor Magee is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an Anglican divine. He became archbishop of York in his career. He lived from 1821 to 1891. He was born at Cork in Ireland in 1821. His father was curate of the cathedral parish there. His grandfather had been archbishop of Dublin before him. Young Magee entered Trinity College, Dublin, at thirteen. 

He was ordained to a curacy at Saint Thomas's, Dublin. Threatened with consumption, he went to Malaga after two years. On his return he took a curacy at Bath. He was soon appointed to the Octagon Chapel there. His fame as preacher and platform speaker kept spreading. In 1860 his delicate health led him to Enniskillen. In 1864 he was made dean of Cork. There his great gifts began to raise him to high office.
britannica-1911-margueritte-paul-and-vic:
