The pope counts as rector of the world in the conferring of the tiara. At some universities, Louvain for example, the actual president bears the title rector magnificus. Rector general names the superior general of certain orders, such as the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God. In ancient times bishops ruling cities and provinces, above all in the Papal States, were called rectors, as were administrators of church lands, like the rector of Sicily. Gregory the Great uses rector as equivalent to pastor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-deus-te:
Rerum Deus Tenax Vigor is the daily hymn for None in the Roman Breviary. Like the hymns for Terce and Sext, it holds only two stanzas of iambic dimeters, with a doxology that varies by feast or season. As in the hymns for Prime, Sext, and Compline, its theme is the sun's steady march marking the hours of the day. God, whose power unmoved controls nature's vastness, marks the day-hours by steady marches of the sun.

The second stanza turns that image to moral use, praying that in life's eventide God's light may abide with us, never failing. The authorship of the Terce, Sext, and None hymns is now given to Saint Ambrose only very doubtfully. The entry sets out the manuscript discussion behind that verdict, with Blume, Dreves, and Daniel among its guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-st:
Richard of St Victor was a twelfth-century Scottish theologian who spent his life inside the Paris monastery of St Victor. The date and place of his birth are unknown. He was professed under the first abbot, Gilduin, and became a disciple of the mystic Hugh of St Victor, whose methods he took up and developed. He rose to sub-prior in 1159 and later to prior.

His career stayed strictly monastic, with few ties to the outside world. Yet his writings travelled widely, and other houses eagerly sought copies. Unlike Hugh, he took no interest in philosophy or in the sharp debates of his day. He distrusted secular learning as an end in itself, valuing it only when joined to knowledge of divine things. His reputation rests on mystical theology, on contemplation as the path to God, and on the orderly teaching methods he borrowed from Abelard. He died in 1173.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-salvador:
San Salvador is the name Columbus gave his first landfall in the New World, one of the Bahamas east of southern Florida at 24 degrees north and 75 degrees west. Native people called it Guanahani, and scholars have argued ever since over which island Columbus actually reached. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs the rival claims without pretending to settle them.

Cat Island, Samana, Mariguana, Grand Turk, and Watling's Island have each had champions. San Salvador was the name given to Cat Island in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, yet Cat Island lacks the low, level shape and inner lagoon Columbus described. Captain Gustavus Fox argued for Samana in the Coast Survey report of 1880, and Navarrete first urged Grand Turk, leaving the puzzle open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-vigor:
Simon Vigor, French bishop and controversialist born at Evreux in Normandy about 1515, died at Carcassonne on 1 November 1575. Son of Raynaud Vigor, a court physician, he went to Paris about 1520 and studied Greek, Hebrew, Latin, then theology. Admitted to the College of Navarre in 1540, he became rector of the University of Paris that same year. In 1545 he took a doctorate in theology and became penitentiary of Evreux.

Thenceforth he preached pastorally and controversially with great success at Rouen, Paris, Metz, and elsewhere. At Saint-Germain in 1562 he defended the Catholic cause against Calvinists led by Theodore Beza. In 1563 he joined twelve Sorbonne theologians at Trent, debating clandestine marriages and indulgences with vast erudition. He also smoothed relations between Cardinal Hosius and Francisco Torres, and won Cardinal de Lorraine's confidence on a mission to Ferdinand I at Innsbruck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded at Rome on 8 December 1881 by Johann Baptist Jordan, as Father Francis Mary of the Cross, the Society of the Divine Savior first bore the name Society of Catholic Instruction. Jordan added a fourth vow of apostolic mission work to poverty, chastity, and obedience. Its rules draw largely on the Society of Jesus, and its black habit bears a black cincture with four knots recalling the four vows.

The Prefecture Apostolic of Assam came under the society in 1889, with 7 principal and 32 dependent stations served by 13 missionaries. A German college rose at Lochau in 1893, a station at Corvallis, Oregon, the same year, and work in Brazil began in 1896. By 1908 missions ran in thirteen languages, and the congregation counted 400 members in 35 foundations across Europe, the United States, Brazil, and Colombia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edward-the:
Edward the Confessor, king of England from 1042 to 1066, earned his title by a reign of unusual gentleness after a youth of exile. Born in 1003 to Ethelred II and Emma of Normandy, he was sent to Normandy at ten when Danish power mastered England. Called to the throne at about forty, he was welcomed even by Danish settlers for his saintly character. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 5 January 1066.

His reign stayed almost unbrokenly peaceful, with the Danegelt tax remitted and no wars beyond a Welsh inroad and aid to Malcolm III against Macbeth. He married Editha, Godwin's daughter, on terms of chastity, and rebuilt Westminster Abbey in place of a promised pilgrimage. Canonized in 1161, he left laws later generations demanded back whenever they felt oppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teresa-lalor:
Teresa Lalor co-founded the Visitation Order in the United States with Bishop Neale of Baltimore. Born in Ireland, she died on 9 September 1846. Her Kilkenny childhood showed so clear a vocation that Bishop Lanigan arranged her entrance into his diocese's convent. Instead she had to accompany her family to America. Arriving at Philadelphia in 1797, she met Father Leonard Neale of St Joseph's, and under him gave herself to piety and charity.

Neale saw in her an instrument for a community, and an academy for girls opened. Yellow fever carried off her companions, and when Neale moved to Georgetown College in 1799, she followed to live with exiled French Poor Clares. After they left America, Lalor and two companions opened their own school within the present Visitation grounds. Pius VII granted them Visitation standing in 1816, and Mother Teresa was professed that Holy Innocents' feast, becoming first superioress of Georgetown Convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodorus-lec:
Constantinople lector Theodorus, compiler of church history from excerpts, is the sixth-century scholar described here. Attached to Saint Sophia's church, he compiled at a friend's request the four-book Historia Tripartita, an epitome of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret made from excerpts. An imperfect manuscript copy survives unpublished, though Valesius used it, perhaps overvaluing its readings, in editing those historians.

A two-book history carried the narrative from Theodosius II's death to Justin I's times, now lost except two long excerpt series under the spurious title Apo phones Nikephorou Kallistou. John of Damascus and the Seventh General Council's Acts quote it. Its value lies in scanty sources for an obscure age, preserved through later excerptors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unjust-aggres: An unjust aggressor, in the moral teaching set out here, is an attacker whose violence may lawfully be met with violence. Defence of life or limb, of property of some importance, and of chastity all allow force in return, even to the point of killing the assailant. The limit is strict: only the force truly needed to stop the attack may be used, so maiming must serve instead of killing wherever maiming suffices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-hugh-tayl:
Hugh Taylor was an English martyr born at Durham, hanged, drawn, and quartered at York on 25 November 1585, not the 26th as sometimes given. He reached Reims on 2 May 1582, was ordained priest there, and was sent out on the mission on 27 March 1585. He became the first to suffer under the newly passed statute 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, against priests.

On 26 November Marmaduke Bowes, a married gentleman, was hanged for harbouring Taylor. Challoner places Bowes at Angram Grange near Appleton in Cleveland, though he appears neither in the will of Christopher Bowes of Angram Grange, proved in 1568, nor in the 1612 pedigree. The sole evidence against Bowes came from a former tutor of his children, an apostate Catholic. The entry weighs that thin evidence with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-roger-cad:
Roger Cadwallador was an English martyr born at Stretton Sugwas near Hereford in 1568, executed at Leominster on 27 August 1610. Ordained subdeacon at Reims on 21 September 1591 and deacon the following February, he was sent in August 1592 to the English College at Valladolid, where he was ordained priest. Back in England from 1594, he worked in Herefordshire to good effect, above all among the poor, for some sixteen years.

Men searched for him in June 1605, but only at Easter 1610 was he arrested, at the house of Mrs Winefride Scroope, widow, within eight miles of Hereford. Brought before Bishop Robert Bennet, he was committed to Hereford jail, where he was loaded with irons night and day. Transferred to Leominster jail, he had to walk the whole way in shackles, though a boy was allowed to carry his cloak, before his trial and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-pa:
Thomas Palasor, or Palliser, was a Yorkshire priest executed at Durham in 1600. He reached Reims in 1592, moved on to Valladolid, and was ordained there in 1596. Returning to England, he was arrested in the house of John Norton near Lamesley in County Durham, together with Norton, his wife, and John Talbot.

All four were tried at Durham. Palasor was condemned for being a priest, and the others for assisting him. A fifth man saved himself by conforming, and Mrs Norton, believed to be pregnant, was reprieved. Palasor and his companions suffered together. The entry adds a curious sequel: an attempt by the gaoler's wife to poison the prisoners led to the conversion of her maidservant, Mary Day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-st-:
Walter of St Victor was a twelfth-century mystic philosopher and theologian known almost solely as prior of St Victor's monastery about 1175. Author about the Third Lateran Council of 1179 of the celebrated polemic Against the Four Labyrinths of France, and dead about 1180.

Its four labyrinths are Abelard, Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers. The work bitterly attacks the dialectical method in theology, condemning in no measured terms the use of logic to elucidate the mysteries of faith. Walter raged at treating Trinity and Incarnation with scholastic levity, discarding St Victor's best traditions to abuse philosophers, theologians, and even grammarians, crying thy grammar be with thee until perdition. That violence defeated its purpose, failing to convince contemporaries and very probably hastening the triumph of the method he attacked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-molit:
Wilhelm Molitor was a Palatinate priest who worked as poet, novelist, church lawyer, and Catholic press organizer. Born at Zweibruecken in 1819, he died at Speyer in 1880. He first trained in law at Munich and Heidelberg and held state legal posts, then turned to theology at Bonn and took orders in 1851. He became secretary to the Bishop of Speyer, a cathedral canon, and a teacher of archaeology and preaching.

Molitor led the Catholic revival in the Palatinate by founding a press association, a daily paper, and a Catholic printing house. His firm ultramontane views, backing Rome over the state, blocked his rise to the Speyer bishopric. His output was vast: poems, plays such as Kynast and Maria Magdalena, novels, sermons, church-law studies, and essays on the press, Goethe, and the stage. Rome called him to help prepare the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-the-c:
William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy and King of England, the bastard son who seized a crown. Born to Robert, Duke of Normandy, and Herleva, a tanner's daughter of Falaise, he was presented to Norman nobles at seven in 1035 before Robert left on the pilgrimage that killed him. Three guardians were murdered and kidnappers threatened the boy, yet after anarchy he ruled Normandy, a youth of clean life, deep piety, and iron resolve.

In 1047 William crushed a noble rising at Val-ès-Dunes with French royal aid, took Alençon and Domfront, and mastered Maine, becoming France's mightiest vassal. A 1051 English visit, a disputed promise of the succession, and Harold's forced oath of 1064 set up his claim. When Harold broke that oath at Edward's death, William, blessed by Pope Alexander II with a consecrated banner, crossed as God's champion against perjury and won England at Hastings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-windsor:
Windsor is the Thames town in Berkshire whose castle has housed English kings for centuries. Of great antiquity, its name comes from the Saxon Windels-or, winding shore, quaintly Latinized as Ventus Morbidus in medieval papers. Saint Edward the Confessor gave the manor to Westminster Abbey, and the town became a free borough under Edward I. A palace and stronghold stood here even in Saxon Heptarchy days.

The castle's fame rests on its Round Tower mound from Saxon times, Henry III's additions, and centuries as the favourite royal home, birthplace of Edward III and Henry VI among others. Edward IV built the sumptuous Saint George's Chapel, finest perpendicular work in England, and lies buried there with successors. Under George IV nearly a million pounds rebuilt the castle to Wyatville's plans, and the chapel remains home of the Knights of the Garter.
caves-of-terror:
Talbot Mundy's adventure novel, copyrighted in 1922 and issued in book form in 1924, sends an agent of the firm Grim, Ramsden and Ross from a New York office straight to India. Meldrum Strange, his chief, has taken up a matter for the British Government. A letter from Simla brings in a former officer of the British Indian army.

Twelve chapters named for the Gray Mahatma, the palace of Yasmini, a pool of terrors, and a cave of bones promise the route. Fire bathers, a river of death, and an earthquake elephant crowd the middle. Secret power in India, half magic and half conspiracy, is what the agents must face. Mundy keeps the pace breathless.
cicero-s-brutus-or-history-of-famous-ora:
Cicero's Brutus and his Orator reach the reader here in an older English translation of Marcus Tullius Cicero. A translator's preface dates the Brutus to Cicero's retirement during the civil war in Africa. It was written in his sixty-first year, in dialogue form, as a fourth book to his three earlier books on the orator's qualifications.

In the Brutus, Cicero talks with Atticus and Brutus in his garden at Rome, under a statue of Plato. Short sketches of every famed Greek and Roman speaker down to his own time fill the talk. The Orator, written soon after at Brutus's request, serves as a fifth part. It sets out Cicero's own plan of the most finished eloquence.
civil-government-for-common-schools-prep:
Henry C. Northam's Civil Government for Common Schools teaches New York children their own government. Northam, a conductor of teachers' institutes at Lowville, prefaces the third edition in April 1878. Textbooks in general use, he complains, stop with theory. Students learn republican principles but not what causes a justice of the peace may try.

His manual begins with the school district and climbs to the President. Names, elections, duties, and salaries of officers fill its question-and-answer lessons. Road, school, and election districts are defined as the smallest units. The constitutions of New York, as amended in 1880, and of the United States are appended, with the Declaration of Independence. Northam wrote the art of government as practised in his state. Progressive schools, he hoped, would find the little book indispensable.
colony-or-free-state-dependence-or-just-:
Colony — or Free State? Dependence — or Just Connection? Empire — or Union?, by Alpheus Henry Snow, was published at Washington in 1907. It joins an essay with an address delivered at Providence on December 29, 1906, before the section for the study of the government of dependencies of the American Political Science Association. Its subject is the bond between the American Union and its annexed insular regions.

Porto Rico and the Philippines, acquired from Spain in 1898, left that bond undefined. Republicans defended good administration and all practicable self-government. Democrats called the same policy imperialism and warned that no nation can endure half republic and half empire. Snow seeks the right terms in the principles of the American Revolution itself.
crayon-and-character-truth-made-clear-th:
Ten-minute chalk talks for Sunday schools and homes fill this guide by B. J. Griswold. Its full title is Crayon and Character: Truth Made Clear Through Eye and Ear. Meigs Publishing Company of Indianapolis issued it in 1913, with a first reprint in 1918.

Each talk pairs spoken words with a drawing in coloured chalks. The picture grows in two scenes while the talk goes on, which holds the eye of the class. Griswold drops old emblems like the anchor and crown for signs from nature and daily life. The foreword says any earnest Christian who can address a class can use the method. Parents are told the talks also teach children a simple way to draw.
doe-osti-17014402-data-driven-instabilit:
Allison Sinnott of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this report, dated September 11, 2026, on forecasting unrest and conflict from data. Forecasting when conflict starts or stops stays an unsolved problem for national security, the author notes. Her case study is Syria, in particular the sudden 2024 rebel offensive that ended the Assad regime after a long frozen phase of the war.

Working with Python tools, Google Earth Engine, and Power BI, she compared fresh data sets against the case timeline. Links were found between sanctions and regime social service provision, and between night lights data, called VIIRS, and which side held ground. The aim is earlier, more accurate warning that leaders can act on.
doe-osti-17031162-hybrid-decision-and-co:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory issued this September 2026 report on keeping a changing power grid stable. Sayak Mukherjee, Kaustav Chatterjee, Ramij Hossain, and colleagues study grids where inverter based gear, such as solar and battery units, replaces spinning generators. Such grids can swing, or oscillate, in new ways and lose their natural grouping behavior.

One part models how grid forming inverters shift coherency, the tendency of areas to swing together. Another builds a learning based control that is aware of those groups and limits risk in a shared way. Later parts assess stability and guide droop settings, a standard inverter control choice. Case studies with numerical tests support each method.
doe-osti-17056536-selective-deposition-o:
Ryan Hensleigh of Lawrence Livermore reports in October 2026 on a new way to make ceramic electronics in three dimensions. Ceramic parts serve well in hot, shaking settings, but making them has meant bulky blocks of metal and ceramic. Future 6G and security gear needs lighter, leaner shapes, project 25-LW-038 notes.

A light based printing method cures thick beams over one millimeter deep in one pass, alongside normal layer by layer printing, cutting print time and waste. The team also showed that surface chemistry differences let metal be deposited, by an electroless process, only where wanted on pre fired ceramic. One intern trained on the project was hired onto lab staff.
doe-osti-17070152-mhdexact-a-cross-refer:
YuHsiang Lan, Paul Fischer, and Mi Sun Min of Argonne National Laboratory assembled mhdExact, a toolbox of exact solutions for standard magnetohydrodynamics flows, in report ANL-26/72. Exact solutions give simulation codes a truth target: if a code cannot match a solved case, its results elsewhere are suspect. Both Python and NekRS versions are provided.

Chapters lay out the governing equations, Ohm law handling, boundary rules, and a stable numerical form. An appendix walks through classic cases, from Hartmann in 1937 and Shercliff in 1953 to Hunt, Gold, and later authors. The report also documents the agent assisted workflow used to build the toolbox, with human steering at each case.
doe-osti-17076516-quantitative-assessmen:
Phase three report ORNL/SPR-2026/4841, by Hevar Palani, Islam Safir, and Andre Desjarlais of Oak Ridge, seeks a measured way to catch water leaking into walls. Hidden moisture rots materials, grows mold, and shortens wall life, yet the standard spray test, ASTM E331, still rests on eyeballing leaks. No set method quantifies water inside the wall layers.

Two steel stud test walls, each eight feet square, were built with known holes, plus one sealed control wall. Handheld moisture meters, capacitance humidity sensors, and pin probes were judged during controlled spray runs. Sensors sat under the water resistive barrier and at set depths in the gypsum sheathing, letting the team compare readings against known entry paths.
doe-osti-17135588-everbess-end-of-life-c:
Jakob Elias, Aravind Baby, and Qiang Dai of Argonne document EverBESS, a model of what happens when grid battery systems reach end of life, in report ANL-26/50 dated September 2026. Battery energy storage is being installed fast, and retirements will follow at scale. Planning that wave early is the point of the model.

Chapters follow the chain step by step. Decommissioning covers taking a site apart safely. Transportation covers moving used batteries under the rules for hazardous goods. Recycling covers routes for recovering materials and their costs. Data sources include labor statistics, energy agency figures, and transport research. The documentation explains model structure and inputs so others can run end of life scenarios.
doe-osti-17197389-keeping-it-cool-action:
Subodh Chaudhari, Jasmine Schmidt, and John O'Neill wrote a January 2026 tip sheet for the Waste Reduction Network on cutting waste from heating, cooling, and ventilation gear. Such systems serve factories, buildings, and data centers. A single rooftop unit or chiller can yield several tons of waste across a 15 to 20 year life, the sheet notes.

A material table for a typical 10 ton rooftop unit shows most mass is recyclable metal: ferrous metals 40 percent, compressors 12 percent, nonferrous metals 12 percent, motors 7 percent. Non recyclable matter is about 25 percent in small units, dropping near 10 percent in larger ones. Five life phases, from factory scrap to end of life, each carry their own waste streams, and the sheet gives actions for each.
doe-osti-1774838-performance-of-quantum-:
Quantum dot coatings for power-generating windows are the subject of National Laboratory of the Rockies report NREL/TP-5K00-79580, issued in February 2026 with Robert Tenent as technical contact. It closes out CRADA project CRD-16-00640. The partner was UbiQD, a Los Alamos materials company working on electricity-generating windows. Its coatings use quantum dots, tiny semiconductor particles, inside a luminescent solar concentrator that guides light to solar cells at the window's edge.

Two main outcomes came out of the collaboration. First, the laboratory modeled the expected performance and cost of the quantum dot windows. Second, its staff ran materials and device tests that the small company could not afford to do in-house. That testing produced third-party validation, including a laboratory-certified conversion efficiency. Results from the work later appeared in print, in ACS Energy Letters in 2018 and ACS Applied Energy Materials in 2020.
doe-osti-2566158-report-for-the-doe-offi:
Workshop report DOE/SC-2022, published in January 2026, records the meeting Envisioning Frontiers in AI and Computing for Biological Research. The Department of Energy's computing and biology programs convened it in Rockville, Maryland, on February 4 to 6, 2025. Daniela Ushizima and Christopher Henry co-chaired the organizing committee, with Prasanna Balaprakash and others on the program committee.

Chapters survey what the two programs already do, from genomics to complex environmental systems, and collect early success stories for AI in biology. The workshop's charge was to find where artificial intelligence, machine learning, and exascale computing meet biological research most fruitfully. Goals named in the summary include predicting and steering how living systems behave, and organizing and simulating biological processes at vast scale. The findings aim to guide a national bioeconomy built on better control of genetic information.
doe-osti-2570872-sesame-the-los-alamos-n:
Daniel G. Sheppard and David A. Pimentel describe the SESAME database and its new multiphase extensions in Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-26258, issued in July 2025. SESAME is the laboratory's tabulated equation-of-state library, holding material data on density and temperature grids since Jack Barnes and Jerry Rood created it in 1971. Simulation codes draw on it whenever they model matter under extreme conditions.

Legacy table structures are documented series by series, from material constants to vapor dome, melt, opacity, and conductivity tables. New phase-specific tables then record each phase's properties separately and tabulate phase boundaries directly. That change improves how mixed-phase regions at equilibrium are represented. It also sets up kinetic modeling of phase transitions that fall out of equilibrium. File formats and ways of working with the data close the report.
doe-osti-2584748-u-statement-of-work-ucd:
Brendan Illingworth, a program manager at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, issued this statement of work in August 2025 as LLNL-TR-2009703. It sets the terms for joint work with UCD on electronics built to survive radiation, known as the RadHard project. The document runs ten pages and names Illingworth as the program manager.

Its first half covers how the work will be run: program controls, project engineering, schedule, gate reviews, and contract steps. Its second half lists what the subcontractor must hand over. The list includes design needs, performance targets, key electrical values, a design approach, and test bench and model run results. It also calls for layout files, pad and pin lists, a package summary, and plans for radiation and reliability tests. A secure work area for chip design is required too.
doe-osti-2586587-low-mass-and-high-effic:
Qigui Wang, a General Motors technical fellow, led this final technical report for Department of Energy grant DE-EE0008877, submitted August 28, 2025. Ronald Petrus shares credit for the project. The goal was a medium-duty truck engine that weighs less and burns less fuel, developed over a grant period from October 2019 through September 2024.

The program began with engine architecture design and analysis, then moved into advanced materials and manufacturing work. Candidate materials and processes were tested and down-selected, with casting studies among them. The best combination went into a full engine, which was evaluated in a test cell and fed into final vehicle simulation. Wang reports that the final engine tests verified the weight reduction and performance the project set out to reach. The stakes are plain: most trucks sold in the next two decades will still run on combustion engines.
doe-osti-2587946-summary-of-dm1200-sbs-h:
Keith Matlack, Ian Pegg, Tevfik Bardakci, and colleagues at the Vitreous State Laboratory of The Catholic University of America prepared this summary, HFO-72185, for the Department of Energy's environmental management program. It was first published in September 2006 as report VSL-06R6410-2 and approved for public release on September 8, 2025. The subject is the DM1200, a test melter system for turning radioactive tank waste into glass.

The report gathers the history and performance of the melter's submerged bed scrubber, the unit that cleans the gases leaving the melter. Test data spans the waste envelopes used in the low-activity waste program, including Envelope A2 runs. Tables record scrubber performance measures run by run, with some entries marked not estimated. As a consolidated record, it preserves two decades of operating experience with a key piece of vitrification equipment in one citable place.
doe-osti-2589165-osw-consortium-1-floati:
Senu Sirnivas, Matthew Hall, and Stein Housner of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5000-96769, dated September 2025. The partner was NYSERDA through the National Offshore Wind Research and Development Consortium, which made this its first funded project in September 2019, with a 300,000 dollar award. The idea: floating wind farms should share moorings.

Station keeping is a heavy cost in deep water. Each turbine traditionally gets its own chains and anchors, so cost scales with depth and size, pushing up the price of energy. Shared systems break that scaling: neighboring turbines share lines and multiline anchors, cutting the hardware count. The project scoped the design space to judge feasibility and savings. Line materials run from chain and wire rope to synthetics. Clump weights and buoyancy structures ride along the lines. Anchor types run from drag embedment anchors to suction piles.
doe-osti-2589589-evaluating-probability-:
Collin Evans and Alan Evans study how well alarm station operators judge what they see, in Sandia report SAND2025-11766R. Central alarm stations guard nuclear and other secure sites. When a sensor trips, an operator must check camera views and decide whether the cause is an intruder, an animal, or a false trigger.

The team built a test bed and a test matrix, then ran operators through set procedures. Every alarm had to be assessed by tagging it in the system or by calling the response team leader. Operators had to name the alarm type from camera views, and a dead camera meant an immediate call for eyes on site. Scored trials turn that judgment into a measured rate, which designers can use to size staffing and camera coverage.
doe-osti-2997166-retro-commissioning-sen:
A cooperative project final report dated 31 July 2025 covers a sensor kit for tuning up small commercial buildings. Jessica Granderson led the work at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, with partners at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and JMATT Construction Services. The Retro-Commissioning Sensor Suitcase packs portable sensors and diagnostic software into a self-installable toolkit. Small buildings rarely get professional commissioning because site visits cost too much.

Upgrades under the project added carbon dioxide sensing, wireless mesh networking, cloud reporting, and easier setup, aiming at sale through utilities and service firms. Field results found common operating faults worth 5 to 15 percent energy savings, with automated reports needing little interpretation by the user. Pacific Northwest reports hold the diagnostic details. The filing closes the agreement, number FP00012262, with the kit readied for commercial deployment.
doe-osti-2998070-ion-exchange-processing:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report, by Amy Westesen, Austin Bachman, Andrew Carney, and co-authors, dated September 2025, runs real Hanford tank waste through cesium-removal columns. Tank AW-105 waste was passed through crystalline silicotitanate, a granular sorbent that grabs cesium ions, in a staged system that grew from two columns to three. Removing cesium early lets the bulk of the waste be treated as lower-activity material.

Columns ran at 16 degrees Celsius under set feed conditions, with batch contact tests run beside them for comparison. Long data tables track cesium and tracer levels stage by stage as liters of waste passed through. Breakthrough behavior across the staged layout tells engineers how much media a full-scale run will consume and when columns must be swapped. The record supports the site's tank-side treatment demonstration.
doe-osti-2998955-commissioning-of-the-tr:
Maria De Luca's Fermilab internship report, FERMILAB-TM-2921-STUDENT, covers commissioning work on the trigger system of the ICARUS T600 detector. ICARUS is the far detector of the Short Baseline Neutrino Program, which hunts for a possible fourth, sterile kind of neutrino. The detector is a liquid argon time projection chamber: particle tracks drift as electric charge through cold argon, while flashes of light mark each event's moment.

A trigger must catch real neutrino events and reject background, without overloading the readout. Working with supervisor Angela Fava, De Luca built two pieces in LabVIEW software. One generates a local trigger signal when scintillation light appears. The other inhibits, or blocks, triggering when the readout cannot safely take more data. Both pieces were working steps toward switching the detector on in the following months.
doe-osti-2998956-design-of-a-remote-cont:
Gabriel Adrian Mihu's Fermilab report, FERMILAB-TM-2922-STUDENT, designs a remote-controlled mount for a magnet undulator in the IOTA storage ring. IOTA, the Integrable Optics Test Accelerator at Fermilab, stores electrons and protons for advanced beam physics tests. An undulator is a row of magnets that wiggles the beam so it emits light. The mount must shift this heavy unit precisely and safely from a distance.

The unit weighs about 763 pounds, and its position must be set to better than a millimetre, with its sideways angle also controlled. Mihu's design drives a scissor jack with a direct-current motor, keeping a hand crank as backup if the motor fails. A linear sensor with 0.01-millimetre resolution reports position, read through a 16-bit converter chip. Control electronics and a feedback loop hold the setting. The report works through motor maths, sensor ranges and safety stops at the travel limits.
doe-osti-2999063-delayed-neutron-tempora:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-13190, printed 30 September 2025, is the final report of a multi-laboratory safeguards project led by Oskar Searfus. Partners came from Oak Ridge, Los Alamos and Lawrence Livermore, plus the University of Michigan. The aim was a new way to measure uranium enrichment without cutting into the material, for inspectors who check that nuclear stock matches its declared use.

When uranium splits, some neutrons arrive late, seconds after the burst, in groups with set half-lives. The timing pattern differs between uranium-235 and uranium-238, so the pattern itself reveals enrichment with no calibration samples. The team paired existing well counters with commercial neutron generators to trigger and read that signature. Choices such as irradiation length change the contrast between the two isotopes. The method suits lumpy, mixed material where gamma-ray assay struggles, and existing inspector gear could be retrofitted around it.
doe-osti-2999092-improving-runtime-perfo:
Kimberly Harding and Daniel Dunlavy of Sandia test a speed trick for tensor computing, in report SAND2025-12493R. Tensors are data arrays with many axes, used in fields from brain research to quantum chemistry. Their Python Tensor Toolbox, pyttb, is flexible but pure Python loops run slowly. The Rust language compiles to fast native code and can be called from Python through add on modules.

The pair rewrote core pyttb steps in Rust, from simple sum and product loops to the multiplication steps behind low rank decomposition and tensor regression. Tests used made up data of many sizes. Rust beat plain Python across the board. It also beat Numba, a just in time Python compiler, on loop based steps, and beat NumPy on the steps tested. The report weighs where the gains come from and what to try next, giving users a proven route to faster runs.
doe-osti-2999552-next-generation-energy-:
Francesco Borrelli's team at the University of California, Berkeley, wrote this final report for ARPA-E award DE-AR0000791, covering March 2021 to June 2025 in the NEXTCAR program. The project built a predictive, data-driven control system for connected and automated vehicles. Rather than reacting moment by moment, the car plans ahead, using traffic light timing, nearby vehicles and road data sent by wireless links to smooth its speed and lane choices.

In testing, the system improved fuel economy by more than 30 percent and cut travel time by about 10 percent, both against a conventional adaptive cruise control baseline. The control spans the car itself and the cloud: a fleet platform gives dispatch and route advice for electric fleets, logging vehicle data along the way. Better dispatch lets operators lean less on diesel backup vehicles. The report presents the design as technically effective and workable at fleet scale.
doe-osti-2999831-next-generation-energy-:
Giorgio Rizzoni, Marcello Canova, Stephanie Stockar and the Ohio State team report on ARPA-E award DE-AR0000794, dated 27 October 2025. The report closes the NEXTCAR project, phases one and two, which ran from April 2017 to June 2025. Their strand paired connected, automated driving with a clever engine trick. Dynamic skip fire shuts down single cylinders moment by moment, letting the rest work at their best load.

A full simulator joined engine, powertrain and vehicle motion controls to test fuel economy across drive scenarios. Delphi hardware was fitted to a real engine and vehicle, and calibration followed. Real-world testing showed a 20 percent fuel economy gain. Simulations pointed to about 30 percent over a representative baseline. The report documents the controls, the test fleet work and the path from bench rigs to road proof.
doe-osti-3000288-integration-and-demonst:
Timothy Johnson, Christopher Strickland, Jonathan Thomle and co-workers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report a bench-scale demonstration, dated September 2025, for the DV-1 amendment. The amendment is a treatment meant to slow contaminants moving through the deep dry soil layer above groundwater. Before field use, its behaviour must be watched, modelled and predicted under controlled conditions, and that three-part test is the subject here.

A laboratory flow rig called GIFT, for Geophysical Imaging of Flow and Transport, carries the experiments. It controls flow, logs pressure and fluid conductivity, and images the sediment with electrical resistivity tomography, essentially X-rays made of electric current. The PFLOTRAN simulator mirrors the rig so predictions can be checked against the images. An AI-based inversion method also learned to read the images back into soil properties, already beating traditional approaches, with thousands more training runs planned.
doe-osti-3000894-technical-and-community:
Sarah Baker of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory closes a standards project in LLNL-TR-2013236, dated November 2025, on measuring carbon dioxide removal honestly. Buyers pay to have carbon taken out of the air, and the market runs on MRV: measurement, reporting and verification. Without trusted standards, investment stalls and weak claims thrive. This umbrella project built shared technical foundations and coordinated three sister projects, each on its own removal pathway.

Its chief product is the Net Flux Framework, an accounting method built for removal itself. Unlike life-cycle assessment, which tracks how emissions change against a baseline, the framework measures fluxes out of the atmosphere directly. Workshops with voluntary market players exposed a basic snarl: groups used different definitions of removal and aimed at different goals. Publications, workshops and this report carry the framework outward, aiming at standards the whole industry can stand on.
doe-osti-3001532-neurosymbolic-approache:
Cuong Ly, Luke Richards, Jessica Yaros and PNNL colleagues propose marrying two kinds of artificial intelligence in a November 2025 report. Neural networks are powerful but opaque and brittle. Symbolic systems reason in rules a human can audit, but cannot learn from raw data. Neurosymbolic models weld them: perception by network, judgement by explicit logic. For defence users who must trust a model's answers, that audit trail is the point.

The testbed is geointelligence. Building on the lab's ISED model, the team applied neurosymbolic methods to aircraft classification in the RarePlanes satellite imagery dataset. A decision tree grown from defined rules shows exactly why an aircraft got its label. Robustness evaluations probe how the hybrid behaves under stress that breaks purely neural systems. Chapters cover attribute automation and model construction. The report argues assured AI, systems whose reasoning can be inspected, is a practical direction, not a slogan.
doe-osti-3001949-developments-in-process:
Harmony Werth, Krista Carlson, Jade Beland and a university lab team refine a waste form recipe in September 2025. Pyroprocessing spent nuclear fuel leaves electrorefiner salt waste, a chloride salt laced with fission products no repository will accept as is. Iron phosphate glass can lock it up, but first the chlorine must be stripped: dehalogenation. The report develops the processing criteria a reliable production line would need.

Processing ranges for the dechlorination step come first, temperatures and conditions mapped in experiments, drawing on a University of Nevada Reno thesis on phosphate dechlorination kinetics. Then crucibles, the unsung constraint. Quartz, alumina, Monofrax K-3, stainless steel 316L and Inconel 693 are each evaluated for surviving hot phosphate melts without contaminating or failing. Later sections treat off gas, product durability and scale up. The aim is a design basis for turning a nasty salt waste into a stable, disposable glass.
doe-osti-3002066-instantiation-of-the-da:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4212, by Stephanie Cooper, Gina Accawi, Abby Barnes, Hayden Esser, Wes Forman, and colleagues, records the setup of a data platform in September 2025. The platform is Damara Tern, configured here for the Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies program. Programs like this one need shared data handling across laboratories and project teams.

The team stood up a working copy of the platform and checked it with real program tasks. Users can build structured records, attach documents, and follow a digital thread that links inputs to outputs. That thread is what makes results traceable back to their source data. The authors present the setup as a tested pattern for later, larger deployments. It now supports cross-site teamwork inside the program.
doe-osti-3002170-burnup-monitoring-for-p:
Robert McElroy Jr., Jianwei Hu, Donald Kovacic, Francisco Parada, and Manit D. Shah address a safeguards problem in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4116, dated September 2025. Pebble bed reactors use thousands of small spherical fuel pebbles that move through the core during operation. Burnup, the share of fuel used up, must be tracked pebble by pebble for both operations and nuclear material accounting.

The report reviews ways to measure burnup as pebbles leave the core, mainly by their gamma and neutron emissions. It draws on post-irradiation studies of TRISO fuel, the coated-particle fuel these reactors use. Good burnup readings tell operators when a pebble is spent and give safeguards staff a check on declared fuel use. The work supports domestic safeguards planning for pebble bed designs now moving toward licensing.
doe-osti-3002237-initial-design-curves-f:
Yanli Wang of Oak Ridge and Mark C. Messner build design curves in ORNL/TM-2025/4072, dated August 2025. The material is Alloy 709, a high-temperature steel meant for advanced reactor parts. The curves support an improved method for judging creep-fatigue damage, the wear that builds when hot metal cycles under load over years.

The method uses elastic-plastic simulation with a simplified material model, called EPP-SMT in the report. Failure is predicted from dissipated work, the energy absorbed in each cycle. Test data appear as stress-strain loops, with model medians and 90 percent prediction bands beside them. Extrapolation rules extend the lab data toward service lifetimes. Designers use such curves when they size parts that must not crack under decades of hot, cyclic duty.
doe-osti-3002356-exploring-nonmotorized-:
Latif Patwary, Majbah Uddin, Melrose Pan, and Hyeonsup Lim study walking and cycling in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/3954, dated November 2025. Like its companion travel study, it was prepared for the New York State Department of Transportation. The subject is nonmotorized travel across New York State: trips made on foot or by bicycle rather than by car or transit.

The analysis uses the 2017 National Household Travel Survey. It profiles who walks or cycles, trip lengths, purposes, and how rates differ between New York City and the rest of the state. Survey definitions are appended so counts can be reproduced. State planners use this picture when they allocate money for sidewalks, bike lanes, and safety programs. Knowing the baseline matters before claiming any program moved the numbers.
doe-osti-3003148-euro-deterrent-analysis:
Harry William Green, an analyst at Los Alamos, weighs a recurring strategic idea in a CNSIS paper, LA-UR-25-31173, issued November 13, 2025. The idea is a Euro-deterrent: a nuclear arsenal under European control, pledged to defend several European countries at once. Such proposals resurface whenever faith in the American security guarantee under NATO wavers.

Green reviews the main proposals and why none was ever built. Sovereignty and credibility problems recur, along with the lack of shared priorities among European states. Public opinion may be shifting, though: a 2019 Körber Foundation poll had 45 percent of Germans preferring French and British protection over the American umbrella. A March 2025 poll found 61 percent of respondents in nine countries welcoming a French umbrella for the continent.
doe-osti-3003995-target-diagnostic-menu-:
Marty D. Galley of Lawrence Livermore wrote a course project report, LLNL-TR-2013706, dated November 2025, for a design thinking and systems engineering class, SYSM-5620. The project built a target diagnostic menu for the laboratory. In inertial confinement fusion work, each experiment needs a chosen set of diagnostic instruments, and planners need that choice organized in advance.

Galley worked through a formal requirements process: acceptance criteria first, then engineering requirements, with the links between them verified one by one. The closing reflection stresses that checking those links is what made the true system requirements definable with confidence. The author contrasts the method with less structured approaches used before. The document doubles as a worked example of systems engineering method applied to a real laboratory planning problem.
doe-osti-3005935-consistent-overline-eva:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-30214, dated October 22, 2025, tracks progress toward a consistent evaluation of prompt fission neutron multiplicity, written nu-bar, for minor uranium isotopes. Amy Lovell, Denise Neudecker, Cole Fritsch, Ionel Stetcu, Patrick Talou, and Toshihiko Kawano use the CGMF model code, updated so it can treat all of these fission reactions at once. The milestone names uranium-233, -234, and -236. Uranium-235 and -238 are included to pin down the model against solid data, and uranium-232, -237, and -239 come out as byproducts.

The team is clear that no final evaluation exists yet. Studies so far point to the parameter choices CGMF needs, and the new results are not meant to displace the current ENDF/B-VIII.1 values for uranium-235 and -238. A stand-alone uranium-233 evaluation, tied to recent cross section work, is reported separately. Fiscal 2026 work is set out at the end.
doe-osti-3010614-esac-v1-enhanced-ai-pow:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4360, by Changwoo Do, Gergely Nagy, and William Heller, dated December 2025, documents version 1 of ESAC, the EQ-SANS Assisting Chatbot. EQ-SANS is a neutron scattering instrument at the Spallation Neutron Source, and ESAC helps researchers run its experiments.

Version 1 fuses in-context learning with retrieval-augmented generation, so the chatbot answers from instrument documentation rather than memory alone. A built-in development environment, one-click copy of generated code into the script editor, and search sorted by recency round out the upgrade. The chat tracks token use and estimated cost in real time and can switch between language models mid-session. Standalone executable distribution freed users from the original setup.
doe-osti-3011816-recommended-practice-se:
Failed electric vehicle charging sessions get a defined second chance in a recommended practice for seamless retry, prepared for the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation. Ed Watt of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and Mayuresh Savargaonkar of Idaho National Laboratory led the author team, with industry contributors from Electrify America, EVgo, and Flo. The practice first issued in December 2024 and was updated in September 2025.

Requirements cover both charging equipment and vehicle sides of the session. A catalogue of errors, from SLAC parameter faults to high attenuation and abrupt link closure, states whether retry follows a failure. Two appendices added in the update give fallback guidance and test cases.
doe-osti-3013885-gridna-multilevel-cyber:
Shamina Hossain-McKenzie of Sandia led the griDNA project report, SAND2025-12328R, printed September 2025, with partners at Texas A&M, SNC, and the Public Service Company of New Mexico. Grid monitoring sensors today watch either the cyber side, network traffic and hosts, or the physical side, voltages and currents, but never both together. Attacks and faults that cross that boundary can hide in the seam.

griDNA fuses cyber and physical sensor data at several levels of a decentralized grid and classifies events jointly with machine learning. An LSTM autoencoder trained only on normal data flags anomalies when reconstruction error passes the 99th percentile of its training distribution. The fused view also connects operators and cyber defenders automatically, so response to a disturbance starts coordinated instead of siloed.
doe-osti-3014040-assessment-and-improvem:
Niccolo Aurigi wrote this assessment, FERMILAB-FN-1285-PIP2-STUDENT-TD, of high-pressure rinsing for superconducting radio-frequency cavities. Aurigi was a University of Pisa aerospace engineering master's student. He worked in Fermilab's Italian Summer Student Program 2025. His supervisors were Leonardo Ristori, Manuele Narduzzi, and Mattia Parise. Dust and debris on a cavity's inner surface cause field emission. Field emission caps accelerator performance. So cavities are blasted with ultra-pure water jets in cleanrooms.

Aurigi characterized the rinse flow with MATLAB estimates. He then ran two-dimensional Ansys Fluent simulations of the multiphase jet. The runs showed how the main parameters shape cleaning action. Chapters cover pressure losses in the delivery ducts. They also cover the Fermilab rinsing facility itself. The report closes with improvement proposals and future developments for the fluid dynamics side of the process.
doe-osti-3014810-monolithic-mesoporous-m:
Window glazing built from monolithic mesoporous metamaterials is reported in a University of Colorado final report under agreement DE-EE0009699, submitted January 28, 2026. The material is a network of hollow polysiloxane nanotubes, highly transparent and super-hydrophobic, formed into slabs as thick as five centimeters and retrofits a square meter in area. Ivan Smalyukh was principal investigator.

Test units reached R-values near 3.24 and 3.65 square-meter kelvin per watt, measured with minus 4 degrees Celsius outside and 16 degrees inside. Hot box tests at 40 degrees and cold box tests at minus 10 degrees compared the new units against a conventional double-pane unit with a 12 millimeter air gap. The work targets the R-10 to R-15 glazing range named in the project title, a large step up from standard windows.
doe-osti-3015072-methods-for-assessing-o:
NLR/TP-6A40-93850, dated January 2026, systematizes siting for ring dam pumped storage. Rosenlieb, Igwe, Ashworth, Ramasamy, and Cohen wrote it. A ring dam plant stores water in a circular reservoir built on high ground. A second reservoir pairs with it. Sites can thus exist where no natural lake or valley fits a conventional design.

The method runs in three parts. First, a resource assessment finds candidate ring dam locations. It pairs them into systems. Second, a cost assessment computes concrete dam volume. It converts that volume into plant cost. Third, supply curve analysis picks the least-cost nonoverlapping systems. It rolls them up for the contiguous United States. The result is a repeatable screen. Developers and planners can apply it before any site visit.
doe-osti-3015697-comstock-measure-docume:
Interior lighting controls for commercial buildings are documented in NLR/TP-5500-96597, a ComStock measure report dated January 2026 by Marlena Praprost. ComStock models the United States commercial building stock building by building, and this measure adds modern lighting controls to the applicable share of that stock.

National results show electricity savings of 3.6 percent, worth 118.3 trillion British thermal units of site energy, while gas use rises 1.5 percent as efficient lights give off less waste heat. Total site energy savings come to 1.9 percent, or 93.4 trillion British thermal units a year. Bill savings are computed at mean available electricity rates, with other rate structures carried in the report and the public dataset for users who need them.
doe-osti-3016088-wind-plant-flow-physics:
Patrick Moriarty and Paula Doubrawa were the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5000-98634. Rebecca J Barthelmie is also named on the record. The project studied how wind flows through whole wind plants in complex settings, and how that flow sets power output. Its centerpiece was the American Wake Experiment, known as AWAKEN.

AWAKEN gathered lidar and other field data at wind plant sites, with instruments run by several partner institutions. The final design tested seven priority hypotheses about wakes, blockage, and wind farm control. Wakes are the slowed, turbulent air behind turbines, which can cut the output of machines downwind. The datasets and papers listed here give modelers real field numbers for checking their wind plant simulations.
doe-osti-3017117-optical-test-bench-sysm:
Zachary A Amadeo and Taylor Davis wrote this February 2026 final report, LLNL-TR-2014124, for the SYSM 5620 optical test bench project at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The bench supports the National Ignition Facility, where experiment sponsors need color photos of the front of diagnostics mounted at a set target chamber position. Camera needs change fast there, sometimes three swaps in one day.

The report is built around stakeholder interviews, recording the voice of the customer group by group. Sponsors asked for a bench that supports several cameras at once, so one experiment can serve many needs. Operations staff asked for quick camera installs that do not pull workers from shot day tasks, plus simple, intuitive handling. Controls for triggering come from facility operations. Engineers designing support gear for big laser facilities get a worked example of needs gathering done properly.
doe-osti-3017430-evaluation-of-pu-solubi:
Fabienne C Johnson, Wesley H Woodham, and Madison C Hsieh of Savannah River National Laboratory wrote this January 2026 report, SRNL-STI-2025-00736, on plutonium solubility in glass for Sludge Batch 11. At Savannah River, radioactive tank sludge is melted into glass logs for permanent disposal. The glass recipe must hold every element in the batch, plutonium included, without crystals forming that would weaken the product.

The report develops glass compositions for the batch and sets out the test procedures, starting with preparing the sludges for testing. Data tables give the batch chemistry, including supernatant values such as 21,700 milligrams per liter for one measured component and under 100 for oxalate. Those data feed the standard equation that predicts the glass REDOX state. One prediction came out below zero because of an unexpected input, which the team flags openly. Waste form chemists get the measured basis for approving this batch's recipe.
doe-osti-3018255-tcf-base-technology-spe:
Gregg Beckham, Michelle Reed, and Jason DesVeaux of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Brenna Norton-Baker and Natasha Murphy, wrote this February 2026 Technology Commercialization Fund report, NLR/TP-2A00-98395. The project engineered enzymes to eat crystalline PET, the plastic of bottles and fleece. Enzymes that digest plastic exist, but the crystalline parts of PET, where chains pack tightly, resist them.

Industry partner Birch Biosciences led the hands-on protein work: iterative enzyme engineering, test-tube characterization and benchmarking, DNA construction, and microfluidics. The laboratory side ran computational enzyme design and enrichment experiments, including work on endoglucanase recovery and testing. The division of labor is spelled out in the report, task by task. For plastic recycling, the prize is a biological route that works on real, partly crystalline waste instead of only easy amorphous material. This close-out records who did what on the way there.
doe-osti-3019234-battery-life-prediction:
Kandler Smith and Paul Gasper of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this CRADA final report, NLR/TP-5700-96031, February 2026. Tristan Simons is the third named author. The partner was the Australian Department of Defense, which ran accelerated aging tests on lithium-ion batteries. The laboratory's job was prediction: turn that aging data into lifetime models for several chemistries. The models rest on physical degradation mechanisms and had prior validation. Phase 1 ran from June 2017 to March 2021, with extensions.

The analysis separates two fade modes. Loss of lithium inventory and loss of active material dominate in different regimes, split by derivative analysis of the data. Calendar fade was fit first, then the inventory-loss region. Defense users care about batteries that sit in storage and then must work. A physics-based model lets them forecast that readiness by chemistry and use pattern. The report closes the CRADA with the method documented.
doe-osti-3019677-establishing-data-analy:
Owen Leiser, Emma Carlson, Javier Flores, Andy Lin, Tony Chiang, and Amy Sims of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Together they built a data pipeline for genomics in this January 2026 report. Their subject is ATAC-seq, an assay that maps open chromatin across the genome. Raw sequencing reads become claims only through a chain of processing steps. The report establishes that chain as a pipeline and tests it on datasets. Test analyses compared treatments, including ultraviolet exposure against infection, for overlap in differential peaks.

The comparison found substantial agreement: 67 percent of differential peak calls were shared between the two treatments. Peaks found in infected cells appeared across the conditions. For laboratory users, a validated pipeline means results stop depending on who ran the scripts. The report lays out the pipeline's stages and its test evidence. Future ATAC-seq studies at the laboratory inherit the code path and its check.
doe-osti-3020107-form-follows-function-f:
The City of Duluth's final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0010419 presents Form Follows Function, or F3, a planning framework that helps small communities prepare for power outages. Many Midwest towns want stronger energy resilience but lack staff to handle data, run scenarios, or engage residents. F3 was built and tested in Duluth, Minnesota, to close that gap.

Instead of picking projects from the top down, F3 starts with the functions a community must protect, such as heating, medical devices, refrigeration, and phone charging. Residents and local operators define those needs together, then plan shared solutions. Solar panels with battery storage at trusted sites, called resilience hubs, are the typical choice for backup power. The report packages the process as a toolkit that other capacity-limited communities can reuse.
doe-osti-3020509-towards-a-more-predicti:
LLNL abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2013144, by Raspberry Simpson, closes LDRD project 23-ER-047 on laser-driven particle sources. Intense lasers striking a target can speed up electrons, ions, and other particles, but the output beam has been hard to predict. Simpson's project worked to make those sources predictable by tying models tightly to test data.

Runs with the LSP code mapped the electric sheath fields that accelerate particles, for laser pulses of 0.6, 5, and 10 picoseconds. The results showed how targets can hold higher electron temperatures and stronger charge separation for longer times. A stretch goal built a physics-informed machine learning framework: neural networks trained on both experiments and simulations to forecast acceleration behavior. The report frames the outcome as working predictive capability for planning future experiments.
doe-osti-3020692-solution-processed-oxid:
National Laboratory of the Rockies CRADA final report NLR/TP-5K00-99016, CRD-23-23493, with Lance Wheeler as technical contact, evaluates coating inks from NexTC as working layers in perovskite solar cells. Perovskite devices stack thin layers on glass: a transparent conductor, then a transport layer that passes one kind of charge carrier and blocks the other, then the perovskite itself. NexTC's solution-processed oxide inks aim to replace or modify those conductor and transport layers.

The laboratory built both PIN and NIP device configurations on NexTC-coated substrates and compared them with its own standard devices. Electrochemical tests measured how well a tin oxide layer blocks holes while passing electrons, using an iron-based electrolyte. The voucher project gives the company an independent first reading on whether its materials can serve the emerging perovskite industry.
doe-osti-3021515-study-of-the-protection:
NLR report NLR/TP-5D00-98333, by Jing Wang and co-authors from the laboratory and Florida Power & Light, studies a protection problem created by the new grid. Protective relays were designed for power flowing from big spinning generators. In weak grid areas fed heavily by inverter-based resources such as solar and batteries, fault currents look different, and relays can misread them.

The team simulated faults across a test network: 40 single phase-to-ground, 41 phase-to-phase, and 25 phase-to-phase-to-ground faults. Faults were placed at 5, 80, and 95 percent of line length to probe each protection zone. Inverter output was tested at a light 0.1 per-unit load and at full load, across 106 scenarios in all. The report evaluates protection improvements against those cases, aiming to keep relays fast and selective where conventional settings fall short.
doe-osti-3022092-structural-calculations:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011604, by D. Westphal, is the structural calculation package for installing a Xradia UltraXRM-L200 X-ray microscope in Building 327, Room B271K. The package works through the anchorage and support checks an equipment installation of this weight and sensitivity requires. It follows the anchor design provisions of ACI 318-08, including concrete breakout strength calculations for the anchor groups.

Dated July 2011 in its calculation sheets and released in this report form later, the document consists largely of worked calculations, anchor schedules, and installation detail drawings rather than prose. It records the assumed loads, embedment details, and code equations behind each check, so a reviewer can retrace every number. For the library it preserves the engineering basis on which the microscope installation was approved.
doe-osti-3022541-fixed-site-kazr-b1-data:
An Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility report, DOE/SC-ARM-TR-330, by Marquette Rocque, Eddie Schuman, Min Deng, and A. Matthews, documents 2025 data processing for the fixed-site KAZR, the Ka-band cloud radar deployed at ARM's fixed observatories. The b1-level product is the quality-controlled, calibrated reflectivity stream that cloud researchers actually use, and this annual report records what changed in producing it.

Case plots track calibration offsets period by period. One documented change is a radar constant adjustment in the precision radial mode, shown by comparing reflectivity fields from January 3 and February 12, 2025 at the Eastern North Atlantic site. The radars are also cross-checked against other instruments, for example comparing KAZR reflectivity at 500 meters with surface disdrometer estimates after near-field and gaseous attenuation corrections.
doe-osti-3022746-kivalina-biomass-reacto:
A Launch Alaska final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0010149, with Ottar Mobley as principal investigator, covers deployment of a community-scale biomass reactor in Kivalina, a remote Alaska Native village. The project attacks a hard local problem: safe sanitation and waste disposal where everything arrives by air or barge. The system, a Biogenic Refinery, turns bagged waste from urine-diverting dry toilets into biochar and usable heat.

The refinery rides in an insulated 20-foot shipping container with a grinder, augers, and controls. Ground material mixed with paper reaches about 35 percent moisture, and exhaust air passes through biochar to strip odor before leaving the container. Project tasks centered on readiness rather than invention: technology assessment, spare parts, key performance indicators, operator manuals, third-party validation of outputs, and on-site training for local operators.
doe-osti-3023091-em-evaluation-of-a-smok:
Vi Rapp, Sharon Chen, Dylan Anacleto-Black of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Noel Putaansuu of Acumentor LLC tested whether a smoke opacity sensor can help wood heaters burn cleaner. Their peer-reviewed report, dated March 2026, looks at home wood heating, a common source of fine particle pollution. A cheap optical signal, if it tracks smoke well, could guide better combustion.

The lab work weighed test filters twice, repeating any weighing that missed agreement by more than 0.0100 milligrams after a test. Particle counters measured number and size from 7 nanometers to 20 micrometers, sampling once per second. Those instruments let the team check the opacity sensor's accuracy across the particle sizes real wood smoke produces.
doe-osti-3024589-hanford-site-rare-plant:
N J Exe and M L Johnson of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions surveyed rare plants across the Hanford Site through calendar year 2025, in report HNF-72997, Revision 0, published March 2026. Hanford's protected shrub-steppe holds plant populations found almost nowhere else, and yearly visits to known occurrences show whether each is holding on. Photo points pair current images with older ones to make change visible.

Suksdorf's monkeyflower, tied to vernal pool complexes, tells a hard story at one site. Surveys in 2025 found no individuals there; it was last detected at that occurrence in 2017. Cheatgrass and other invasive species have heavily degraded the ground, and the site burned in the May 2020 Gable Mountain fire. The authors judge the monkeyflower possibly extirpated at that occurrence, while monitoring continues at the Gable Butte complex.
doe-osti-3028322-variation-in-surface-pr:
M C Akin of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory studies a quiet error source in LLNL-TR-2011344, dated September 2025: when temperature is measured fast and from a distance, the surface itself can lie. Optical temperature readings depend on how the surface emits and reflects, and those properties vary with finish, oxidation, and coating. Under dynamic conditions, that variation becomes measurement error.

The report works the problem numerically. Tables sweep surface emissivity settings from five hundredths to nine tenths against true temperatures of 6000 and 7000. The computed apparent readings swing widely, from about 5085 to 6195 in the 7000 rows as the second parameter runs from five hundredths to two tenths. Rows like these are the point: two surfaces at one real temperature can report very different temperatures unless their properties are pinned down.
doe-osti-3029528-permittec-v0-1-standard:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-39193, dated April 2026, introduces PermitTEC version 0.1. Kaustav Bhattacharjee, Narmadha Mohankumar, Julianna Puccio, and a large team built a standardized metadata corpus of court cases tied to the National Environmental Policy Act. That 1969 law makes federal agencies study and record the environmental effects of planned actions before they decide. Lawsuits over those studies are hard to track without clean records.

The corpus links each case to the project it challenged. Matching leans on fuzzy title scores blended with search scores, checks that the agencies named in court match the project agencies, and tests for shared states. A perfect agency match scores 100, and missing agency data is scored as neutral. The system aims to make permit disputes searchable on one footing.
doe-osti-3030127-atf-cladding-mechanical:
M. Nedim Cinbiz, Ben Garrison, Ethan Blount, and colleagues at Oak Ridge National Laboratory show off a testing skill in report ORNL/SPR-2025/4125, dated September 2025. The subject is accident tolerant fuel cladding, the metal tubes that wrap reactor fuel. Chromium-coated and plain advanced zirconium alloy tubes went through the High Flux Isotope Reactor. The fiscal 2025 work proved the lab can measure how such tubes stretch and bend after irradiation, data that safety cases need.

Hot cell crews opened the capsules and moved silicon carbide heat monitors to a low-activation lab for study. Eight monitors per capsule were read by dilatometry, a method that tracks tiny length changes with heat. Averaged readings gave each specimen true exposure temperature, checked against model forecasts, with spread shown as error bars.
doe-osti-3030407-atf-cladding-mechanical: ATF cladding got capability-demonstrated again, and this DOE report covers properties. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The demonstration was capability. The data were nuclear. The again were demonstrated. The properties were report. The data were DOE.
doe-osti-3185150-integrated-anaerobic-me:
Prathap Parameswaran of Kansas State University led this wastewater project under award DE-EE0009504, running from October 2021 to December 2025, with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the universities of Kansas and Pittsburgh. The platform pairs an anaerobic membrane bioreactor with electro-assisted fermentation. Bugs break down waste without oxygen, a membrane keeps them in the tank, and electric nudges steer what they make. The goal was total resource recovery from farm and other wastewaters.

The target was to lock away over half the incoming carbon as volatile fatty acids or methane gas. Those acids are saleable chemicals, and longer chains are worth more. Extraction trials pulled the acids out in a clear order: hexanoic acid first, then butyric, propionic, and acetic. Computer models of the acid and solvent mixes matched the lab order.
doe-osti-3344861-final-report-for-electr:
Adam Holewinski and Michael J. Janik report final results under award DE-SC0023322 on turning biomass into chemicals with electricity. The project studied electro-oxidative valorization: using electric power to partly oxidize multi-carbon molecules from plants, stepping alcohols to aldehydes and aldehydes to acids without burning them all the way down. Test chemistry used the furan platform, furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural, to draw lessons that carry to other feedstocks.

Most older work ran in alkaline baths, where more materials survive, but plant feed prep often yields acidic mixes. The team hunted acid-stable catalysts instead. On gold, aldehyde oxidation was selective but slow; platinum ran faster but risked surface poisoning from carbon-carbon cuts and bound acid films. Live spectroscopy watched the surface while quantum models explained the steps.
doe-osti-3362775-merged-aerosol-value-ad:
John E. Shilling and Brian D. Ermold of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory describe a data product in report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-338, dated May 2026, for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility. Aerosol data pour in from many instruments at once, and picking the best stream for each variable is slow, fussy work. The Merged Aerosol Value-Added Product does that sorting for scientists, merging the strongest inputs into one clean record.

The product runs in two modes. A near-real-time stream, labeled c0, posts fast but may carry early versions of some inputs and skips final quality reports. A yearly stream, labeled c1, waits for final inputs and folds in those quality checks. Input quality flags are boiled down to three verdicts, so users can screen data without reading every instrument log.
doe-osti-3364265-realization-of-a-quantu:
A final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0020160, led by Vladimir E. Manucharyan, describes a superconducting circuit built to simulate quantum field theories that ordinary computers cannot calculate. The device is a long transmission line of thousands of tiny superconducting junctions, forming a one-dimensional vacuum for microwave photons. A tunable Josephson junction at the end controls how strongly the photons interact.

Tuning the line's impedance past the quantum resistance of about 6.5 kilo-ohms switched the end junction between superconducting and insulating behavior. The switch happened exactly at the predicted point, settling the forty-year-old Schmid-Bulgadaev transition prediction. At the transition, single photons split into lower-frequency pairs with near-unit probability. The team also saw photon decay blocked by many-body localization. One adjustable chip now stands in for several hard quantum models.
doe-osti-3365006-responsible-artificial-:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated September 2025 for the Office of International Nuclear Security examines how artificial intelligence can hunt insider threats without becoming a threat itself. Jessica Baweja, Jonathan Barr, and Chantell Murphy wrote it. Nuclear facilities increasingly use AI to watch behavior patterns for warning signs. Continuous monitoring, though, creates privacy, accountability, and security risks of its own.

Guidance covers the full deployment: define how alerts escalate, who responds to each kind of behavioral flag, and what actions system outputs may trigger. Programs must also avoid duplicating existing security capabilities or opening new gaps. The framework targets facilities that need insider mitigation strong enough for nuclear work yet governed tightly enough to respect the workforce it watches.
doe-osti-3365080-high-power-amplifier-co:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-23965, by Maria Sanchez Barrueta, Wes Hall, John T. McCaw Lyles, Ray Bratton, and John Lewellen, works out how to power tests of the LAMP accelerator's first accelerating cavities. The radio frequency quadrupole needs an estimated 430 kilowatts and the first drift tube linac cavity 366 kilowatts, before coupling and line losses. An existing amplifier test stand at the lab will be reconfigured to deliver that power.

Two amplifier topologies could excite the first drift tube cavity with minimal redesign, and their merits are under discussion. The plan adds a 90-kilowatt solid-state amplifier, a 2-megawatt circulator, and a high-power switch, with procurement already running. A low-level radio frequency system will supply fast feedback control, and hardware interlocks will block unsafe switch states during conditioning.
doe-osti-3365147-lib81-ace-neutron-subli:
A Los Alamos National Laboratory memorandum, XCP-5:26-011 dated April 27, 2026, from Amanda Lewis, Wim Haeck, Nathan Gibson, and Noah Kleedtke, issues 80 errata files for the Lib81 neutron data library. Lib81 packages the ENDF/B-VIII.1 nuclear data evaluations into ACE files that transport codes read. The erratum fixes neutron capture gamma-ray energy distributions for platinum isotopes 190 through 198 and for tantalum-180m; it is a library processing fix, not a new evaluation.

The bug: processing code collected discrete gamma-ray energies into a union list, but primary gamma energies depend on incident neutron energy, so primaries were counted once per outgoing distribution. One platinum-190 list ballooned to 1,592 entries with wrong energies. Shielding and energy balance calculations depend on these spectra, so users are told to replace the files.
doe-osti-3367322-strong-mitchell-feed-st:
Sargent & Lundy summary report, Revision D dated June 4, 2026, presents the front-end engineering design study for carbon capture at the Mitchell plant, DOE project DE-FE0032222. A FEED study is the detailed engineering package that fixes a design's cost and schedule before construction money commits. This unlimited-rights version summarizes the design for public release.

The study covers the full capture scope for the plant: absorber and regeneration equipment, compression, utilities, and integration with the existing station, prepared for the National Energy Technology Laboratory. Utilities commission FEED studies to learn whether a retrofit pencils out; the summary format lets competitors and researchers see the engineering approach without the proprietary detail. Mitchell joins a series of such studies benchmarking capture costs across the coal fleet.
doe-osti-3369028-fy25-electric-grid-secu:
Sandia National Laboratories annual report SAND2026-21966R tallies the Electric Grid Security program's fiscal 2025 year. The program guards the grid against cyber attack, electromagnetic events, and extreme weather. The report is its scoreboard: 70 publications, 81 intellectual property items, and 19 patents by the cover counts. Journal articles, conference proceedings, and invited talks are listed behind them.

Bibliographies dominate the back half, paper by paper, from spectral clustering for power network reduction to sensor-based phase identification in distribution systems. Acronym tables and award lists fill the front. Annual reports like this exist so sponsors can audit output; the sheer count of venues, from IEEE journals to Electrochemical Society meetings, shows the program's spread across power engineering and security.
doe-osti-3374934-summary-of-responses-to:
A Department of Energy summary dated June 22, 2026, gathers public input on partnerships for transformational artificial intelligence models.
