Saswata Hier-Majumder of the Office of Science is the point of contact. The department issued its request for information in December 2025. The topic is the Genesis Mission Consortium, a planned public-private platform. It would curate lab data and build self-improving AI models on top of it.

More than two hundred submissions came in. The summary covers the nonproprietary parts, from one hundred ninety-four distinct responders. Three questions framed the replies. They asked how labs should curate data with privacy intact, which fields deserve priority models, and how models should reach working scientists. Suggested answers include a federated science cloud with an inference service. Responders also urged open licenses for code, weights, and data, plus a consortium open to small firms.
doe-osti-3375371-the-aerosol-model-bench:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated December 2025 introduces the Aerosol Model Benchmarking Repository, a toolkit for comparing aerosol models head to head. Six authors built it. Laura Fierce of the lab leads the list. Benjamin Murphy of the Norwegian Meteorological Institute and Nicole Riemer of the University of Illinois are among the partners. Aerosol models drive air quality and climate forecasts, yet each team tests its model in its own way.

The repository fixes that gap with shared test cases. A case spells out the particle mix in code: modes for primary carbon, set size ranges, and mass shares for organic matter and black carbon. Gas levels, humidity, and temperature are drawn from set ranges to build an ensemble. Every model then runs the same scenes, so gaps in the output point at the models, not the setup.
doe-osti-3376002-pte-results-from-overpo: Idaho National Laboratory poster INL/MIS-25-88944, dated December 2025, shows results from an overpower run on MOX fuel. Jason L. Schulthess leads the author team; Takayuki Ozawa of the Japan Atomic Energy Agency is a co-author. Its panels lay out aim, test marks, and microscope views, with one results slot a placeholder. The JAEA and INL test pushed a pin from 43 kilowatts per meter to between 120 and 126, at one percent of power per second. Its aim is the failure line for fuel-clad contact in fast reactor MOX.
doe-osti-3377662-three-dimensional-grid-:
Three-Dimensional Grid Visualization for Planning Activities, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A40-98585 from July 2026, is a Dubai case study built with the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority. Five laboratory authors are printed, Nicholas Brunhart-Lupo, Tengis Dashmunkh, Shibani Ghosh, Kenny Gruchalla, and Gayathri Krishnamoorthy, joined by Sajan K. Sadanandan and Tareg Ghaoud of the Dubai utility.

The work puts distribution grid simulations into a three-dimensional view that planners can read directly. It also sets out a battery sizing method whose inputs are simulation results showing thermal and voltage violations, rated line capacities, feeder topology, and impedance data. A line loaded past 100 percent counts as a thermal violation, and the method then sizes storage to support the peak.
doe-osti-3377908-lahaina-energy-partners:
Slides from a Lahaina Energy Partnership community workshop, held May 18, 2026 at Lahainaluna High School in Lahaina, Hawaii, update residents on technical assistance work in progress. The National Laboratory of the Rockies presented with local partners Lahaina Strong, Ha Sustainability, and Shake Energy Collaborative. The evidence record names Jenny Sumner, Evan Rosenlieb, and Maya Fein-Cole among the laboratory contributors. An open house followed the session.

Updates run task by task. Task 1 covers resource assessment, Task 2 building modeling, and Task 3 microgrids. Task 4 treats the distribution grid and undergrounding of lines. Task 5 splits into workforce development, policy and regulatory analysis, and finance. Appendices carry the detail for each task, and residents were invited to question task leads and shape next steps.
doe-osti-3382464-tcf-base-technology-spe:
Christopher P. Muzzillo of the National Laboratory of the Rockies reports on negative cracked film lithography for PERC cadmium telluride solar cells in a Technology Commercialization Fund final report, NREL/TP-5K00-95085, dated July 2026. The project start date is printed as October 1, 2023. Funding came from the Solar Energy Technologies Office. The report was produced while the laboratory still operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

Cadmium telluride is a thin-film solar material. The PERC design, borrowed from silicon practice, adds a passivated rear contact to catch more light and lose less energy. Patterning that rear contact cheaply is the problem the project attacked: a cracked film itself serves as the lithography pattern, a negative of the usual mask-making process. The report closes the fund's base technology work on the method.
doe-osti-3402005-domestically-manufactur:
Plug Power Inc. closes out award DE-EE00009248 with a final report on fuel cells built in the United States for heavy duty use. Dr. Cynthia Rice led the work as principal investigator. The project ran from October 1, 2020 to September 30, 2025.

Teams tuned cell active area for system needs and shop processes. They also built test methods for stacks at sizes between lab cells and full systems. Plug Power chose not to use the standard single-cell stress test, since its voltages run well above real use. The results point toward fuel cells that can be made at scale for trucks and other heavy work.
doe-osti-3409012-genesis-mission-enabled:
Argonne report ANL-26/27 sets out Genesis-SAFE, a plan to use secure AI to strengthen energy process safety. Hyekyung Kim, Bruce Hamilton, Allison Fischman, and co-authors wrote the study. The plan draws on a confidential industry safety data set called SafeOCS in the text.

A framework named AI-EPS was deployed and tested inside a secure enclave called ABLE. Setup steps that failed to move cleanly between systems were written down for reuse. The work shows what safe AI use takes when data cannot leave a guarded space. Gulf energy operators gain a model for learning from shared safety records.
doe-osti-3426936-stereo-vision-thermal-i:
Pacific Northwest abstract PNNL-39677, dated August 2026, describes ThermalTracker-3D, a stereo thermal camera system for tracking flying animals near wind farms. Alicia M. Mahon and Jennifer Wehof wrote the abstract for CRADA number 763 with Sightir, Inc. The hosted text is an abstract only, so this note stays brief.

Two thermal views combine into three-dimensional tracks of birds or bats in flight. Wind farm operators need such tracks to judge collision risk and time shutdowns. The abstract frames the system and its purpose without test data. Readers learn what the tool is and why wind sites would deploy it.
doe-osti-3435803-development-of-sam-code:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-26/24 develops SAM code features for safety analysis of air-ingress events in gas-cooled reactors. Gang Yang, Zhiee Jhia Ooi, and Ling Zou are among the authors. Air leaking into a hot graphite reactor can start damaging oxidation.

Test data show oxygen in the inlet plenum fell fast once argon flooded in. It dropped to about 11 percent within 2 seconds. By about 6 seconds it reached about 1.8 percent. Natural circulation stalled, then heat rose and recovery began. Safety analysts can check SAM against this sharp, well-timed record.
doe-osti-3484809-solar-resource-measurem:
NLR/TP-5D00-100533 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that sums up solar resource measurements in Eugene, Oregon. Aron Habte was the lab contact. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-07-00252, a long-running measurement effort.

Quality checks cover the station record from 2017 to 2025. The data set is largely complete, the report finds. Gaps came from broken instruments, logger faults, tracker failures, and upkeep downtime. One table flags diffuse light data for 2023 in the yearly summary. Long, checked sun records anchor solar design for the Pacific Northwest. Yearly summaries flag those gaps so users know which periods carry thinner records.
doe-osti-3520295-high-temperature-chlori:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4774, by Phillip Halstenberg, Shannon Mahurin, and Sheng Dai and dated August 2026, builds a high-temperature reference for actinide chloride salts. Reference electrodes let chemists measure salt potentials on a shared scale. Molten salt reactor work needs such anchors at high heat.

In one salt system, the chloride signal rose toward unity as heat increased. Two readings at 600 degrees Celsius differed by 15.8 millivolts in one run. That gap shows the deviation was not repeatable within a run. Salt chemists learn where the reference holds and where readings drift.
doe-osti-3520598-thermal-scattering-law-:
Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4357, dated February 2026, measures the thermal scattering law for lithium aluminate with the ARCS and VISION instruments. Iyad Al-Qasir, Kemal Ramic, Luiz Leal, and Alex Lang wrote the report. Scattering laws tell modelers how neutrons bounce in a material.

Measurements ran at 295 kelvin and 600 kelvin for two sample types. One sample used natural lithium; the other was fully enriched in lithium-7. Measured spectra matched computed density-of-states curves in fine detail. Fusion blanket studies use lithium aluminate, so checked scattering data sharpen their neutron models.
doe-osti-3676872-interconnection-timelin:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory slide set, dated September 2026, sums up data on hooking distributed energy projects to United States distribution grids. Five authors are printed: Kathryn Chelminski, Johnny Wong, Lisa Schwartz, Margaret Pigman, and Katherine Carlson. The period covered runs from 2000 to 2025. Data came from utilities, state commissions, and the Interconnection.fyi site. The slides make no policy recommendations.

Interconnection covers the technical, legal, and step-by-step rules for adding a local generator or storage unit. Charts track applications, timelines, and costs by project size and state. One finding is that average time from application to a signed service agreement improved by about a quarter in recent years, across the states studied. For the largest class studied, median timelines fell a great deal between 2019 and 2023. Yet most of those projects were still in process, without permission to operate, by 2024.
doe-osti-3682473-validation-of-ultrasoni:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4764, dated August 2026, checks sound-based ways to read stress in reinforcing bar inside concrete. Four authors are printed: Hongbin Sun, Adam Brooks, Marco Martinez, and Samantha Sabatino. Sound speed in steel shifts with stress, an effect called acoustoelasticity. Heat also shifts sound speed, so the two effects must be split first.

Tests pulled bare bars in tension while sensors tracked guided sound waves. Other bars were cast in concrete and pulled the same way, with heating pads wrapped on. A chamber test swung heat between twenty and fifty degrees at four set rates. The link between sound speed and heat stayed tightly linear at every rate, with near-equal slopes. So heating rate, in the tested range, does not bend the correction. The work supports field checks on hidden bars.
doe-osti-3816575-technoeconomic-opportun:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A20-97066, dated September 2026, tests whether Falls City, Nebraska should build its own power plant. Simon Sandler, Meenakshi Narayanaswami, William Carron, and Jamie Lopp are the printed authors. The town weighed solar panels, battery storage, or both against buying wholesale power. Models ran fifty-four scenarios across price paths and weather years.

Only four scenarios came out ahead in present value. All four paired solar with high wholesale prices and the fastest price growth path. Storage alone never won, and its revenue failed to cover upkeep under the base outlook. The authors note what could flip the maths: cheaper build costs, grants, or pay for grid services.
doe-osti-3818368-a-button-type-beam-posi:
Brookhaven technical note NSLSII-ASD-TN-446, dated August 2026, models a button-type beam position monitor for the NSLS-II storage ring. Victor Smaluk is the sole printed author. The monitor supports a test of a new complex-bend magnet design. Four small button electrodes pick up the passing beam's image current. Smaluk traces that faint signal through every stage to the readout electronics.

The chain runs through a combiner, then a twenty metre coaxial line to the front end. A twenty decibel amplifier lifts the signal before a filter centred at five hundred megahertz. In user mode, a thousand bunches carrying five hundred milliamps yield a clean wave near one and a half volts. In study mode, a hundred bunches at low current give only about fifty millivolts. The note also checks readout straightness as the beam wanders off centre.
doe-osti-3818369-ion-effects-in-the-eic-:
Brookhaven technical note NSLSII-ASD-TN-447, dated August 20, 2026, studies ion effects in the Electron-Ion Collider's Beam Accumulator Ring. Six authors from Brookhaven and Argonne are printed, led by Victor Smaluk. The ring stacks about thirty linac pulses into one bunch of twenty-eight nanocoulombs. Such a dense electron bunch ionizes the thin gas left in the vacuum pipe. Trapped ions then shake the beam, swelling its size and hurting hand-off to the next ring.

The team estimated the growth rate with formulas and tracking runs on the current lattice file. Four gas species fill the model: hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide. Ion sway frequencies spread around the ring as beam size changes, and that spread damps the growth. The effect caps itself and rarely dumps the beam. Still, modest swelling cuts injection efficiency downstream. Results feed the ring's vacuum and mitigation choices.
doe-osti-3874830-marsame-radiological-re:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-27737, issued September 11, 2026, documents the radiological release survey of Technical Area 43 Building 1. Mary Jo Chastenet and Jamie Gerard are the printed authors. Before a building with past radiological work can be released, crews must prove its surfaces meet free-release limits. The MARSAME method structures that proof: the building splits into survey units, each with a class and a sampling plan. Floors, walls, and ceilings all get direct readings and wipe smears.

Tables log every unit, from the elevator shaft to basement closets and roof machine rooms. Each entry lists alpha and beta readings, scan coverage, and quality repeats near ten percent. Survey dates run from September 2025 through March 2026. Most closets could not be entered, and the report says plainly that not all were surveyed. Final calls on waste disposition rest with the lab's waste management programs.
doe-osti-3874840-excitons-and-polaritons:
Los Alamos project report LA-UR-26-28337, issued September 16, 2026, adapts a vibration algorithm into a tool for tiny semiconductor crystals. Serguei Goupalov is the sole printed author. The xyz method was built in 1991 for vibration modes of elastic objects. Goupalov reworks it, inside the effective mass picture, to compute hole states in colloidal nanocrystals. The test case is indium phosphide, a safer stand-in for toxic quantum dots.

Applied to a spherical crystal, the tool shows where the simple rounded picture breaks. For the lowest one or two hole levels, it gives sound guidance. From the second or third level up, it misses level order, symmetry, and degeneracy. The cause is the strong directional character of the real crystal lattice. The report also computes how light-matter waves travel along a nanowire of a lead-halide crystal. The tool is pitched as decisive for rods and ellipsoidal dots.
doe-osti-3989379-advanced-moderator-modu: Argonne National Laboratory closes out a joint project with AlphaTech Research Corp in this short final CRADA report, ANL/CFC-C2023-A00104. Sumit Bhattacharya, Yinbin Miao, and Abdellatif Yacout are the named Argonne staff, and Los Alamos National Laboratory also took part. Most of the hosted pages are the standard closeout form. The scope note says Argonne built a moderator module for the AlphaTech micro molten salt reactor and ran tests whose data showed how it behaves and whether it suits the design.
draft-of-a-plan-for-beginning-animal-san:
Lieutenant-Colonel William Wood of Quebec drafted a plan for wild animal sanctuaries in Labrador, meant for the fourth annual meeting of Canada's Commission of Conservation at the start of 1913. The paper is marked for private circulation. It follows his 1911 address on the same theme and a supplement from 1912, both nearly out of print by the time he wrote.

Wood thanks an odd crew of experts: friends who fish, seal, hunt, trap, and guide for a living, men never called experts before. The plan asks for patrol help from the Dominion Fisheries Protection Service and the government telegraph line, and for offenders to be handed to the province for punishment. Sections verify the facts, then set out a full scheme for the Canadian Labrador. It is an early, practical sketch of wildlife protection in the north.
eleanor:
Mrs. Humphry Ward gives her 1900 novel Eleanor to Italy, the beloved and beautiful, in a warm dedication. Albert Sterner drew the illustrations. The scene opens at an Italian villa, where Miss Manisty, a small elderly lady in a cap, breaks news to her nephew Edward. A young American woman, Lucy Foster, will arrive within the half hour.

Eleanor, Edward's cousin and the villa's reigning spirit, must help decide what to do with the visitor. Portraits in the plate list promise the beautifying of Lucy and a Father Benecke. An old man's advice to Lucy, whispered at table, is to learn Persian and get the dictionary. Ward writes the clash of old Europe and young America as a drama of manners and faith. Lucy, fresh and direct, unsettles a house built on reserve, art, and quiet renunciations.
every-man-in-his-humor:
Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour, in the anglicized edition, carries an introduction calling Jonson the greatest English dramatist except Shakespeare. The introduction traces his Westminster schooling under Camden, to whom the play was dedicated. Jonson's soldiering in Flanders and his duels precede the comedy. The play itself reset the Italian original in London.

Old Knowell worries over his son Edward's wild companions, and sends his servant Brainworm spying after him. Master Kitely's jealousy of his wife, the water-bearer Cob, and the braggart Bobadill fill the city scenes. Every character serves his humour, the ruling obsession Jonson made a dramatic system. The comedy of humours founded a school that English drama followed for decades. Jonson's London is exact: shops, taverns, and tobacco talk. The introduction's scholarship and the play's energy make this the standard gateway to his work.
fonvizin-der-landjunker-the-minor:
A spoiled young nobleman who cannot learn and will not grow up anchors Denis Fonvizin's comedy The Minor, given here in German translation as Der Landjunker. Written in 1782, the play effectively invented Russian social comedy. Mitrofanushka's doting, tyrannical mother raises him into perfect uselessness while lecturing everyone on virtue.

Fonvizin aims his satire at the ignorant gentry of Catherine's age: brutal to serfs, proud of empty titles, hostile to learning. Honest officials and a wise uncle supply the standard the household fails. Humane as well as sharp, the comedy is still performed in Russia today. Its schoolroom scenes remain painfully funny anywhere exams are dodged. The German version opens Russia's first great play to new readers.
girlhood-and-womanhood-the-story-of-some:
Sarah Tytler, author of Papers for Thoughtful Girls, gathers tales of girls and women in this 1883 volume, subtitled The Story of some Fortunes and Misfortunes. The book falls into parts with heads such as Cain's Brand, On the Stage and Off the Stage, and A Cast in the Waggon. Stories nest inside each part, each with its own heroine.

One tale follows Mistress Betty from the stage to nursing and to a journey into Somersetshire. Another sends Dulcie off in a waggon to join her company. The women face work, travel, pride, and loss, and Tytler treats their choices with sympathy. The tales reflect Victorian ideas of a woman's path, yet they give their heroines grit. Readers get a set of linked portraits of young lives under pressure.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALabor_CIA_La:
William Greider reported for the Washington Post on a quiet change in the labor movement's Cold War. After the CIA pulled out of funding overseas labor work, its exposure in 1967 having made the arrangement untenable, the AFL-CIO turned to subsidies from the Agency for International Development.

For two decades the CIA had channeled money to American unions fighting Communist labor federations abroad, and the pullout left the programs hunting for a new patron. AID money was overt, which changed both the politics and the paperwork. Greider's article records the handover as it happened, a small marker of the post-exposure cleanup.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIUSRecordingC:
In January 1978, the U.S. Department of Justice issued a report on the relationship between the United States Recording Company and the FBI. The report also covers certain other matters pertaining to the Bureau. It is an internal reckoning made public: the department examining a private company's tie to its own police force.

A recording company linked to the FBI raises obvious questions about surveillance work and who performed it. The department's report was the official effort to answer them. Readers get the findings in the government's own words, from a period when the Bureau's practices faced hard public scrutiny.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FordGeraldRPort:
An FBI memorandum dated February 24, 1964 was prepared for Clyde Tolson, J. Edgar Hoover's deputy. It records a call from J. Lee Rankin, chief counsel of the Warren Commission. Rankin's call concerned Marina Oswald, the accused assassin's widow, and James Herbert Martin, a figure in her affairs.

Marina's testimony and her handling were live issues between the commission and the Bureau. A call from the commission's lawyer became a memo to the director's right hand the same day. The paper shows how closely the two bodies coordinated, and how quickly their contacts were written up.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrankelSandor_F:
Harold Weisberg wrote on April 14, 1973 to Sandor Frankel, a New York lawyer, asking to be represented. Weisberg had disputes with publishers and book wholesalers over money he said they owed him. He wanted counsel to pursue what his books had earned.

The letter shows the business underside of dissent publishing. Weisberg's books challenged official history, but they still moved through ordinary contracts, print runs, and wholesale accounts. When the money did not arrive, he hired the law like any author. The request preserves that practical fight in his own words.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewOrleansDupli: An unidentified author left this fragment of an essay about Jack Ruby's shooting of Lee Harvey Oswald. The writer asks how Ruby, a known gambler and nightclub owner, managed to shoot Oswald in front of the Dallas police. That question has been asked since November 24, 1963, when the shooting happened in a police basement crowded with officers and cameras. The fragment gives the question, but its author and its full argument are not preserved.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PearlHarbor_Pea: nsia-PearlHarbor Pearl Harbor: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RockwellGeorgeL: nsia-RockwellGeorgeLincoln Rockwell George Lincoln: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SocialistWorker: nsia-SocialistWorkersParty Socialist Workers Party: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VaganovIgor_Vag: An FBI memorandum dated February 20, 1967, records a phone call from Domingo Benavides. Benavides was a key witness to the shooting of Dallas police officer J. D. Tippit, killed shortly after President Kennedy. The file is cataloged under the name Igor Vaganov. The memo shows the bureau still logging witness contacts years later, as new names and claims kept entering the assassination files.
govdocs-archive_org-theory-of-geometrica: Ludwig Bieberbach, a German mathematician, wrote a treatise on geometrical construction, and this volume gives it in English in a machine-made translation. Its German title is Theorie der geometrischen Konstruktionen. The subject is classic: what can be drawn with straightedge and compass, and what cannot. The edition includes an introduction. It serves readers of mathematics history who can work past the rough edges of an automatic translation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Tru:
Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump's Florida resort, hosted official business while also operating as a private club. Lists of its visitors would show who gained access to the president there. This posting reports that the White House refused to keep or release such lists, citing ProPublica reporting.

Visitor logs matter because access is influence. Earlier administrations released White House logs as a transparency practice. The refusal at Mar-a-Lago broke that pattern at the very place where club members could mix with officials. The record is short, but it documents a specific gap in the public trail of a presidency.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran-nuc:
From the late 1940s into the early 1960s, the United States and Britain planned for a Soviet invasion of the Middle East. Part of that planning was denial: disabling or destroying the region's oil facilities before the Soviets could take them. This briefing book, posted in June 2016, publishes recently discovered British documents.

The documents give a new account of the CIA's role in the top-secret plan to ravage the Middle East oil industry. Scorched-earth planning against allied oil fields sounds extreme, yet it sat in official files for years. The record shows how completely Cold War planners subordinated the world economy to a single feared invasion.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iraq-nuc:
On June 7, 1981, Israeli jets attacked Iraq's Osirak nuclear research reactor at Tuwaitha and partially destroyed it. Joyce Battle edited this briefing book, posted exactly forty years later in June 2021. The aircraft and much of the equipment were American supplied, a fact the documents explore.

The posting's question has divided analysts ever since: was the strike a setback for Saddam Hussein's bomb program, or an impetus that drove it deeper underground? Declassified records let readers weigh both readings against what officials knew then. Few single air strikes have carried forty years of argument, which makes the file unusually instructive.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Seventy-five years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki opened the atomic era, this briefing book, posted in May 2020, surveys American nuclear forces during the Cold War. Its themes are overkill and assured destruction: arsenals built far beyond any plausible military need.

The posting frames the hard questions that still follow the weapons. Their value, danger, and morality challenge politicians, strategists, and ordinary citizens alike. A survey built on the documentary record gives those debates a factual spine. Readers can see how the arsenal grew, what its builders said it was for, and why alternatives kept being searched for and not found.

In 1978 and 1979 American officials discovered the scale of Pakistan's secret nuclear program, and it posed what they called an acute dilemma. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 773, published in August 2021. New documents center on A. Q. Khan, the program's central figure.

Khan led shopping expeditions abroad for nuclear supplies, buying the parts of a bomb piece by piece. Officials even discussed the brutal possibility that some other country might destroy Pakistan's nuclear plants. The dilemma was real: punish an ally and push it closer to the bomb, or tolerate a program Washington publicly opposed. The papers show both horns of it.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-intelligence:
In April 2018, the National Security Archive sued the CIA in federal court in Washington under the Freedom of Information Act. The suit sought twelve specific cables from November and December 2002, written or approved by Gina Haspel. She had just become the agency's acting director and was awaiting confirmation as its permanent head.

Those cables came from the Thailand black site Haspel ran, where prisoners were waterboarded and held in secret. Supporters said her record showed experience; critics said the cables would show exactly what she authorized. The Archive's suit is a case study in disclosure law used at a confirmation moment. That is when the public's need to know and the agency's wish for secrecy collide hardest. The posting lays out the filing and what each side wanted.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_2nd_Circuit_:
Who visits the White House is a basic record of who has the president's ear, and the Obama administration published about six million such visitor records. A National Security Archive news post from May 2020 reports a Second Circuit ruling in Doyle v. DHS that helped the White House keep later visitor logs secret, in a defeat for the groups that sued.

The Archive notes, with some bite, that the ruling never mentions Obama's six million released records at all. The case, brought with CREW and the Knight Institute, exposed how weak federal records laws can be when an administration simply refuses disclosure. For readers, the posting is both a case report and an argument: transparency that depends on a president's goodwill can vanish the moment goodwill does.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Breaking_New: On July 27, 2018, the National Security Archive reported a court ruling in its running fight over White House visitor logs. A judge let the Secret Service keep the logs hidden. Visitor logs show who walks into the seat of power, and administrations publishing them surrender real secrecy. The ruling kept the Trump White House's visitors out of public view. The posting here is the Archive's same-day account of its own defeat, for readers tracing how disclosure law bends in court.
grain-and-chaff-from-an-english-manor:
Arthur H. Savory farmed an English manor at Aldington and set down its life in Grain and Chaff from an English Manor, published at Oxford in 1920. The contents begin with the village, the manor house, and the farm. Then come the people: the farm bailiff, the hop foreman and hop drier, the head carter, the carpenter, and an old-fashioned shepherd.

Later chapters treat the character of farm laborers and villagers, machinery, asparagus, and village politics. Savory tells of his three vicars, church restoration, and his years as churchwarden and school board man. The tone is fond, dry, and exact. The book is a store of how an English farm really ran before tractors took over, told by the man who paid the wages and knew every worker by name.
how-and-when-to-be-your-own-doctor:
Isabelle A. Moser, a doctor of natural hygiene, wrote How and When to Be Your Own Doctor with Steve Solomon. Solomon tells in his foreword how Moser's advice restored his own failing health. The book teaches hygienist practice, a system that treats disease as the body's effort to cleanse itself. Its home ground is Oregon, where Moser ran a health school.

Chapters explain how she became a hygienist and what she believes causes disease. Long sections give practical direction on fasting, colon cleansing, diet, and food supplements. A final chapter works through particular disease states and how the body recovers. Appendices gather further guidance for home care. Readers get a complete statement of one alternative tradition, written for laypeople willing to take charge of daily habits.
iamblichus-life-pythagoras-taylor:
Iamblichus, a Neoplatonic philosopher, wrote his Life of Pythagoras around 300 CE. Thomas Taylor translated the biography into English in 1818. Pythagoras appears here as philosopher, mathematician, and miracle-working sage together.

Iamblichus tells of Pythagoras taming a bear and recalling past lives. The sage hears the music of the spheres and founds a disciplined community. Rules for diet, silence, and study governed his followers' daily lives. Taylor, England's great Platonist translator, prized this late-antique portrait. The Life blends history, legend, and Neoplatonic teaching without separating them. Readers seeking the historical Pythagoras must filter carefully, but the legend itself shaped centuries. The book is part life, part myth, and part a guide for those who would live well and think deep.
in-the-reign-of-terror:
G. A. Henty placed a Westminster boy in France during the Terror in this 1887 tale. His short preface says the story speaks for itself, more than history lessons do. He notes one change, that the drownings at Nantes are placed earlier than they fell. A journey to France opens the plot.

Parents debate letting their son live among the French after the Bastille fell. Later a nurse reports a patient too weak to rave, whose fate two days will decide. Escape, rescue, and terror in Paris drive the tale. Henty gives boys the Revolution as adventure.
jack-mason-the-old-sailor:
Francis C. Woodworth wrote Jack Mason, the Old Sailor for children, under the name Theodore Thinker, in 1850. Jack is shown in a pea-jacket with a book, telling tales to a boy on a coil of rope. He has sailed almost all over the world, the narrator says. He does not swear or drink rum, unlike many sailors.

A native man asks the sailors daily for rum and tobacco in one tale. Some give him rum till he gets drunk, which the book blames on them, not him. He dives farther than anyone the narrator ever saw. Short sea tales teach children temperance and kindness.
jane-allen-junior:
Edith Bancroft's Jane Allen: Junior brings her basketball heroine to the third year at Wellington College. The title page lists her earlier volumes, from Jane Allen of the Sub-Team onward. Late September sunshine opens the get-together on the poplar slope. Judith Stearns hopes the weird shadows are not a sign.

A misfit freshman and thrilling news start the year in earnest. Threats and defiance bring Jane to the rescue of her friend Judith. A hidden chamber and the ghost of Lenox Hall supply the mystery. The dance, the big night, and startling disclosures crowd the close. Bancroft writes college fiction for girls in the series manner: sport, loyalty, and a spook explained. Jane's junior year mixes examinations with adventure, and friendship carries both. The real story, as the last chapter promises, corrects every rumour.
john-jacob-astor:
John Jacob Astor is Elbert Hubbard's sketch of the fur trader who became America's first multimillionaire. It belongs to Hubbard's Little Journeys to the Homes of Great Business Men. The sketch opens with a saying credited to Astor: the man who goes to bed at nine gets rich and stays reliable. Hubbard builds on it a sermon about habit.

Wealth, Hubbard argues, is a result of good habits, and honest men work by day. He quotes Victor Hugo: when you open a school, you close a prison. Education, for Hubbard, must make people self-reliant and efficient, not merely honored. His Astor is less a life story than a lesson in industry, told in Hubbard's brisk, preaching style.
literary-blunders-a-chapter-in-the-histo:
Henry B. Wheatley studies literary mistakes in this book. He calls it a chapter in a history of human error. His preface borrows the frame from Bulwer-Lytton's novel The Caxtons. Augustine Caxton there plans a great History of Human Error.

That fictional work forms the pivot of the novel's incidents. Wheatley modestly offers his blunders as one real chapter. Printers, authors, and translators all contribute errors to his store. Readers meet amusing mistakes that survived into print. The Caxtons' charming novel inspired Wheatley's modest framing device. His history grows gradually around Augustine Caxton's pivot work.
literary-taste-how-to-form-it-with-detai:
Arnold Bennett first published this guide to reading in August 1909. The text here follows the seventh edition of February 1914. Bennett promises to show readers how to form literary taste. Detailed instructions help them collect a complete English library.

His lists organize poets and prose writers by periods. Beaumont and Fletcher appear among the Period One poets. Plain advice suits busy beginners who need a starting shelf. Bennett plays friendly mentor rather than distant scholar throughout. Hyphenation choices in six words troubled the modern text editor. Canterbury Poets editions supply several of Bennett's recommended texts.
lorna-doone-a-romance-of-exmoor:
R. D. Blackmore called Lorna Doone a romance, and his 1869 preface says why. The scenes, people, and deeds are all romantic, drawn from Exmoor nurse-tales. At its heart stands John Ridd, a farmer of great strength and simple heart. Against him stand the Doones, outlaws of Bagworthy Forest, feared across the moor.

John loves Lorna, the beautiful girl raised among the Doones against her will. Their story runs through raids, escapes, and open war on the moor. Blackmore said he shaped the old tale with care and warm color. The result is a classic tale of love across a blood feud. Generations of readers have kept it in print ever since.
martin-hewitt-investigator:
Arthur Morrison published Martin Hewitt, Investigator in 1894. Seven cases make up the book, each named on the contents page. They run from the Lenton Croft robberies to the affair of the tortoise.

The first case starts with a great will suit, Bartley v. Bartley. A young clerk's sharp work built proof that stunned the other side. That clerk is Hewitt, and the book follows the skill that made his name in such work. Other heads name a jewel theft, a cameo, and a torpedo plot. Each case turns on small facts that most eyes would pass by.
masterpieces-of-american-wit-and-humor:
Thomas L. Masson edited Masterpieces of American Wit and Humor, dated 1903 here. Mark Twain's face fronts the book as its first picture. The contents mix short prose, verse, and comic sketches by many hands.

Agnes Repplier opens with a plea for humor. Marietta Holley, Fitzhugh Ludlow, and Robert Jones Burdette follow. Burdette offers a rheumatism movement cure, and Seba Smith tells of his first visit to Portland. William Cullen Bryant's Mosquito shows how wide the net is cast. John Carver and Oliver Wendell Holmes add New England wit to the mix. The range runs from school room verse to sharp prose sketches.
meyer-us4613304-gas-electrical-hydrogen-:
Stanley A Meyer won United States Patent 4,613,304 on September 23, 1986, for a gas electrical hydrogen generator. The device sits at the heart of his water fuel cell family of eight patents. It was the box meant to split water into fuel gas with pulses of power.

The patent describes the cell plates, the gas space above them, and the circuit that drives the split. Meyer claimed the cell made far more gas than plain electrolysis should allow. A patent only records that a design was filed as new. In 1996, an Ohio court found Meyer's fuel claims fraudulent.
meyer-us4613779-electrical-pulse-generat:
United States Patent 4,613,779 went to Stanley A Meyer on September 23, 1986, the same day as his generator patent. It covers the electrical pulse generator that powered his water fuel cell. The filing is one of eight patents in the Meyer family gathered here.

The circuit builds sharp pulses of voltage and feeds them to the cell that splits water. Meyer said the pulses, timed to a set frequency, shook water apart with very little power. That claim was never proven by outside tests. A patent shows a design was filed, not that it works, and Meyer's claims were ruled fraudulent in 1996.
modern-broods-or-developments-unlooked-f:
Charlotte Mary Yonge published this late novel with Macmillan in 1900. It was reprinted within two months of its first edition. Her epigraph, from Tennyson, says youth and age are scholars yet in the lower school. The title promises modern broods and developments nobody expected.

The first chapters are named Tortoises and Hares, The Goyle, and The First Sunday. A chapter called Cycles hints at generations repeating and diverging. Yonge, the Victorian novelist of family life, watches a new generation grow up under changed conditions. Her interest is moral as much as social: what the young keep, and what they quietly discard.
mona-or-the-secret-of-a-royal-mirror:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon published this romance in 1891. Sheldon wrote popular novels like Virgie's Inheritance and Trixy. Her first chapter introduces a fascinating young widow. Two gentlemen in a Chicago hotel dining room watch her pass, and one raves over her face and figure.

The widow's hair starts the comedy: her admirer has always detested red hair. Hers, he insists, is a deep, rich shade, unlike any he has seen. Her diamonds alone are worth a small fortune. The title promises a royal mirror and its secret, the kind of hidden-identity machinery Sheldon's dime-novel readers loved.
my-aunt-margaret-s-mirror:
Sir Walter Scott wrote this short tale for The Keepsake Annual of 1828. His introduction tells how such gift annuals came from Germany. Mr. Ackermann first brought the fashion to Britain. The Keepsake's fine engravings cost its owners a fortune.

Scott gave the editor fragments meant for his Chronicles of the Canongate. The tale itself turns on a mirror with strange powers. V1 says a young woman dares to look and sees what is to come. Scott mixes Scots wisdom with a ghostly chill. The piece is a neat, compact sample of his short fiction, framed by his own chatty account of its birth.
my-home-in-the-field-of-honor:
Frances Wilson Huard tells how war came to her French home in 1914. Her chateau at Villiers sits near the Marne, an hour from Paris. In late July her guests talk theatre and play bridge. War is the farthest thing from their minds.

Guests include an artist, a magazine editor, and French friends. A walk ends under a purple beech above the river. Days later one guest leaves for Paris as news darkens. Huard writes as an American wife in France. Her home soon lay in the field of honor, and her tale shows peace breaking, hour by hour, at one house.
my-life-as-an-author:
Martin Farquhar Tupper published his autobiography in London in 1886. Sampson Low issued it from 188 Fleet Street. Chapter one sets out sonnets, self-judgment, and samples from his books. He says the book treats his public life, not his private one.

Chapter two recalls his schooldays at Brentford, Brook Green, and Charterhouse. His father knew King George III and held a patent gaslight post. Germany, Guernsey, America, and Canada all touched his youth. Tupper had been a famed poet of proverbial verse. His memoir shows a Victorian man of letters taking stock of fame, faith, and a long writing life.
my-summer-with-dr-singletary-part-2-from:
John Greenleaf Whittier calls this tale a fragment from his works. It opens with bold news: Dr. Singletary is dead. The narrator asks why one old man's death should claim notice. His answer lifts the doctor into every reader's kin.

Singletary shared our joy, sorrow, sin, and folly, Whittier argues. Death has stripped his odd, repulsive traits away. He stands now as God's child and our brother. The doctor was single, little known, and little missed. His village paper gave him one stock line of praise. Whittier's sketch turns that slight notice into a tender plea for how we judge the obscure.
nasa-tm-19630010328-the-purposes-of-envi:
John H. Boeckel wrote this NASA paper on February 12, 1963. Boeckel led test and evaluation work in the Office of Technical Services. His subject is why scientific satellites get harsh tests before launch. Explorer XII serves as his typical satellite case.

The contents move from test philosophy to plans and levels. Vibration, shock, heat, cold, and vacuum each get a section. Spin, acceleration, and humidity are covered as well. Boeckel asks if test levels are strong enough, based on past programs. The paper is a guide to proving a satellite can survive launch and space before it ever leaves Earth.
nasa-tm-19650020204-a-mutual-visibility-:
G D Repass and R G Chaplick at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this May 1965 description of a computer program for communication satellites. Two satellites can relay signals only when each can see the other, or when a ground path links them. The program works out those periods of mutual visibility.

Scheduling contact time was a daily problem for early satellite networks. A program that predicts visibility windows saves hours of hand work. It also reduces missed contacts and idle ground stations. Repass and Chaplick present the program for users who planned such contacts. Their work belongs to the quiet computer support that kept early networks running.
nasa-tm-19650020211-a-soft-x-ray-photoio:
R M Young and A K Stober at Goddard described a detector for soft X-rays in April 1965. Soft X-rays carry little energy and are hard to sense. Their detector works by photoionization, where the X-rays free electric charge in a gas. The catalog note calls it a simple ceramic device, used as a direct-current, gas-filled ionization chamber.

A simple, sturdy detector suits space instruments well. It has few parts to fail and gives a steady current to measure. Such detectors let satellites study the Sun and other X-ray sources. Young and Stober present the design and its working principle for other builders.
nasa-tm-19660001939-investigation-of-res:
Joseph G Haynos at Goddard investigated glues for solar cell covers in this September 1965 study. Each solar cell wears a thin glass cover for protection. The glue must hold that glass through prelaunch handling, launch shaking, and the harsh conditions of orbit. Haynos tested resinous, or polymer, materials made for that bonding job.

A failed bond can cloud a cell or let the cover slip. Either fault cuts the power a spacecraft lives on. Simulated orbital conditions formed part of the test setting. Studies of humble materials like glue rarely draw notice. Yet whole missions have rested on whether such a joint held in space.
nasa-tm-19660020119-the-status-of-reliab:
William Wolman at Goddard reviewed how well his center judged satellite reliability before flight. The assessment methods had been in use for about five years, he notes. His review covers the method itself and its usefulness in practice. It also compares the pre-flight judgments with what actually happened in flight, satellite by satellite in effect.

Wolman names major problem areas in plain view. Sound mathematical models were hard to build. Failure rates for systems and parts were hard to obtain. Correction factors used to patch those gaps get their own scrutiny. An honest status report of this kind is how a young discipline improves its own tools.
nasa-tm-19670015071-long-lived-radioacti:
Ira T. Myers and James A. Kish, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in May 1967. It concerns concrete for the NASA Plum Brook Space Propulsion Facility near Sandusky, Ohio. If that facility ran nuclear tests, neutrons would slowly make its own concrete radioactive.

The authors measured trace element concentrations in cement, sand, and gravel from northern Ohio. Their purpose was practical: choose materials that would minimize neutron activation of the finished facility. They also considered the exposure rates that best-case and worst-case material choices would produce. The work let builders pick safer concrete before construction.
nasa-tm-19670025679-design-and-performan:
Robert N. Gibson Sr. and Thomas A. Cygnarowicz wrote this report at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. It covers the design and performance of a thermal storage resistojet, a small electric rocket thruster. A resistojet heats gas electrically to make gentle thrust, and a thermal storage type banks heat in its structure for later use. The device was built for Goddard by the General Electric Company.

An electrical resistance element heats ammonia propellant past eighteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit. At twenty millipounds of thrust, it delivered a specific impulse of two hundred thirty seconds on thirty watts. The design is modular, in three parts: heating element, thruster body, and heat shield package, an approach that eases design changes. The whole package is a flange-mounted cylinder about two inches across and five inches long, weighing roughly one and seven-tenths pounds. Layered metal foil forms its heat shielding.
nasa-tm-19670027073-a-resettable-monosta:
Norman M. Garrahan, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, describes an electronics circuit in this paper. The circuit is a resettable monostable pulse generator, a device that fires one clean pulse of set length when triggered. The catalog record adds that the design serves galactic X-ray work, sampling and measuring individual X-ray events.

A galactic X-ray detector must pick single genuine X-ray hits out of a constant rain of other cosmic particles. Garrahan's low-power solid-state memory circuit answers one particle pulse with a blocking output lasting a preset ten microseconds. That pause proves no pileup came before and lets the sensors settle back to rest. If a second pulse follows closely, the circuit ends the first interval and starts a fresh one, without dropping the blocking state. A companion section describes a constant-amplitude pulse generator, with schematics and waveforms.
nasa-tm-19670031007-some-flight-mechanic:
Clyde D. Baker, James C. Blair, and Wilton E. Causey, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this memorandum on September 8, 1967. Numbered TM X-53654, it sets out flight mechanics considerations for the Voyager mission. Voyager was a planned uncrewed voyage to Mars, to be launched by the Saturn V. The paper began as a status review given to center management.

Four study areas from the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory are discussed. First come the effects of Earth-Mars-Sun geometry on launch opportunities, since the planets align only in certain windows. Second is the influence of trajectory design requirements on the mission as a whole. Third, the authors report the present performance capabilities of the Saturn V configured for Voyager. Fourth, they describe a proposed load relief control system, meant to ease the structural loads the huge vehicle suffers while climbing through the atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19670031199-aeronautics-in-revie:
James F. Connors, of the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, gave this talk to the Lewis Aerospace Explorers on September 30, 1967. He reviews aviation in historical perspective. The airplane, he opens, has had a huge impact on society and daily life, shrinking the world.

Connors notes how completely people now take flight for granted. In 1966, he points out, American airlines carried well over a hundred million passengers. The airplane had also become a primary element in the national defense posture. He then asks how all this came about, and turns to the dramatic steps of powered flight's history.
nasa-tm-19680017689-a-study-of-artificia:
Charles E. Shepard, John W. Vorreiter, Howard A. Stine, and Warren Winovich of Ames Research Center test artificial meteors in this study. Photographs of real meteors could better reveal the meteoroid hazard to spacecraft. That use depends on knowing how meteors ablate and radiate light.

Static tests in an ultrahigh-enthalpy plasma jet compared lab-made samples with natural meteorite pieces. Artificial meteors of gabbro or basalt ablated and radiated much like natural stone meteorite samples. Steel specimens likewise matched natural iron meteorite material. During ablation, matching materials grew in frontal area, dropped in average density, and gave off light in the same manner.
nasa-tm-19680020522-effect-of-variable-s:
Edward M. Szanca, Frank P. Behning, and Harold J. Schum of Lewis Research Center report turbine stator tests in this 1968 memorandum, part one of a series. The single-stage turbine suits air cooling duties. Its stator can open or close to change flow area from the design setting.

Part one covers the stator opened to 130 percent of design area. Results include weight flow, outlet flow angle, and blade surface pressures and velocities. Inner and outer wall pressures were also recorded across a range of pressure ratios. At this setting the stator acted as a convergent-divergent blade row, most strongly at the tip section. Mass flow exceeded the value expected from area change alone.
nasa-tm-19680027792-effect-of-variable-s:
Frank P. Behning, Bernard Bider, and Edward M. Szanca of Lewis Research Center report stator tests in this 1968 memorandum, part four of a series. The single-stage turbine suits air cooling duties. Here the stator sits closed, at seventy percent of its design flow area.

Results cover mass flow, outlet flow angle, and blade surface pressures and velocities. Inner and outer wall pressures were recorded across a range of stator pressure ratios. At choked conditions, mass flow fell by exactly the area reduction, the authors found. Findings are compared against earlier tests at the design setting. The series helps designers predict how variable stators reshape turbine behavior.
nasa-tm-19690000965-effect-of-variable-s:
Herman W. Prust, Thomas P. Moffitt, and Bernard Bider of Lewis Research Center detail stator losses in this report, part five of a turbine series. The single-stage turbine suits air cooling. Here the stator sits closed at seventy percent of design area, and losses are examined closely.

Experimental loss values sat close to analytical predictions. Final results appear as kinetic-energy loss coefficients plotted against velocity level. The closed stator reached an efficiency of about ninety-six percent. Values for the closed setting are compared with design and open settings from earlier parts. Together the parts map how stator area changes affect turbine losses. Designers can use the map when sizing variable-geometry turbines.
nasa-tm-19690018830-the-thermospheric-ti:
H. Volland wrote this March 1969 Goddard preprint, numbered X-621-69-88, treating the thermospheric tides as an oscillator circuit system. Tides are great daily waves in the thin upper air, and their density swings add drag on satellites. Volland models the wave-making energy equation as an electric circuit in series, with density amplitude playing the role of current.

In his circuit, the heat source acts as voltage, and ion drag acts as resistance. Wave heat and convection supply the parts that store and return energy. His simplified calculations agree well enough with exact full-wave results, he reports. He applies the model to daily and twice-daily tides, magnetic activity effects, and longer rhythms. The circuit even explains the afternoon lag of peak density.
nasa-tm-19690020371-satellite-data-recov:
Thomas J. Karras and Richard C. Lee of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this May 1969 preprint, X-560-69-208. They study satellite data recovery and quality at low elevation tracking angles. Near the horizon a ground station sees a satellite briefly and through the thickest air. The pair ask how much of each low pass is actually usable.

A telemetry performance monitor built by Goddard's Information Processing Division anchors the study. It scores recovery and quality for each pass and draws signal strip charts. First used on OGO-D and OSO-F passes from several tracking stations, it confirmed a harsh pattern. Data gathered near the horizon, the authors find, is generally either lost or severely degraded.
nasa-tm-19690029280-maintainability-supp:
Ward H. Cook and Chester B. May, of Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this July 1969 report, number 53855, on maintainability and support requirements. Cook wrote from the Advanced Program Support Office, May from the Mission and Payload Planning Office. Long-duration missions cannot improvise repairs, spares, and support after launch, so those needs must be identified from the start.

Chapters survey NASA's space programs, then phase the support functions against mission requirements. Test planning for operational support and its philosophy come next. Trade-off chapters weigh space's natural conditions, crew and equipment capability, and maintenance modes. Simulation methods, from mock-ups to weightless habitats, and resupply requirements close the study before its conclusion.
nasa-tm-19690029389-a-method-for-separat:
I. Litant of the Electronics Research Center in Cambridge devised a better way to break semiconductor wafers into chips, reported in this October 1969 memorandum. A scribed wafer sits face-up on a convex surface. A rubber diaphragm driven by air pressure then contacts it rapidly.

Stress lands uniformly in all directions at once. Breakage follows the pre-scribed lines almost completely. Dust and debris are minimized compared with older breaking methods. Cleaner, more complete breaks raise chip yields in electronics fabrication. The method serves the single-crystal wafers used for the era's semiconductor devices. NASA electronics work depended on reliable chips for spacecraft systems.
nasa-tm-19700014979-a-laser-velocity-mea:
George R. Grant and Ralph W. Donaldson of the Ames Research Center wrote this report in April 1970. It describes a laser system for measuring air speed in hot wind tunnels. Normal probes stuck into the flow work poorly in very fast, very hot gas streams.

The system shines laser light into the tunnel and reads the scattered light. Shifts in that light reveal how fast the gas is moving. Light-based measuring leaves the flow itself untouched. The report sets out the system for use in high-temperature tunnels, where heat and speed defeat older tools.
nasa-tm-19700016517-third-compilation-of:
NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, issued this volume in August 1969. It is the third compilation of papers on trajectory analysis and guidance theory. Contractors working with the center's Computer Research Laboratory prepared the papers.

The volume holds twelve papers in all. They deal with celestial mechanics, numerical methods, optimization theory, and guidance theory. In plain terms, they cover how to steer spacecraft, choose best paths, and do the math behind both. The collection pulled current contractor work into one place. Staff across the space program could then build on the same set of studies.
nasa-tm-19700028107-position-of-sun-and-:
George E. Kowalski and Lloyd T. Davis of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in June 1970. It gives the position of the Sun and the magnetic vector for three launch sites. The sites are Wallops Island, White Sands, and Fort Churchill, all used for sounding rocket work.

The heart of the report is a series of graphs covering every day of the year. From them a reader can find the Sun's direction and height at each site, and the direction of Earth's magnetic field as well. Instructions explain how the graphs were built and how to use them, including finding a launch window. A computer program section and a note on leap year errors round out the tools.
nasa-tm-19700030106-film-boiling-transit:
Robert C. Hendricks of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 engineering meeting in New York. It seeks the temperature at which film boiling ends for tissue cooled with liquid nitrogen. Liquid nitrogen can freeze tissue fast enough to store it.

Hendricks ran a series of tests on pig skin in the laboratory. He looked for the point where a vapor film around the tissue breaks down. No single unique value was found, he reports. Work of this kind serves organ preservation, where the full freeze and thaw cycle must be controlled. It also bears on handling living samples brought back from other planets.
nasa-tm-19710015774-improved-parasitic-s:
H L Wimmer and B D Ingle of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an August 1971 energy conversion meeting in Boston. It concerns speed controllers for dynamic space power systems. Those systems spin an alternator to make electricity. A parasitic controller burns off extra power as load falls, holding speed and frequency steady.

Working controllers had run for many thousands of hours. Still, they warped the line voltage and loaded the alternator unevenly. The authors studied design changes to fix those faults. Ideas included more load stages, each handling a smaller share. Added feedback networks and a fully digital design were also under study.
nasa-tm-19710016307-nuclear-powered-air-:
Frank E Rom and Charles C Masser of the Lewis Research Center wrote this May 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2293. It sizes up giant nuclear air cushion vehicles for ocean cargo work. These craft ride on a bubble of air above the waves. The study covered vehicles heavier than four thousand tons, cruising near one hundred knots.

Rom and Masser found the big craft could haul cargo at roughly one to two cents per ton mile. Nuclear versions clearly beat chemical ones on long routes. At the longest range studied, chemical craft cost about three times more to run. Nuclear performance also held steadier when cost guesses changed. The study still called for a fleet of over a thousand craft.
nasa-tm-19710021800-data-received-by-wor:
World Data Center A for Rockets and Satellites issued this catalogue in March 1971. It lists the data the center received from July 1 through December 31, 1970. The center archived records from sounding rocket flights and artificial satellites. Researchers worldwide sent their mission data there for safekeeping. A printed catalogue told other scientists what material existed.

The catalogue covers the second half of 1970. Entries record what arrived, mission by mission. Such listings let researchers request data they did not collect themselves. They also served as a receipt of record for the space science community. World Data Centers formed an international system for sharing geophysical data. This volume is one regular part of that system.
nasa-tm-19710029098-the-8-july-1966-inte:
A NASA preprint dated September 1971, numbered X-692-71-365, estimates the normal of the 8 July 1966 interplanetary shock near Earth. Its author's name does not survive legibly in the scan. On that date a shock wave in the solar wind swept past Earth. Knowing the shock's speed and which way its surface faced helps scientists read the records it left.

The author estimated both quantities under two constraints. The shock conservation equations had to hold, and sighting times from Explorers 28 and 33 had to fit. The new values disagreed seriously with earlier estimates. The Vela 3A satellite, sitting in the magnetosheath, saw the shock later than a simple flat, steady front model predicted. The author concludes the shock probably slowed rapidly and bent out of its flat shape in the sunward magnetosheath.
nasa-tm-19720004464-a-study-of-the-nords:
A Study of the Nordsieck-Type Predictor-Corrector Methods is a NASA preprint on computer methods for solving initial value problems step by step. Such problems start from a known value and ask a computer to follow a changing quantity forward. Predictor-corrector schemes guess the next value of a solution, then refine that guess before moving on.

The authors explain why multistep methods are popular: they usually need fewer function evaluations per step than single-step methods. The established Adams formulas rate well on speed and accuracy, but changing the step size and interpolating are awkward with them. Nordsieck devised a method equivalent to one of the Adams formulas that eases those problems. The study focuses on the Descloux formulas, modified Nordsieck formulas prized for steady behavior and small truncation errors.
nasa-tm-19720013635-final-environmental-:
NASA issued this final environmental impact statement for the Langley Research Center on August 17, 1971. It runs to sixty nine pages, as NASA TM X-67680. New federal law required agencies to weigh the environmental effects of their sites. The statement describes Langley and what its laboratories and tunnels do each day. From that account, it argues the center counts as only a minor source of pollution. Langley's tunnels and laboratories were the main subjects.

The document also describes the site itself in detail. Its geography, geology, and climate shape how any emissions would spread. Local water, soil, and air conditions enter the judgment. Tables of contents show a summary and sections on mission and the center. The statement belongs to the first wave of such federal reviews.
nasa-tm-19720015402-a-reliable-all-silve:
John H Lamneck Jr and Lawrence Schwartz of the Lewis Research Center reported this solar cell advance in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2544. A silicon solar cell needs a metal contact on its sunlit face to gather current. Silver contacts worked, but sticking and damp air failures plagued them. The team asked whether an all silver front contact could be made reliable. Space power systems depended on such cells.

They showed that the contact can indeed be made well. It sticks firmly and resists damage from moisture. The best making processes and their order were worked out. The contacts also showed good electrical behavior in tests. A matching back contact of aluminum and silver was developed. It proved very satisfactory for cooler applications.
off-hand-sketches-a-little-dashed-with-h:
Timothy Shay Arthur published these comic sketches in Philadelphia in 1851. The preface promises smiles that never mock virtue. Many incidents, he says, rest on real facts. He adds only a few touches of fancy. Each short piece carries a small moral lesson.

The contents list tales about preachers, debt, drink, and vanity. Titles include Trying to Be a Gentleman and Taking a Prescription. Other sketches treat marriage, bargains, and false honor. Arthur writes for general readers in plain, lively prose. The book shows popular moral humor of its era. Short pieces make the book easy to read in sittings.
operation-terror:
Murray Leinster begins Operation Terror on an ordinary morning for surveyor Lockley, camped on a mountain flank to measure a base line for a new map of Boulder Lake National Park. He wakes in his sleeping bag annoyed at himself for dreaming again of Jill Holmes, who is engaged to someone else, and prepares for a commonplace day's work.

The same morning, far away, radar stations in Alaska and Oregon are the only ones watching a long stretch of Pacific sky, for reasons nobody on the ground understands. Then the Alaskan installation reports something strange in space. Leinster cross-cuts between the quiet survey camp, the park construction crews, and distant command centers as the ordinary day turns into first contact with the unknown.
robert-s-rules-of-order-pocket-manual-of:
Major Henry M. Robert, of the Corps of Engineers, U.S.A., wrote this pocket manual of rules of order for deliberative assemblies. S. C. Griggs of Chicago published it in 1876, the year of its copyright. Part one gives the rules of order as a compendium of parliamentary law, based on the rules and practice of Congress.

Part two explains, in simple terms, how societies, conventions, and other assemblies organize and conduct their business. Robert's preface states the need: a work fitted to ordinary societies, not only to legislatures. For each motion it gives the object and effect, whether it can be amended or debated, and when it can be made. Cross-references keep each rule complete in itself.
robur-the-conqueror:
Jules Verne's Robur the Conqueror is mapped in twenty-three chapters of contents, from Mysterious Sounds to The Grand Collapse. The early chapters bring a visitor, a new character, and another disappearance, while a president and secretary suspend hostilities. Chapter seven puts the company on board the Albatross, though the balloonists refuse to be convinced.

The voyage then runs across the prairie, the wide Pacific, the Himalayas, and the Caspian. A skirmish in Dahomey, the Atlantic, a shipwrecked crew, and a volcano follow. The Albatross is wrecked, the Institute meets again, and the Go-Ahead is launched before the close. Chapter one opens with two pistol shots and a cow killed by accident near Niagara.
romance-of-california-life-illustrated-b:
John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, gathered these Pacific Slope stories in 1880, billed in his subtitle as thrilling, pathetic, and humorous. The Schoolteacher at Bottle Flat leads the contents. Jim Hockson's Revenge and Making His Mark follow, in the rough settlements their names suggest.

Codago, The Last Pike at Jagger's Bend, and First Prayer at Hanney's keep the mining and town colour. The New Sheriff of Bunker County and A Story of Ten Mile Gulch bring law and gold together. Miss Fewne's Last Conquest, Markson's House, Grump's Pet, and Old Twitchett's Treasure close the list, in tales of California life told plain and warm.
studies-in-love-and-in-terror:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes, Marie Adelaide Belloc Lowndes, published Studies in Love and in Terror in 1913; the printing at hand is a library reprint from Freeport, New York. Five long stories make up the book: Price of Admiralty, The Child, St. Catherine's Eve, The Woman from Purgatory, and Why They Married.

The first tale opens under lines from Baudelaire calling on Death, the old captain, to weigh anchor at last. Lowndes, a skilled hand at quiet dread, builds her effects from ordinary marriages, households, and chance meetings that tilt toward terror. Love and fear share each story, as the title promises, with the chill arriving by small steps.
t-haviland-hicks-senior:
J. Raymond Elderdice wrote T. Haviland Hicks, Senior, a college football novel dedicated to Master Lloyd Elderdice. The hero, Hicks of Yale ninety-six, returns to Bannister College as the beloved old grad whose hunches and speeches steer the eleven through its season.

The contents run from Hicks, Wild West Bad Man, through Leave It to Hicks, Hicks Makes a Speech, and Coach Corridan Surprises the Eleven, to Vale, Alma Mater. The first chapter opens on Big Butch Brewster, captain and fullback of the Bannister squad, dreaming under heavy blankets of a western bad man ballad, Chuckwalla Bill and his notched six-gun. Football, college loyalty, and a mystery Hicks starts and solves fill the tale, which belongs to the hearty school-story line of its day.
the-adventures-of-hugh-trevor:
Thomas Holcroft wrote The Adventures of Hugh Trevor, a novel told in the first person, with a mocking verse from Gay at its head. This first volume opens with heads that promise the hero's birth, a slight to family pride, and his grandfather's wrath.

Hugh starts by granting that each man may think his own life the most grave of all histories. His own has mixed gloom and sunshine enough, he says, to interest others. He then notes that some date his woes from before his birth: his grandfather, a rector vain of his line, felt shamed when his daughter wed a mere farmer. Readers get a sharp, comic tale of pride, class, and a young man's hard road up.
the-american-senator: A contents list for both volumes opens Anthony Trollope's The American Senator. A head note states it ran in Temple Bar Magazine from May 1876 through July 1877. It came out in book form in 1877, from Chapman and Hall. Early chapters settle in Dillsborough with the Morton and Masters families, a town club, and a feud. Arabella Trefoil arrives, a party is held at Bragton, and Mr. Gotobed's good works are weighed. Volume Two opens with Mounser Green and the senator's letter.
the-annals-of-the-poor:
The Reverend Legh Richmond, late rector of Turvey in Bedfordshire, gathered these accounts of poor Christians, shown in a 1900 edition from T. Nelson and Sons of London. A line from the sixty-eighth Psalm heads the book: God has prepared his goodness for the poor. The first and best-known piece is The Dairyman's Daughter.

Richmond calls it a delight to trace grace at work in the lives of God's real children. Among the poor, he says, mercy often shines with a plain and sincere light. Riches, rank, and fine manners can clog the spirit, while low homes show faith clear and simple. His tales aim to prove that claim through lives he knew.
the-apartment-next-door: Contents and picture captions open William Johnston's 1919 mystery, The Apartment Next Door, with drawings by Arthur William Brown. Johnston, also billed as author of The House of Whispers, dedicates the book to Carolyn Wells. Chapter heads promise a face of hate, a clue in a book, a missing message, a woman on the roof, and a sealed packet. Captions speak of Jane, who alone may know who the murderer was, and of a man she loves whose secret she cannot bring herself to tell.
the-bride-of-lammermoor: Sir Walter Scott wrote The Bride of Lammermoor. The pages shown hold a list of its parts and the head of a first word, but no tale text. The list counts thirty-five chapters, each named by number alone, from Chapter I to Chapter XXXV. An introduction to the book is named at the head of the list. Scott's name and the title are all the facts the opening pages give, apart from the count of chapters.
the-canadian-dominion-a-chronicle-of-our:
The Canadian Dominion, by Oscar D. Skelton, was published by Yale University Press in 1919, and its preface is dated from Queen's University, Kingston, in July of that year. Skelton divides Canada's history since the close of the French regime into three half-centuries: a separate existence under the British flag, then self-government and Confederation, then expansion from sea to sea.

He arranges the chronicle by that scheme, and the contents begin with The First Fifty Years and The Fight for Self-Government. The book is thus a survey with an argument built into its structure. Canada's story is told as three long movements. Each lasts about fifty years. Together they carry the country from colony to self-governing dominion. That dominion stretches across the continent.
the-coverley-papers-from-the-spectator:
O. M. Myers edited The Coverley Papers from the Spectator, with an introduction and notes. In his preface he explains that the selection holds every Spectator number dealing with Sir Roger de Coverley's history or character. It adds those arising from the Spectator's visit to Sir Roger's country house.

Sir Roger's name turns up in some seventeen other papers, Myers notes, but there he gets only passing mention or speaks in talks where the topic, not the man, holds the interest. Two papers are left out: No. 410, which Addison condemned as out of character for Sir Roger, and No. 544, an unconvincing try at reconciling it. Myers also decodes the paper's marks: C, L, I, and O stand for Addison, R and T for Steele, and X for Budgell.
the-crusade-of-the-excelsior: Bret Harte's The Crusade of the Excelsior is shown here only through its contents, split into two parts. Part I, In Bonds, runs from A Crusader and a Sign through Vigilancia, In the Fog, and Todos Santos. It ends with The Captain Follows His Ship. Chapters treat gentle castaways, an open-air prison, and Todos Santos solving the mystery. Part II is headed Freed and begins with The Mourners at San Francisco. Only the title page and this contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-dancing-mouse-a-study-in-animal-beha: Robert M. Yerkes of Harvard University wrote The Dancing Mouse, of The Animal Behavior Series, dated 1907. A note records the Cartwright Prize of Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons Alumni, awarded in 1907. The prize honored an essay forming its twelve chapters. Yerkes dedicates the volume to his mother. Chapter I's contents list the dancing mouse's traits, origin, and history, its keeping and marking, and accounts from China and Japan. Views of how the breed arose follow, including breeding, mutation, and sickness. Only front matter and contents are present here.
the-devil-doctor: Sax Rohmer bills The Devil Doctor as hitherto unpublished adventures in the career of the mysterious Dr. Fu-Manchu. The London edition from Methuen and Company is a sixth edition; the first publication is dated March 2, 1916. Its contents open with chapters called A Midnight Summons, Eltham Vanishes, The Wire Jacket, The Cry of a Nighthawk, and The Net, running on to Enter Mr. Abel Slattin and Dr. Fu-Manchu Strikes. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here.
the-diving-bell-or-pearls-to-be-sought-f: The Diving Bell; or, Pearls to Be Sought For is a story book by Francis C. Woodworth, writing as Uncle Frank. The Boston title page, entered in 1851, lists him as editor of Woodworth's Youth's Cabinet. Only the title matter and contents are present here. First pieces named are The Name of My Book, Thinking and Laughing, and The Scheming Spider. Tinted pictures are promised, with a fox and crab up front.
the-double-traitor:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's spy novel The Double Traitor, dated 1915, opens in a plush Berlin restaurant. A woman chides her young dining partner, Norgate, for calling his move from Paris an exile, and hints that surprises wait for him. He looks round at oak panels, flowers, soft carpets, hidden music, and officers in bright dress, and owns that Germany has changed.

Berlin's new wealth hides a web of spies on the eve of war. Norgate, a British agent, must judge who plays false. Oppenheim builds dread through manners, dinners, and small slips.
the-dream-doctor:
Arthur B. Reeve's The Dream Doctor belongs to his Craig Kennedy series, as its front pages state. Chapter heads run from The Dream Doctor and The Soul Analysis through The Sybarite, The Beauty Shop, and The Phantom Circuit. Later heads name the Detectaphone, the Green Curse, a mummy case, and an elixir of life.

Kennedy solves crimes with lab science: wires, tests, and new machines. Each chapter works like a case file. Reeve wrote the tales as America's answer to Sherlock Holmes, with news prose and bold gear. Will Foster drew the frontispiece.
the-elevator:
The Elevator, a farce from The Sleeping Car and Other Farces in its 1911 Houghton Mifflin printing, opens in Mrs. Edward Roberts's pretty drawing room at the Hotel Bellingham. A dinner table gleams through a curtained door, burners low, while Mr. Roberts checks his watch: six o'clock, and his wife's aunt still not come. The children, keen to talk Christmas, are near tears.

Mrs. Roberts soothes him and fusses with small touches round the room. A late guest, a stuck lift, and mixed-up callers will wreck the dinner's calm. William Dean Howells wrote the piece as light stage fun.
