the-fortieth-door: Mary Hastings Bradley wrote The Fortieth Door as a tale of Egypt, printed in 1920. The book is given to Arthur Mills Corwin. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name a rash promise, masks, and a pasha's palace. They name the forty doors and an uninvited guest. A tomb of a king and the bazaars close the list. All this points to a tale of Cairo intrigue and a hidden bride. No chapter text can be read here.
the-gem-collector:
P. G. Wodehouse wrote The Gem Collector as a comic novel of Jimmy Pitt, a young baronet bored with life, first placed in Ainslee's Magazine in December 1909. A note at the front tells the book's later fate.

The tale was reworked in 1910 as The Intrusion of Jimmy, also called A Gentleman of Leisure. Jimmy sits in the bright supper room of the Savoy, rich, young, and glum, feeling the world is flat. Nine years away from London have left him a stranger in his own town. Wodehouse sends his idle hero toward house parties, jewel theft, and love, in the light style that would make his name.
the-grand-inquisitor:
Feodor Dostoevsky wrote The Grand Inquisitor. H. P. Blavatsky translated it. An editor's note explains that the piece is an extract. It comes from Dostoevsky's last novel, The Brothers Karamazof. The note calls it a cutting satire on modern theology. It aims in particular at the Roman Catholic religion. Blavatsky dedicates the translation to sceptics. They demand to be shown wonders before they will believe.

The note sets the scene of the poem within the novel. Ivan tells the tale to his youngest brother Alyosha. Ivan is a rank materialist and atheist. Alyosha is a young Christian mystic, raised by a saint in a monastery. In Ivan's poem, Christ comes back to earth in Spain. The time is the days of the Inquisition. He is at once arrested as a heretic by the Grand Inquisitor. The extract is that poem and the talk it sparks.
the-green-door:
Mary E. Wilkins-Freeman wrote The Green Door. Mary R. Bassett made the pictures. Dodd, Mead and Company published it in New York in 1931. Letitia lives in the house where her grandmother and great-grandmother lived and died. Her own parents died when she was very young. She came there to live with her Great-aunt Peggy. Peggy is her grandfather's sister, a very old woman. She is active, bright, and good company.

Aunt Peggy plays grace-hoops with Letitia. She plays dominoes and checkers, and even dolls. Yet Letitia is not a contented child. She is naturally rather idle. Her aunt, a wise old woman, believes in the proverb about Satan and idle hands. She keeps the girl always busy: sewing, study, dusting, or a set portion of a story-book. Letitia wants new treasures, fine clothes, and plenty of candy.
the-keeper-of-the-door: Ethel M. Dell's novel appears here in an A. L. Burt edition of 1915, in its fourth impression, published by arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. Only the title pages and a list of Dell's works are present here. The story itself does not appear. The list testifies to her popularity. The Way of an Eagle and The Knave of Diamonds appear. The Rocks of Valpré, The Swindler, and Bars of Iron follow. Rosa Mundi, The Hundredth Chance, and Greatheart come next. The Lamp in the Desert closes the list shown.
the-life-of-captain-james-cook-the-circu:
Arthur Kitson wrote his life of Captain James Cook with portrait and map, first issued in 1907. A preface dated London 1912 explains this popular edition. Kitson condensed his larger work, cut nothing of importance, fixed slight errors, and added fresh notes on Cook documents.

Contents run from Cook early years through service on the Eagle, Pembroke, and Northumberland to Newfoundland survey work. Later chapters cover three Pacific voyages that charted Australia east coast and New Zealand. Readers get a careful naval life trimmed for general readers rather than specialists. Portrait and map front the narrative.
the-little-warrior:
P. G. Wodehouse's The Little Warrior runs to twenty-one chapters. Chapter one opens at a breakfast table, where Freddie Rooke inspects through a gleaming eye-glass a revolting object his man Parker has set before him. Told that it is a poached egg, Freddie averts his eyes with a shudder, says it looks just like an old aunt of his, and orders it removed.

The scene is pure Wodehouse farce: a fussy young man of leisure, a faithful servant, and a breakfast disaster played dead straight. Readers meeting Freddie first get the book's comic tone at once, all polished dialogue and exaggerated horror over small things, before the wider plot gets moving.
the-lost-ambassador: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Lost Ambassador is dated 1910 in its heading. Only a table of contents is present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The twenty-two chapter titles shown trace an intrigue. A Rencontre, A Café in Paris, Delora, and Dangerous Play come first. Delora Disappears, Through the Telephone, Felicia Delora, and A Dangerous Impersonation follow. The list shown closes with Wheels Within Wheels and A Formal Call. A companion record gives the same book's Boston publication details and illustrator.
the-love-sonnets-of-a-car-conductor:
Wallace Irwin's The Love Sonnets of a Car Conductor, copyrighted in 1908 by Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco and New York, carries a mock-scholarly introduction. Its author, Wolfgang Copernicus Addleburger, styled Professor of Literary Bi-Products at the University of Monte Carlo, insists that science does nothing by jumps. He consented to preface the sonnet cycle, he says, only after supreme deliberation.

His stated reasons parody academic method. As a botanist he wants to watch genius flower; as a psychologist he wants to settle, once and for all, the status of slang. He even turns to zoology for the answer. The introduction frames Irwin's comic sonnets, written in the voice of a streetcar conductor, as a serious experiment in what slang can do in a strict poetic form.
the-major: Ralph Connor wrote The Major. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The twenty chapters begin with The Coward, A Fight for Freedom, and The Escutcheon Cleared. Then they move west: Westward Ho!, Jane Brown, The Girl of the Wood Lot, The Spirit of Canada, and The Shadow of War. Titles include Men and a Mine, An Extraordinary Nurse, The Coming of Jane, and The Tragedies of Love. A final chapter, The German Type of Citizenship, suggests a story reaching into wartime.
the-malefactor: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Malefactor appears with only its title page and contents, so the novel does not appear. It is divided into two books. Book one runs from A Society Scandal through The Gospel of Hate, Lord of the Manor, The Heart of a Child, and The Hidden Hand. Book two opens with "Mr. Wingrave, From America" and continues through Guardian and Ward. One chapter quotes "I am Misanthropos, and Hate Mankind." Nemesis at Work, Revenge is—Bitter, and "Love Shall Make all Things New" follow.
the-marriage-of-elinor: Mrs. Oliphant's The Marriage of Elinor, dated 1892 in its heading, was issued as number 95 of The English Library in two volumes. Only the title pages and a volume listing are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The listing shows volume one carrying chapters one through twenty-three and volume two continuing from twenty-four through forty-eight, a long courtship-and-marriage novel by its scale alone. Oliphant's other works named in the same series include The Railway Man and his Children, also in two volumes.
the-merry-wives-of-windsor: Only an editor's note stands in this record, the same note carried by another Shakespeare record in this set, and it does not present The Merry Wives of Windsor. Signed by Michael S. Hart, the note discusses old printers' spelling substitutions, such as u for v, and quotes the opening lines of Hamlet as the example. It announces the file it introduces as Shakespeare's First Part of Henry the Sixth. No scene or speech from the Windsor comedy appears here.
the-moravians-in-labrador:
Only a hymn and a title page are present here for The Moravians in Labrador, so the mission history itself does not appear. Verses by Heber, beginning From Greenland's icy mountains, serve as epigraph. The title page shows the book printed by J. Ritchie in Edinburgh and sold by booksellers in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London, dated in Roman numerals as 1833.

A transcriber's note at the head of the record gives a different date, saying the document was originally published in 1822, with archaic spelling and corrected misprints. The two dates stand side by side without explanation. The note also warns that original page images were of very poor quality, so some punctuation had to be inferred.
the-nursery-volume-17-no-101-may-1875-a-: Number 101 of The Nursery is dated May 1875, in volume XVII of the Boston monthly for the youngest readers, published by John L. Shorey at $1.60 a year. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories and poems themselves do not appear. Listed pieces include The Dog Who Lost His Master by Uncle Charles, The Doll-Baby Show by George Cooper, Day and Night by Aunt Winnie, and Daddy Dandelion, a song with music.
the-path-of-empire-a-chronicle-of-the-un:
Carl Russell Fish wrote The Path of Empire, a chronicle of the United States as a world power. The contents list seventeen chapters, from The Monroe Doctrine through Alaska, Blaine and Pan-Americanism, the war with Spain, Dewey at Manila Bay, the Open Door, and the Panama Canal, to World Relationships.

Chapter One begins in 1815, when the world found peace after twenty-two years of war. Men and women from Canada to Palestine prayed its horrors would never return. Czar Alexander I invited governments into a Holy Alliance to prevent war, while Metternich of Austria spun his web of secret diplomacy to the same end. Fish starts America's road to empire in that hopeful, scheming peace.
the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-volume-: Volume XVI of The Philippine Islands is devoted to the year 1609. Much of it gives Antonio de Morga's Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The opening here is broken: the contents stop after a stray line. The rest is a list of pictures and the heading of the Sucesos. Morga's text itself does not appear. The pictures include the 1609 title page of the Sucesos and Morga's own signature.

Volume XXI of The Philippine Islands is devoted to the single year 1624. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Title page and contents are present here; the documents themselves do not appear. The list names church affairs of the Philippines from 1574 to 1624. A clash between civil and church rulers in Manila appears. A school for Japanese missionaries and royal orders on the religious are listed. Extracts on the early Recollect missions close the list.
the-radio-amateur-s-hand-book-a-complete:
A. Frederick Collins, who calls himself inventor of the wireless telephone in 1899, offers a complete guide to wireless telegraphy and telephony, dedicated to William Marconi. His introduction recalls that popular interest has surged in two or three years after a quarter century of experiment.

Collins dates Marconi's first dot-and-dash signals of 1896 to a few hundred feet, and his own voice transmission of 1899 to three blocks in Narberth, Pennsylvania. History thus frames practical instruction. Amateur readers of the early radio boom get both a pioneer's memoir and a handbook meant to be used at the workbench.
the-reverberator:
Henry James opens in a Paris hotel reading room, where journalist George Flack asks after Miss Francina Dosson. Her father rises at once from the hotel court and leads the way with docile, almost servile eagerness to fetch his daughter.

James notes the symmetry: Mr. Dosson thinks it natural that anyone should want to see Francina, while Flack thinks it natural that a father should run errands for a visitor. A heavy drapery hangs in the doorway as the search begins. Money, publicity, and American innocence abroad stand behind the small courtesy, and James lets manners carry the satire.
the-rover-boys-in-new-york-or-saving-the:
Saving Their Father's Honor is the subtitle of the seventeenth Rover Boys volume. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the series for young Americans. Its introduction stresses that the story is complete in itself. Winfield notes the line's sales with pride. They had reached nearly one million and a quarter copies.

The boys have grown older by this volume. Dick, the eldest, marries and settles down to business. Tom remains as full of fun as ever. In New York City the brothers face strenuous times. Their father is in deep trouble. They aid him and clear up quite a mystery. Chapter one opens at Brill. Sam proposes a trip in the Dartaway that afternoon.
the-ruby-of-kishmoor:
Howard Pyle built The Ruby of Kishmoor from a prologue, five chapters, and an epilogue. The chapter titles introduce Jonathan Rugg. They also promise a mysterious lady with a silver veil. A one-eyed little gentleman in black appears. So does a stranger with silver ear-rings. A sea-captain with a broken nose completes the cast.

The prologue tells of Captain Robertson Keitt. He was once a reputable merchant in Jamaica. From there he entered the African trade. By regular degrees he became a pirate. His fame rests on one capture. He took the Rajah of Kishmoor's great ship, The Sun of the East. The Rajah's favorite queen was aboard, bound for Mecca. Her attendants and a treasury traveled with her. The prize in gold and jewels was incredible.
the-story-of-the-big-front-door: Mary F. Leonard wrote this children's story, copyrighted by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company in 1898. Only the title pages and the start of a contents list appear in this record. A motto heads the list. It speaks of helping every one his neighbour. The opening chapters are The Outlaws and In the Star Chamber. The Lady of the Brown House and Dora follow. The story itself does not appear.
the-survivor: E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this novel of Douglas Guest's career, presented here through its contents alone. Forty chapters promise much incident. A sermon was never preached. A strange betrothal follows. Guest makes his exit and takes his chance. The author of No Man's Land appears. A Scotland Yard visitor calls. Emily de Reuss tells a lie. Joan Strong plays the avenger. A supper at the Milan and the wooing of Cicely close the heads. The story itself does not appear.
the-survivors-of-the-chancellor:
Charles F. Horne introduces Jules Verne's tale in his edition of Verne's works. The story was issued in 1875, he records. It is Verne's only tale devoted wholly to shipwreck. In it, Horne says, Verne gathered all the sea's tragedy. Mystery and suffering fill the tale. Every form of disaster falls on the unhappy voyagers. Shame and agony heap up too. The pile is complete, Horne claims, and unforgettable.

The idea came from a painting, Horne explains. Géricault painted the wreck of the Medusa. The French frigate was lost off Africa in 1816. Her survivors endured many days on a raft. Verne also drew on the British troopship Sarah Sands, which caught fire off Africa in 1857 with gunpowder aboard, fought explosion, storm, and flooding together for ten days, and still reached port.
the-talking-deaf-man-a-method-proposed-w:
John Conrade Amman, a Swiss doctor, wrote The Talking Deaf Man to set out his method for teaching people born deaf to speak. Printed at Amsterdam in 1692 and Englished in 1693, it opens with Amman's letter to Peter Kolard, whose daughter he taught. He says the age finds his results hard to believe, and some people deny outright that the deaf can be brought to speak. Kolard himself once doubted, until he heard a formerly dumb maiden talking with Amman.

Amman promises to expose his whole artifice openly so that no more dumb persons need be found. His dedication argues from results witnessed in his own pupils. The treatise stands as an early, practical landmark in deaf education, written by a teacher eager to share, not guard, his method.
the-trumpet-major:
Thomas Hardy's Trumpet-Major, first published in 1880 and reissued by Macmillan in 1920 with a map of Wessex, carries Hardy's preface on its sources. The tale, he says, rests on testimony, spoken and written, more fully than any other of his books. Its external incidents mostly reproduce, unexaggerated, the recollections of old people he knew in childhood who had witnessed the scenes. Those recollections alone would have filled a volume three times the novel's length.

Hardy recalls relics surviving into his own time around the Dorset coast. One was an outhouse door riddled with bullet-holes from firelock practice, when Napoleon's landing was hourly expected. Another was a beacon-hut's remains on a hill. His story of John Loveday, who soldiered against Buonaparte, and his brother Robert of the merchant service grows from that living memory of invasion fear.
the-village-rector:
Honoré de Balzac dedicates The Village Rector to Helene, asking her to protect the book as sailors place an emblem on a launched boat. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the novel. Part one, The Sauviats, opens a generation back in the lower town of Limoges, at a corner shop little changed since the middle ages.

Balzac lingers over the building: cracked tiles laid on damp soil, walls mosaicked from wood, brick, stone, and iron, and colossal beams bent under upper storeys for a century. Windows lean every way, rain-hollowed nooks sprout spring flowers, and moss carpets the roof. The loving, decaying detail establishes a provincial world before its people fully enter.
the-virgin-birth-of-our-lord-a-paper-rea:
B. W. Randolph, principal of Ely Theological College and canon of Ely, read his paper on the virgin birth before the Confraternity of the Holy Trinity at Cambridge. Longmans, Green published the paper in London in 1903. Randolph dedicates the work to Vincent Henry Stanton, Ely professor of divinity at Cambridge, with respect and affection.

The argument opens by naming two miracles confessed in every form of the Creed. One is the miraculous conception and birth that brought about the Incarnation, and the other is the Resurrection. These, Randolph says, are the fundamental miracles. They form the battleground where defenders and assailants of Christianity chiefly meet, and his paper takes up the first of them.
the-war-terror: Arthur B. Reeve's War Terror belongs to his Craig Kennedy series of scientific detective stories. The pages present here give a full contents list and an introduction heading, so the stories themselves do not appear. Thirty-six chapters promise an electromagnetic gun, a murder syndicate, an air pirate, and an ultra-violet ray. Wireless wiretappers, a radio detective, a radium robber, and a burglar's microphone follow. Later headings turn stranger: a germ letter, an artificial kidney, devil worshippers, a psychic curse, and a lie detector.
the-youth-of-the-great-elector: L. Mühlbach wrote The Youth of the Great Elector, an historical romance translated from the German by Mary Stuart Smith in 1909. A contents list of three books is what appears here. George William, the Elector, opens the story amid evil tidings. Count Adam von Schwarzenberg figures as a favorite. The electoral prince, a warning, and love's sacrifice follow. The romance chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
three-articles-on-metaphor:
The Society for Pure English issued Three Articles on Metaphor as tract number eleven at the Clarendon Press in 1922. Its authors are listed as E. B., H. W. Fowler, and A. Clutton-Brock. The first article, notes on the function of metaphor, opens the tract.

A writer, it argues, must arouse full consciousness of an idea or emotion by suggesting a comparison. Readers reject unlike qualities and keep the like ones with satisfaction. A good metaphor leaves no distracting by-products of imagery. Readers get practical criticism about how figurative language works, and why similes may stay looser than metaphors.
through-the-magic-door:
Arthur Conan Doyle invites readers through a magic door in an essay collection whose contents list twelve numbered chapters without titles. Chapter one begins at a humble bookshelf in a lowly room. Close the door, Doyle says, and outer cares fall away.

Books stand like noble, silent comrades, each a mummified soul holding a writer's concentrated essence. Shakespeare could be summoned for an hour, yet readers hardly reach for him. Readers get Doyle celebrating reading as travel into dreamland, where great dead authors wait at every reader's elbow in ordinary domestic rooms.
tom-swift-and-his-giant-cannon-or-the-lo: The Longest Shots on Record is the subtitle of the Tom Swift giant cannon story by Victor Appleton, opening with twenty-five chapter headings. Tom starts on a live wire, plans a big gun, tests another gun at Sandy Hook, and meets failure and success. A powerful blast and casting the cannon follow. Chapter one starts with a visitor insisting Mr. Swift should believe him, then breaks off. The contents and that fragment are what is held in this record.
travels-in-arabia-comprehending-an-accou:
John Lewis Burckhardt's Travels in Arabia, printed at London in 1829, reports on the Hedjaz, the region Muslims hold sacred. The African Association published the book after his death. Its editor explains that Burckhardt's Nubia and Syria volumes had already won a strong reception.

Burckhardt lived at Mecca through the whole pilgrimage season without suspicion, the editor reports. His Arabic and his grasp of Muslim manners let him pass as a believer. The volume gave Europe its fullest account yet of Mecca and Medina, cities closed to Christians. Colonel Leake's praise, quoted in the preface, sets the terms on which readers meet the journal.
troop-one-of-the-labrador: Dillon Wallace's Troop One of the Labrador appears in the Talbot Baines series, from the Boy's Own Paper office in London. The opening pages are mostly the publisher's series list. It advertises school stories by Talbot Baines Reed, sea tales, and a fifth form mystery. A frontispiece caption declares, It was Dr. Joe beyond a doubt. Wallace had already written Grit-a-Plenty and The Ragged Inlet Guards. Only the series pages and title page are present here, so the Labrador story itself does not appear.
un-doc-joint-statement-on-holodomor:
Governments joined at the United Nations in 2003 to issue a joint statement on the Holodomor, the famine that killed millions of people in Ukraine in 1932 and 1933. The statement marked seventy years since the disaster. It was backed by many member states and placed the famine on the formal UN record.

The text honors the victims and calls the famine a result of the cruel policies of the Soviet regime of that era. It also urges teaching and remembrance so such crimes are not repeated. The statement remains a key record of how the world first spoke jointly about the Holodomor.
warlord-of-kor:
Terry Carr's Warlord of Kor opens on an alien world, where the huge, slow Horng sits facing a tiny creature with a microphone wired to an interpreting machine. Horng's stiff mouth fumbles words of a tongue his race has not used for thirty thousand years. Kor, he tells the small invaders, was and is God and knowledge, yet the humans do not heed him. They mean to dig out the forbidden directives of Kor, and Horng's buried race memory holds a warning: they must be stopped.

A cast list fills out the stakes. Rynason's mental quest leads him too close to a dangerous secret. Manning's plans for colonizing the world leave no room for its native beings to live. Malhomme, a ruffian-preacher, may be the one man everyone must trust. Carr pits a dying race's god-machine against human greed, in a short and thoughtful space tale.
white-slaves-or-the-oppression-of-the-wo: The opening here holds a dedication and an introductory letter for Louis Albert Banks's White Slaves, while Banks's own chapters do not appear. Banks, a minister, gave the book to his parents, who taught him love of liberty and hate of oppression. The letter speaks to a department of the Epworth League. It charges that churches waste most of their spiritual power, as coal plants waste the force in coal. Banks's book, the writer says, spurs real work to change society. Its vivid pictures of poor workers' lives are praised.
william-the-conqueror:
Edward A. Freeman wrote William the Conqueror as a portrait of a man, not a tale of events. His preface, dated February 6, 1888, sets the book apart from his Short History of the Norman Conquest. That work told a long story of years. Here Freeman studies William's personal character and will. No man's choices, he argues, shaped English law and rule more directly.

William, though a Norman stranger and conqueror, earns a place among English statesmen, Freeman holds. Macmillan printed the edition of 1913 in London. Freeman was Oxford's Regius Professor of Modern History. Readers get a short, dense life of the Conqueror as a maker of England.
